The funnel above is the hierarchy every request walks on a miss: each level is larger and slower, so the goal of cache-friendly code is to stop as high as possible. Quote the orders of magnitude in interviews: L1 hit 1 ns, DRAM 100 ns, SSD 100 microseconds.

Practical rules that follow:

  • Keep hot working sets under L2/L3 size. A hash table that fits in L3 beats a theoretically better tree that spills to DRAM.
  • Favor sequential over random: arrays over pointer chains, column scans that match layout, batch allocations from arenas.
  • Pad or shard contended counters to separate cache lines (@Contended in Java, 64-byte alignment in Go and Rust).
  • Use huge pages for large heaps and read-mostly dictionaries; measure TLB misses with perf stat -d.

docs.title: 7.2 Try It: Measure the Hierarchy on Your Machine
docs.text:
$ lscpu | grep -i cache        # L1/L2/L3 sizes per core
$ perf stat -d ./server        # L1 misses, LLC misses, MPKI, IPC in one run
$ valgrind --tool=cachegrind ./small_input   # simulated miss attribution

Rising MPKI with flat IPC means memory-bound: fix layout before scaling out.

docs.title: 7.3 Cache Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text:
1. Explain L1/L2/L3 and why cache locality decides backend speed. L1 (~1 ns, per core) feeds the pipeline; L2 (~5 ns) backs it; shared L3 (~15-40 ns) spans cores; DRAM costs ~80-100 ns and disk 100,000x an L1 hit. Data moves in 64-byte lines, so sequential scans use full lines while strided or pointer-chasing access wastes them. Keep hot sets in L2/L3, prefer arrays over linked nodes, shard hot counters to separate lines.
  2. What are the three Cs of cache misses? Compulsory (first touch), capacity (working set exceeds cache), conflict (too many addresses share a set). Profilers report miss rate and MPKI.
  3. Write-through vs write-back? Write-through pushes every store down: simple, slow. Write-back marks lines dirty and flushes on eviction: fast, the standard for L1/L2/L3. Write-allocate fetches the line on a store miss.
  4. MESI in one minute? Each line is Modified, Exclusive, Shared, or Invalid across cores. A core writing a Shared line must invalidate every other copy. Two threads writing different fields on one 64-byte line ping-pong ownership: false sharing. (MOESI/MESIF add Owned/Forward states to cut that traffic on AMD/Intel.)
  5. Your service shows high CPU but low IPC. How do you debug it? High CPU with low instructions-per-cycle means stalls. perf stat -d for miss rates and MPKI, flame-graph on-CPU stacks, perf record -b for branch misses, cachegrind for line attribution. Check TLB pressure, false sharing, NUMA remote access. Fix layout first; scale out only after IPC recovers.

docs.title: Part 8. Concurrency Cores Threads and SMT
docs.text:
Three different things share the name parallelism: instruction-level parallelism inside one core (pipelining, superscalar), thread-level parallelism across cores, and data-level parallelism across vector lanes. Interviews test whether you map each to the right primitive: ILP is the compiler and core's job, thread parallelism is your thread-pool and locking design, data parallelism is SIMD or GPU batches.

  • Cores: independent execution engines with private L1/L2 and shared L3. More cores raise throughput for parallel work but do nothing for single-thread latency. Scaling stops at Amdahl's Law: if 10 percent of work is serial, even infinite cores cap speedup at 10x.
  • Hardware threads and SMT: Simultaneous Multithreading (Intel Hyper-Threading, AMD SMT, IBM POWER) exposes two threads per core sharing execution units. When one thread stalls on a cache miss, the other issues. Typical gain is 15-30 percent throughput on mixed server workloads, near zero on fully saturated vector code. Cloud vCPUs usually equal one hardware thread, so an 8-vCPU box may be 4 cores with SMT.
  • Performance vs Efficiency cores: Apple M-series, Intel Core 12th-gen plus, and ARM server chips mix wide fast cores with narrow efficient cores. The OS scheduler parks background work on E-cores and bursts latency-sensitive work on P-cores. Backend relevance: tail latency depends on which core served the request, and noisy-neighbor effects grow when threads migrate between core types.
  • Processes vs threads vs green threads: processes isolate memory (separate page tables, expensive fork); OS threads share memory with per-thread stacks and kernel scheduling (~microseconds to switch); green threads (goroutines, Java virtual threads, Tokio tasks) multiplex thousands onto few OS threads with user-space switching (~tens of nanoseconds). Modern backends run tens of thousands of virtual threads or goroutines over dozens of OS threads.
  • Affinity and pinning: binding latency-critical threads to specific cores (taskset, cpuset, isolcpus) cuts migration misses and jitter. Databases and event loops commonly pin; stateless web tiers usually do not need to.
  • Coherence cost of sharing: atomics and locks bounce the line between cores. An uncontended CAS costs ~10-20 ns; heavily contended it costs hundreds of nanoseconds plus pipeline stalls. Shard counters per core and combine on read.
flowchart TD
    P["Process with shared address space"] --> T1["OS thread pinned to P-core"]
    P --> T2["OS thread on E-core"]
    P --> T3["OS thread with 2x SMT siblings"]
    T1 --> G1["Many green threads multiplexed"]
    T2 --> G2["Many green threads multiplexed"]
    T3 --> G3["Many green threads multiplexed"]

The diagram above separates what the OS schedules from what the runtime schedules: a few OS threads occupy cores and SMT slots while thousands of green threads take turns on top. If green threads block on I/O, the runtime parks them; if OS threads block, the kernel pays a full context switch.

docs.title: 8.2 Try It: Size Pools and Pin Threads
docs.text:
import os
print(os.cpu_count())  # logical CPUs: cores x SMT siblings, not physical cores

$ nproc && lscpu | grep -E "Thread|Core|Socket"   # disentangle threads vs cores
$ taskset -c 0-3 ./latency-critical               # pin to specific cores
$ vmstat 1            # watch cs column: collapsing throughput past a thread count = oversubscription

CPU-bound pools to cores (discount SMT), I/O-bound pools to Little's Law concurrency, event loops to one thread per core with blocking work hived off. Never size by request count.

docs.title: 8.3 Concurrency Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text:
1. Cores vs threads vs SMT: how do you size a thread pool? Cores execute independently; SMT threads share one core's units for 15-30 percent extra throughput on mixed work. OS threads are kernel-scheduled; green threads multiplex in user space. CPU-bound to cores, I/O-bound to concurrency from Little's Law, event loops one per core.
  2. Why do P-cores vs E-cores matter for tail latency? The scheduler parks background work on E-cores and bursts latency-sensitive work on P-cores, so which core served a request changes its latency and noisy-neighbor effects grow on migration.
  3. What does a context switch cost, and how do you reduce them? Direct cost 1-10 microseconds plus cold caches, TLB churn, NUMA migration. Size pools to cores, use non-blocking I/O and virtual threads or goroutines, batch syscalls, avoid 20x vCPU oversubscription, pin latency-critical threads, diagnose with vmstat and perf sched.
  4. Processes vs threads vs green threads? Processes isolate memory with expensive fork; OS threads share memory with microsecond kernel switching; green threads multiplex thousands onto few OS threads with nanosecond user-space switching. Modern backends run tens of thousands of virtual threads or goroutines over dozens of OS threads.
  5. What is Amdahl's Law in one line? If 10 percent of work is serial, even infinite cores cap speedup at 10x. Parallelize the serial fraction or stop adding cores.

docs.title: Part 9. What Backend Developers Must Know
docs.text:
You rarely program the CPU directly, but its costs leak into every p99, every capacity plan, and every Why is this slow after deploy thread. These five effects cover the majority of backend CPU questions.

  • Context switches: what they cost and when they bite. A voluntary switch (blocking on I/O, lock, await) saves registers, swaps stacks, and traps into the scheduler; an involuntary switch (timeslice expiry, higher-priority wakeup) adds TLB pressure and cache pollution. Direct cost is 1-10 microseconds, but the indirect cost — cold L1/L2, migrated NUMA locality, woken cache lines — dominates. Symptoms: high cs in vmstat, high scheduler latency, throughput that collapses past a thread count. Fixes: size pools to cores not requests (one event-loop thread per core, bounded worker pools), use non-blocking I/O and virtual threads or goroutines so parking is cheap, batch syscalls, and stop oversubscribing vCPUs 20x on latency-sensitive tiers.
  • Cache locality: the cheapest optimization. Sequential array scans run at memory bandwidth; pointer-chasing linked structures run at pointer latency, often 10-50x slower on the same data volume. Prefer flat arrays, struct-of-arrays, arena allocation, and batching. Keep per-request hot state small enough for L1/L2: a 200-byte request context stays hot, a 200 KB context does not. Columnar formats (Parquet, Arrow) exist precisely because analytics scans one column sequentially instead of hopping across rows. Compression helps twice: less I/O and smaller cache footprint.
  • Branch prediction and predictable hot paths. Sorted or biased branches predict well; random branches mispredict and flush 10-20 cycles each. Real examples: checking if (user == null) on a path where it is almost never null is free; a hash-bucket chain with unpredictable comparisons is not. Prefer lookup tables, branchless selects (Math.min, masked moves), and separating hot from cold paths so the instruction cache holds the common case. Profile with perf record branch-miss rate before rewriting conditions by hand.
  • SIMD and vectorization: doing 4-16 values per instruction. SSE, AVX2, AVX-512 (x86) and NEON, SVE2 (ARM) apply one op to a whole register: 8 floats with AVX2, 16 with AVX-512. Compilers auto-vectorize simple counted loops over contiguous arrays with no aliasing or early exits; they give up on pointer hops and data-dependent branches. Help them: use for i in range(n) over slices, restrict-style non-aliasing guarantees (separate arrays, typed memoryviews), and library kernels (NumPy, Arrow compute, Java Vector API, Go assembly kernels) instead of hand-rolled scalar loops. GPUs extend the same idea to thousands of lanes; SIMD is the on-CPU version you get for free.
  • Syscalls, user vs kernel, and I/O batching. Every read, send, fsync, or futex crosses protection rings, validates buffers, and may block. High-QPS services win by crossing rarely: buffered writes, readv/writev, sendfile, epoll/kqueue/io_uring instead of one-thread-per-connection blocking reads, and connection pooling to avoid TLS handshake syscalls per request. strace -c showing 30 percent of time in futex means lock contention; showing millions of tiny read calls means missing buffering.
  • Memory model and safe publication. x86 TSO makes most reorderings invisible, but ARM needs explicit acquire-release barriers, which the JVM, Go runtime, and C++ atomics insert for you. Rules: never roll your own double-checked locking with plain fields, publish shared state via volatile, AtomicReference, sync.Mutex, or channels, and keep mutable sharing narrow. The MESI traffic from one hot atomic counter can cap an entire service; shard it per core and aggregate.
  • GC, allocators, and CPU interplay. Allocation is cheap (bump pointer in TLAB), but cache misses during marking and page faults from heap growth are not. Keep young-gen churn low (reuse buffers, stream instead of materializing lists), size heaps so working sets fit DRAM on the local NUMA node, and prefer off-heap or pooled direct buffers for I/O paths.

Latency numbers to memorize (approximate, modern server):

Operation Cost Mental model L1 hit ~1 ns Free in a hot loop Branch mispredict ~5-15 ns 15 wasted cycles L3 hit ~15-40 ns Cross-core share DRAM random ~80-100 ns 300 stalled cycles Uncontended CAS ~10-20 ns Line stays local Contended CAS ~100-500 ns Line ping-pong Context switch ~1-10 us 10,000 L1 hits lost Syscall round trip ~0.5-2 us Batch them SSD 4K read ~50-100 us 1M L1 hits lost Cross-AZ RPC ~0.5-2 ms 10M L1 hits lost

Quote the ratios, not just absolutes: a cache miss costs 100x an L1 hit, a context switch 10,000x, a disk read 100,000x.

docs.title: 9.2 Try It: Find Your Bottleneck
docs.text:
$ perf stat -d ./server            # IPC + MPKI: compute-bound (high IPC) vs memory-bound (high MPKI)
$ perf record -b ./server && perf report   # branch-miss rate before rewriting conditions
$ strace -c -p $PID                # 30% futex = lock contention; millions of tiny reads = missing buffering
$ py-spy record -o flame.svg -- ./app.py    # Python flame graph without code changes

docs.title: 9.3 Backend Performance Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text:
1. Cache locality: the cheapest optimization? Sequential scans run at bandwidth; pointer-chasing runs at latency, 10-50x slower on the same data. Flat arrays, struct-of-arrays, arenas, small hot state, columnar formats for analytics.
  2. Branch prediction and hot paths? Sorted or biased branches predict well; random ones flush 10-20 cycles each. Lookup tables, branchless selects, separate hot from cold code paths. Profile branch-miss rate first.
  3. SIMD in one minute? One op on 4-16 values per register (AVX2/AVX-512, NEON/SVE2). Compilers vectorize simple counted loops over contiguous non-aliasing arrays. Counted index loops, separate arrays, library kernels.
  4. Syscalls and I/O batching? Every crossing costs 0.5-2 microseconds and may block. Buffered writes, readv/writev, sendfile, epoll/kqueue/io_uring, connection pooling. strace -c tells you whether locks or tiny reads dominate.
  5. Memory model and safe publication? x86 TSO hides most reorderings; ARM needs explicit acquire-release barriers, inserted by the JVM, Go runtime, and C++ atomics. Publish via volatile, AtomicReference, mutexes, or channels; shard hot atomics per core to avoid MESI ping-pong.

docs.title: Part 10. Branch Prediction and Speculative Execution
docs.text: Guessing right keeps a 14-19 stage pipeline full; guessing wrong flushes 10-20 cycles of work. This part turns the one-line mentions in Parts 4 and 9 into the full mechanism: what predictors track, how speculation recovers, and what Spectre and Meltdown taught the industry.

docs.title: 10.1 How Predictors Learn Your Branches
docs.text:
• 1-bit and 2-bit saturating counters: remember taken/not-taken per branch address. The 2-bit version needs two consecutive surprises before flipping, which stops loops with one odd iteration from thrashing. State machine: Strongly-Not-Taken -> Weakly-Not-Taken -> Weakly-Taken -> Strongly-Taken.
  • Pattern and history tables (TAGE): index by branch address XOR global history, so if (x) after different call paths predicts differently per path. The longest matching history wins.
  • Perceptron predictors: tiny neural nets per branch; modern AMD and Intel ship these for hard, data-dependent branches.
  • Indirect branch predictors and BTB: switch, virtual calls, and function pointers need a Branch Target Buffer predicting the destination, not just taken/not-taken.
flowchart TD
    F["Fetch branch PC"] --> L{"BTB hit?"}
    L -- "Yes" --> P["Predict direction from history"]
    P --> S["Speculatively fetch and execute ahead"]
    S --> R{"Actual outcome matches?"}
    R -- "Yes" --> K["Commit: prediction was free"]
    R -- "No" --> X["Flush pipeline, 10-20 cycles lost, update tables"]
    L -- "No" --> D["Static predict not-taken or fall through"]

docs.title: 10.2 Spectre, Meltdown, and What Changed
docs.text:
• Meltdown (2018): out-of-order loads bypassed permission checks before the fault retired, leaking kernel memory via cache timing. Fixed with KPTI (separate kernel page tables): correct, costs 5-30 percent on syscall-heavy workloads.
  • Spectre v1/v2: tricked the victim's own speculation (bounds-check bypass, branch-target injection) into leaking. Fixed with retpolines, IBRS/STIBP microcode, bounds clipping (array_index_nospec), and site isolation in browsers.
  • Backend cost you still pay: KPTI page-table switches on every syscall, retpoline-throttled indirect calls, and disabled SMT on some security-sensitive fleets. When someone says "post-2018 cloud got 10 percent slower," this is a big slice of it.

docs.title: 10.3 Try It: Make a Branch Predictable
docs.text:
import random, time

data = [random.random() for _ in range(200_000)]
t0 = time.perf_counter()
s1 = sum(1 for x in data if x > 0.5)          # random: predictor helpless
t1 = time.perf_counter()
data.sort()
s2 = sum(1 for x in data if x > 0.5)          # sorted: predictor nearly perfect
t2 = time.perf_counter()
print(f"random {(t1-t0)*1000:.1f}ms, sorted {(t2-t1)*1000:.1f}ms")

The sorted pass runs dramatically faster on identical comparisons: that gap is pure branch prediction. Compilers do this transformation for you when they can (lookup tables, branchless selects, cmov).

docs.title: 10.4 Prediction Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text:
1. What does a mispredict cost, and why? 10-20 cycles: every speculatively fetched instruction after the branch is flushed and the pipeline refills. Correct predictions are free, which is why biased branches are nearly invisible.
  2. 2-bit counter vs TAGE in one minute? 2-bit counters remember per-branch bias with hysteresis. TAGE indexes by branch plus global history so the same branch predicts differently on different paths. Perceptron predictors learn data-dependent patterns no table catches.
  3. Spectre vs Meltdown in one minute? Meltdown: faulty out-of-order loads read kernel memory before the fault retires; fixed by KPTI. Spectre: attacker steers the victim's own speculation into leaking; fixed by retpolines, microcode, bounds clipping, site isolation.
  4. How do you write predictor-friendly code? One predictable exit per loop, sort or bias branches so the common path falls through, hoist unpredictable tests out of hot loops, prefer tables and branchless selects over data-dependent ifs.

docs.title: Part 11. Power, Clocks, and Thermals
docs.text: Clock speed stalled near 5-6 GHz because power did not scale with transistors. This part explains why, what vendors do instead, and how it changes benchmarking.

docs.title: 11.1 Why GHz Stopped Growing
docs.text:
Dynamic power follows P = C x V^2 x f: each switch charges capacitance at voltage V, f times per second. Dennard scaling (shrink transistors, drop voltage, hold power density) ended around 2006; since then smaller transistors leak more at rest and the voltage floor barely moves, so higher clocks mean melting silicon.

What vendors do instead:

  • DVFS: scale voltage and frequency to the workload. Bursty request handlers turbo up, idle cores park.
  • Turbo and thermal headroom: boost one core far above base while the package stays under its thermal and current budget. Sustained all-core loads clock lower than single-thread bursts.
  • Gating and dark silicon: clock-gate idle units, power-gate whole cores, leave accelerators dark until needed. A phone SoC can only light a fraction of its transistors at once without throttling.
  • Wider, not faster: spend the transistor budget on more cores, wider decode, bigger caches, and matrix engines at modest clocks. Apple Silicon, Graviton, and Zen all bet this way.
flowchart TD
    L["Load rises"] --> T["Turbo to higher frequency"]
    T --> H{"Within thermal and current budget?"}
    H -- "Yes" --> S["Sustain boost"]
    H -- "No" --> D["Step frequency down"]
    D --> H

docs.title: 11.2 Try It: See Turbo and Throttling
docs.text:
$ cat /proc/cpuinfo | grep -m1 "model name"   # advertised vs base clock
$ sudo cpupower frequency-info                # current governor and boost state
$ dmesg | grep -i -E "thermal|throttl"          # kernel saw heat pressure
$ lscpu | grep -i mhz                          # compare before / during load

Benchmark at a pinned frequency (performance governor) or turbo noise drowns real deltas.

docs.title: 11.3 Power Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text:
1. Why did clocks stop near 5 GHz, and how should that change benchmarking? Dennard scaling ended so voltage stopped dropping while leakage rose; P = C x V^2 x f turns extra GHz into cubic power for linear speed. Vendors went wider with turbo as borrowing against thermal budget. Pin the governor, compare at fixed clocks, size capacity at sustained all-core frequency.
  2. DVFS vs turbo vs throttling? DVFS is deliberate scaling to the workload. Turbo is opportunistic boost inside thermal budget. Throttling is forced slowdown when the budget is blown. Same knob, different intent.
  3. Dark silicon in one line? A modern SoC can only power a fraction of its transistors at once without melting, so accelerators stay dark until their workload arrives.

docs.title: Part 12. Virtual Memory, Paging, and the TLB
docs.text: Every process gets a private address space and the OS oversubscribes physical RAM. The MMU translates each virtual address, checks permissions, and faults to the OS when the mapping is missing or forbidden.

docs.title: 12.1 Pages, Tables, and the TLB
docs.text:
Paging splits both spaces into fixed pages (4 KB standard, 2 MB and 1 GB huge pages). A multi-level page table is a tree: each level indexes the next with 9 bits on x86-64 and ARM64, so unmapped regions cost no memory. Translating means walking that tree; the TLB caches recent translations so the walk happens only on miss.

flowchart LR
    VA["Virtual address from CPU"] --> TLB{"TLB hit?"}
    TLB -- "Yes" --> PA["Physical address to cache"]
    TLB -- "No" --> W["Hardware page table walk"]
    W --> OK{"Mapping valid?"}
    OK -- "Yes" --> F["Fill TLB and retry"]
    F --> PA
    OK -- "No" --> PF["Page fault to OS"]
Page size TLB reach with 1024 entries Best for 4 KB 4 MB General processes, fine-grained protection 2 MB 2 GB Databases, JVM heaps, vector stores 1 GB 1 TB Terabyte in-memory engines on bare metal

docs.title: 12.2 What the OS Does on a Fault
docs.text:
• Minor fault: page exists in memory (file cache, copy-on-write zero page) but is not yet mapped. Cheap: wire the page-table entry and resume. mmap startup and first-touch allocation look like this.
  • Major fault: page is on disk or network. The faulting thread sleeps while the page is read in. One major fault costs more than a million L1 hits, which is why cold-start scans spike p99.
  • Swap or reclaim: under pressure the OS evicts cold pages. Containers with tight memory limits die by thrashing here long before any OOM headline.
  • Copy-on-write: fork shares pages read-only until either side writes, then copies. This is why forking a 10 GB process is instant until the child touches memory.

docs.title: 12.3 Try It: Watch Faults and TLB Pressure
docs.text:
$ /usr/bin/time -v ./server 2>&1 | grep -E "faults|Maximum resident"   # minor vs major faults
$ perf stat -d ./server 2>&1 | grep -i tlb    # dTLB miss rates: huge pages help here
$ sar -B 1 3                                   # paging activity under load
$ free -h && vmstat 1                          # swap use + si/so columns climbing = thrashing

Pre-touch or pre-fault memory-mapped files before serving; keep NUMA-local allocation (first-touch or explicit pinning) so the page walk and the data land on the same socket.

docs.title: 12.4 Virtual Memory Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text:
1. Explain virtual memory and what happens on a TLB miss. Every process sees a private virtual address space; the MMU translates each address via multi-level page tables with permission checks. The TLB caches recent translations. On a miss the hardware walks the tables: hit means fill the TLB and retry, miss means page fault to the OS. Minor faults map an in-memory page and resume; major faults sleep the thread for disk or network.
  2. Huge pages: when and why? 2 MB pages shrink page tables 512x and cut TLB misses for multi-GB heaps: standard Postgres, Redis, and JVM tuning. Verify with perf stat dTLB miss rates before and after.
  3. Minor vs major fault? Minor: page already in RAM, just unmapped — microseconds. Major: page on disk or network — the thread sleeps milliseconds. time -v reports both; major faults in a hot path are a p99 emergency.
  4. How do NUMA and paging interact? On multi-socket hosts, memory local to the socket answers faster at 1.3-2x latency. First-touch allocation or numactl keeps pages near their threads; remote walks and remote data stack the penalty.

docs.title: Part 13. I/O, PCIe, Interrupts, and DMA
docs.text: The CPU never bit-bangs a modern SSD or NIC. It programs a controller, goes back to useful work, and learns the transfer finished via an interrupt or by polling a completion queue.

docs.title: 13.1 Three I/O Styles
docs.text:
Style How the CPU moves data Cost profile Programmed I/O CPU reads and writes every byte Simple, burns a core per byte Interrupt-driven Device interrupts when done Good for rare events, storms at high rate DMA Controller moves bulk memory itself Best throughput, CPU free during transfer

PCIe is the fabric: lanes of high-speed serial, devices exposing memory-mapped registers and doorbells, MSI-X interrupts routed per-queue so each core handles its own completions. NVMe queues, NIC rings, and GPU command queues all sit on this model: the driver writes descriptors, rings the doorbell, the device DMAs data and posts a completion.

sequenceDiagram
    participant CPU as CPU
    participant DEV as NVMe or NIC
    participant MEM as Memory
    CPU->>DEV: Write descriptors, ring doorbell
    DEV->>MEM: DMA data directly
    DEV-->>CPU: MSI-X interrupt or completion flag
    CPU->>MEM: Consume completed buffers

docs.title: 13.2 Interrupts, Affinity, and Why They Matter
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    E["Device event"] --> Q{"Interrupts enabled?"}
    Q -- "Yes" --> S["Finish instruction, save context"]
    S --> ISR["Run interrupt handler"]
    ISR --> R["Restore and resume"]
    Q -- "No" --> P["Event waits as pending"]

Affinity and MSI-X route each device queue's interrupts to one core so caches stay warm — check /proc/interrupts when NIC load looks lopsided.

docs.title: 13.3 SATA vs NVMe vs PCIe
docs.text:
SATA and NVMe are often confused with the physical plug. Separate the three layers: the connector (2.5-inch, M.2), the bus (SATA, PCIe), and the protocol (AHCI, NVMe). Performance comes from the bus plus the protocol, not the shape.

Property SATA SSD (AHCI) NVMe SSD (PCIe) Designed for Spinning disks, 2004 Flash, 2011, parallelism from day one Queues 1 queue, 32 commands 64k queues x 64k commands each CPU cost per I/O Legacy path, heavier locking MSI-X per-core queues, doorbell registers Bandwidth ~550 MB/s ceiling (SATA III 6 Gbps minus encoding) PCIe 3.0 x4 ~3.5 GB/s, Gen4 x4 ~7 GB/s, Gen5 x4 ~14 GB/s Latency ~100 us ~20-50 us Random 4K read IOPS ~50-100k ~500k-1M+ Best for Drop-in laptop upgrades, bulk cheap flash Databases, boot, scratch, ML data, WAL

How an NVMe read actually flows:

1. Driver builds a command (opcode READ, namespace, LBA, length,
   destination memory address) in a submission queue in RAM.
2. Driver rings the doorbell register on the SSD: new work waiting.
3. SSD DMAs the command in, reads NAND pages into its buffer.
4. SSD DMAs the data straight into host RAM (no CPU copy).
5. SSD posts a completion entry to the completion queue and raises
   one MSI-X interrupt to the core that owns that queue.
6. Driver reaps completions in a batch and hands pages to the app.

SATA/AHCI does one queue shared across cores with heavier locking and one interrupt style from the spinning-disk era. Same NAND behind either interface benchmarks 10x apart on random I/O because the plumbing, not the flash, is the bottleneck.

M.2 confusion cleared: an M.2 stick can speak SATA (B-key, ~550 MB/s) or NVMe (M-key, GB/s). U.2 is the 2.5-inch NVMe form for servers. Always check lspci link speed, not the physical size.

docs.title: 13.4 The PCI Bus and PCIe: How Devices Talk to the CPU
docs.text:
PCI (Peripheral Component Interconnect) was the 1990s parallel shared bus: every card shared one set of wires, one device spoke at a time, 133 MB/s at best. PCIe (PCI Express) replaced it with serial point-to-point links and kept the PCI software model (configuration space, enumeration, BARs), which is why lspci still works on a machine with no physical PCI slots.

  • Lanes: each lane is a full-duplex differential pair (one transmit, one receive). A x1 link has 1 lane, x4 has 4, x16 (GPUs) has 16. Bandwidth scales linearly with lanes.
  • Generations: each doubles per-lane speed. Per-lane each direction: Gen3 ~1 GB/s, Gen4 ~2 GB/s, Gen5 ~4 GB/s. A Gen4 x4 NVMe drive: 4 x 2 = ~8 GB/s raw, ~7 GB/s after encoding.
  • Packets, not wires: devices exchange Transaction Layer Packets (memory reads/writes, completions, messages) routed by address. Switches fan one root port out to many endpoints like a network.
  • Root complex: the CPU-side agent that owns the hierarchy. Everything the CPU reads or writes to a device address crosses it.
  • BARs (Base Address Registers): during enumeration the BIOS/OS sizes each device's memory windows and maps them into physical address space. MMIO to those addresses hits device registers; DMA from the device writes to RAM addresses it was given.
  • MSI-X interrupts: devices write a message to a special address instead of toggling a shared pin, so each queue can interrupt its own core with no sharing.
flowchart TD
    CPU["CPU cores"] <--> RC["Root complex"]
    RC <--> SW["PCIe switch"]
    SW <--> NVME["NVMe SSD x4"]
    SW <--> NIC["NIC x8 or x16"]
    SW <--> GPUC["GPU x16"]
    RC <--> DRAM["DRAM controller"]

Reading lspci -vv output: LnkSta: Speed 16GT/s, Width x4 means Gen4 x4, healthy. A drive rated for x4 showing Width x1 or Gen1 speed means a bad slot, bifurcation limit, or power-saving ASPM state, and it directly caps throughput. NUMA adds one more rule: a device behind socket 1's root complex is faster for socket 1's cores, so pin latency-sensitive I/O threads near their device.

PCI vs PCIe vs SATA vs NVMe in one line: PCI is the dead parallel bus, PCIe is the live serial fabric everything plugs into, SATA/AHCI is the old disk protocol that can ride SATA (or M.2 SATA), and NVMe is the modern flash protocol that rides PCIe.

docs.title: 13.5 Try It: Trace an I/O Path
docs.text:
$ cat /proc/interrupts | grep -E "nvme|eth"   # one queue per core = MSI-X balanced
$ ethtool -S eth0 | grep -i -E "queue|drop"    # queue balance and drops
$ iostat -x 1                                   # device queue depth and utilization
$ sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:block:block_rq_issue { @[args->dev] = count(); }'  # live block I/O

docs.title: 13.6 I/O Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text:
1. Interrupts vs polling vs DMA: which for a 100 Gbps NIC? Interrupts per packet drown at that rate, programmed I/O burns cores per byte. DMA with per-queue MSI-X, interrupt coalescing, batched doorbells, and user-space polling (io_uring, DPDK) on dedicated cores. The driver posts descriptor rings, the NIC DMAs into memory, completions are consumed in batches.
  2. Level-triggered vs edge-triggered (epoll) and io_uring? Level-triggered suits steady streams (re-notified while ready). Edge-triggered plus io_uring completion queues suit millions of small ops with fewer syscalls. Coalescing plus batched doorbells is why sendmmsg and jumbo frames exist.
  3. What does a DPU offload, exactly? The whole dance: TLS, virtual switching, tunnel encapsulation, storage initiators, eBPF or P4 pipelines — off the host cores onto the NIC computer.
  4. PCI vs PCIe vs SATA vs NVMe in one minute? PCI is the dead parallel shared bus. PCIe is the live serial fabric everything plugs into. SATA/AHCI is the old disk protocol over SATA links. NVMe is the modern flash protocol over PCIe.
  5. Why does a Gen4 x4 NVMe drive show 7 GB/s not 8? 4 lanes times ~2 GB/s per lane is ~8 GB/s raw; encoding overhead lands around 7 GB/s usable.
  6. What does Width x1 in lspci mean for an x4 drive? Negotiated one lane instead of four: bad slot, bifurcation limit, or ASPM power saving. Throughput caps at a quarter until fixed.

docs.title: 14.1 Memory Hierarchy
docs.text:
Fast storage is small, large storage is slow. Every access checks the fastest level first.

flowchart TD
    R["Registers: ~1 KB, under 1 ns"] --> L1["L1: ~64 KB per core, ~1 ns"]
    L1 --> L2["L2: ~1-2 MB per core, ~5 ns"]
    L2 --> L3["L3: shared ~16-128 MB, ~20 ns"]
    L3 --> DRAM["DRAM: GBs, ~80 ns"]
    DRAM --> SSD["SSD: TBs, ~50 us"]
    SSD --> HDD["HDD or network: ms"]
Level Size Latency Role Registers ~1 KB <1 ns Current operands L1/L2 KB–MB 1–5 ns Hot loops L3 tens of MB 15–40 ns Shared working set DRAM GBs ~80 ns Running processes SSD TBs ~50–100 us Persistent fast data HDD/network TBs+ ms Archive, cold data

Locality makes it work: temporal (recently used is reused) and spatial (neighbors of used data are used next). Caches exploit both with 64-byte lines and prefetchers.

docs.title: 14.2 SRAM vs DRAM
docs.text:
Property SRAM DRAM Cell 6 transistors, flip-flop 1 transistor + 1 capacitor Speed Very fast (~1 ns) Slower (~50 ns + refresh) Density Large, expensive Dense, cheap Refresh Never, holds while powered Every few ms or charge leaks Used for Caches, register files Main memory

How RAM stores and retrieves: the address splits into row and column. Wordlines open one row, bitlines sense each column's charge (DRAM) or flip-flop state (SRAM), sense amplifiers latch the row into a buffer, and column muxes pick the requested bytes. Writing reverses the flow. DRAM then precharges for the next access and the memory controller refreshes idle rows in the background.

docs.title: Storing a bit in SRAM
docs.text: An SRAM cell is two cross-coupled inverters (4 transistors) that hold each other at 1/0, plus 2 access transistors to the bitlines. To store a 1: drive bit = 1, bit_bar = 0, raise the wordline, the latch flips and holds. To read: precharge both bitlines high, raise the wordline, one side pulls its line down, and the sense amplifier detects which side moved. No refresh needed because the inverters keep driving the value while powered. That is why SRAM is fast and why 6 transistors per bit make it big and expensive.

docs.title: Storing a bit in DRAM, step by step
docs.text:
A DRAM cell is 1 transistor plus 1 capacitor. Charged capacitor = 1, empty = 0. Charge leaks within milliseconds, so every read is destructive and must be written back, and every row is refreshed periodically whether you touch it or not.

1. Idle: bitlines precharged to Vdd/2, wordline closed.
2. ACTIVATE row: controller sends row address, wordline opens every
   transistor in that row at once.
3. Charge sharing: each capacitor nudges its bitline slightly up (1)
   or down (0). The swing is tiny, tens of millivolts.
4. Sense: sense amplifiers detect the direction and drive each bitline
   to full 0 or Vdd, latching the whole row (typically 8 KB) into the
   row buffer. This also restores the capacitors.
5. READ/WRITE: column address picks bytes from the row buffer.
   A second access to the same row is a fast row-buffer hit.
6. PRECHARGE: close the row, reset bitlines for the next access.

flowchart TD
    A["Controller sends ACTIVATE plus row address"] --> B["Wordline opens all cells in the row"]
    B --> C["Capacitors nudge bitlines up or down"]
    C --> D["Sense amplifiers latch full row into row buffer"]
    D --> E["READ or WRITE columns from the buffer"]
    E --> F["PRECHARGE row, refresh idle rows in background"]

Row-buffer hits serve in ~15 ns, row conflicts (close one row, open another) cost ~50 ns plus. That is why sequential access within a row is fast, random rows are slow, and the controller reorders requests to favor hits. Refresh touches every row about every 64 ms (8192 refresh commands), briefly blocking that bank, which is one source of tail latency in RAM-heavy services.

docs.title: 14.3 RAM and ROM Types
docs.text:
Type Volatile Behavior SRAM Yes Cache, no refresh DRAM (DDR4/DDR5) Yes Main memory Mask ROM No Factory-fixed firmware PROM/EPROM/EEPROM No One-time or electrically erasable firmware Flash (NOR/NAND) No BIOS chips, SSDs, USB sticks

NOR flash executes code in place (firmware); NAND flash stores bulk data (SSDs). Your SSD is an array of NAND plus a controller that hides its quirks.

docs.title: 14.4 Cache Memory
docs.text:
L1 splits into instruction and data caches per core; L2 backs each core or cluster; L3 (or system-level cache) is shared. Three mapping policies:

Policy Rule Trade-off Direct-mapped Each block has exactly one home Simple, most conflicts Set-associative (4–16 ways) Each block has a small set of homes The standard balance Fully associative Anywhere Flexible, expensive, small TLBs only

On a miss the line (64 bytes) is fetched from below and possibly evicts a victim (LRU approximation). Writes use write-back (dirty lines flushed on eviction, the norm) or write-through (every store goes down, simple but slow). Miss types: compulsory (first touch), capacity (working set too big), conflict (too many addresses share a set).

docs.title: 14.5 HDD Architecture
docs.text:
A hard drive stacks spinning platters coated with magnetic grains. Each surface has a head on an actuator arm. Data lives on concentric tracks divided into sectors (traditionally 512 bytes or 4 Kn). A cylinder is the same track across all platters.

Reading and writing: to write, the head magnetizes grains in one of two orientations. To read, the head senses the magnetic transitions as it flies nanometers above the spinning surface. Seek time moves the arm (ms), rotational latency waits for the sector (~4 ms at 7200 RPM), transfer streams the bits.

Access time ≈ seek + rotation + transfer. Sequential reads stream at 100–200 MB/s; random 4 KB reads collapse to under 1 MB/s because each seeks. That 100x gap is why databases love sequential layouts and why indexing exists.

docs.title: How a write physically lands on a platter
docs.text:
1. OS sends a 4 KB block write. It sits first in the HDD's DRAM cache.
2. Firmware translates the logical block address (LBA) to a physical
   zone, track, and sector, skipping grown defect lists.
3. Voice-coil actuator seeks the arm to the target track (2–8 ms).
4. Controller waits for the target sector to rotate under the head.
5. Write current through the head magnetizes grains vertically
   (perpendicular recording) as they pass. ECC bytes are written
   alongside the data.
6. Optional read-after-write verifies the sector; failures remap to
   a spare sector transparently.
7. Drive acknowledges. Write-back cache acks early for speed,
   write-through acks after the platter for safety.

Reading reverses it: seek, wait for rotation, sense magnetic transitions as resistance changes in the read head, correct up to a few bad bits with ECC, return the sector.

flowchart LR
    OS["OS block write"] --> CACHE["HDD DRAM cache"]
    CACHE --> SEEK["Seek arm to track"]
    SEEK --> WAIT["Wait for sector rotation"]
    WAIT --> MAG["Magnetize grains, write ECC"]
    MAG --> ACK["Acknowledge to OS"]

CMR vs SMR: conventional (CMR) tracks sit side by side and allow random rewrites. Shingled (SMR) tracks overlap like roof tiles for 20–25 percent more capacity, but rewriting one track requires rewriting its neighbors, so random writes stall. SMR suits archives; databases and RAID rebuilds want CMR. Check the datasheet before buying bulk drives.

docs.title: 14.6 SSD and NAND Flash
docs.text:
NAND flash stores charge in floating-gate or charge-trap cells arranged in strings. No moving parts: any page reads in tens of microseconds regardless of location.

Type Bits per cell Relative speed and endurance Use SLC 1 Fastest, ~100k cycles Industrial, write cache MLC 2 Balanced, ~3k cycles Older consumer drives TLC 3 Slower, ~1k cycles Mainstream SSDs QLC 4 Slowest, ~hundreds of cycles Cheap bulk storage

Hierarchy: cell → string → page (4–16 KB, read/write unit) → block (hundreds of pages, erase unit). Rules that shape everything: pages write once before erase, erases happen per block, blocks wear out. So the controller does garbage collection (copy live pages, erase the block), wear leveling (spread erases evenly), over-provisioning (spare blocks for GC and bad blocks), and an FTL flash translation layer that remaps logical addresses so the OS never sees the churn.

docs.title: Program, read, and erase: the three NAND operations
docs.text:
A NAND cell is a transistor with an extra isolated gate that traps electrons. More trapped electrons raise the threshold voltage. Reading applies reference voltages and checks at which point the cell conducts; TLC needs 7 references to distinguish 8 levels, QLC needs 15 for 16 levels, which is why denser NAND reads slower and wears faster.

READ a page (fast, ~50 us): apply reference voltages, sense each
  cell's level, run ECC (LDPC) to fix borderline cells.
PROGRAM a page (slower, ~1 ms): only on an erased page. Pulse
  electrons in (ISPP), verify, repeat until the level is right.
ERASE a block (slowest, ~ms): whole block at once, high voltage
  clears every cell. The only way to reuse a page.

Golden rule: no in-place overwrite. Every write goes to a fresh erased page elsewhere (out-of-place write). The old page is marked invalid. Garbage collection later copies the still-live pages out of a mostly-invalid block and erases it. Write amplification = NAND bytes written ÷ host bytes written; random small writes can push it to 2–4x, sequential writes keep it near 1x.

flowchart TD
    H["Host 4 KB write"] --> BUF["SSD DRAM buffer"]
    BUF --> FTL["FTL picks an erased page, updates LBA to PBA map"]
    FTL --> PROG["Program page, mark old page invalid"]
    PROG --> ACK["Acknowledge"]
    PROG -.-> GC["Later: GC copies live pages, erases block"]

Power-loss protection (capacitors on enterprise drives) flushes the DRAM buffer to NAND on outage. Consumer drives without it can lose seconds of acknowledged writes, which is why databases demand enterprise SSDs or fsync on a filesystem that orders correctly.

docs.title: 14.7 Controllers, Sectors, Blocks, Pages, File Systems
docs.text: The storage controller (HDD PCB, SSD controller, RAID card, cloud EBS backend) translates OS block reads and writes into device operations, queues them, and hides retries and remapping. File systems (ext4, XFS, APFS, NTFS) layer files, directories, permissions, and journals on top of that block interface. A journal (or copy-on-write design like ZFS and Btrfs) replays interrupted writes after a crash so metadata stays consistent.

docs.title: 14.8 RAID Levels
docs.text:
Level Layout Usable of N disks Failures tolerated Notes RAID 0 Stripe, no parity 100 percent 0 Fast, any disk kills the array RAID 1 Mirror 50 percent 1 per pair Simple, good for boot RAID 5 Stripe + 1 parity (N−1)/N 1 Rebuilds are slow and risky on TB drives RAID 6 Stripe + 2 parity (N−2)/N 2 Standard for large HDD arrays RAID 10 Mirror then stripe 50 percent 1+ (if lucky) Best random I/O, database default

Parity math is XOR across stripes: any one missing chunk is the XOR of the survivors. RAID is availability, not backup: it survives disk death, not deletion, corruption, or fire.

docs.title: 14.9 Persistence, Durability, Reliability
docs.text:
• Persistence means data survives power loss (flash, disk, not RAM).
  • Durability means acknowledged writes survive crashes (fsync, journal, replication).
  • Reliability means data stays correct over time: ECC, checksums, scrubbing, SMART monitoring, and backups.

SSDs lie a little: without power loss protection, writes in the DRAM cache can vanish on outage. Databases call fsync and enterprise drives add capacitors for exactly this reason.

Misconception: deleting a file erases it. Deletion usually unlinks metadata; the bytes remain until overwritten, which is why forensics and secure-erase exist.

Interview questions: SRAM vs DRAM cell and use. Why random HDD reads are 100x slower than sequential. What TLC means. Usable capacity and fault tolerance of RAID 5 vs RAID 10. Where does an acknowledged write live after fsync. Why a Gen4 x4 NVMe drive shows 7 GB/s not 8. What Width x1 in lspci means. CMR vs SMR for a database. What write amplification is and what drives it up.

docs.title: 14.10 Try It: Know Your Own Storage Stack
docs.text:
$ lsblk -t && iostat -x 1              # alignment, queue depth, utilization
$ nvme list && nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0n1  # drives, wear percentage, temperature
$ sudo smartctl -a /dev/sda | grep -i -E "realloc|pending|wear|power_on"  # drive health
$ df -h && mount | grep -E "ext4|xfs|apfs"   # filesystem per mount
$ cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/scheduler       # none (NVMe) vs mq-deadline/kyber (SATA)

Checklist: NVMe on PCIe Gen4 x4 for databases and WAL; none scheduler on NVMe; utf8mb4 on MySQL text; enterprise SSDs with power-loss protection where fsync durability matters.

docs.title: 14.11 Storage Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text:
1. SRAM vs DRAM cell and use? SRAM: 6 transistors, latch, no refresh, ~1 ns, big and expensive: caches and register files. DRAM: 1 transistor plus 1 capacitor, leaks in milliseconds, needs refresh, dense and cheap: main memory.
  2. Walk the DRAM read path. ACTIVATE row, charge sharing nudges bitlines, sense amplifiers latch the 8 KB row into the row buffer, column reads serve from the buffer, PRECHARGE closes. Row-buffer hits ~15 ns, conflicts ~50 ns.
  3. Why are random HDD reads 100x slower than sequential? Every random read pays seek (ms) plus rotation (~4 ms); sequential streams at 100-200 MB/s while random 4 KB collapses under 1 MB/s. CMR allows random rewrites; SMR suits archives.
  4. TLC vs QLC: what does it cost? TLC: 3 bits per cell, 7 reference voltages, ~1k program-erase cycles. QLC: 4 bits, 15 references, hundreds of cycles. Denser and cheaper, slower and shorter-lived.
  5. What is write amplification, and what drives it up? NAND bytes written divided by host bytes written. No in-place overwrite plus garbage collection means random small writes hit 2-4x; sequential stays near 1x.
  6. SATA vs NVMe: same NAND, 10x apart on random I/O — why? One shared AHCI queue with legacy interrupts vs 64k NVMe queues with per-core MSI-X, doorbells, and GB/s PCIe bandwidth. See Part 13 for the full queue and doorbell flow. The plumbing, not the flash, is the bottleneck.
  7. RAID 5 vs RAID 10 for a database? RAID 5: (N-1)/N usable, survives 1 disk, slow risky rebuilds on TB drives. RAID 10: 50 percent usable, best random I/O, database default. Neither is a backup.
  8. Where does an acknowledged write live after fsync? On durable media or power-loss-protected buffers, ordered through journal and device cache flush. Consumer SSDs without capacitors can lose DRAM-cached writes on outage.

docs.title: 15.1 ASCII and Unicode
docs.text: ASCII assigns 0–127 to English letters, digits, and control codes. A is 65, a is 97, 0 is 48. Unicode extends this to every script plus emoji: each character gets a code point like U+0041 (A) or U+1F600 (grinning face). Encodings (UTF-8, UTF-16) decide how code points become bytes.

docs.title: 15.2 UTF-8 and UTF-16
docs.text:
UTF-8 is variable-length and ASCII-compatible, the backend default:

Code point range Bytes Pattern U+0000–U+007F 1 0xxxxxxx U+0080–U+07FF 2 110xxxxx 10xxxxxx U+0800–U+FFFF 3 1110xxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx U+10000–U+10FFFF 4 11110xxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx

Example: é (U+00E9) encodes as 11000011 10101001 (0xC3 0xA9). UTF-16 uses 2 bytes per unit with surrogate pairs for characters above U+FFFF (JavaScript strings, Java char, Windows APIs). The MySQL utf8 versus utf8mb4 trap: the former stores 3 bytes max and rejects emoji; always use utf8mb4.

docs.title: 15.3 Integers and IEEE 754 Floats
docs.text:
Integers follow Part 1.5. Floats follow IEEE 754: a double is 1 sign bit, 11 exponent bits (bias 1023), 52 mantissa bits. Value = (−1)^sign × 1.mantissa × 2^(exponent−bias) for normals.

Worked example: 13.25. Binary 1101.01 = 1.10101 × 2^3. Sign 0, exponent 3+1023 = 1026 = 10000000010, mantissa 101010...0. So 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 in every hardware-float language, and money belongs in integer cents or decimal types.

Special values: all-zero exponent with zero mantissa is ±0; all-one exponent with zero mantissa is ±infinity; all-one exponent with nonzero mantissa is NaN.

docs.title: 15.4 Endianness
docs.text:
Little-endian (x86, ARM as you deploy it, RISC-V) stores the least significant byte at the lowest address. Big-endian (network order, some file formats) stores the most significant first.

Value 0x12345678 at address 0x100:

Address Little-endian byte Big-endian byte 0x100 0x78 0x12 0x101 0x56 0x34 0x102 0x34 0x56 0x103 0x12 0x78

Use htons/ntohs at network boundaries and specify byte order in every binary protocol, Parquet footer, and hex dump you read.

docs.title: 15.5 How Data Types Sit in Memory
docs.text:
A 32-bit int is 4 consecutive bytes in whatever endianness the machine uses. A C struct gets padded so each field aligns to its size: struct { char a; int b; char c; } is typically 12 bytes, not 6 (3 padding after a, 3 after c). Reorder fields largest-first to shrink hot structs.

Pointers are just addresses-sized integers; arrays are contiguous elements (index math is base + i × size); strings are bytes plus a convention (NUL terminator in C, length prefix in Go, Java, and Rust).

Misconception: char is one character. In UTF-8 a character is 1–4 bytes, and one visible glyph can be several code points (base + combining marks + variation selectors).

Interview questions: encode é in UTF-8. Break down an IEEE 754 double. What breaks when code assumes 1 char = 1 byte. How is 0x12345678 laid out in little-endian memory.

docs.title: 15.6 Try It: Encoding Bugs in the Open
docs.text:
print(0.1 + 0.2)                    # 0.30000000000000004: binary, not decimal
print((0.1 + 0.2) == 0.3)           # False: never == floats

print("é".encode("utf-8"))          # b'\xc3\xa9': 2 bytes, not 1 char
print(len("é"), len("é".encode("utf-8")))  # 1 character, 2 bytes
print(b"\xc3\xa9".decode("latin-1"))       # Ã©: mojibake from wrong charset

import struct
print(struct.pack("<I", 0x12345678).hex())  # 78563412: little-endian layout
print(struct.pack(">I", 0x12345678).hex())  # 12345678: big-endian layout

-- MySQL trap: utf8 is 3-byte, rejects emoji. Always real UTF-8.
ALTER TABLE posts MODIFY body TEXT CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;

docs.title: 15.7 Encoding Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text:
1. Encode é in UTF-8. U+00E9 falls in the 2-byte range: 11000011 10101001 (0xC3 0xA9).
  2. Break down an IEEE 754 double. 1 sign bit, 11 exponent bits (bias 1023), 52 mantissa bits: value = (-1)^sign × 1.mantissa × 2^(exponent-bias), with all-zero/all-one exponents reserved for zero, infinity, NaN.
  3. What breaks when code assumes 1 char = 1 byte? Truncation splits multi-byte sequences, VARCHAR(10) counts characters not bytes, emoji vanish under utf8 instead of utf8mb4, and string offsets drift across languages.
  4. How is 0x12345678 laid out in little-endian memory? Lowest address holds the small end: 78 56 34 12. Network order is the reverse; htons/ntohs bridge the boundary.
  5. Money math is off by a cent. Where do you look first? Encoding before logic: float rounding, decimal scale, timestamp truncation. Then serialization, column types, and API contracts, with a regression test asserting exact decimals.

docs.title: Part 16. Models, Boards, and Boot
docs.text: How the machine is organized: one shared memory or two, what the ISA promises, what the motherboard connects, and how the whole thing wakes up when you press power.

docs.title: 16.1 Von Neumann vs Harvard
docs.text:
Property Von Neumann Harvard Memory One store for code and data Separate instruction and data memories Buses Shared Separate, parallel access Examples Laptops, servers, phones at system level Microcontrollers, DSPs; split L1 I/D cache inside every core Strength Flexible, self-modifying code, one memory to manage No fetch-vs-data contention, deterministic timing 
flowchart LR
    subgraph Von["Von Neumann"]
    VCPU["CPU"] <--> VMEM["Single memory: code plus data"]
    end
    subgraph Har["Harvard"]
    HCPU["CPU"] <--> HIM["Instruction memory"]
    HCPU <--> HDM["Data memory"]
    end

Modern cores are modified Harvard locally (split L1) on a von Neumann system (shared DRAM). Self-modifying code and JITs must flush the I-cache precisely because the two views can disagree.

docs.title: 16.2 RISC vs CISC and the Open-ISA Wave
docs.text:
Property RISC (ARM, RISC-V) CISC (x86-64) Instructions Few, fixed-size, load/store only touches memory Many, variable-size, memory operands allowed Philosophy Compiler + simple decoder + wide execution Hardware does more per instruction Today Both decode to RISC-like micro-ops internally Difference is code density, decoder cost, extensions

The ISA matters less than implementation quality: Apple Silicon, Graviton, and Zen all win through wide decode, huge reorder buffers, and integration, not acronyms.

  • RISC-V: the open third pole. No license fees, modular extensions (M, A, F, D, C, V), moving from microcontrollers into data-center silicon and hyperscaler fleets. Your code is ready if it avoids inline assembly and builds multi-arch (see Part 5.2); the CPU-vs-accelerator placement stays where Part 6 put it: cheapest generalist that meets the SLO, promote only on proof.

docs.title: 16.3 Booting: From Power Button to PID 1
docs.text:
Pressing power replays the whole stack in miniature. Firmware initializes what software assumes:

1. Power-on and BootROM: on-chip ROM runs first, initializes clocks and RAM just enough
   to load the next stage, verifies signatures (Apple Silicon, phones, Secure Boot PCs).
2. Firmware (UEFI or BIOS): discovers hardware, trains DRAM, enumerates PCIe devices
   (this is when BARs from Part 13 get assigned), picks a boot device.
3. Bootloader (GRUB, systemd-boot, Apple iBoot): loads the kernel and initramfs into memory.
4. Kernel start: sets up page tables (Part 12), interrupt handlers (Part 13), schedulers,
   and drivers, then starts PID 1.
5. Cloud twist: on EC2 or GCE most of this already happened on the host. Your VM or
   container starts at step 3 or 4 under a hypervisor — which is why cloud boot is seconds
   while bare-metal POST can take minutes.

flowchart LR
    ROM["BootROM: clocks, RAM, verify"] --> FW["UEFI/BIOS: train DRAM, enumerate PCIe"]
    FW --> BL["Bootloader: load kernel"]
    BL --> K["Kernel: page tables, IRQs, drivers"]
    K --> INIT["PID 1: userspace"]

Backend takeaway: every cold start, from Lambda init to Kubernetes pod scheduling, replays a slice of this chain. Knowing which stage is slow (firmware, bootloader, kernel, image pull, runtime init) tells you where to optimize instead of guessing.

$ dmesg | head -50                  # firmware + kernel boot log, with timestamps
$ systemd-analyze blame | head      # which userspace unit ate your boot time
$ lsusb && lspci -tv               # bus topology: what hangs off what
$ sudo dmidecode -t baseboard      # motherboard and chipset identity

docs.title: 16.4 Buses, Chipset, and Motherboard
docs.text:
Classic three buses: address (which device or cell), data (the bytes), control (read/write, clock, interrupts). Modern form: DDR channels to DRAM, PCIe lanes to NVMe/GPU/NIC, USB/SATA for peripherals, and on-chip fabrics (Infinity Fabric, Apple fabric, Intel mesh) between cores, caches, and memory controllers.

flowchart TD
    CPU["CPU package: cores, caches, memory controller"] <--> DRAM["DDR5 DIMMs"]
    CPU <--> PCIE["PCIe switch"]
    PCIE <--> NVME["NVMe SSD"]
    PCIE <--> NIC["NIC"]
    PCIE <--> GPUC["GPU"]
    CHIP["Chipset"] <--> USB["USB, SATA, audio, BIOS flash"]
    CPU <--> CHIP

The chipset is the slower I/O hub; the motherboard is power delivery, clocks, and these traces. When a device misbehaves, lspci, link-width checks, and reseating are the hardware equivalents of reading the stack trace.

Misconception: the CPU does all the work. On a modern machine the CPU programs accelerators and controllers, and DMA engines, GPUs, NICs, and SSD controllers move the bytes.

See Part 22 for the capstone drill on these questions.

docs.title: 16.5 Models and Boards Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text:
1. Von Neumann vs Harvard with an example of each? Von Neumann: one store for code and data — laptops, servers, phones at system level. Harvard: separate instruction and data memories — microcontrollers, DSPs, and the split L1 I/D cache inside every modern core (modified Harvard locally, von Neumann globally).
  2. Why does the split L1 exist if the system is von Neumann? Fetch-vs-data contention: the core fetches the next instruction every cycle while loading data. Separate L1s give both full bandwidth; self-modifying code and JITs must flush the I-cache because the two views can disagree.
  3. RISC vs CISC in one minute? RISC: few fixed-size instructions, load/store only touches memory. CISC: many variable-size instructions with memory operands. Both decode to RISC-like micro-ops today; difference is code density, decoder cost, extensions.
  4. What does the chipset do, and what is the motherboard? The chipset is the slower I/O hub (USB, SATA, audio, BIOS flash); the motherboard is power delivery, clocks, and the traces connecting CPU, DRAM, PCIe, and chipset. lspci link-width checks are the hardware equivalent of reading a stack trace.
  5. Walk a cold boot to first request. BootROM verifies, UEFI trains DRAM and enumerates PCIe (BAR assignment), bootloader loads the kernel, kernel sets up page tables and IRQs, PID 1 starts, image pulls, runtime inits, app binds its port. Profile each stage (dmesg, systemd-analyze) before optimizing.

docs.title: Part 17. Memory Models: From Barriers to volatile
docs.text: Part 9 named the rules; this part shows the mechanism. x86's Total Store Order hides most reorderings while ARM64's weaker model exposes them, and your language runtime inserts the barriers you never see.

docs.title: 17.1 What the Hardware Reorders, and How Languages Hide It
docs.text:
• x86-64 TSO: stores become visible in order, loads can pass older stores to different addresses. Dekker-style flag protocols mostly work by accident; you still need barriers for publication safety.
  • ARM64 / RISC-V: loads and stores to different addresses can both reorder. The compiler and the JVM/Go/C++ runtime emit dmb/fence instructions around volatile, atomics, mutexes, and channels.
  • The contract ladder: hardware guarantees little; the ISA adds acquire/release; the language memory model (Java JMM, Go memory model, C++11 atomics) promises what your code can rely on. Program to the language model, never to observed hardware behavior.
flowchart TD
    HW["Hardware: cores, store buffers, caches"] --> ISA["ISA ordering: TSO on x86, acquire-release on ARM"]
    ISA --> LANG["Language model: volatile, atomics, locks, channels"]
    LANG --> APP["Your code: publish once, share narrowly"]

docs.title: 17.2 Try It: Watch Reordering (or Its Absence)
docs.text:
// Compile for both ISAs and compare the barriers the compiler emits.
#include <stdatomic.h>
atomic_int flag = 0;
int data = 0;

void publish(void) { data = 42; atomic_store_explicit(&flag, 1, memory_order_release); }
int consume(void) {
    if (atomic_load_explicit(&flag, memory_order_acquire)) return data;
    return -1;
}

$ gcc -O2 -S mm.c -o mm.s && grep -E "mfence|dmb|sync" mm.s   # x86: often nothing extra
$ aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc -O2 -S mm.c -o mm_arm.s && grep -E "dmb|stl|lda" mm_arm.s  # ARM: barriers present

Same source, different fences: the runtime pays for ordering only where the ISA needs it.

docs.title: 17.3 Memory Model Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text:
1. Why does double-checked locking need volatile (or an atomic)? Without it the reference can publish before the object is constructed (reordered stores on weak models, compiler motion everywhere). Acquire/release on the flag makes construction happen-before use.
  2. TSO vs weak ordering in one minute? TSO (x86) keeps stores ordered; weak models (ARM) reorder both. Language runtimes insert barriers so volatile, atomics, locks, and channels behave the same everywhere.
  3. One hot atomic counter caps my service. Fix? MESI ping-pong on one line. Shard per core (or per thread), sum on read. Same pattern as Part 7's false-sharing rule, now at the language level.

docs.title: Part 18. Code Labs: Locality and Vectorization
docs.text:
Python will not show cycle-level truth (the interpreter hides vectorization and pinning), but it demonstrates the two effects interviewers ask you to reason about: sequential locality beats strided access, and batching vector work beats scalar loops. Both snippets use only the standard library plus NumPy, run anywhere, and print timings you can quote.

Row-major sequential scan versus strided column scan over the same matrix:

import time
import numpy as np

# 4000x4000 float64 matrix: 128 MB, spills out of any L3.
# C-order (row-major) means a[i, :] is contiguous, a[:, j] strided.
a = np.random.rand(4000, 4000)

def row_sum(m: np.ndarray) -> float:
    total = 0.0
    # Sequential: each 64-byte line serves 8 doubles before the next miss.
    for i in range(m.shape[0]):
        total += float(np.sum(m[i, :]))
    return total

def col_sum(m: np.ndarray) -> float:
    total = 0.0
    # Strided: each access touches a new line, wasting 7/8 of every fetch.
    for j in range(m.shape[1]):
        total += float(np.sum(m[:, j]))
    return total

for name, fn in (("row-major", row_sum), ("column-strided", col_sum)):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    fn(a)
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
    print(f"{name}: {elapsed:.2f}s")

This example allocates one large row-major matrix, then sums it both ways. The row pass streams contiguous lines and lets the hardware prefetcher run ahead, while the column pass jumps 32 KB per element and thrashes sets and TLB entries. Expect the strided version to run several times slower on identical FLOPs; that gap is pure memory hierarchy, and it is why columnar stores transpose data before scanning.

Scalar Python loop versus batched NumPy (SIMD-backed) over the same vector:

import time
import numpy as np

# One million floats: small enough for L3, large enough to matter.
x = np.random.rand(1_000_000)
y = np.random.rand(1_000_000)

def scalar_dot(xs: np.ndarray, ys: np.ndarray) -> float:
    total = 0.0
    # Pure-Python loop: one interpreter iteration per element, no vectorization.
    for i in range(len(xs)):
        total += float(xs[i]) * float(ys[i])
    return total

def vector_dot(xs: np.ndarray, ys: np.ndarray) -> float:
    # One call into a C kernel compiled with SIMD: 4-8 doubles per instruction.
    return float(np.dot(xs, ys))

# Warm up imports and caches, then time each path once.
vector_dot(x[:1000], y[:1000])
t0 = time.perf_counter(); scalar_dot(x, y); t1 = time.perf_counter()
vector_dot(x, y); t2 = time.perf_counter()
print(f"scalar loop: {(t1 - t0) * 1000:.1f}ms")
print(f"numpy dot:   {(t2 - t1) * 1000:.1f}ms")

This example contrasts interpreter overhead plus scalar execution against a single dispatched kernel that the BLAS and SIMD units chew through at bandwidth speed. Expect 50-500x difference. The lesson transfers to every runtime: batch work into contiguous kernels (NumPy, Arrow, Java Vector API, DB vectorized scans) instead of per-element callbacks, and keep the hot loop free of branches the vectorizer cannot prove safe.

docs.title: 18.2 Try It: Run the Locality Lab
docs.text:
import time
import numpy as np

a = np.random.rand(4000, 4000)  # 128 MB: spills out of any L3

def row_sum(m):
    return sum(float(np.sum(m[i, :])) for i in range(m.shape[0]))

def col_sum(m):
    return sum(float(np.sum(m[:, j])) for j in range(m.shape[1]))

for name, fn in (("row-major", row_sum), ("column-strided", col_sum)):
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); fn(a); t1 = time.perf_counter()
    print(f"{name}: {(t1 - t0):.2f}s")

Expect the strided version several times slower on identical FLOPs: pure memory hierarchy, and the reason columnar stores transpose before scanning.

docs.title: 18.3 Vectorization Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text:
1. Why is the NumPy dot 50-500x faster than the scalar loop? One dispatched C kernel running SIMD at bandwidth speed vs one interpreter iteration per element. Batch contiguous work into kernels (NumPy, Arrow, Java Vector API, DB vectorized scans).
  2. What stops auto-vectorization? Pointer hops, aliasing, data-dependent exits, unpredictable branches. Counted index loops over separate contiguous arrays vectorize; linked traversal never does.
  3. How do you verify instead of hoping? -fopt-info-vec (GCC), -Rpass=loop-vectorize (Clang), perf stat IPC lift on the hot loop.

docs.title: Part 19. Tools and Ecosystem
docs.text:
• Profilers: perf stat/record/report (cycles, IPC, cache-misses, branch-misses), perf top for live hotspots, async-profiler and JFR for JVM (CPU plus allocation flames), py-spy and cProfile for Python, pprof for Go, Instruments (Time Profiler, Allocations) on Apple Silicon. Always profile optimized builds; debug builds hide inlining.
  • Flame graphs and traces: Brendan Gregg flame graphs turn perf stacks into boxes you can read; perf sched and bpftrace expose run-queue latency and off-CPU time. If CPU is idle but latency is high, the answer is locks or I/O, not ALU.
  • Cache and topology inspection: lscpu, lstopo (hwloc), /sys/devices/system/cpu, numactl --hardware for NUMA layout; perf stat -d for L1/LLC miss rates; valgrind --tool=cachegrind for simulated miss attribution on small inputs.
  • Benchmarking discipline: hyperfine for CLI timing, JMH for Java, pytest-benchmark or timeit with repeats for Python, taskset plus nice to isolate cores. Pin frequency governors (performance), disable turbo during comparison only if you say so, warm up JITs and caches, and report medians with variance, never single runs.
  • Compilers and flags: -O2/-O3, -march=native, link-time optimization, and profile-guided optimization decide whether loops vectorize. Check with -fopt-info-vec (GCC) or -Rpass=loop-vectorize (Clang); on JVM inspect with -XX:+PrintCompilation and the Vector API instead of JNI for kernels.
  • Accelerator stacks: CUDA and cuDNN (NVIDIA GPU), ROCm (AMD), XLA and TPUs on GCP, Metal Performance Shaders and MLX on Apple Silicon, ONNX Runtime and TensorRT for portable inference. DPUs program via DOCA, P4, or eBPF offload SDKs.

  • Capacity planning: track IPC, MPKI, and context-switch rate per service, not just CPU percent. A service at 40 percent CPU with high MPKI is memory-bound and needs layout work; one at 90 percent with IPC near 2 is compute-bound and needs scale-out or vectorization.

  • Numbers and encoding: python3 -c for two's complement and struct layouts, Compiler Explorer for codegen, pahole for struct padding, utf8mb4 checks for MySQL text.

  • Memory and I/O path: numastat and numactl --hardware for locality, sar -B for major faults, iostat -x and nvme list for device queues, ethtool -S plus cat /proc/interrupts for NIC queue balance.
  • Disassembly and inspection: objdump -d, perf annotate, Compiler Explorer for ISA comparison.
  • Power and boot: cpupower frequency-info, dmesg thermal lines, systemd-analyze blame for cold-start attribution.

docs.title: 19.2 Try It: One Pass Over a Sick Server
docs.text:
$ uptime && free -h && iostat -x 1 3        # load, memory, device pressure
$ perf stat -d -p $PID sleep 5              # IPC + MPKI + TLB in one shot
$ sudo perf record -g -p $PID sleep 10 && sudo perf report --no-children  # who burns cycles
$ strace -c -p $PID                         # syscall profile: locks vs tiny I/O
$ dmesg | tail -20                           # OOM kills, thermal events, link errors

Five commands separate compute-bound (scale out) from memory-bound (fix layout), from lock-bound (fix sharing), from I/O-bound (fix the path) — in that order.

docs.title: 19.3 Tools Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text:
1. Which one command separates compute-bound from memory-bound? perf stat -d: high IPC means compute-bound, high MPKI means memory-bound. Fix layout before scaling out.
  2. Flame graph shows wide flat boxes under one frame setup — what is it? Allocation or frame-construction overhead (see Part 4.9's stack-frame discussion): copying, boxing, or oversized frames. Reduce churn, reuse buffers, shrink hot state.
  3. What do Width x1 and Gen1 speed in lspci tell you? Negotiated below capability: bad slot, bifurcation, or power saving. Fix the plumbing before blaming NAND, drivers, or the app.

docs.title: 20.1 Building an Adder from Gates
docs.text: Goal: 1 + 1 with a half adder. Inputs A=1, B=1. XOR gives Sum = 0. AND gives Carry = 1. Read as binary 10 = 2. Correct. Chain four full adders for a nibble, eight for a byte, 64 for a register.

docs.title: 20.2 Building a 1-Bit ALU Slice
docs.text: Inputs A, B, Op. Compute AND, OR, and ADD in parallel with gates and a full adder, then select with a mux. Op=10, A=1, B=1, Cin=0: AND=1, OR=1, ADD sum=0 carry=1. Mux picks sum 0, carry-out 1. Tile 64 slices with carries chained and you have the integer heart of a CPU core.

docs.title: 20.3 How Registers and RAM Hold Bits
docs.text: Loading 1011 into a 4-bit register: present the bits on D inputs, raise write-enable, clock edge captures all four flip-flops at once (Part 3.8). Until the next enabled edge they hold. RAM is the same idea at scale: decode the address to one row, sense or drive the columns, write back and refresh on DRAM (Part 14.2).

docs.title: 20.4 How HDDs and SSDs Store Bits
docs.text: HDD write of 10: firmware maps the LBA, seeks the arm, waits for rotation, and magnetizes two grain regions north-up then south-up as they pass under the head (Part 14.5, CMR vs SMR). Read: sense the transitions, fix bits with ECC. SSD write of 10: the FTL picks an erased page, programs charge levels into two NAND cells, marks the old page invalid (Part 14.6). Read: apply reference voltages and correct with LDPC. Erase clears whole blocks for reuse. One spins rust, the other traps electrons; both present the same block interface to the OS.

docs.title: 20.5 How a CPU Executes LOAD x1, [0x1000]
docs.text: Fetch the instruction bytes at PC. Decode: opcode LOAD, dest x1, address 0x1000. Execute: MMU translates 0x1000 (TLB hit or page walk), L1D checked, then L2, L3, DRAM on miss. Data returns up the hierarchy and lands in x1. PC advances. A cache hit costs ~1 ns; a DRAM trip ~80 ns; a major page fault milliseconds.

docs.title: 20.6 Data Journey: CPU to Disk and Back
docs.text: A Postgres SELECT: NIC DMAs packets to RAM over PCIe (lane width and NUMA affinity from Part 13), CPU parses the query, buffer pool checked (DRAM row-buffer hit or NVMe submission queue read (Part 13.3)), pages land in L3/L2/L1 as scanned, results formatted in registers, socket buffers DMA back to the NIC. Every layer caches the one below; sizing each layer is capacity planning.

docs.title: Part 21. Cheat Sheet and Misconceptions
docs.text:
• Deleting is not erasing; formatting is not destruction. Bytes persist until overwritten.
  • More GHz is not faster; more cores do not speed single requests. IPC, locality, and sharing dominate.
  • 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 in floats; money goes in cents or decimals with explicit scale.
  • RAID is not backup; flushing is not durability without fsync and power-loss protection.
  • Registers and RAM forget on power loss; only flash and disk persist.
  • 1 char is not 1 byte in UTF-8; VARCHAR(10) counts characters, and MySQL utf8 rejects emoji.
  • A cache miss costs ~100x an L1 hit, a context switch ~10,000x, a disk read ~100,000x.
  • Little-endian stores the small end first; network order is big-endian.
  • Turbos are borrowing, not income; size capacity at sustained all-core clocks.
  • Width x1 for an x4 drive is a plumbing fault, not a NAND fault.

Must-know one-liners: two's complement negate is flip-plus-one. NAND is universal. Sum is triple-XOR, carry is majority. SRAM is caches, DRAM is memory. TLC is 3 bits per cell. NVMe wins on queues, not just NAND. DMA moves data while the CPU does other work. MESI ping-pong is why you shard hot counters. Huge pages cut TLB pressure 512x.

docs.title: Part 22. Final Interview Drill
docs.text:
Ask each aloud, answer in under two minutes, then check the part cited. Fifteen confident answers means the guide did its job.

  1. Convert 0xD3 to binary and decimal, and give -1 in 8-bit two's complement. (Part 1) 11010011 = 211; -1 is 11111111 (flip-plus-one wraps to zero).
  2. Build OR from NAND only. (Part 2) NOT from NAND by tying inputs; A OR B = (A' NAND B'). Universality in one gate.
  3. Add 13 + 9 in binary and name the flags. (Parts 1, 4) 1101 + 1001 = 10110 (22). Zero = 0, Carry = 0, Overflow = 0; 127 + 1 in int8 would set Overflow.
  4. Full adder from two half adders? (Part 3) HA1 adds A and B; HA2 adds that sum and Cin; Cout is either carry ORed together.
  5. Latch vs flip-flop, and what is metastability? (Part 3) Level-sensitive vs edge-triggered; sampling too close to the edge hovers. Two-flop synchronizers on every clock-domain crossing.
  6. Walk fetch-decode-execute for ADD x2, x0, x1. (Part 4) Fetch at PC, decode opcode and registers, ALU adds, write back x2, PC advances. Modern cores do it pipelined, superscalar, out-of-order, speculative.
  7. RISC vs CISC in one minute, with a Graviton recommendation. (Parts 5, 16) Fixed vs variable, load/store vs memory operands, both micro-op based today. Trial one stateless tier; runtimes abstract the ISA, native deps do not.
  8. GPU, TPU, DPU, QPU: place each workload. (Part 6) GPU for batched parallel math, TPU for dense GCP matmul at scale, DPU for infra offload, QPU for research only. CPUs win at batch 1.
  9. Explain L1/L2/L3 and fix a high-CPU low-IPC service. (Parts 7, 9) 1 ns / 5 ns / 15-40 ns / 80 ns / 50 us ladder; 64-byte lines; three Cs; MESI; perf stat -d, fix layout and sharing before scaling out.
  10. Size a thread pool for CPU-bound vs I/O-bound work. (Part 8) Cores for CPU-bound (discount SMT), Little's Law concurrency for I/O-bound, one event loop per core. Amdahl caps the rest.
  11. Spectre vs Meltdown, and the cost we still pay. (Part 10) Meltdown: faulty loads read kernel memory, fixed by KPTI. Spectre: victim speculation leaks, fixed by retpolines, microcode, bounds clipping. Syscalls and indirect calls cost more forever.
  12. Minor vs major page fault, and when huge pages help. (Part 12) Minor maps in-memory pages in microseconds; major sleeps for disk. 2 MB pages shrink tables 512x for multi-GB heaps; verify with perf stat dTLB rates.
  13. Walk an NVMe read, and explain a Width x1 link. (Parts 13, 14) Doorbell, DMA to RAM, completion plus MSI-X, batched reaping. x1 on an x4 drive is slot, bifurcation, or power saving — fix plumbing first.
  14. Why is random HDD I/O 100x slower, and RAID 5 vs 10 for a database? (Part 14) Seek plus rotation per random read; CMR for rewrites. RAID 10 for random I/O and rebuilds; RAID 5 for cheap bulk. Neither is a backup.
  15. UTF-8 é, IEEE 754 13.25, and little-endian 0x12345678. (Part 15) C3 A9; sign 0, exponent 1026, mantissa 101010...; bytes 78 56 34 12 at increasing addresses. Money in cents, utf8mb4 for text, htons at boundaries.
