Interview Questions: - What triggers a WiredTiger checkpoint by default? — A checkpoint is triggered by default every 60 seconds or after 2GB of journal data has accumulated, whichever comes first. - How do checkpoints relate to crash recovery time? — Checkpoints bound crash recovery time by limiting how much journal data must be replayed on restart, since recovery only needs to reapply operations recorded after the most recent checkpoint. - Why might a filesystem snapshot backup want to be taken right after a checkpoint? — Taking a snapshot right after a checkpoint captures the data files in the most recently known consistent, fully-flushed state, minimizing the amount of journal replay needed to make the backup usable.

docs.title: Cache Management
docs.text:
WiredTiger maintains an in-memory cache (default: 50% of (RAM - 1GB), or 256MB, whichever is greater) that holds frequently accessed, uncompressed data and indexes for fast access. When the working set exceeds the cache size, WiredTiger must evict pages to disk, which increases I/O and can degrade performance; monitoring cache utilization and eviction rates is a key part of MongoDB performance tuning.

// Check current WiredTiger cache statistics
db.serverStatus().wiredTiger.cache

Advantages: - Keeps hot data in memory for low-latency access - Configurable size lets operators tune for available hardware

Disadvantages: - Undersized cache relative to working set causes excessive eviction and disk I/O - Oversized cache can starve the OS file system cache and other processes on the same host

Interview Questions: - What is the default WiredTiger cache size formula? — By default, WiredTiger's cache size is 50% of (total RAM minus 1GB), or 256MB, whichever is greater. - What happens when the working set doesn't fit in the WiredTiger cache? — WiredTiger must evict pages from cache to make room for new data, increasing disk I/O and degrading performance since frequently accessed data may need to be re-read from disk. - Which serverStatus metrics would you check to diagnose cache pressure? — Check wiredTiger.cache metrics such as "bytes currently in the cache", "tracked dirty bytes in the cache", and eviction-related counters like "pages evicted by application threads" to diagnose cache pressure.

Real-life scenario: Writes stall every hour when checkpoints flush a flood of dirty pages; splitting the bulk load into smaller batches with pauses lets eviction keep up — the engine needs steady pacing, not tidal waves.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
1. WiredTiger = LSM-ish write path (skip-list memtable → SSTable-like files) + B-tree-ish reads with MVCC snapshots.
  2. Cache defaults to 50% of (RAM − 1 GB); dirty-page pressure stalls writers — monitor eviction counters.
  3. Checkpoints + journal give crash recovery; compression (snappy/zstd) trades CPU for I/O per collection.
  4. Size cache for the working set and pace bulk writes — the engine rewards steady flow.

docs.title: Single Document Atomicity
docs.text:
MongoDB guarantees that all changes within a single document — including nested arrays and subdocuments — are applied atomically, even across multiple fields. This built-in atomicity is why well-designed document models (embedding related data in one document) often avoid the need for multi-document transactions entirely.

db.accounts.updateOne(
  { _id: "acc1" },
  { $inc: { balance: -100 }, $push: { history: { type: "DEBIT", amount: 100 } } }
);

Interview Questions: - Why is single-document atomicity considered a core design principle in MongoDB's data modeling philosophy? — Because MongoDB guarantees atomic changes across all fields, arrays, and subdocuments within a single document, schema designs that embed related data into one document can rely on this built-in atomicity for consistency, reducing the need for more expensive multi-document transactions. - How can embedding data to leverage single-document atomicity reduce the need for multi-document transactions? — By co-locating related data that must change together (e.g., an account balance and its transaction history) within one document, a single atomic update operation can satisfy consistency requirements that would otherwise require wrapping multiple documents in a transaction.

docs.title: Multi-Document Transactions
docs.text:
Multi-document transactions (available since MongoDB 4.0 for replica sets, and 4.2 for sharded clusters) allow multiple read/write operations across multiple documents, collections, or even databases to be grouped into a single all-or-nothing unit, with snapshot isolation. They're used when operations spanning several documents must all succeed or all fail together, such as transferring funds between two account documents.

const session = client.startSession();
try {
  session.startTransaction();
  accounts.updateOne({ _id: "acc1" }, { $inc: { balance: -100 } }, { session });
  accounts.updateOne({ _id: "acc2" }, { $inc: { balance: 100 } }, { session });
  session.commitTransaction();
} catch (e) {
  session.abortTransaction();
  throw e;
} finally {
  session.endSession();
}

@Transactional
public void transferFunds(String fromId, String toId, BigDecimal amount) {
    mongoTemplate.updateFirst(query(where("_id").is(fromId)),
        new Update().inc("balance", amount.negate()), Account.class);
    mongoTemplate.updateFirst(query(where("_id").is(toId)),
        new Update().inc("balance", amount), Account.class);
}

Advantages: - Guarantees atomicity/consistency across multiple documents and collections - Simplifies application logic for genuinely multi-document invariants

Disadvantages: - Higher latency and resource cost than single-document operations - Long-running transactions can hold locks/snapshots and impact throughput

Interview Questions: - When would you reach for a multi-document transaction instead of relying on document embedding? — Use a multi-document transaction when an operation must atomically update multiple separate documents, collections, or databases that cannot reasonably be embedded together, such as transferring funds between two independent account documents. - What is snapshot isolation, and how does it apply to MongoDB transactions? — Snapshot isolation means a transaction sees a consistent point-in-time view of the data for its entire duration, unaffected by concurrent writes from other transactions, and its own writes aren't visible to others until it commits. - How would you implement a multi-document transaction using Spring Data MongoDB's @Transactional? — Annotate a service method with @Transactional, ensure a MongoTransactionManager bean is configured, and perform multiple repository/template operations inside that method; Spring Data automatically starts, commits, or rolls back the underlying MongoDB session transaction around the method boundary.

docs.title: ACID Properties
docs.text:
MongoDB transactions provide the classic ACID guarantees: Atomicity (all operations in the transaction succeed or none do), Consistency (the database moves from one valid state to another), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't see each other's uncommitted changes, via snapshot isolation), and Durability (committed changes survive failures, backed by the write-ahead journal and replication).

Interview Questions: - How does MongoDB implement isolation for concurrent transactions? — MongoDB implements isolation through snapshot isolation, giving each transaction a consistent view of data as of its start time and hiding uncommitted changes from other concurrent transactions until commit. - How does write concern relate to the durability guarantee of a committed transaction? — The write concern (e.g., majority) used when committing a transaction determines how many replica set members must acknowledge the write before it's considered durable, directly controlling the strength of the durability guarantee. - Can you explain atomicity in the context of a MongoDB multi-document transaction with an example? — In a funds transfer transaction that debits one account and credits another, atomicity guarantees that either both updates succeed and are committed together, or if either fails, both are rolled back, so the system never ends up with money debited from one account without being credited to the other.

docs.title: Transaction Lifecycle
docs.text:
A transaction moves through a defined lifecycle: start a client session, start the transaction, execute one or more operations against that session, then either commit (making all changes visible/durable) or abort (rolling back all changes). Retryable logic is often layered on top to handle transient errors like TransientTransactionError.

sequenceDiagram
    participant App
    participant Session
    participant MongoDB
    App->>Session: startSession()
    App->>Session: startTransaction()
    App->>MongoDB: op1 (with session)
    App->>MongoDB: op2 (with session)
    alt success
        App->>Session: commitTransaction()
        Session->>MongoDB: apply changes durably
    else error
        App->>Session: abortTransaction()
        Session->>MongoDB: discard changes
    end

Interview Questions: - What are the distinct phases of a MongoDB transaction's lifecycle? — A transaction starts a client session, starts the transaction itself, executes one or more operations scoped to that session, and finally either commits (making changes durable and visible) or aborts (discarding all changes). - What kinds of errors should trigger a transaction retry versus an abort? — Errors labeled TransientTransactionError (e.g., transient network issues or replica set elections) should trigger a retry of the whole transaction, while non-transient errors like application-level validation failures should trigger an abort without retrying. - Why is a client session required before starting a transaction? — A client session provides the context (including the transaction number and causal consistency guarantees) that MongoDB uses to associate a sequence of operations with a single transaction and to support retryable writes.

docs.title: Transaction Limitations
docs.text:
MongoDB transactions have practical constraints: a default 60-second maximum runtime, restrictions on certain DDL operations (e.g., creating collections/indexes inside a transaction, though this improved in later versions), increased oplog/cache pressure for large transactions, and a general recommendation to keep transactions short and touch a limited number of documents.

Disadvantages: - Not designed for bulk/batch operations touching very large numbers of documents - Can increase contention and WiredTiger cache pressure if overused

Interview Questions: - What is the default time limit for a MongoDB transaction, and what happens if it's exceeded? — MongoDB transactions default to a 60-second maximum runtime; if exceeded, the transaction is automatically aborted and any changes made within it are rolled back. - Why are multi-document transactions discouraged for large bulk-update workloads? — Large transactions touching many documents increase oplog size, WiredTiger cache pressure, and contention/lock hold time, risking timeouts and degraded throughput, so bulk updates are generally better handled with bulkWrite() outside a transaction. - What operations were historically restricted from running inside a transaction? — Certain DDL-like operations, such as creating collections or indexes, were historically restricted from running inside a transaction, though later MongoDB versions relaxed some of these restrictions.

docs.title: Retryable Writes
docs.text:
Retryable writes automatically retry a single write operation (insert, update, delete, findAndModify) once if it fails due to a transient network error or replica set election, using a unique transaction number to ensure the operation isn't applied twice. This is enabled by default in modern drivers and improves resilience during failovers without requiring application-level retry logic for simple writes.

// Enabled by default via connection string option
mongodb://host1,host2,host3/?retryWrites=true

Differences:

Aspect Retryable Writes Multi-Document Transactions Scope Single write operation Multiple operations/documents Purpose Resilience against transient failures Atomicity across multiple operations Overhead Low Higher (snapshot, locks)

Interview Questions: - How does MongoDB avoid applying a retried write twice? — Retryable writes are tagged with a unique transaction number per session, which the server uses to detect and deduplicate a retried attempt, ensuring the operation's effect is applied only once even if the client resends it. - What kinds of failures trigger a retryable write to automatically retry? — Transient failures such as network errors or a replica set election (temporary loss of a Primary) trigger an automatic retry of the write by the driver. - How do retryable writes differ from multi-document transactions in purpose and scope? — Retryable writes provide resilience for a single write operation against transient failures with low overhead, while multi-document transactions provide atomicity across multiple operations/documents at a higher performance cost.

Real-life scenario: A booking flow reserves a seat + charges + writes an audit record inside one transaction with TransientTransactionError retry — a crash between steps rolls back cleanly instead of charging for an unreserved seat.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
1. Single-document writes are atomic by default; multi-document transactions add cross-document atomicity at a latency cost (and require replica sets+).
  2. Always retry TransientTransactionError whole-transaction; dedupe retried writes via session transaction numbers.
  3. Keep transactions short with snapshot reads — long ones abort on WriteConflict and hurt throughput.
  4. Prefer embedded documents (single-write atomicity) over transactions; use transactions only where document boundaries truly split.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Update operations modify existing documents in a MongoDB collection. Unlike SQL UPDATE which directly sets column values, MongoDB uses update operators ($set, $inc, $push, etc.) to precisely control what changes.

Update Operation Flow:

  db.collection.updateOne(filter, update, options)
       │              │         │         │
       │              │         │         └── {upsert, writeConcern, arrayFilters}
       │              │         └──────────── {$set: {...}, $inc: {...}, ...}
       │              └────────────────────── Which document(s) to match
       ↓
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 1. Find matching document(s)         │
  │ 2. Apply update operators            │
  │ 3. Validate constraints/schema       │
  │ 4. Write changes (atomic per doc)    │
  │ 5. Update indexes if needed          │
  │ 6. Return {matchedCount, modifiedCount}│
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

Update Methods:

Method Behavior updateOne() Updates the first document matching the filter updateMany() Updates all documents matching the filter replaceOne() Replaces the entire document body (except _id) findOneAndUpdate() Updates one document and returns it (before or after)

Key distinction: updateOne/Many uses operators to modify specific fields. replaceOne replaces the whole document — if you forget a field, it's gone.

In the Users db Info collection all the documents in the following type

{
  "_id": {
    "$oid": "62ac4ff719cc703713ba43c0"
  },
  "name": "Max",
  "hobbies": [
    {
      "title": "Sports",
      "frequency": 3
    },
    {
      "title": "Cooking",
      "frequency": 6
    }
  ],
  "phone": 131782734
}
But the object with name chris has the different type of hobbies array

So, we need to update the hobbies. We have two methods for update any object updateOne and updateMany. The names are self-explanatory.

The update method takes two mandatory input one is filter for search and what to update.

$set keyword is used to set the change the field value. Other fields will be untouched.

> db.infos.updateOne(
    {"name" : "Chris"},
    { $set: 
        {"hobbies": [
            {title:"Sports",frequency:5},
            {title:"Cooking",frequency:3},
            {title:"Hiking",frequency:1}
        ]}
    }
)
{ "acknowledged" : true, "matchedCount" : 1, "modifiedCount" : 1 } 

## If I again run the same query then the modifiedCount will be 0
{ "acknowledged" : true, "matchedCount" : 1, "modifiedCount" : 0 }

We can update multiple documents at the same time 

> db.infos.updateMany(
    {"hobbies.title": "Sports"},
    {$set: {isSporty: true}}
)
{ "acknowledged" : true, "matchedCount" : 3, "modifiedCount" : 3 }
With $set operator we can change more than one field at a time as well.

We also have incrementor or decrement operator as these two are very common operation. 

> db.infos.updateOne(
    {name: "Manuel"}, 
    { $inc : { age : 1 }}
)
{ "acknowledged" : true, "matchedCount" : 1, "modifiedCount" : 1 }

With $inc we can also decrement. 

> db.infos.updateOne(
    { name: "Manuel" } , 
    { 
        $inc : { age :  -1 } , 
        $set : { isSporty : false }
    }
)
{ "acknowledged" : true, "matchedCount" : 1, "modifiedCount" : 1 }
We can operate on different field on the same time, but we cannot set age and increment age at the same time.

We have other 3 operators like $inc. those are $min, $max, $mul.

The field age will be updated as the max value between what we have passed and what is the previous value. If the previous value is 20 then the new value of age will be 31 but if its already 35 then the value will not be changed. 

db.infos.updateOne(
    { name : "Manual" },
    { $max :{ age : 31 }}
)

$min and $max is quite similar operation just that one is taking minimum value and another is taking maximum value. The $mul operator will multiply the field with the value that we have passed. If the previous value of age is 30 then the new value will be 30*1.1 = 33 

db.infos.updateOne(
    { name : "Manual" },
    { $mul :{ age : 1.1 }}
)

We can also drop any field with $unset operator. With this command we can remove the phone field. The value of phone here will be ignored. We can assign any value. 

db.infos.updateOne(
    { name : "Manuel" },
    { $unset :{ phone : "" }}
)

We also can rename the field using the $rename operator. The field age will now be converted to totalAge 

db.infos.updateMany(
    {},
    { $rename :{ age : "totalAge" }}
)

{ "acknowledged" : true, "matchedCount" : 4, "modifiedCount" : 2 }

We can do update and insert operation at the same time, and it is called upsert. Suppose we don’t know we have a document with name as Abhishek or not and we also want to change its value if it is there. So, we can use upsert here. So, to use upsert we must pass the upsert value in the last parameter. By default, its value is true. 

> db.infos.updateOne(
    { name : "Abhishek" }, 
    { $set : 
        { 
            "hobbies": [
            { "title": "Sports", "frequency": 3 },
            { "title": "Cooking", "frequency": 6 }], 
            "phone": 131782734, 
            "isSporty": true 
        }
    } , 
    { upsert : true }
)


{
        "acknowledged" : true,
        "matchedCount" : 0,
        "modifiedCount" : 0,
        "upsertedId" : ObjectId("62da1c2f60336bad54ef7227")
}
MongoDB is smart enough to determine that if we are querying with equality operator then the name value must be there. So, in the new object name, hobbies, phone, isSporty all these values will be present.

Array update operations:

Suppose we have to find the documents where hobbies array has title value of Sports and frequency value greater than 3. Then the query will be like. 

db.infos.find({ 
    hobbies : { 
        $elemMatch : { 
            title : "Sports" , 
            "frequency" : { $gte : 3}
            }
        }
    }
)
{ 
    "_id" : ObjectId("62ac4ff719cc703713ba43be"), 
    "name" : "Chris", 
    "hobbies" : [ 
        { "title" : "Sports", "frequency" : 5 }, 
        { "title" : "Cooking", "frequency" : 3 }, 
        { "title" : "Hiking", "frequency" : 1 } 
    ], 
    "isSporty" : true 
}
{ 
    "_id" : ObjectId("62ac4ff719cc703713ba43c0"), 
    "name" : "Max", 
    "hobbies" : [ 
        { "title" : "Sports", "frequency" : 3 }, 
        { "title" : "Cooking", "frequency" : 6 } 
    ], 
    "phone" : 131782734,
    "isSporty" : true 
}
{ 
    "_id" : ObjectId("62da1c2f60336bad54ef7227"), 
    "name" : "Abhishek", 
    "hobbies" : [ 
        { "title" : "Sports", "frequency" : 3 }, 
        { "title" : "Cooking", "frequency" : 6 } 
    ],
    "isSporty" : true, 
    "phone" : 131782734 
}

Suppose we want to update the inner array document that we have found and highlighted above. 

> db.infos.updateMany({ 
    hobbies : {
        $elemMatch : { 
            title : "Sports" , 
            "frequency" : { $gte : 3}
        }
    }}, 
    { $set : { 
        "hobbies.$.highFrequency" : true 
    }}
)
{ "acknowledged" : true, "matchedCount" : 3, "modifiedCount" : 3 }
This $ represents the same element. Here we are adding new field that is why we are using "hobbies.$.highFrequency" but if we want to override that document then we can simply do this "hobbies.$" : {"title" : "Sports", "frequency" : 5}

Suppose we want to update all the documents of the array. So, we can use $[] operator it means all the array documents. goodHobby field added for all the inner array documents. 

> db.infos.updateMany({ 
    hobbies : { 
        $elemMatch : { title : "Sports" , "frequency" : { $gte : 3}}
    }}, 
    { $set : { "hobbies.$[].goodHobby" : true }}
)
{ "acknowledged" : true, "matchedCount" : 3, "modifiedCount" : 3 }
> db.infos.find({ 
        hobbies : { 
            $elemMatch : { title : "Sports" , "frequency" : { $gte : 3}}
        }}
    ).pretty()
{
        "_id" : ObjectId("62ac4ff719cc703713ba43be"),
        "name" : "Chris",
        "hobbies" : [
                {
                        "title" : "Sports",
                        "frequency" : 5,
                        "highFrequency" : true,
                        "goodHobby" : true
                },
                {
                        "title" : "Cooking",
                        "frequency" : 3,
                        "goodHobby" : true
                },
                {
                        "title" : "Hiking",
                        "frequency" : 1,
                        "goodHobby" : true
                }
        ],
        "isSporty" : true
}

Let's say if we have a criterion to upadate only some certain documents then we can $[ el ] and later we will define the el condition in the thir parameter arrayFilers part. In array filter we can pass as many conditions as we want. 

> db.infos.updateOne(
    { name: "Abhishek"}, 
    { $set : { "hobbies.$[el].goodFrequency" : true}} , 
    { arrayFilters : [{ "el.frequency" :{ $gte : 3}} ]} 
)
{ "acknowledged" : true, "matchedCount" : 1, "modifiedCount" : 1 }

> db.infos.find({name:"Abhishek"})
{ 
    "_id" : ObjectId("62da1c2f60336bad54ef7227"), 
    "name" : "Abhishek", 
    "hobbies" : [ 
        { "title" : "Sports", "frequency" : 3, "highFrequency" : true, "goodHobby" : true, "goodFrequency" : true }, 
        { "title" : "Cooking", "frequency" : 6, "goodHobby" : true, "goodFrequency" : true } 
    ], 
    "isSporty" : true, 
    "phone" : 131782734 
}

We can also add new element in our array. With $push we can add new element to the existing array. 

> db.infos.updateOne(
    { name: "Abhishek"}, 
    { $push : 
        { hobbies : { title: "Hiking" , frequency : 1}}
    } 
)
{ "acknowledged" : true, "matchedCount" : 1, "modifiedCount" : 1 }

> db.infos.find({name:"Abhishek"})
{ 
    "_id" : ObjectId("62da1c2f60336bad54ef7227"), 
    "name" : "Abhishek", 
    "hobbies" : [ 
        { "title" : "Sports", "frequency" : 3, "highFrequency" : true, "goodHobby" : true, "goodFrequency" : true }, 
        { "title" : "Cooking", "frequency" : 6, "goodHobby" : true, "goodFrequency" : true }, 
        { "title" : "Hiking", "frequency" : 1 } 
    ], 
    "isSporty" : true, 
    "phone" : 131782734 
}

We can also add more than one documents with $each operator. 

> db.infos.updateOne(
    { name: "Abhishek"}, 
    { $push : { 
        hobbies : { 
            $each : [
                { title: "Hiking" , frequency : 1},
                { title : "wine", frequecy: 1}
            ]
        }}
    }
)
{ "acknowledged" : true, "matchedCount" : 1, "modifiedCount" : 1 }

> db.infos.find({name:"Abhishek"})
{ 
    "_id" : ObjectId("62da1c2f60336bad54ef7227"), 
    "name" : "Abhishek", 
    "hobbies" : [ 
        { "title" : "Sports", "frequency" : 3, "highFrequency" : true, "goodHobby" : true, "goodFrequency" : true }, 
        { "title" : "Cooking", "frequency" : 6, "goodHobby" : true, "goodFrequency" : true }, 
        { "title" : "Hiking", "frequency" : 1 }, 
        { "title" : "Hiking", "frequency" : 1 }, 
        { "title" : "wine", "frequecy" : 1 } 
    ], 
    "isSporty" : true, 
    "phone" : 131782734 
}
We can also add sort or slice operator to add the element in sorted order or we can also take only one element.

But there is issue with $push operator. If the values are already existing, then also it will add the value. We can use $addToSet operator for to add unique element in the array. 

> db.infos.updateOne(
    { name: "Abhishek"}, 
    { $addToSet : { 
        hobbies : { 
            $each : [
                { title: "Hiking" , frequency : 1},
                {title : "wine", frequecy: 1}
            ]
        }}
    }
)
{ "acknowledged" : true, "matchedCount" : 1, "modifiedCount" : 0 }

> db.infos.find({name:"Abhishek"})
{ 
    "_id" : ObjectId("62da1c2f60336bad54ef7227"), 
    "name" : "Abhishek", 
    "hobbies" : [ 
        { "title" : "Sports", "frequency" : 3, "highFrequency" : true, "goodHobby" : true, "goodFrequency" : true }, 
        { "title" : "Cooking", "frequency" : 6, "goodHobby" : true, "goodFrequency" : true }, 
        { "title" : "Hiking", "frequency" : 1 }, 
        { "title" : "Hiking", "frequency" : 1 }, 
        { "title" : "wine", "frequecy" : 1 } 
    ], 
    "isSporty" : true, 
    "phone" : 131782734 
}

We can also pull the element from an array with $pull operator. 

> db.infos.updateOne(
        { name: "Abhishek"},
        { $pull : { hobbies : { title : "Hiking" }}}
    )
{ "acknowledged" : true, "matchedCount" : 1, "modifiedCount" : 1 }

> db.infos.find({name:"Abhishek"})
{ 
    "_id" : ObjectId("62da1c2f60336bad54ef7227"), 
    "name" : "Abhishek", 
    "hobbies" : [ 
        { "title" : "Sports", "frequency" : 3, "highFrequency" : true, "goodHobby" : true, "goodFrequency" : true }, 
        { "title" : "Cooking", "frequency" : 6, "goodHobby" : true, "goodFrequency" : true }, 
        { "title" : "wine", "frequecy" : 1 } 
    ], 
    "isSporty" : true, 
    "phone" : 131782734 
}
{ $pull : { hobbies : { title : "Hiking" }}} it means pull from the hobbies array where title is Hiking. We can also add other queries.

If we want to remove the last element from the array, then we can use $pop operator with value of 1 and if we want to remove the first element then we can assign the value with -1. 

> db.infos.find({name:"Abhishek"})
{ 
    "_id" : ObjectId("62da1c2f60336bad54ef7227"), 
    "name" : "Abhishek", 
    "hobbies" : [ 
        { "title" : "Sports", "frequency" : 3, "highFrequency" : true, "goodHobby" : true, "goodFrequency" : true }, 
        { "title" : "Cooking", "frequency" : 6, "goodHobby" : true, "goodFrequency" : true }, 
        { "title" : "wine", "frequecy" : 1 } 
    ], 
    "isSporty" : true, 
    "phone" : 131782734 
}

> db.infos.updateOne(
        { name: "Abhishek"}, 
        { $pop : { hobbies : 1}}
    )
{ "acknowledged" : true, "matchedCount" : 1, "modifiedCount" : 1 }

> db.infos.find({name:"Abhishek"})
{ 
    "_id" : ObjectId("62da1c2f60336bad54ef7227"), 
    "name" : "Abhishek", 
    "hobbies" : [ 
        { "title" : "Sports", "frequency" : 3, "highFrequency" : true, "goodHobby" : true, "goodFrequency" : true }, 
        { "title" : "Cooking", "frequency" : 6, "goodHobby" : true, "goodFrequency" : true } 
    ], 
    "isSporty" : true, 
    "phone" : 131782734 
}

> db.infos.updateOne(
        { name: "Abhishek"}, 
        { $pop : { hobbies : -1}}
    )
{ "acknowledged" : true, "matchedCount" : 1, "modifiedCount" : 1 }

> db.infos.find({name:"Abhishek"})
{ 
    "_id" : ObjectId("62da1c2f60336bad54ef7227"), 
    "name" : "Abhishek", 
    "hobbies" : [ 
        { "title" : "Cooking", "frequency" : 6, "goodHobby" : true, "goodFrequency" : true } 
    ], 
    "isSporty" : true, 
    "phone" : 131782734 
}

docs.title: Basic Updates
docs.text:
Intent: These are the most common field-level update operations — set values, remove fields, rename, increment counters, and track timestamps.

db.coll.updateOne({"_id": 1}, {$set: {"year": 2016, name: "Max"}})
db.coll.updateOne({"_id": 1}, {$unset: {"year": 1}})
db.coll.updateOne({"_id": 1}, {$rename: {"year": "date"} })
db.coll.updateOne({"_id": 1}, {$inc: {"year": 5}})
db.coll.updateOne({"_id": 1}, {$mul: {price: NumberDecimal("1.25"), qty: 2}})
db.coll.updateOne({"_id": 1}, {$min: {"imdb": 5}})
db.coll.updateOne({"_id": 1}, {$max: {"imdb": 8}})
db.coll.updateOne({"_id": 1}, {$currentDate: {"lastModified": true}})
db.coll.updateOne({"_id": 1}, {$currentDate: {"lastModified": {$type: "timestamp"}}})

docs.title: Array Updates
docs.text:
Intent: These operators modify array fields — add elements, remove elements, update specific elements by position or condition.

db.coll.updateOne({"_id": 1}, {$push :{"array": 1}})
db.coll.updateOne({"_id": 1}, {$pull :{"array": 1}})
db.coll.updateOne({"_id": 1}, {$addToSet :{"array": 2}})
db.coll.updateOne({"_id": 1}, {$pop: {"array": 1}})  // last element
db.coll.updateOne({"_id": 1}, {$pop: {"array": -1}}) // first element
db.coll.updateOne({"_id": 1}, {$pullAll: {"array" :[3, 4, 5]}})
db.coll.updateOne({"_id": 1}, {$push: {"scores": {$each: [90, 92]}}})
db.coll.updateOne({"_id": 2}, {$push: {"scores": {$each: [40, 60], $sort: 1}}}) // array sorted
db.coll.updateOne({"_id": 1, "grades": 80}, {$set: {"grades.$": 82}})
db.coll.updateMany({}, {$inc: {"grades.$[]": 10}})
db.coll.updateMany({}, {$set: {"grades.$[element]": 100}}, {multi: true, arrayFilters: [{"element": {$gte: 100}}]})

Array Update Operators Summary:

Operator Action Duplicates Allowed? $push Append element to array Yes $addToSet Append only if not exists No (set semantics) $pull Remove all matching elements N/A $pullAll Remove specific values N/A $pop Remove first (-1) or last (1) element N/A $each Used with $push/$addToSet to add multiple Depends on parent $sort Used with $push + $each to maintain order N/A $slice Used with $push + $each to cap array size N/A

docs.title: FindOneAndUpdate
docs.text:
Intent: Atomically finds a document, updates it, and returns either the original or updated document. Useful for implementing atomic counters, queue-like processing, or when you need the document value.

db.coll.findOneAndUpdate({"name": "Max"}, {$inc: {"points": 5}}, {returnNewDocument: true})

// Atomic counter — increment and return the new value
db.counters.findOneAndUpdate(
    { _id: "orderId" },
    { $inc: { seq: 1 } },
    { returnNewDocument: true, upsert: true }
)
// Returns: { _id: "orderId", seq: 43 } (the new value)

// Queue pattern — claim the next unprocessed job
db.jobs.findOneAndUpdate(
    { status: "pending" },
    { $set: { status: "processing", worker: "worker-1", startedAt: new Date() } },
    { sort: { priority: -1, createdAt: 1 }, returnNewDocument: true }
)

docs.title: Upsert
docs.text:
Intent: Update if exists, insert if not. Combines update + insert in a single atomic operation. The $setOnInsert operator sets fields only when inserting (not when updating an existing document).

db.coll.updateOne({"_id": 1}, {$set: {item: "apple"}, $setOnInsert: {defaultQty: 100}}, {upsert: true})

// Track daily page views — create if first visit, increment if exists
db.pageViews.updateOne(
    { page: "/home", date: "2024-06-15" },
    {
        $inc: { views: 1 },
        $setOnInsert: { page: "/home", date: "2024-06-15", firstViewAt: new Date() }
    },
    { upsert: true }
)

docs.title: Replace
docs.text:
Intent: Replace the entire document body (except _id). Use when you want to overwrite a document completely rather than modifying individual fields. Any fields not in the replacement document will be removed.

db.coll.replaceOne({"name": "Max"}, {"firstname": "Maxime", "surname": "Beugnet"})

docs.title: Write Concern
docs.text: db.coll.updateMany({}, {$set: {"x": 1}}, {"writeConcern": {"w": "majority", "wtimeout": 5000}})

docs.title: Update Operations — Concepts and Interview Q&A
docs.text:
Update operations modify existing documents using updateOne(), updateMany(), or findOneAndUpdate(), typically applying update operators like $set, $inc, $unset, or $push rather than replacing the whole document. By default, only matched fields specified with update operators are changed — other fields remain untouched.

db.orders.updateMany(
  { status: "PENDING" },
  { $set: { status: "PROCESSING" }, $currentDate: { updatedAt: true } }
)

Interview Questions: - What is the difference between updateOne(), updateMany(), and findOneAndUpdate()? — updateOne() modifies the first matching document, updateMany() modifies all matching documents, and findOneAndUpdate() updates a single matching document while also atomically returning either its pre- or post-update state. - What is the difference between using $set versus passing a plain replacement document to updateOne()? — Using $set only modifies the specified fields and leaves the rest of the document untouched, whereas passing a plain document without operators replaces the entire matched document (equivalent to replaceOne()), removing any fields not included. - How would you atomically increment a counter field on a document? — Use the $inc update operator, e.g. { $inc: { count: 1 } }, which atomically increments the field's numeric value on the server without a separate read-modify-write cycle.

Real-life scenario: A like button fires { $inc: { likes: 1 } } directly — 10k concurrent tappers each increment atomically server-side, where read-then-write would lose thousands of likes to lost updates.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
1. Update operators ($set, $inc, $push, $pull) patch in place atomically — never read-modify-write counters.
  2. updateOne (first match), updateMany (all matches), findOneAndUpdate (match + return old/new atomically).
  3. Bare-document updates replace the whole document — $set is almost always what you meant.
  4. Array operators ($push, $pull, $addToSet, positional $) modify elements without fetching the array.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    F["Filter (indexed)"] --> Match["Matched docs"]
    Match --> Ops["Update operators ($set/$inc/$push)"]
    Ops --> Atom["Atomic per-document apply"]

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
• SurrealDB in 100 Seconds
  • Beyond Surreal? A closer look at NewSQL Relational Data
  • Rust Powered Database SurrealDB (It's Pretty Ambitious)
  • SurrealDB - Rust Embedded Database - Quick Tutorial

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
SurrealDB is a multi-model database (document + relational rows + graph edges + key-value + time series) with a Rust core, SurrealQL query language, and built-in realtime (live queries), auth, and server-side functions. One binary covers embedded to distributed modes, which makes it attractive for prototypes and edge deployments that would otherwise need Postgres + Redis + a queue.

Treat it as a consolidation bet for small-to-medium workloads: great when one team wants documents, relations, and graph traversals without operating three systems; not yet the answer for massive scale, strict compliance ecosystems, or workloads needing the mature tooling of Postgres/Mongo.

docs.title: Multi-model in one engine
docs.text: Model How it looks Use when Document Nested records, flexible fields Product catalogs, profiles Relational Tables + typed fields + constraints Ledgers, inventories Graph RELATE edges with properties Friends, fraud, recommendations Key-value / series Fast lookups, time-ordered data Sessions, metrics

docs.title: SurrealQL highlights
docs.text:
• RELATE author:1->wrote->post:9 SET time = time::now() creates a graph edge inline.
  • LIVE SELECT streams matching changes to subscribed clients (realtime without a separate pub/sub).
  • Schemafull tables enforce types; schemaless tables allow iteration — pick per table, not per database.
  • Namespaces → databases → tables scope multi-tenancy (USE NS app DB prod).

Real-life scenario: A hackathon team ships a collaborative app with documents for posts, RELATE edges for follows, and LIVE SELECT for the activity feed — one SurrealDB instance replaces what would have been Postgres + Redis Pub/Sub + a graph prototype.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    App[Application / SDK] --> API["SurrealQL API (WS / HTTP)"]
    API --> Auth["Auth + namespace / DB scope"]
    Auth --> Engine["Query engine: doc + relational + graph"]
    Engine --> Store[("Storage: RocksDB / TiKV / memory")]
    Engine -.->|LIVE SELECT| Subs[Subscribed clients]
Layer Responsibility Scaling note Protocol WebSocket realtime + HTTP queries WS for live, HTTP for request/response Auth Users, scopes, row-level rules Define access at table level early Functions Server-side logic, future WASM Keep hot logic close to data, not in clients Storage Embedded RocksDB → distributed TiKV Start embedded, plan the TiKV jump past one node

docs.title: Deep Dive / How it works
docs.text:
Write path: SurrealQL statement → auth/scope check → storage transaction (single-node ACID in embedded mode) → secondary indexes updated → live-query subscribers notified for matching LIVE selections. Graph edges are first-class records, so traversals avoid join tables.

Read path: query planner uses indexes for anchored filters, then traverses RELATE edges by record links; unanchored full-graph scans cost like full-table scans anywhere else. Realtime is change-data-capture built in — clients hold a LIVE cursor instead of polling.

Trade-offs: young distributed story (consensus/scaling less battle-tested than Postgres/Cassandra), smaller ecosystem (drivers, ORMs, DBAs-for-hire), and migration risk if you outgrow single-node. Mitigate by keeping domain boundaries clean so extraction to specialist stores stays possible.

docs.title: Practical Examples
docs.text:
-- Schemafull users, schemaless posts, graph follows
DEFINE TABLE user SCHEMAFULL;
DEFINE FIELD name ON user TYPE string;
DEFINE FIELD email ON user TYPE string ASSERT string::is::email($value);

CREATE user:1 SET name = 'Ava', email = 'ava@example.com';
CREATE post:9 SET title = 'Hello Surreal', author = user:1;
RELATE user:1->wrote->post:9 SET at = time::now();
RELATE user:2->follows->user:1 SET at = time::now();

-- Traverse: who follows Ava, and what did they write?
SELECT <-follows<-user.name AS followers,
       ->wrote->post.title AS posts
FROM user:1;

-- Realtime feed: clients subscribe once, get deltas
LIVE SELECT * FROM post WHERE author = user:1;

# Run it locally (single binary) and connect
surreal start --user root --pass root memory
# then: USE NS app DB demo; CREATE user:1 SET name = 'Ava';

docs.title: Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Q: What does multi-model mean here? A: One engine querying documents, relations, graph edges, and KV without ETL between systems — SurrealQL spans all four in one statement.
  • Q: How do live queries replace polling? A: LIVE SELECT holds a subscription; matching writes push deltas to clients — realtime feeds/notifications without a separate broker for moderate scale.
  • Q: When would you still choose Postgres over SurrealDB? A: Strict compliance/tooling needs, massive scale with proven HA, PostGIS/pgvector-class extensions, or teams that need hireable operational expertise.
  • Q: How do you avoid lock-in with a young database? A: Clean bounded contexts, keep the system of record exportable (CDC/dumps), and isolate Surreal-specific features (live queries, graph edges) behind repository interfaces.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
1. SurrealDB consolidates document + relational + graph + realtime in one binary.
  2. RELATE edges and LIVE SELECT are the two features that replace extra infrastructure.
  3. Scope with namespaces/databases; choose schemafull vs schemaless per table.
  4. Great consolidation bet under moderate scale; plan extraction seams for growth.
  5. Evaluate the distributed/HA story against your RPO/RTO before committing production data.

docs.title: Udemy
docs.text:
• Learn Apache Cassandra in 2 hours | NoSQL Database
  • Learn Apache Cassandra from Scratch
  • Apache Cassandra : Everything You Need To Know

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Apache Cassandra is a masterless, wide-column NoSQL store built for linear horizontal scale and always-on availability across racks, regions, and clouds. Born at Facebook (Dynamo + BigTable ideas), it powers write-heavy workloads like time series, messaging inboxes, and IoT telemetry at Discord, Netflix, and Apple scale.

Choose it when you need multi-datacenter active-active writes with tunable consistency and can model data around known query patterns. Avoid it for ad-hoc joins, secondary-index-heavy access, or strongly-consistent transactional workloads.

docs.title: Partitioning and tokens
docs.text: Concept What it is Interview note Partition key First part of PRIMARY KEY; decides the node Wrong key = hotspots Clustering key Sorts rows inside a partition Range scans only within a partition Token ring Murmur3 hash space split across nodes vnum_tokens spreads load Replication SimpleStrategy / NetworkTopologyStrategy NTS with RF=3 per DC is the prod default

docs.title: Consistency tuning
docs.text: ONE / QUORUM / LOCAL_QUORUM / ALL per read and write, plus EACH_QUORUM for multi-DC. W + R > RF gives strong consistency; LOCAL_QUORUM both sides is the common low-latency strong-ish default. Hinted handoff + read repair cover transient misses.

docs.title: LSM storage engine
docs.text:
Memtable → immutable SSTables → leveled/size-tiered compaction, with commitlog as WAL and Bloom filters skipping SSTables. Writes are sequential; tombstones mark deletes until gc_grace_seconds passes.

Real-life scenario: A messaging team models messages_by_conversation (conversation_id, message_id) so one partition holds one thread in time order — fetching a page is a single-partition slice, while cross-conversation search is deliberately pushed to Elasticsearch instead of Cassandra.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    App[Application] --> Coord["Coordinator (any node)"]
    Coord --> N1[("Node 1: token range A")]
    Coord --> N2[("Node 2: token range B")]
    Coord --> N3[("Node 3: token range C")]
    Coord -.->|hinted handoff| N4[("Down node: replay later")]
    N1 -.->|gossip + repair| N2
Component Responsibility Scaling note Gossip Membership + failure detection Seed nodes bootstrap, all nodes equal Commitlog + memtable Durable write buffer Size memtables for write bursts SSTables + compaction Sorted persistent storage STCS for write-heavy, LCS for read-heavy Repair / anti-entropy Replica convergence Run incrementally; never skip with deletes

docs.title: Deep Dive / How it works
docs.text:
Write path: coordinator hashes partition key → forwards to RF replicas → each appends to commitlog + memtable → acknowledges per CL → coordinator returns after W acks. Later memtable flush creates SSTables; compaction merges and evicts tombstones after grace.

Read path: coordinator asks RF replicas → digest comparison → read repair on mismatch → returns after R acks. Partition too large (>100 MB guideline) causes heap pressure and slow repair — split by time bucketing (..._by_month) before it hurts.

Failure story: single-node loss is absorbed by RF replicas; quorum reads during a partition stay consistent or fail loudly with LOCAL_QUORUM; ALL maximizes consistency and maximizes outage blast radius — pick deliberately.

docs.title: Practical Examples
docs.text:
-- Model around the query: one partition per conversation, clustered by time
CREATE TABLE messages_by_conversation (
  conversation_id uuid,
  message_id timeuuid,
  sender_id uuid,
  body text,
  PRIMARY KEY (conversation_id, message_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (message_id DESC);

-- Single-partition page fetch (fast path)
SELECT sender_id, body FROM messages_by_conversation
WHERE conversation_id = 123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000
LIMIT 50;

-- Time-bucketed sensor table avoids unbounded partitions
CREATE TABLE readings_by_sensor_month (
  sensor_id uuid,
  month text,
  ts timestamp,
  value double,
  PRIMARY KEY ((sensor_id, month), ts)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (ts DESC);

# Operate it like prod: status, repair, cleanup after topology change
nodetool status
nodetool repair -pr -j 2 mykeyspace
nodetool cleanup mykeyspace

docs.title: Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Q: Partition key vs clustering key? A: Partition key picks the node (hash); clustering key orders rows inside that partition. Cross-partition range scans are the modeling smell.
  • Q: How do you get strong consistency from Cassandra? A: W + R > RF, e.g., QUORUM/QUORUM with RF=3. LOCAL_QUORUM both sides keeps it single-DC fast.
  • Q: What happens on node failure during a write? A: Coordinator writes to remaining replicas + stores hints; the down node replays hints on return, with read repair and anti-entropy repair converging the rest.
  • Q: Why do deletes come back (zombie data)? A: Tombstones expire after gc_grace_seconds; a down node that missed the tombstone resurrects data. Run repair within the grace window, always.
  • Q: When is Cassandra the wrong choice? A: Ad-hoc analytics, joins, heavy secondary-index queries, or serializable transactions — use Postgres/warehouse/search alongside it.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
1. Model queries first: partition key places, clustering key orders.
  2. Tune consistency per operation; QUORUM/QUORUM over RF=3 is the default strong answer.
  3. LSM + tombstones explain both write speed and the repair discipline deletes demand.
  4. Bucket unbounded partitions by time before repair and heap suffer.
  5. Cassandra owns write-heavy keyed access; pair it with search/analytics stores for the rest.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
• Why Elasticsearch Is So Fast
  • How Elastic Search Work ? System Design Deep Dives Podcast

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Elasticsearch is a distributed search and analytics engine built on Apache Lucene. It stores JSON documents in an inverted index plus columnar doc-values, exposing full-text relevance ranking, aggregations, and vector (kNN) search behind a REST API. It powers product search, log analytics (ELK/EFK), SIEM, and RAG retrieval.

Use it when queries are "find and rank by relevance / aggregate over billions of events" rather than relational joins or strict transactions. Keep the system of record in Postgres/Mongo; index a denormalized projection into Elasticsearch.

docs.title: Documents, indices, shards
docs.text: Concept What it is Interview note Document JSON unit (products/1) Immutable-ish; updates reindex Index Collection of documents with mappings Like a table, but sharded Shard Lucene instance (primary + replicas) Unit of parallelism and recovery Mapping Field types + analyzers Wrong mapping = wrong search; plan before indexing Relevance BM25 score of term match Tune with match vs term deliberately

docs.title: Analysis chain
docs.text: character filter → tokenizer → token filter (lowercase, stem, synonyms) turns "Running Shoes!" into [run, shoe]. Same analyzer at index and query time, or recall silently breaks.

docs.title: Inverted index vs doc values
docs.text:
• Inverted index: term → posting list (doc ids + positions). Serves full-text search.
  • Doc values / columnar: doc → field values on disk. Serves sorting and aggregations.
  • HNSW graph (8.x kNN): vector field for semantic search alongside BM25 (hybrid retrieval).

Real-life scenario: A marketplace indexes 20M products with an english analyzer plus a synonym filter (sneakers ⇔ sports shoes), so a query for "running sneakers" still matches listings titled "men's running sports shoes" with BM25 ranking the best matches first.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    App[Application] --> LB["Coordinating node / LB"]
    LB --> S1[("Shard P1 + replicas")]
    LB --> S2[("Shard P2 + replicas")]
    LB --> S3[("Shard P3 + replicas")]
    S1 --> Disk1[(Lucene segments)]
    S2 --> Disk2[(Lucene segments)]
    S3 --> Disk3[(Lucene segments)]
    LB --> Agg[Scatter-gather + merge + rank]
    Agg --> App
Component Responsibility Scaling note Data nodes Store shards, execute search Add nodes + rebalance past ~30–50 GB/shard Master-eligible nodes Cluster state, shard assignment Dedicated 3-node quorum in prod Ingest / coordinating Pipeline + fan-out merge Isolate hot indexing from search ILM snapshots Rollover + force-merge + S3 backup Hot → warm → cold → frozen

Real-life scenario: A logging platform rolls daily indices (logs-2026.10.08), force-merges warm indices to one segment, and snapshots to S3 — hot nodes stay fast while 90 days of history remains searchable from cheap frozen storage.

docs.title: Deep Dive / How it works
docs.text:
Write path: POST /idx/_doc → routing hash picks shard → primary validates mapping, writes to in-memory buffer + translog (WAL) → refresh (default 1 s) opens a new Lucene segment for search → flush commits segments + clears translog. Refresh interval is the visibility-vs-indexing-throughput knob.

Read path: coordinating node fans out to one copy of each shard → each shard scores locally (BM25) with distributed term statistics → coordinator merges, re-sorts, returns top-K. Deep pagination (from: 100000) is expensive — use search_after or PIT + point-in-time readers.

Failure handling: replica promotion on node loss (yellow → green), split-brain prevented by master quorum, translog replay on unclean restart. Shard count is fixed at index creation — over-sharding burns heap (each shard ~20–50 MB heap overhead), under-sharding caps parallelism.

Real-life scenario: After a data-node OOM, the cluster goes yellow with unassigned replicas; the on-call confirms primaries are intact, restarts the node, and watches replicas re-sync from translog/segments instead of panicking — yellow means degraded redundancy, not data loss.

docs.title: Practical Examples
docs.text:
# Create an index with explicit mapping (do this BEFORE bulk load)
curl -s -X PUT localhost:9200/products -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "settings": {"number_of_shards": 3, "number_of_replicas": 1},
  "mappings": {"properties": {
    "name": {"type": "text", "analyzer": "english"},
    "price": {"type": "double"},
    "tags": {"type": "keyword"},
    "embedding": {"type": "dense_vector", "dims": 384}
  }}
}'

# Index one document
curl -s -X POST localhost:9200/products/_doc/1 -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "name": "Trail running shoes", "price": 129.99, "tags": ["outdoor", "footwear"]
}'

# Full-text search with filter + aggregation
curl -s -X GET localhost:9200/products/_search -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "query": {"bool": {
    "must": [{"match": {"name": "running shoes"}}],
    "filter": [{"term": {"tags": "outdoor"}}]
  }},
  "aggs": {"avg_price": {"avg": {"field": "price"}}},
  "size": 5
}'
# match = analyzed relevance query; term = exact keyword filter (cached, unscored)

# Hybrid BM25 + kNN (Elasticsearch 8.x)
curl -s -X GET localhost:9200/products/_search -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "knn": {"field": "embedding", "query_vector": [0.11, -0.02, 0.43], "k": 10, "num_candidates": 100},
  "query": {"match": {"name": "running shoes"}},
  "size": 10
}'

docs.title: Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Q: Why is Elasticsearch faster than LIKE '%...%' in Postgres for full text? A: Inverted index jumps straight to the posting list per term with BM25 ranking; LIKE '%x%' scans. The index pays build cost once for O(terms) lookups.
  • Q: text vs keyword — when does the wrong choice hurt? A: text is analyzed for relevance search; keyword is exact-match/sort/aggregate. Filtering on text or full-text on keyword gives wrong or empty results.
  • Q: What does refresh interval control? A: How often in-memory writes become searchable segments. 1 s default = near-real-time; raising it (30 s / -1 for bulk) boosts indexing throughput at the cost of visibility lag.
  • Q: How do you handle deep pagination? A: Avoid large from/size (each shard sorts then discards); use search_after with a tiebreaker sort or point-in-time readers for stable deep scans.
  • Q: Primary vs replica shard in a search answer? A: Primaries take writes; replicas serve reads and take over on failure. Replica count = read parallelism + fault tolerance; shard count = write parallelism set at creation.
  • Q: Sketch an ELK logging pipeline in a system-design answer. A: App → Filebeat/Fluent Bit → (Kafka buffer) → Logstash/ingest pipeline → hot data nodes → ILM rollover to warm/cold + S3 snapshots; Kibana + alerting on top; mention backpressure and index templates.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
1. Elasticsearch = distributed Lucene: inverted index for search, doc values for aggregations, kNN for vectors.
  2. Mappings and analyzers must be designed before bulk load; reindex to change them.
  3. Shard count is fixed at creation — size for ~10–50 GB per shard, keep heap per shard in mind.
  4. Refresh trades visibility for indexing speed; deep pagination needs search_after, not big from.
  5. Use it as a searchable projection of a system of record, with ILM + snapshots for lifecycle and recovery.

docs.title: Youtube
docs.text: • Graph Databases Will Change Your Freakin' Life (Best Intro Into Graph Databases)

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
A graph database stores nodes (entities), relationships (edges), and properties natively, making multi-hop traversals ("friends of friends who bought X") first-class operations instead of expensive recursive joins. Neo4j, Amazon Neptune, and TigerGraph dominate; SurrealDB and others add graph flavors.

Reach for one when the queries are about connections — fraud rings, recommendations, knowledge graphs, access-control hierarchies, network topology — and the relational version needs 5+ joins or recursive CTEs that get slower with depth.

docs.title: Property graph vs RDF
docs.text:
Model Structure Query language Best for Property graph Nodes + directed edges, both with key-value properties Cypher, Gremlin, GSQL Applications, recommendations, fraud RDF triple store Subject-predicate-object triples + ontologies SPARQL Knowledge graphs, linked data, reasoning

Most interviews mean property graphs (Neo4j-style) when they say "graph DB".

docs.title: Why not recursive joins
docs.text: A 4-hop "friends of friends of friends" query in SQL needs recursive CTEs whose cost explodes with fan-out. A graph DB stores adjacency with each node (index-free adjacency), so each hop is a pointer chase — O(degree) per hop regardless of total graph size.

docs.title: Storage patterns
docs.text:
• Native graph storage (Neo4j): nodes/records with direct relationship pointers; traversals never touch a global index.
  • Layered on KV/document (some multi-model stores): edges as documents; simpler ops, slower deep traversals.

Real-life scenario: A fraud team models accounts, devices, and transactions as a graph; a new account sharing a device with three previously-flagged accounts is caught by a 2-hop traversal in milliseconds — the same check in SQL needed four joins over hundred-million-row tables and timed out.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    App[Application] --> Q[Query engine: Cypher planner]
    Q --> Cache[Page cache: hot nodes + rels]
    Cache --> Store[("Native graph store: node / relationship / property files")]
    Store --> Idx[Index: label + property lookup]
    Q --> Idx
    Store -.->|raft / causal clustering| Replica[Read replicas]
Component Responsibility Scaling note Transaction log + checkpoints Durability (like WAL) Same replay-on-crash story Page cache Hot subgraph in RAM Size for working set, not full graph Causal clustering Read replicas + core consensus Writes on core, scale reads horizontally Full-text / vector index Entry-point lookup ("find start node") Graph traversal starts from indexed anchors

Real-life scenario: A social app keeps the 2-hop neighborhood of active users in page cache, routes writes to the 3-node core and feed reads to 5 replicas — p99 feed latency stays flat as reads scale 10×.

docs.title: Deep Dive / How it works
docs.text:
Write path: CREATE/MERGE appends node and relationship records with properties, updates label/property indexes, commits via transaction log. Relationship creation is O(1) pointer wiring — no join-table inserts, no foreign-key fan-out.

Read path: anchor (indexed label/property lookup, e.g., MATCH (u:User {id: 42})) → expand (follow relationship pointers hop by hop, filtering by type/direction/properties) → project/aggregate. The planner chooses expand direction by degree estimates; PROFILE shows estimated vs actual rows per hop — cardinality misestimates compound exactly like relational misestimates.

Supernodes (a celebrity with 50M followers, a popular product) are the classic pathology: traversals touching them explode. Mitigations include degree caps, time-windowed edges, relationship partitioning, and bidirectional BFS from both ends.

Real-life scenario: A recommendation query slows from 40 ms to 4 s after a viral product becomes a supernode; the team adds a RECENT edge window (only last-90-day purchases traversed) plus a degree-aware planner hint, restoring latency without changing results users see.

docs.title: Practical Examples
docs.text:
-- Anchor on an indexed property, traverse 2 hops, rank
MATCH (u:User {id: 42})-[:PURCHASED]->(p:Product)<-[:PURCHASED]-(other:User)
MATCH (other)-[:PURCHASED]->(rec:Product)
WHERE NOT (u)-[:PURCHASED]->(rec)
RETURN rec.name, count(*) AS bought_together
ORDER BY bought_together DESC
LIMIT 10;

-- Fraud ring: accounts sharing devices within 2 hops of a flagged account
MATCH (flagged:Account {flagged: true})-[:USES_DEVICE|SHARES_IP*1..2]-(suspect:Account)
WHERE suspect <> flagged
RETURN suspect.id, count(*) AS signals
ORDER BY signals DESC;

-- Shortest path for access or routing questions
MATCH path = shortestPath(
  (a:Employee {id: 7})-[:REPORTS_TO*1..10]->(ceo:Employee {title: 'CEO'})
)
RETURN [n IN nodes(path) | n.name] AS chain, length(path) AS hops;

# Sanity checks worth running before blaming the database
# 1. Is the anchor indexed?  2. PROFILE the hop fan-out
echo "CREATE INDEX user_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (u:User) ON (u.id);"

docs.title: Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Q: When does a graph DB beat Postgres for connected data? A: When queries traverse 3+ hops with selective anchors — index-free adjacency makes each hop O(degree) instead of join cost that grows with table size and depth.
  • Q: What is index-free adjacency? A: Each node physically stores pointers to its relationships, so traversal is pointer chasing from the start node rather than global index lookups per hop.
  • Q: What is a supernode and how do you handle it? A: A node with extreme degree that blows up traversals. Mitigate with degree caps, time-windowed edges, bidirectional search, and separating hot edges from traversal paths.
  • Q: How do you enter the graph — can you traverse without an index? A: You need an anchor: a label/property or full-text/vector index locates start nodes, then traversal proceeds by pointers. Unanchored full-graph scans are the graph equivalent of full table scans.
  • Q: Sketch fraud detection in a system-design answer. A: Stream transactions/edges into the graph, run periodic 1–3 hop pattern queries (shared device/IP/account, velocity fan-out), score and push to a review queue; mention supernode guards and read-replica scaling.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
1. Graph DBs make relationship hops O(degree) via index-free adjacency — depth is cheap, anchors matter.
  2. Property graphs + Cypher cover most app cases; RDF/SPARQL covers ontology reasoning.
  3. Every fast query starts at an indexed anchor; profile hop fan-out like join cardinality.
  4. Supernodes are the #1 production pathology — bound degree explicitly.
  5. Choose graphs for connection queries, keep tabular/aggregate workloads in relational or columnar stores.

docs.title: Comparisions
docs.text:
• Kafka vs RabbitMQ
  • The Best Queue System for Scaling - Not Kafka!
  • What is a Message Queue and When should you use Messaging Queue Systems Like RabbitMQ and Kafka
  • When to Use Kafka or RabbitMQ | System Design
  • Kafka vs. RabbitMQ - who wins and why? | Systems Design Interview 0 to 1 with Ex-Google SWE

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
A message queue decouples producers from consumers in time, topology, and speed: producers append, the broker durably buffers, consumers process at their own pace with retries. The payoff is resilience (traffic spikes buffer instead of cascading), independent scaling, and clean failure isolation between services.

Use queues when work can be asynchronous — order processing, emails, ETL, webhook delivery. Keep synchronous request/response for reads needing immediate consistency or sub-100 ms user-facing latency.

docs.title: Queue vs log vs pub/sub
docs.text: Pattern Model Replay Best for Point-to-point queue Each message → one consumer Ack removes Task distribution, RPC Log (Kafka) Append-only partitions, offsets Rewind/replay any offset Event sourcing, stream processing Pub/sub topic Each message → all subscribers Depends on retention Notifications, cache invalidation

docs.title: Delivery semantics
docs.text:
• At-most-once: fast, may lose. Metrics, best-effort signals.
  • At-least-once: ack + redelivery, may duplicate. The sane default — pair with idempotent consumers.
  • Exactly-once: transactions/idempotence scoped to one system (Kafka EOS). True end-to-end exactly-once needs idempotency keys at the sink.

docs.title: Ordering, retries, dead letters
docs.text:
Ordering is per-partition/per-queue with a single active consumer group — global ordering and horizontal scale conflict, so scope ordering keys narrowly (per user, per order). Retries need backoff + jitter + a cap, then a dead-letter queue with alerting and replay tooling, or one poison message stalls everything.

Real-life scenario: A checkout flow publishes payment.authorized once; inventory, email, and analytics consume independently with idempotency keys on order_id. A duplicate redelivery after a consumer crash debits nothing twice — the key makes at-least-once behave exactly-once.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    P[Producers] --> B["Broker: exchange / topic + durable queues"]
    B --> Q1[(Queue: inventory)]
    B --> Q2[(Queue: email)]
    B --> Q3[(Queue: analytics)]
    Q1 --> C1[Consumers: ack + prefetch + idempotent]
    Q2 --> C2[Consumers]
    Q3 --> C3[Consumers]
    Q1 -.->|retries exhausted| DLQ[(Dead-letter queue)]
    DLQ --> Ops[Alerts + replay tool]
Decision Options Rule of thumb Broker RabbitMQ / Kafka / SQS / Pulsar Routing richness → RabbitMQ; replay + throughput → Kafka; managed simplicity → SQS Durability Persistent + confirms Always on for money/mutations Consumption Push vs poll, prefetch Bound unacked work (prefetch/MAX poll) Failure path DLQ + cap + alert Design before the first incident

Real-life scenario: A flash sale spikes checkouts 20×; the queue absorbs the burst, inventory consumers autoscale on queue depth, and p99 checkout latency stays flat — without the buffer, the inventory DB would have fallen over in the first minute.

docs.title: Deep Dive / How it works
docs.text:
Publish path: producer sends with durability flags → broker routes (exchange binding / topic partition) → fsync per persistence settings → confirm/ack back. No confirm means "accepted by TCP", not "stored".

Consume path: broker delivers up to prefetch → handler runs business logic → ack deletes, nack redelivers, reject routes to DLQ. Visibility timeouts (SQS) and session heartbeats (Kafka) detect crashed consumers; tune them shorter than the business SLA but longer than p99 processing time, or healthy work redelivers spuriously.

Backpressure is the design center: bounded queues + consumer autoscaling on depth/age + load shedding (reject with Retry-After upstream) + circuit breakers. An unbounded buffer just moves the OOM from the service to the broker.

Real-life scenario: An image-resize queue uses visibility timeout 5 min (p99 job 90 s) plus a 3-retry cap to DLQ; a bad image that segfaults workers lands in quarantine with its payload id after 15 minutes instead of wedging the queue all night.

docs.title: Practical Examples
docs.text:
# Idempotent consumer sketch (works on any broker)
seen = set()  # prod: Redis/Dynamo with TTL on the idempotency key

def handle(msg):
    key = msg["order_id"]
    if not seen_add(key):   # SETNX semantics
        return "duplicate-skip"
    debit_inventory(msg)
    send_email(msg)

# Kafka: durable topic + consumer group with bounded fetch
kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create \
  --topic orders --partitions 12 --replication-factor 3 \
  --config min.insync.replicas=2 --config retention.ms=604800000

kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
  --topic orders --group inventory-svc \
  --from-beginning --max-messages 5

# RabbitMQ: durable topology with dead-lettering
rabbitmqadmin declare exchange name=orders type=topic durable=true
rabbitmqadmin declare queue name=orders.inventory durable=true \
  arguments='{"x-dead-letter-exchange":"orders.dlx"}'
rabbitmqadmin declare binding source=orders destination=orders.inventory routing_key="order.*"

docs.title: Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Q: Why put a queue between services instead of direct HTTP calls? A: Time/topology/speed decoupling: bursts buffer, consumers scale and deploy independently, and one slow downstream stops cascading into timeouts upstream.
  • Q: How do you choose between RabbitMQ and Kafka? A: RabbitMQ for routing flexibility, per-message acks, moderate throughput; Kafka for replayable high-throughput logs and stream processing. Often both: RabbitMQ for tasks, Kafka for events.
  • Q: How do you get effectively-exactly-once processing? A: At-least-once delivery + idempotent consumers (dedupe keys at the sink) + transactional produce where the broker supports it. No magic — the sink idempotency is the load-bearing piece.
  • Q: What breaks with one poison message? A: Infinite redelivery head-of-line-blocks the partition/queue. Fix: retry cap with exponential backoff + jitter, then DLQ quarantine with alerts and replay.
  • Q: How do you preserve order and still scale? A: Order per key (user/order id → partition/routing key) with one active consumer per partition; scale by key cardinality, not by abandoning ordering.
  • Q: Sketch checkout with a queue under flash-sale load. A: API validates → publishes order.created → broker buffers burst → inventory/email/analytics consume independently with prefetch bounds → autoscale on queue depth/age → DLQ + idempotency keys for safety.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
1. Queues buy decoupling, buffering, and isolated failure — the backbone of async system design.
  2. Default to at-least-once + idempotent consumers; exactly-once is scoped, not universal.
  3. Order per key, retry with cap + backoff, quarantine to DLQ with replay.
  4. Bound everything (prefetch, visibility timeout, queue depth) and autoscale on age/depth.
  5. RabbitMQ for routing, Kafka for replayable scale, managed queues for simplicity — match the broker to the pattern.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Neo4j is the reference native property-graph database: nodes, relationships, and properties stored with index-free adjacency, queried in Cypher, with causal clustering for HA and Bloom/Browser for visualization. It is the default answer for "we need a graph database" in interviews and in production alike.

Use it for connected-data workloads — recommendations, fraud rings, identity resolution, access graphs, knowledge graphs — where traversals beat joins. See Graph Database for the general model; this page is Neo4j-specific operations and Cypher.

docs.title: Data model recap
docs.text: (person:Person {id: 7})-[:FOLLOWS {since: 2024}]->(friend:Person): labels group nodes, relationship types direct edges, properties live on both. Multiple labels per node, multiple properties per relationship — schema-optional with constraints added deliberately.

docs.title: Indexes and constraints
docs.text: Feature Syntax Purpose Range index CREATE INDEX FOR (u:User) ON (u.email) Anchor lookups Full-text index CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX ... FOR (p:Post) ON EACH [p.title] Text entry points Vector index (5.x) CREATE VECTOR INDEX ... OPTIONS {dimensions: 384} Semantic anchors + hybrid search Uniqueness CREATE CONSTRAINT FOR (u:User) REQUIRE u.id IS UNIQUE Identity + upsert safety Existence / type REQUIRE u.email IS NOT NULL Application invariants in the DB

docs.title: Transactions and clustering
docs.text:
Single-node ACID transactions; causal clustering (3+ core members via Raft) gives HA with read replicas scaling horizontally. Bookmark chaining (dbms.routing + bookmarks) provides read-your-write across the cluster.

Real-life scenario: A fraud team adds CREATE CONSTRAINT FOR (a:Account) REQUIRE a.id IS UNIQUE before backfilling, so concurrent ingestion jobs MERGE safely on account id instead of creating duplicate nodes that later corrupt ring queries.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    App[Application + driver] --> Router["Bolt routing / load balancer"]
    Router --> Core["Core cluster (Raft, 3 nodes): writes"]
    Router --> RR1[Read replica 1]
    Router --> RR2[Read replica 2]
    Core --> Store[("Graph store + indexes + txn logs")]
    Core -.->|raft replication| RR1
    Core -.->|raft replication| RR2
Component Responsibility Scaling note Core members Writes + consensus Keep at 3–5; never scale writes by adding cores Read replicas Scale traversal reads Add freely; mind replication lag for fresh writes Page cache Hot subgraph in RAM Size for active working set Bloom / Browser Exploration + stakeholder demos Great for query development, not prod access

Real-life scenario: A recommendations API routes writes to the core and feed reads to six replicas with bookmark-aware sessions — users see their own new follows immediately while read throughput scales past 50k qps.

docs.title: Deep Dive / How it works
docs.text:
Write path: Cypher CREATE/MERGE → constraint validation → transaction log append → page-cache mutation → commit + Raft replication to core majority. MERGE is match-or-create in one atomic step — the idempotent ingestion primitive.

Read path: planner anchors on the most selective index (or vector/full-text entry point) → expands relationship pointers hop by hop → filters, aggregates, projects. PROFILE exposes estimated vs actual rows per operator; a 100× misestimate at hop 2 compounds into seconds of wasted expansion — add or rewrite the anchor before touching the traversal.

Supernode defense in Neo4j specifically: degree caps in the pattern (-[r:BOUGHT]-> with WHERE size((p)<-[:BOUGHT]-()) < 100000), time-windowed relationship types (BOUGHT_2026), bidirectional shortestPath, and APOC batching for backfills (apoc.periodic.iterate) so billion-edge loads don't blow the heap.

Real-life scenario: A backfill creating 200M edges OOMs on one giant transaction; rewriting it as apoc.periodic.iterate batches of 50k with periodic commit finishes in 40 minutes with flat heap — batching is the production ingestion pattern.

docs.title: Practical Examples
docs.text:
-- Upsert-safe ingestion with constraints
MERGE (u:User {id: 42})
ON CREATE SET u.name = 'Ava', u.created = date()
ON MATCH SET u.lastSeen = date();

-- Recommendations: friends-of-friends products, anchored and ranked
MATCH (me:User {id: 42})-[:FOLLOWS]->(f:User)-[:BOUGHT]->(p:Product)
WHERE NOT (me)-[:BOUGHT]->(p)
RETURN p.name, count(*) AS score
ORDER BY score DESC
LIMIT 10;

-- Fraud ring expansion with a degree guard
MATCH (a:Account {id: 'a-1'})-[r:TRANSFER*1..3]-(b:Account)
WHERE size((b)-[:TRANSFER]-()) < 5000
RETURN b.id, length(r) AS hops, count(*) AS paths
ORDER BY paths DESC
LIMIT 20;

# Operate it: backup, check consistency, run migrations versioned
neo4j-admin database backup --to-path=/backups neo4j
neo4j-admin database check-consistency --database=neo4j
# neo4j-migrations: versioned Cypher changelogs in CI, applied in order

docs.title: Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Q: MATCH vs MERGE vs CREATE? A: MATCH finds, CREATE always inserts, MERGE matches or creates atomically — use MERGE with uniqueness constraints for idempotent ingestion.
  • Q: How do you make traversals fast? A: Selective indexed anchor first, expand by lowest-degree direction, filter early, cap supernodes, and PROFILE every hop's cardinality.
  • Q: Core vs read replica — where do writes go? A: Writes to core members (Raft majority); reads fan out to replicas. Scale reads by adding replicas; never by adding cores.
  • Q: How do you load a billion edges without OOM? A: apoc.periodic.iterate in 10–100k batches with periodic commit, indexes/constraints created first, parallel where the graph structure allows.
  • Q: How do migrations work in Neo4j? A: Versioned Cypher changelogs (neo4j-migrations) applied in order via CI — same expand-contract discipline as relational migrations.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
1. Neo4j = native property graph + Cypher + causal clustering; the default graph answer.
  2. Anchor on indexes/constraints, then traverse; PROFILE hop fan-out like join cardinality.
  3. MERGE + uniqueness constraints make ingestion idempotent.
  4. Cores take writes, replicas take reads; batch backfills with APOC.
  5. Bound supernodes explicitly — viral nodes are a correctness-of-latency issue, not just data.
