Real-life scenario: A social app stores profiles in Postgres (ACID friendships), timelines in Cassandra (write-heavy fan-out), sessions in Redis (sub-ms), and the follow-graph in Neo4j (traversals) — four stores, each justified by a measured access pattern, synced via CDC events.

docs.title: Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Q: SQL vs NoSQL in one minute? A: SQL for relational integrity, joins, and ACID at moderate scale; NoSQL for horizontal write scale, flexible schemas, or specialized access (KV, wide-column, graph, search, vectors). Most real systems use both behind a polyglot design.
  • Q: What does BASE give up relative to ACID, and when is that OK? A: Immediate consistency — reads may be stale. Acceptable for feeds, carts, counters, and analytics where availability/scale beats instant agreement; unacceptable for money and inventory.
  • Q: How does CAP constrain a NoSQL choice? A: Partitions are inevitable, so choose CP (consistent, fail on partition — MongoDB, HBase) or AP (available, serve possibly-stale — Cassandra, DynamoDB). There is no CA distributed system.
  • Q: Key-value vs document vs wide-column vs graph — when each? A: KV for opaque blobs by key (sessions, cache); documents for nested objects with secondary indexes (catalogs, profiles); wide-column for massive ordered writes by partition key (metrics, timelines); graph for multi-hop traversals (fraud, recommendations).
  • Q: How do you keep polyglot stores consistent? A: One system of record per domain, CDC/outbox events to projections, idempotent consumers, and reconciliation jobs — eventual consistency with named bounds, not hope.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
1. NoSQL = specialized access at horizontal scale: KV, document, wide-column, graph, search, vector — each earns its place by pattern.
  2. BASE and eventual consistency trade instant agreement for availability and scale — choose per workload, not by default.
  3. CAP forces CP vs AP during partitions; quorum tuning (W + R > N) moves along the spectrum deliberately.
  4. Polyglot persistence is the endgame: Postgres for truth, specialists for scale/shape/speed, events keeping them converged.

docs.title: Youtube
docs.text: • I Would Never Use an ORM, by Matteo Collina

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
An ORM (Object-Relational Mapper) maps classes to tables and objects to rows, so application code works with user.orders instead of hand-written JOINs. SQLAlchemy, Hibernate/JPA, Django ORM, Prisma, TypeORM, and ActiveRecord dominate. It is a productivity layer: schema migrations, query building, identity maps, and unit-of-work come bundled.

Use one when domain logic is object-shaped and CRUD-heavy; drop to raw SQL or a query builder for hot paths, bulk loads, and reporting queries where the abstraction hides cost.

docs.title: What the ORM actually does
docs.text: Concern ORM handling Leaks when Mapping Class ↔ table, field ↔ column, relations ↔ FK Composite keys, legacy schemas Identity map One object per row per session Stale reads across sessions Unit of work Batches inserts/updates, flushes on commit Surprise write bursts at flush Lazy vs eager loading Loads relations on access or up front N+1 queries, cartesian explosion Migrations Versioned DDL from model diffs Data backfills, zero-downtime renames

docs.title: Lazy loading and the N+1 problem
docs.text:
# N+1: 1 query for users + N queries for orders
users = session.query(User).all()
for u in users:
    print(u.orders)  # lazy load fires one SELECT per user

# Fix: eager load in 1-2 queries
users = session.query(User).options(selectinload(User.orders)).all()
Strategy Queries Risk Lazy 1 + N N+1 latency death Joined eager 1 with JOIN Row multiplication, wide rows Select-in eager 2 (parents + children IN) Usually the sweet spot Explicit batch 2 with manual mapping Most control

Real-life scenario: A Django list endpoint slows from 80 ms to 4 s at 500 rows because the template touches order.customer.name per row; adding select_related/prefetch_related collapses 1001 queries to 2 with identical output.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    Code[Domain objects] --> Session["Session / Unit of Work"]
    Session --> Identity["Identity map (1 object per row)"]
    Session --> Builder[Query builder]
    Builder --> SQL[(Generated SQL)]
    SQL --> DB[("Relational database")]
    Session --> Txn[Flush on commit / rollback]
    Txn --> DB
Layer Responsibility Interview note Models Schema + relations + validations Fat-model vs anemic trade-off Session Change tracking, flush ordering Flush ≠ commit; know both Migrations Versioned DDL + rollbacks Expand-contract for zero downtime Cache (L1/L2) Identity map + optional shared cache Invalidation is the hard part

Real-life scenario: A checkout service keeps business rules in models, runs writes through one request-scoped session with explicit commit, and routes a slow admin report to raw SQL — the ORM owns the domain, SQL owns the analytics.

docs.title: Deep Dive / How it works
docs.text:
Write path: mutate objects → session tracks dirty state → flush() topologically orders INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE (parents before children, nullables deferred) → single transaction commit. Bulk inserts bypass this (use bulk_save_objects / COPY / batch JDBC) because per-object bookkeeping is O(n) Python/Java overhead.

Read path: query builder emits SQL → rows hydrated into objects → identity map dedupes → lazy proxies queue follow-ups. The planner you must carry in your head: every dot-access on an unloaded relation is a potential query; every eager join multiplies rows. EXPLAIN the generated SQL, not the Python.

Failure modes: stale reads across sessions (identity map is per-session, not global), lost updates without optimistic locking (version column + WHERE version = ?), migration locks (ALTER TABLE rewriting billion-row tables), and connection-pool exhaustion from long sessions holding connections.

Real-life scenario: Two admins edit the same product; without a version column the second save silently overwrites the first. Adding optimistic locking turns it into a clean 409 conflict with a retry prompt instead of lost data.

docs.title: Practical Examples
docs.text:
# SQLAlchemy: explicit session, eager loading, optimistic locking
from sqlalchemy import Column, Integer, String, ForeignKey, select
from sqlalchemy.orm import relationship, selectinload, Session

class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"
    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    name = Column(String, nullable=False)
    version_id = Column(Integer, nullable=False, default=1)
    orders = relationship("Order", back_populates="user")
    __mapper_args__ = {"version_id_col": version_id}

with Session(engine) as s:
    users = s.execute(
        select(User).options(selectinload(User.orders)).limit(100)
    ).scalars().all()

# Zero-downtime rename: expand then contract across two deploys
# Deploy 1: add new column, dual-write, backfill
# Deploy 2: switch reads, drop old column
# Alembic sketch
def upgrade():
    op.add_column("users", sa.Column("display_name", sa.String(), nullable=True))

-- What to check when the ORM is slow: read the generated SQL
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT users.*, orders.* FROM users LEFT JOIN orders ON orders.user_id = users.id;
-- look for: seq scans on hot filters, missing index on FK, row explosion

docs.title: Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Q: What is the N+1 problem and how do you fix it? A: One query for parents plus one per child via lazy loading. Fix with joined/select-in eager loading or explicit batching; verify with a query counter in tests.
  • Q: When should you bypass the ORM? A: Bulk loads, complex reporting/aggregations, recursive queries, and latency-critical hot paths — anywhere generated SQL hides cost or the abstraction adds O(n) overhead.
  • Q: How does optimistic locking work? A: A version column checked in UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND version = ?; a mismatch raises a concurrency error instead of silently overwriting.
  • Q: ORM session vs database transaction? A: The session tracks object changes; flush writes SQL; commit commits the DB transaction. Holding sessions open holds connections — keep them request-scoped.
  • Q: How do you rename a column with zero downtime? A: Expand-contract: add new column, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, drop old — across two deploys, never a single rewriting ALTER on a hot table.
  • Q: Defend or critique ORMs in a system-design answer? A: ORMs win on velocity and consistency for domain writes; raw SQL/query builders win on bulk, reporting, and hot paths. Mature answer: ORM by default, SQL escape hatch measured, N+1 tests enforced.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
1. ORMs map objects to rows with identity map + unit of work — productivity for domain writes.
  2. N+1 is the #1 pathology: eager-load deliberately, count queries in tests.
  3. Flush ≠ commit; sessions are request-scoped and hold connections.
  4. Optimistic locking prevents silent overwrites; expand-contract enables safe migrations.
  5. Default to the ORM for the domain, drop to SQL for bulk, reporting, and hot paths.

docs.title: Blogs
docs.text: • RabbitMQ: A Complete Guide to Message Broker, Performance, and Reliability

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text: • RabbitMQ beginners guide

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
RabbitMQ is a general-purpose message broker speaking AMQP (plus MQTT/STOMP plugins): producers publish to exchanges, bindings route to queues, consumers acknowledge. It excels at flexible routing, per-message acknowledgments, and operational simplicity for task queues, RPC, and event distribution at moderate throughput.

Pick RabbitMQ when routing logic (topics, headers, delayed, dead-letter flows) and broker-managed delivery guarantees matter more than raw log throughput — the complement to Kafka, not its clone.

docs.title: Exchanges, bindings, queues
docs.text: Exchange type Routes by Use for Direct Exact routing key Task queues per type Fanout Broadcast to all bound queues Notifications, cache invalidation Topic *.critical.# patterns Log levels, multi-tenant events Headers Header key-values (no key needed) Content-based routing Consistent-hash / plugins Hash spread Work distribution

docs.title: Delivery semantics
docs.text:
• Ack modes: auto-ack (fast, lossy) vs manual ack (at-least-once with redelivery).
  • Durability: durable exchange + durable queue + persistent delivery mode — all three, or a restart eats messages.
  • Prefetch (basic.qos): caps unacked messages per consumer; the fairness knob that prevents one slow consumer hoarding work.
  • Dead-letter exchanges (DLX): rejected/expired/overflowed messages route to a quarantine queue for inspection and replay.

Real-life scenario: An order pipeline publishes order.created to a topic exchange; bindings fan out to inventory, email, and analytics queues, each with its own retry/DLX policy — one publish, three independent consumers with isolated failure handling.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    P[Producers] --> X["Exchange (direct / topic / fanout)"]
    X -->|binding key| Q1[(Queue: inventory)]
    X -->|binding key| Q2[(Queue: email)]
    X -->|binding key| Q3[(Queue: analytics)]
    Q1 --> C1[Consumers: ack + prefetch]
    Q2 --> C2[Consumers: ack + prefetch]
    Q3 --> C3[Consumers: ack + prefetch]
    Q1 -.->|reject / expire| DLX[(Dead-letter queue)]
Component Responsibility Scaling note Virtual hosts Tenancy + permissions boundary One vhost per service/domain Classic vs quorum queues Classic = speed; quorum = Raft safety Quorum for anything you cannot afford to lose Mirroring / clustering HA across nodes Quorum queues replace old mirroring Management UI + Prometheus Queue depth, publish/ack rates Alert on depth growth, not just consumer count

Real-life scenario: A payments team runs quorum queues with producers confirms on, consumers manual-ack with prefetch 10, and depth/latency alerts — a consumer deploy that slows processing pages before the queue becomes a swamp.

docs.title: Deep Dive / How it works
docs.text:
Publish path: channel → exchange match → routed copies appended to bound queues (durable → fsync per persistence settings) → publisher confirm (confirm.select) asynchronously acks. No confirm = "sent to TCP", not "stored".

Consume path: broker pushes (or consumer polls) up to prefetch → handler processes → basic.ack removes; nack(requeue) redelivers, reject without requeue plus DLX policy quarantines. Poison messages need a retry cap + DLX, otherwise one bad payload redelivers forever and head-of-line-blocks the queue.

Failure story: node loss with classic queues loses unmigrated messages; quorum queues keep majority-confirmed messages with minutes-scale leader re-election. Split-brain demands operator policy (pause-minority) — decide before the partition, not during.

Real-life scenario: A PDF-render queue without DLX gets one corrupt file that crashes every worker; redelivery loops burn CPU for an hour. After adding 5-retry cap → DLX + alerting, the sixth failure quarantines the file and pages with the payload id attached.

docs.title: Practical Examples
docs.text:
# Declare topology once (durable exchange + queues + DLX), then publish persistent
rabbitmqadmin declare exchange name=orders type=topic durable=true
rabbitmqadmin declare queue name=orders.inventory durable=true \
  arguments='{"x-dead-letter-exchange":"orders.dlx"}'
rabbitmqadmin declare binding source=orders destination=orders.inventory routing_key="order.*"

# Producer: confirms on, persistent delivery
import pika
params = pika.ConnectionParameters("localhost")
conn = pika.BlockingConnection(params)
ch = conn.channel()
ch.confirm_delivery()
ch.basic_publish(exchange="orders", routing_key="order.created",
                 body=b'{"id": 9001}', properties=pika.BasicProperties(delivery_mode=2))

# Consumer: manual ack, bounded prefetch, DLX on repeated failure
ch.basic_qos(prefetch_count=10)
def on_msg(ch, method, props, body):
    try:
        handle(body)
        ch.basic_ack(delivery_tag=method.delivery_tag)
    except TransientError:
        ch.basic_nack(delivery_tag=method.delivery_tag, requeue=True)
    except Exception:
        ch.basic_nack(delivery_tag=method.delivery_tag, requeue=False)  # -> DLX
ch.basic_consume(queue="orders.inventory", on_message_callback=on_msg)

docs.title: Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Q: RabbitMQ vs Kafka in one minute? A: RabbitMQ = smart broker, flexible routing, per-message acks, moderate throughput; Kafka = dumb-fast log, replayable partitions, huge throughput. Routing complexity favors RabbitMQ; event sourcing at scale favors Kafka.
  • Q: How do you guarantee a message survives a broker restart? A: Durable exchange + durable queue + persistent (delivery_mode=2) messages + publisher confirms — miss any one and loss is possible.
  • Q: What does prefetch control and what breaks without it? A: Max unacked messages per consumer. Unbounded prefetch lets one fast consumer grab everything while others idle, and a crash redelivers a mountain.
  • Q: How do you handle poison messages? A: Retry counter (header/x-death) with a cap, then reject to a DLX quarantine queue with alerting and a replay tool — never infinite requeue.
  • Q: Classic vs quorum queues? A: Classic for max speed/tolerable loss; quorum (Raft) for safety and HA. New durable workloads should default to quorum.
  • Q: Sketch an order pipeline with failures considered. A: Topic exchange → per-domain queues → manual ack + prefetch → retry with backoff → DLX quarantine → idempotent consumers (dedupe on order id) → depth/age alerts.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
1. Exchanges route, queues buffer, consumers acknowledge — design all three deliberately.
  2. Durability is a trio (exchange + queue + persistent + confirms); partial durability is no durability.
  3. Prefetch bounds blast radius; DLX bounds poison damage.
  4. Quorum queues for anything valuable; classic only where loss is acceptable.
  5. Idempotent consumers + depth alerting turn the broker from a hope into a system.

docs.title: Youtube
docs.text:
• The Power of Vector Databases For Knowledge Search
  • Vector databases are so hot right now. WTF are they?

docs.title: Medium
docs.text: • The Simplified Introduction of Vector Databases

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
A vector database stores high-dimensional embeddings (arrays of floats produced by ML models) and answers nearest-neighbor queries — "find the 10 documents most similar to this query" — at scale. It is the memory layer behind semantic search, RAG chatbots, recommendation engines, and image/audio similarity search.

Use one when ranking by meaning or similarity matters more than exact keyword match or relational joins. Keep ground-truth records in your primary database; store embeddings plus a pointer (document id) in the vector store.

docs.title: Embeddings
docs.text: An embedding maps text, images, or audio to a dense vector (e.g., 384–3072 dimensions) where distance ≈ semantic dissimilarity. Same meaning, different wording → nearby vectors. Common models: sentence-transformers, OpenAI text-embedding-3-*, Cohere embed, CLIP for images.

docs.title: Distance metrics
docs.text:
Metric Formula idea When to use Cosine similarity Angle between vectors (normalized) Text search, most RAG setups Euclidean (L2) Straight-line distance Image embeddings, clustering Dot product Unnormalized alignment Retrieval with trained bi-encoders Hamming Bit differences Binary/quantized vectors

Pick the metric your embedding model was trained with — mismatching metric and model silently degrades recall.

docs.title: Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN)
docs.text:
Exact search is O(n·d) per query — impossible at millions of vectors. ANN indexes trade a few percent recall for 100–1000× speedups:

  • HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World): graph-based, best recall/latency balance, higher memory. Default choice (pgvector, Qdrant, Weaviate, Pinecone).
  • IVF (Inverted File Index): partitions space into clusters, probes top-k clusters. Lower memory, needs training step (FAISS, Milvus).
  • PQ (Product Quantization): compresses vectors into codes. Massive memory savings, slight recall loss; often combined as IVF-PQ.
  • LSH (Locality-Sensitive Hashing): hash collisions ≈ similarity. Simple, rarely best today.

docs.title: Metadata filtering
docs.text:
Production queries are hybrid: "top-10 similar support tickets from tenant X, filed this year." The store must combine vector similarity with scalar filters (tenant_id = ? AND year = ?). Pre-filtering (filter then search) vs post-filtering (search then filter) changes recall — prefer engines with native pre-filtered HNSW.

Real-life scenario: A help-desk RAG bot embeds 2M past tickets with a 768-dim model, stores them in HNSW with a tenant_id payload filter, and answers new questions by retrieving the 8 most similar same-tenant tickets as LLM context — cutting hallucinations because the model grounds on real tickets.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    Docs[Documents / chunks] --> Embed[Embedding model]
    Embed --> Store[("Vector index (HNSW / IVF) + payload")]
    Query[User query] --> QEmbed[Embed query]
    QEmbed --> Search[ANN search + metadata filter]
    Search --> TopK[Top-K hits + ids]
    TopK --> App[App / LLM / ranker]
    Store -.->|filter| Search
Component Responsibility Scaling note Chunker Splits docs into retrievable units Chunk size ~200–800 tokens typical Embedder Query + doc vectors in same space GPU batch for backfill, CPU ok for queries Index ANN structure + payload store Shard by tenant or collection past ~10–50M vectors Ranker (optional) Cross-encoder re-rank of top-K Rerank top-50 → top-5 for quality wins

Real-life scenario: An e-commerce site shards its 40M product vectors by category, keeps HNSW ef_search tuned for p99 < 50 ms, and re-ranks the top-30 with a cross-encoder — search feels instant while conversion-relevant ranking stays high quality.

docs.title: Deep Dive / How it works
docs.text:
Write path: chunk → embed → insert vector with payload (doc_id, tenant_id, ts). HNSW inserts walk the layered graph and link the new node to its nearest neighbors per layer — O(log n). IVF instead assigns the vector to the nearest centroid.

Read path: embed query → enter graph at top layer → greedy walk down to ef_search candidates → score exact distances → apply payload filter (pre-filter prunes the graph walk; post-filter over-fetches then discards) → return top-K with scores.

Trade-offs worth internalizing: higher M (graph degree) and ef_construction raise recall and build cost; higher ef_search raises recall and query latency. Quantization (PQ/scalar) cuts memory 4–8× at ~1–3 points of recall loss. Recall is measured against brute-force ground truth on a sample — always benchmark with your data, not vendor numbers.

Real-life scenario: A team chasing p99 latency halves ef_search from 200 to 100, loses 0.5% recall, and gains 35% latency headroom — an acceptable trade because the downstream LLM tolerates one slightly-off passage in eight.

docs.title: Practical Examples
docs.text:
# Chunk, embed, upsert with Qdrant
from qdrant_client import QdrantClient
from qdrant_client.models import VectorParams, Distance, PointStruct

client = QdrantClient(host="localhost", port=6333)
client.recreate_collection(
    collection_name="tickets",
    vectors_config=VectorParams(size=768, distance=Distance.COSINE),
)

client.upsert(collection_name="tickets", points=[
    PointStruct(id=1, vector=[0.12, -0.03, 0.44, 0.01],
                payload={"tenant_id": "acme", "year": 2026}),
])

# Filtered similarity search: same tenant, this year, top 5
hits = client.search(
    collection_name="tickets",
    query_vector=[0.11, -0.02, 0.43, 0.02],
    query_filter={"must": [
        {"key": "tenant_id", "match": {"value": "acme"}},
        {"key": "year", "match": {"value": 2026}},
    ]},
    limit=5,
)
for h in hits:
    print(h.id, round(h.score, 4), h.payload)

-- Same idea in Postgres with pgvector (HNSW + pre-filter)
CREATE EXTENSION vector;
CREATE TABLE docs (
  id bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id text NOT NULL,
  embedding vector(768) NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX ON docs USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);

SELECT id, 1 - (embedding <=> '[0.11,-0.02,0.43,0.02]'::vector) AS score
FROM docs
WHERE tenant_id = 'acme'
ORDER BY embedding <=> '[0.11,-0.02,0.43,0.02]'::vector
LIMIT 5;

docs.title: Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Q: Why not just store embeddings in Postgres as arrays and scan? A: Brute-force distance over millions of high-dim vectors is O(n·d) per query — milliseconds become seconds. ANN indexes (HNSW/IVF) give ~100× speedups at ~99% recall.
  • Q: Cosine vs Euclidean — does it matter? A: Yes: use the metric the embedding model trained with (usually cosine for text). Mixing metrics silently shifts rankings with no error raised.
  • Q: What is HNSW's ef_search trade-off? A: Higher ef_search explores more candidates: better recall, higher latency. Tune it against a recall-vs-p99 curve on your own data.
  • Q: Pre-filter vs post-filter for tenant isolation? A: Pre-filtering constrains the ANN walk to matching vectors (correct with small tenants); post-filtering over-fetches then discards (can return too few results for selective filters). Prefer native pre-filter support.
  • Q: How do you evaluate a vector-search setup? A: Recall@K against brute-force ground truth on a sampled query set, plus p50/p99 latency and index memory — report all three, never recall alone.
  • Q: Where do vectors fit in a RAG system-design answer? A: Ingest (chunk → embed → upsert with metadata) → retrieve (embed query → filtered ANN top-K → optional re-rank) → generate (LLM with cited passages). Mention chunking, metric choice, and freshness/invalidation.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
1. Vector DBs answer "most similar" queries over embeddings — the memory behind semantic search and RAG.
  2. Match the distance metric to the embedding model; mismatches degrade recall silently.
  3. HNSW is the default ANN index; tune M/ef_*, quantize when memory binds.
  4. Native metadata pre-filtering is what makes multi-tenant vector search correct.
  5. Evaluate with recall@K + p99 latency + memory on your own data, and keep ground truth in the primary DB.

docs.title: Key Mental Models
docs.text:
• Connections: app → TCP → listener → auth → backend process → session → query.
  • Queries: SQL → parse → rewrite → plan → execute → access method → buffers → storage.
  • Writes: tuple change → buffers → WAL → flush → commit → lazy page writeback.
  • MVCC: transaction → snapshot → xmin/xmax → versions → VACUUM.
  • Recovery: WAL → checkpoint → crash → replay → consistency.
  • Replication: primary → WAL → sender → network → receiver → replay → standby.

docs.title: Architecture Recap
docs.text:
flowchart TB

    Pool --> Be["Backends + shared memory"]
    Be --> MVCC["MVCC snapshots + WAL"]
    MVCC --> Store[("Heap/index/TOAST + WAL archive")]
    Store -.->|streaming / logical| Rep[("Replicas / CDC sinks")]

Real-life scenario: A new backend engineer reads this roadmap top to bottom over two weeks, tracing one slow checkout query through connections, memory, storage, MVCC, and vacuum — by the end they diagnose a bloat-driven seq scan from n_dead_tup velocity alone, without senior help.

docs.title: Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Q: How do you use this roadmap in an interview? A: Follow the failing symptom down the stack: connections → memory → storage → MVCC/vacuum → WAL → replication — naming the file (mechanism) at each step instead of guessing.
  • Q: What is the single highest-leverage internals topic for interviews? A: MVCC + VACUUM + WAL as one story (versions → reclaim → durability) — it answers half the "why is Postgres slow/expensive" questions.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
1. Foundations (processes, connections, memory, storage) precede MVCC, which precedes WAL, which precedes everything distributed.
  2. Every file ends with takeaways; every mechanism links its metrics — read mechanism plus meter together.
  3. The interview file compresses all of this into 31 questions; the case-studies file turns it into design judgment.
  4. Learn by tracing one real query down the whole stack, not by memorizing files in order.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
RLS, generated/identity columns, rich types (range, multirange, arrays, JSONB), full-text search, LISTEN/NOTIFY, advisory locks, event triggers, exclusion constraints, and matviews — the features that make PostgreSQL a platform. Internals-first notes per feature with planner/lock implications.

See also:

  • PostgreSQL as More Than a Database
  • PostgreSQL Security Internals
  • Index Internals

docs.title: Feature Notes
docs.text:
• Row-Level Security (CREATE POLICY, USING/WITH CHECK): predicates injected at rewrite; planner can't always push them optimally — verify plans per role. BYPASSRLS for owners; table-owner bypass is a footgun in multi-tenant designs.
  • Security barrier views: prevent predicate-pushdown leaks in RLS/view stacks (security_barrier).
  • Generated columns (GENERATED ALWAYS AS (...) STORED): computed at write, WAL-logged, indexable — materialized-expression trade (write cost vs read speed).
  • Identity columns (GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY): sequence-backed, SQL-standard successor to SERIAL.
  • Domains / composite / enum / range / multirange / arrays / JSONB: typed constraints with GiST/GIN support (range exclusion, array containment). Multirange aggregates disjoint ranges — scheduling/availability modeling without app code.
  • Full-text search (tsvector, tsquery, GIN, ts_rank): indexable lexeme search with dictionaries/stop-words per language.
  • LISTEN/NOTIFY (8000 B payload, transient, coalesced): signaling, not messaging — see platform.
  • Advisory locks: app mutexes; no MVCC interaction; crash releases with session.
  • Event triggers: DDL hooks (audit/migration guardrails) firing on ddl_command_end.
  • Logical replication / matviews (REFRESH ... CONCURRENTLY with unique index): covered in replication / CDC.
  • Exclusion constraints (EXCLUDE USING gist): generalized uniqueness (no-overlap bookings) enforced via index — concurrent inserts serialize on the predicate; design hot paths accordingly.
  • Deferrable constraints: checked at commit (DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED) — enables cyclic FK loads, costs holding checks to commit.
  • Partitioning / FDW: see dedicated files.
CREATE POLICY tenant_iso ON orders USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant')::int);
ALTER TABLE orders ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

docs.title: Hands-on Experiment
docs.text: Enable RLS on a test table, SET app.tenant, and EXPLAIN the same query as different tenants — observe injected quals and plan changes. Add an exclusion constraint on a booking table and collide two concurrent inserts to feel the predicate-lock serialization.

docs.title: Intermediate
docs.text:
• RLS vs application WHERE clauses? — Enforcement in the database survives every client/ORM/reporting tool; misplanned policies cost performance, so EXPLAIN per role.
  • Stored generated vs view expression? — Generated pays at write (WAL + storage) for indexed/fast reads; view pays per read.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Features compose (RLS + partitioning + logical replication) but each adds planner/lock surface — verify combined plans.
  • Prefer database enforcement (constraints, RLS, exclusion) for invariants; app code for presentation.

Real-life scenario: A SaaS puts tenant_id RLS on every table with SET app.tenant per request — one developer's missing SET in a background job leaks cross-tenant rows in staging, caught by a per-role EXPLAIN test in CI before prod. The policy that wasn't verified per role is the policy that fails.

docs.title: Architecture Recap
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Q[Query] --> RW["Rewrite: inject RLS policy quals"]
    RW --> Plan["Planner (verify per role!)"]
    Plan --> Exec["Execute: constraints + indexes + locks"]
    Exec --> Rows[Rows]

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Physical base backup + continuous WAL archiving = point-in-time recovery to any LSN/timestamp. Logical dumps (pg_dump) serve migration and selective restore, not RPO/RTO. This file explains the backup chain, recovery targets, verification, and DR math.

See also:

  • WAL: Write-Ahead Logging
  • Crash Recovery Internals
  • Replication Internals

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text: Backups that have never been restored are hopes, not backups. PITR mechanics determine whether "restore to 5 min before the bad deploy" is a command or a fantasy.

docs.title: Physical vs Logical / pg_dump / pg_basebackup / Filesystem / Archiving / PITR
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Base[Base backup: pg_basebackup] --> WALs[WAL archive chain]
    WALs --> Target[Recovery target: LSN / time / xid / name]
    Target --> DB[Restored cluster]
  • Physical (pg_basebackup -Ft -z -D, or pgBackRest/Barman with parallel+compress+encrypt): whole-cluster byte copy + backup_label with start LSN. Fast, complete, version-coupled.
  • Logical (pg_dump/pg_restore, COPY): per-database SQL/custom-format; portable across versions, slow at scale, no PITR.
  • Continuous archiving (archive_mode = on, archive_command = 'test ! -f /arc/%f && cp %p /arc/%f'): every completed segment preserved. Miss one segment → PITR gap.
  • PITR (recovery_target_time/lsn/xid/name, restore_command = 'cp /arc/%f %p'): replay base + WAL to the target, then recovery_target_action = promote/pause/shutdown. Named restore points (pg_create_restore_point('deploy')) beat timestamps for deploy rollbacks.

docs.title: Consistency / Verification / DR / RPO / RTO / Corruption
docs.text:
• Consistency: base backups are fuzzy (taken while running) + WAL makes them consistent — pg_verifybackup checks manifest checksums (v13+).
  • Verification: automated restore to a sandbox + amcheck + app-level row counts, on schedule. Alert on pg_stat_archiver.failed_count and archive age.
  • RPO/RTO: RPO = archive lag (seconds with streaming archive like pgBackRest async); RTO = base size/bandwidth + WAL volume to replay. Size both from measured restores, not vendor claims.
  • Corruption: checksum failures (--data-checksums) surface at restore/replay; keep multiple base generations + off-site archive copies.
SELECT * FROM pg_stat_archiver;  -- archived_count vs failed_count
SELECT pg_create_restore_point('pre_migration');

docs.title: Hands-on Experiment
docs.text:
1. pg_basebackup -D /tmp/bak -Ft -z -P, note start LSN.
  2. Write rows, SELECT pg_switch_wal();, archive segments.
  3. Restore to a scratch PGDATA, set restore_command, recovery_target_time, boot, verify rows present/absent per target.

docs.title: Symptom: FATAL: requested WAL segment has already been removed
docs.text: Archive gap or retention purge. Fix: rebuild from a newer base; extend retention; never let archive storage share fate with pg_wal disk.

docs.title: Intermediate
docs.text:
• Why can't pg_dump give you PITR? — It's a logical snapshot at dump time with no WAL chain to roll forward through.
  • Base + WAL vs filesystem snapshot? — Snapshots need crash-recovery replay too (fuzzy without pg_start_backup coordination); basebackup + archive is the supported portable chain.

docs.title: Advanced
docs.text: • How do you prove RPO/RTO, not assert them? — Timed restore drills measuring archive lag at incident start and wall-clock to promoted + verified traffic.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Physical + archive = time travel. Logical = portability. Run both, drill the former.
  • pg_stat_archiver + restore drills are the backup monitoring that matters.
  • Restore points beat timestamps for human-driven rollbacks.

Real-life scenario: A dropped production table at 14:07 restores to 14:06 via base backup + WAL replay to a named restore point created before the deploy — 20 minutes of restore, zero data loss, because the drill last quarter proved the archive chain was complete.

docs.title: Architecture Recap
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Base["Base backup"] --> WAL["Archived WAL stream"]
    WAL --> PITR["Replay to LSN / timestamp / restore point"]
    PITR --> Verify["Sandbox verify, then promote"]

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Dirty pages in shared buffers are crash-safe (WAL has them) but must eventually reach heap files to bound recovery time. Checkpoints draw the recovery line; the background writer smooths the flow between checkpoints. Mistuning either turns steady writes into latency spikes.

See also:

  • WAL: Write-Ahead Logging
  • PostgreSQL Write Path
  • PostgreSQL Memory Architecture
  • Crash Recovery Internals

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text: Checkpoint spikes are a top-3 "mystery p99 latency" cause. Understanding dirty-page lifecycle converts them from mystery to arithmetic.

docs.title: Checkpoints / Why They Exist / Lifecycle / Segments
docs.text:
A checkpoint (src/backend/postmaster/checkpointer.c):

  1. Writes a checkpoint WAL record (with current LSN = redo point).
  2. Flushes all dirty buffers up to that LSN to heap/index files (+ fsync).
  3. Updates pg_control with the new redo pointer.
  4. Allows recycling of older WAL segments.

Recovery replays only WAL after the last redo point — checkpoints bound RTO at the cost of write I/O.

flowchart LR
    Dirty[Dirty buffers] --> CKPT[Checkpoint: flush to LSN N]
    CKPT --> Control[pg_control redo=N]
    Control --> Recycle[Recycle WAL < N]
    Crash --> Replay[Replay WAL from N]

docs.title: Checkpoint Timeout / Completion Target / max_wal_size
docs.text:
Setting Effect checkpoint_timeout (5 min default) max time between checkpoints max_wal_size (1 GB default) WAL growth forces an early checkpoint — the usual trigger on write-heavy systems min_wal_size WAL retained even when idle (avoids recycle churn) checkpoint_completion_target (0.9) spread flush over 90% of the interval — the smoothing knob

Whichever hits first (time or WAL volume) triggers. On busy systems max_wal_size dominates; the default 1 GB checkpoints far too often — 4–16 GB is common in production with adequate disk.

docs.title: Background Writer vs Checkpointer / Dirty Buffers / Flushing
docs.text:
• Background writer: continuously writes a trickle of dirty/aged buffers (bgwriter_delay, bgwriter_lru_maxpages) so checkpoints find less work. Opportunistic, throttled, never fsyncs for durability (WAL already has that).
  • Checkpointer: the periodic full flush + redo-pointer advance. Does the fsyncs that actually move the recovery line.

Mental model: bgwriter keeps the sink dripping; checkpointer empties the tub on schedule.

docs.title: Checkpoint I/O / Spikes / Latency / WAL Volume
docs.text:
A checkpoint flushes potentially gigabytes in seconds → data-device saturation → foreground queries queue on buffer locks and I/O. log_checkpoints = on + log_autovacuum_min_duration reveal the correlation:

LOG: checkpoint starting: time
LOG: checkpoint complete: wrote 45012 buffers (351 MB); ... sync=12.4s

If p99 spikes align with these lines, it's checkpoint I/O, not queries.

docs.title: Tuning Checkpoints / Checkpoint Storms
docs.text:
1. Raise max_wal_size (fewer, larger checkpoints) and keep checkpoint_completion_target = 0.9.
  2. Ensure bgwriter is actually cleaning (pg_stat_bgwriter.buffers_clean growing; buffers_backend high means backends do the flushing = under-tuned bgwriter).
  3. Separate pg_wal onto its own device so checkpoint reads don't fight WAL fsyncs.
  4. Checkpoint storms: many replicas/hosts checkpointing simultaneously after a shared event (failover, deploy) — stagger checkpoint_timeout or accept one slower cycle.
SELECT buffers_checkpoint, buffers_clean, buffers_backend,
       buffers_backend_fsync FROM pg_stat_bgwriter;
-- healthy: clean >> backend; sick: backend dominates

docs.title: What Actually Happens Internally?
docs.text:
Time-based checkpoint:

  1. Checkpointer signals backends to pause buffer allocation briefly, records redo LSN.
  2. Sorts dirty buffers, writes them (spread over completion_target × interval), fsyncs files.
  3. Writes checkpoint record to WAL, updates pg_control, signals archiver/recycler.

docs.title: Hands-on Experiment
docs.text:
ALTER SYSTEM SET log_checkpoints = on; SELECT pg_reload_conf();
CHECKPOINT;  -- watch log: buffers written, sync time
SHOW max_wal_size; SHOW checkpoint_timeout; SHOW checkpoint_completion_target;
-- run pgbench write load, observe checkpoint cadence in logs vs p99

docs.title: Symptom: periodic latency spikes every few minutes
docs.text: Diagnose: enable log_checkpoints, correlate spike timestamps with checkpoint-complete lines; check pg_stat_bgwriter. Fix: raise max_wal_size, set completion_target = 0.9, tune bgwriter lru_maxpages, isolate pg_wal device.

docs.title: Intermediate
docs.text:
• What does a checkpoint guarantee vs what WAL already guarantees? — WAL guarantees durability; checkpoint bounds recovery time by moving the redo pointer forward and allowing WAL recycling.
  • Bgwriter vs checkpointer in one sentence each? — Bgwriter trickles dirty pages early to smooth load; checkpointer periodically flushes everything to advance the recovery line.

docs.title: Advanced
docs.text:
• Why does raising max_wal_size reduce spikes but increase recovery time? — Fewer checkpoints = larger flush batches spread thinner, but more WAL to replay after a crash. RTO vs smoothness trade, explicitly.
  • What is buffers_backend telling you when it dominates? — Backends are flushing their own victims because bgwriter/checkpointer can't keep up — I/O or tuning deficit.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Checkpoints trade recovery time for I/O smoothness; size them from WAL rate, not defaults.
  • completion_target = 0.9 + adequate max_wal_size + working bgwriter = flat p99.
  • log_checkpoints is non-negotiable in production.

Real-life scenario: Commit p99 spikes every 5 minutes in lockstep with checkpoint start; log_checkpoints shows sync-heavy flushes and max_wal_size too small. Raising it with checkpoint_completion_target = 0.9 spreads writes and the spikes vanish — sized from WAL rate, not defaults.

docs.title: Architecture Recap
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Dirty["Dirty buffers"] --> BG["Background writer (trickle)"]
    Dirty --> CKPT["Checkpoint (redo pointer + flush)"]
    CKPT --> Replay["Bounded crash replay"]

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
postgresql.conf + ALTER SYSTEM + per-database/role SET form a precedence stack, with restart-vs-reload semantics per parameter. This file explains the layers, the dangerous knobs by subsystem, and how to change production safely.

See also:

  • PostgreSQL Logging and Debugging
  • PostgreSQL Memory Architecture
  • Monitoring PostgreSQL Internals

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text: Most PostgreSQL outages from "tuning" come from precedence surprises (ALTER SYSTEM overriding the file edit) or restart-required changes applied without restart. Know the stack and the context column.

docs.title: Files / ALTER SYSTEM / Reload vs Restart / Session / Transaction / Precedence / pg_settings
docs.text:
defaults → postgresql.conf → conf.d/*.conf → postgresql.auto.conf (ALTER SYSTEM)
  → per-database → per-role → per-session SET → per-transaction SET LOCAL
  (later wins; command line -c/-o beats all files)

SELECT name, setting, unit, context, source, sourcefile
FROM pg_settings WHERE source <> 'default' ORDER BY name;
-- context: internal | postmaster(restart) | sighup(reload) | superuser | user
  • Reload (pg_reload_conf()): sighup parameters (most logging, vacuum costs, timeouts).
  • Restart: postmaster parameters (shared_buffers, max_connections, wal_level, shared_preload_libraries, ports).
  • ALTER SYSTEM writes postgresql.auto.conf — it overrides hand-edited conf; always inspect source when a change "doesn't take".

docs.title: Knob Map by Subsystem
docs.text:
Area Key parameters Change class Memory shared_buffers, work_mem, maintenance_work_mem, effective_cache_size restart / reload(user) — see Memory WAL wal_level, synchronous_commit, wal_compression, max_wal_size, archive_mode mixed; wal_level needs restart Connections max_connections, superuser_reserved_connections, timeouts, keepalives restart for max; reload for timeouts Autovacuum thresholds, scale factors, cost limits, workers reload — safe to iterate live Planner random_page_cost, effective_cache_size, *_cost, jit reload; session-testable via SET Parallelism max_worker_processes (restart), max_parallel_workers* (reload) split contexts — check pg_settings

Safe-change protocol: stage on a replica/canary → ALTER SYSTEM + reload → watch pg_settings.source + metrics → commit to config management (Ansible/Terraform/operator CRD) so the DB isn't the source of truth.

docs.title: Hands-on Experiment
docs.text:
SHOW work_mem;  -- session value
SET work_mem = '64MB'; SHOW work_mem;          -- session override
BEGIN; SET LOCAL work_mem = '256MB'; SHOW work_mem; COMMIT;
SHOW work_mem;  -- back to session
SELECT name, context, source FROM pg_settings WHERE name IN ('shared_buffers','work_mem','max_connections');

docs.title: Intermediate
docs.text:
• Why didn't my postgresql.conf edit take effect? — postgresql.auto.conf (ALTER SYSTEM) overrides it, or the parameter needs restart/reload you didn't perform. pg_settings.source tells you.
  • Session vs transaction settings? — SET lasts the session; SET LOCAL lasts the transaction — used for per-report work_mem boosts without global risk.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Read pg_settings (context + source) before changing anything.
  • Reload-safe knobs (vacuum, timeouts, planner costs) iterate live; restart knobs plan with failover.
  • Config management owns the files; the database is the runtime, not the repo.

Real-life scenario: An engineer edits postgresql.conf to raise max_connections but an old ALTER SYSTEM SET in postgresql.auto.conf silently wins — the restart changes nothing and the outage repeats. SELECT * FROM pg_settings WHERE source <> 'default' would have shown the real winner in 5 seconds.

docs.title: Architecture Recap
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    D["Defaults"] --> F["postgresql.conf + conf.d"]
    F --> A["postgresql.auto.conf (ALTER SYSTEM)"]
    A --> R["Per-db / per-role / session SET"]
    R --> Eff["Effective value (later wins)"]

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
After any unclean shutdown, the startup process replays WAL from the last checkpoint's redo pointer, reconstructing dirty pages forward to consistency. This file explains REDO mechanics, torn-page defense, and recovery performance.

See also:

  • WAL: Write-Ahead Logging
  • Checkpoints and Background Writer
  • Backup and Recovery Internals

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text: Crash recovery is the proof of the WAL design: committed data survives anything except WAL loss. Recovery time is the single-instance RTO floor — size checkpoints and WAL accordingly.

docs.title: After Crash / REDO / Checkpoint Records / Start-End Points / Dirty Pages / Durability
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Control[pg_control: last redo LSN] --> Scan[Scan WAL forward]
    Scan --> Redo[REDO each record: apply to pages]
    Redo --> FPI[Full-page images fix torn pages]
    FPI --> End[End-of-WAL: consistent, new checkpoint]
  1. Startup reads pg_control for the last checkpoint's redo LSN.
  2. Replays every WAL record after it (heap/index mutations, FPIs, commit markers).
  3. Dirty pages in buffers at crash time are irrelevant — replay reconstructs them from WAL + surviving files.
  4. Writes an end-of-recovery checkpoint; postmaster opens for connections.

fsync + full_page_writes are the load-bearing guarantees: without durable WAL fsyncs, "committed" is fiction; without FPIs, torn pages (half-written 8 KB) can't be repaired by delta replay.

docs.title: Torn Pages / Corruption / Performance / Conflicts
docs.text:
• Torn pages: OS writes 8 KB in sectors; crash mid-page leaves halves from different eras. First-touch FPI after each checkpoint gives replay a whole-page baseline — the reason disabling full_page_writes needs page-atomic storage proof.
  • Recovery performance: proportional to WAL since last checkpoint (hence max_wal_size/checkpoint_timeout set RTO) + FPI volume + storage replay bandwidth. recovery_prefetch/recovery_init_sync_method tune replay I/O.
  • Corruption: checksum mismatch during replay halts recovery at the bad record — restore from base + archive skipping past it (data loss window) or page-level salvage (zero_damaged_pages as last resort, with acknowledged data loss).

docs.title: Hands-on Experiment
docs.text:
SHOW data_checksums;  -- on for modern initdb
CHECKPOINT;
-- kill -9 a backend-heavy pgbench run's postmaster (test host!), restart, watch:
-- LOG: database system was not properly shut down; automatic recovery in progress
-- LOG: redo starts at ... ; LOG: database system is ready (replay time visible)

docs.title: Intermediate
docs.text:
• Why does restart take minutes after a crash but seconds after clean shutdown? — Clean shutdown checkpointed everything; crash replays all WAL since the last redo pointer.
  • What exactly do full-page images repair? — Torn pages: replaying deltas onto a half-written page diverges; FPI restores the whole page first, then deltas apply cleanly.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• REDO-forward from the last checkpoint is the entire recovery model — everything else is tuning its cost.
  • full_page_writes + honest fsync are non-negotiable on ordinary storage.
  • Checkpoint cadence sets crash RTO; measure replay time, don't assume it.

Real-life scenario: A kill -9 on a loaded primary restarts in 4 minutes replaying WAL since the last checkpoint; the team measures replay rate, raises max_wal_size slightly, and crash RTO drops under 90 s — recovery time is a tunable, once measured.

docs.title: Architecture Recap
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Crash["Unclean shutdown"] --> Redo["REDO from redo LSN"]
    Redo --> FPI["Full-page images repair torn pages"]
    FPI --> Ready["Consistent + new checkpoint"]

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
FDWs expose remote systems (PostgreSQL, files, S3, Chánh APIs) as local tables with pushdown optimization. postgres_fdw enables federated queries and online migration patterns. This file explains the architecture, pushdown economics, and performance cliffs.

See also:

  • PostgreSQL Extensions
  • Query Execution Internals

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text: FDW queries look local but execute remotely — without pushdown understanding, a "simple join" fetches entire remote tables. Know what ships where before using FDWs past prototyping.

docs.title: Architecture / Servers / Tables / postgres_fdw / Pushdown / Remote Txns
docs.text:
CREATE EXTENSION postgres_fdw;
CREATE SERVER remote FOREIGN DATA WRAPPER postgres_fdw OPTIONS (host 'db2', dbname 'app');
CREATE USER MAPPING FOR app SERVER remote OPTIONS (user 'app', password '...');
CREATE FOREIGN TABLE remote_orders (...) SERVER remote OPTIONS (schema_name 'public', table_name 'orders');
  • Pushdown (src/backend/foreign/ + fdw callbacks): WHERE clauses, joins (v14+ full outer/cross improvements), aggregates, LIMIT ship remotely when the FDW proves semantic equivalence. EXPLAIN (VERBOSE) shows Remote SQL: — the shipped fragment. Non-pushable expressions (custom functions, collations) force local fetch + filter.
  • Remote transactions: each foreign scan opens a remote txn; 2PC across servers is not coordinated — cross-server writes are best-effort consistent, not atomic.

docs.title: Performance / Federation / Cross-DB Queries
docs.text:
Cost model: remote startup + row-transfer dominates; one selective pushed-down query is fine, join-heavy analytics across servers is not. Use FDWs for: migrations (dual-read cutover), rare admin joins, archiving to cheap stores. Avoid for: hot-path joins, high-frequency OLTP fan-out, anything needing cross-server transactions.

EXPLAIN (VERBOSE, COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM remote_orders WHERE status='shipped' LIMIT 10;
-- check Remote SQL includes WHERE + LIMIT; if not, add indexes remotely or restructure

docs.title: Intermediate
docs.text:
• What determines whether a filter runs remotely? — FDW deparse proof: built-in ops on remote columns push; volatile/custom functions don't.
  • Why no atomic cross-server writes? — Independent remote transactions without 2PC coordination; failure mid-write leaves partial effects.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Remote SQL in EXPLAIN is the whole performance story — read it before shipping FDW queries.
  • Federate reads for migrations and admin; don't build hot paths on cross-server joins.

Real-life scenario: A "simple" dashboard join between local users and a foreign orders table fetches 40M remote rows because the WHERE on a custom function can't push down — EXPLAIN VERBOSE shows an empty Remote SQL, and adding a remote index + sargable predicate drops it to 200 rows shipped.

docs.title: Architecture Recap
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Q[Local query] --> Deparse["FDW deparse: what ships?"]
    Deparse -->|pushable| Rem["Remote SQL (WHERE + LIMIT + agg)"]
    Deparse -->|custom fn| Local["Fetch all + filter locally (slow!)"]
    Rem --> Merge["Merge + return"]
    Local --> Merge

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
PostgreSQL indexes are pluggable access methods over the same buffer/WAL/MVCC substrate as the heap. B-tree dominates, but GiST/SP-GiST/GIN/BRIN/hash/bloom each solve a shape B-tree can't. This file explains page-level mechanics, MVCC interaction, bloat, and maintenance.

See also:

  • PostgreSQL Storage Architecture
  • Query Execution Internals
  • VACUUM Internals
  • Partitioning Internals

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text: "Add an index" is the most prescribed and most mispredicted optimization. Index choice determines write amplification, vacuum load, and whether plans can use index-only scans. This file makes the trade-offs mechanical.

docs.title: Index Architecture / Access Methods
docs.text: src/backend/access/ hosts one directory per AM (nbtree/, hash/, gist/, gin/, brin/, spgist/, bloom/ via extension), each implementing the IndexAmRoutine interface (insert, vacuum cleanup, scan paths, cost estimates). pg_am + pg_opclass/pg_opfamily map SQL operators (<, &&, @>, <->) to the AMs that can serve them — an index is only usable for operators in its family.

docs.title: B-tree Internals / Pages / Root / Internal / Leaf / Splits
docs.text:
Default AM, general ordered search (src/backend/access/nbtree/):

flowchart TB
    Root[B-tree root] --> Int[Internal pages: high keys + downlinks]
    Int --> Leaf[Leaf pages: index tuples + heap TIDs, doubly linked]
  • Inserts descend to the leaf, insert the (key, heap-TID) tuple; full leaf → page split (half moves to a new page, parent gets a downlink; splits can cascade to the root, growing depth).
  • Rightmost behavior: append-only keys (sequence PK, now()) always split the rightmost page — contention point + half-empty pages; v11+ suffix-truncation and v13+ deduplication (identical key payloads share one posting list) mitigate it.
  • Versions: pg_index.indnatts/indclass evolve (deduplication, bottom-up index deletion in v14+ lets backends prune dead entries during scans, reducing vacuum urgency).

docs.title: Index Tuples / Deduplication / Versioning
docs.text: Index tuples lack MVCC headers — they point at heap TIDs and inherit visibility from the heap. Dead heap versions leave dead index entries until vacuum cleanup (or bottom-up deletion prunes them during scans). Deduplication compresses repeated keys (low-cardinality + non-unique indexes shrink dramatically).

docs.title: Index-Only Scans / Visibility Map / Bitmap Scans
docs.text:
• Index-only scan: possible when all needed columns are in the index (INCLUDE covering) and the VM all-visible bit is set for each heap page touched. Without maintained VM bits (weak vacuum), "index-only" degrades to heap fetches — monitor heap fetches in EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS).
  • Bitmap heap scan: index builds a TID bitmap, heap fetched in physical order — the random-to-sequential I/O conversion for medium-selectivity queries. Bitmaps spill at work_mem (lossy pages → rechecks).

docs.title: Other AMs: Hash / GiST / SP-GiST / GIN / BRIN / Bloom
docs.text:
AM Shape Use when Hash equality only = lookups where B-tree comparison overhead matters; no ordering/scans GiST balanced tree, custom consistent/union geometry (PostGIS), ranges, nearest-neighbor (<-> with ORDER BY ... LIMIT) SP-GiST partitioned search (quad/radix tries) non-overlapping ranges, IPs, texts with prefix structure GIN inverted index (item → row list) jsonb @>, arrays @>, full-text @@, trigram pg_trgm BRIN per-page-block summaries append-only time series, TB-scale scans with tiny index Bloom (bloom ext) probabilistic multi-column many-column equality filters where compound B-tree is too big

Operator classes matter: text_pattern_ops for LIKE 'abc%', jsonb_path_ops for small GIN on containment-only workloads.

docs.title: Expressions / Partial / Covering / Multicolumn / Ordering / Correlation
docs.text:
• Expression: CREATE INDEX ON t ((lower(email))) — queries must match the expression exactly.
  • Partial: WHERE status = 'active' — small index over the hot subset; planner uses it only when the query implies the predicate.
  • Covering (INCLUDE): payload columns without ordering overhead — index-only scan enabler.
  • Multicolumn: leftmost-prefix rule; order by equality-first, range/sort-last; write cost per extra column.
  • Correlation (pg_stats.correlation): physical vs logical order alignment — high correlation favors index scans, low favors bitmap/seq.

docs.title: Size / Bloat / Maintenance / REINDEX / Concurrent Builds
docs.text:
• Indexes bloat from dead entries + splits; pgstatindex() (pgstattuple ext) shows leaf density.
  • REINDEX CONCURRENTLY (v12+) rebuilds without blocking writes; plain REINDEX locks.
  • CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY: two-pass build (scan + catch-up) that doesn't block writes but takes longer and can leave INVALID indexes on failure (check pg_index.indisvalid).
  • Write amplification: each index adds heap-TID entries per INSERT/UPDATE(non-HOT) + WAL + vacuum cleanup. The 6th index on a hot table costs more than the first five combined in operational terms.

docs.title: What Actually Happens Internally?
docs.text:
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx ON orders (customer_id):

  1. First snapshot scan builds initial entries while writes continue.
  2. Wait for old snapshots to drain; second pass catches entries written concurrently.
  3. Validate, mark valid, update planner stats (needs ANALYZE for best plans immediately).

B-tree split: leaf full → allocate sibling, move upper half, post downlink to parent (WAL-logged, possibly cascading).

docs.title: Hands-on Experiment
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE i(id serial primary key, v int);
INSERT INTO i(v) SELECT (random()*100)::int FROM generate_series(1,200000);
CREATE INDEX i_v ON i(v);
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM i WHERE v = 42;       -- index scan
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT v FROM i WHERE v BETWEEN 10 AND 90;  -- bitmap?
VACUUM i; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT v FROM i WHERE v > 0;      -- index-only after VM set

docs.title: Symptom: index exists but planner seq-scans
docs.text: Diagnose: selectivity (EXPLAIN rows estimate vs actual), correlation, enable_seqscan left off in debugging, stale stats (last_analyze), operator not in index's opfamily, parameterized generic plan. Fix: ANALYZE, correct opclass, covering INCLUDE, or accept the seq scan (small tables should seq-scan).

docs.title: Intermediate
docs.text:
• Why do index-only scans still hit the heap sometimes? — VM bit unset (vacuum lag) or columns not covered; heap fetches counts it.
  • Leftmost-prefix rule in practice? — (a,b) serves a = ? and a = ? AND b = ?, not b = ? alone.

docs.title: Advanced
docs.text:
• How does bottom-up deletion change vacuum urgency? — Backends prune dead leaf entries during scans, so read-heavy indexes self-clean; write-only indexes still need vacuum cleanup.
  • When is BRIN better than B-tree on a TB table? — Append-ordered data (time series): KB-sized summary vs GB-sized B-tree, at the cost of block-range rechecks.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• AM first, columns second: match the data shape and operators to the access method.
  • Every index is a write-amplification and vacuum liability — count them like dependencies.
  • VM maintenance determines whether index-only scans actually skip the heap.

Real-life scenario: WHERE email = ? ignores the btree because the column is citext and the index is on text — opfamily mismatch. A matching expression index restores 1 ms lookups; EXPLAIN plus pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan = 0 found the unused index first.

docs.title: Architecture Recap
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Q["Predicate + operator"] --> AM{"Access method? (btree/GIN/GiST/BRIN)"}
    AM --> Idx["Index scan → heap fetch (or index-only via VM)"]
    Idx --> Rows[Rows]

docs.title: Introduction to PostgreSQL
docs.text:
PostgreSQL is an open-source, process-based, MVCC relational database with an extensible architecture: pluggable index access methods, extensions (PostGIS, pgvector, TimescaleDB), logical replication, and JSONB support that let it serve as OLTP store, analytics engine, queue, search index, and CDC source.

This section covers PostgreSQL from the user level up; the deep internals series starts at PostgreSQL Internals.

docs.title: Why PostgreSQL
docs.text:
• Correctness-first: MVCC + WAL + SSI give strong guarantees without read locks.
  • Extensible: types, indexes, functions, FDWs, and background workers without forking the server.
  • Operational maturity: streaming/logical replication, PITR, and a large HA ecosystem (Patroni, CloudNativePG, managed clouds).

docs.title: Core Concepts (User Level)
docs.text:
-- databases hold schemas, schemas hold tables
CREATE DATABASE app;
CREATE TABLE users (id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, email text UNIQUE NOT NULL);

-- transactions are atomic, consistent, isolated, durable
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;
  • Schemas namespace tables; constraints (PK, FK, unique, check, exclusion) enforce invariants in the database, not the app.
  • Indexes (B-tree default, plus GIN/GiST/BRIN/hash) trade write cost for read speed — see Index Internals.
  • Transactions with Read Committed (default), Repeatable Read, or Serializable isolation — see Isolation and Transaction Internals.

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
psql "host=localhost dbname=app user=app"

Authentication (pg_hba.conf, SCRAM), TLS, and pooling (PgBouncer) are covered in PostgreSQL Connection Internals.

docs.title: Where Next
docs.text:

  • Architecture overview: PostgreSQL Architecture
  • External resources: Links

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    App[Application] --> Pool["PgBouncer / pool"]
    Pool --> Be["Backend process (one per connection)"]
    Be --> Engine["MVCC + WAL + planner"]
    Engine --> Data[("Heap + indexes + WAL files")]
    Engine -.->|streaming / logical| Replica[("Replicas")]

Real-life scenario: A team outgrows slow checkout queries; they add a covering index (see Index Internals), move sessions to PgBouncer, and cut p99 from 900 ms to 60 ms — the user-level playbook before touching internals.

docs.title: Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Q: Why is Postgres the default choice for new OLTP services? A: Correctness-first MVCC + WAL durability, extensibility (types, indexes, extensions), and a mature HA/replication ecosystem.
  • Q: When does Postgres stop being enough? A: Single-writer WAL/vacuum saturation on extreme writes, or specialist ceilings (vectors, search relevance, streams) — then extract via logical replication/CDC.
  • Q: What are the first three things to check when Postgres is slow? A: Connection pressure (pg_stat_activity + pool stats), the plan (EXPLAIN — seq scan? misestimate?), and bloat/vacuum lag (dead tuples) — in that order.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
1. Postgres = process-based MVCC relational DB with WAL durability and deep extensibility.
  2. Schemas/constraints/indexes enforce integrity in the DB; transactions default to Read Committed.
  3. Pool connections (PgBouncer), index hot paths, and read EXPLAIN before scaling hardware.
  4. This page is the user-level map; the internals series traces every mechanism underneath.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
PostgreSQL transactions are XID-stamped snapshot scopes with three isolation levels implemented three different ways: per-statement snapshots (Read Committed), one snapshot per transaction (Repeatable Read), and predicate-tracked SSI (Serializable) — plus subtransactions, 2PC, and wraparound discipline. This file connects isolation theory to the XID/snapshot machinery.

See also:

  • MVCC Internals
  • Locks and Concurrency Internals
  • VACUUM Internals (wraparound)

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text: Choosing an isolation level without knowing its implementation means choosing anomalies you can't predict. This file makes each level's guarantees and failure modes mechanical.

docs.title: Lifecycle / XIDs / Snapshots / Boundaries
docs.text: BEGIN (assigns no XID until first write — lazy XID assignment saves IDs for read-only txns) → statements (snapshots per level) → COMMIT (assign commit LSN, mark pg_xact, flush WAL) or ABORT (mark aborted, release locks). src/backend/access/transam/xact.c owns the state machine; GetSnapshotData() owns visibility.

docs.title: Read Committed Internals
docs.text: Default. New snapshot per statement: each statement sees data committed before it started. Consequences: non-repeatable reads and phantom rows across statements in one transaction — but also the level where UPDATE ... WHERE re-evaluates the latest committed version on write-conflict retry (PostgreSQL's EvalPlanQual recheck), so concurrent updates serialize rather than fail.

docs.title: Repeatable Read Internals
docs.text: One snapshot for the whole transaction: repeatable reads, no phantoms — at the price of write conflicts. Updating a row changed after your snapshot aborts with could not serialize access due to concurrent update. Long RR transactions pin old snapshots → vacuum/wraparound pressure. Use for consistent multi-statement reports, not for OLTP update loops.

docs.title: Serializable / SSI / Serialization Failures / Snapshot Visibility
docs.text:
True serializability via Serializable Snapshot Isolation (src/backend/storage/predicate/): tracks read predicates (SIREAD locks) and write dependencies, aborts transactions whose commit order would be non-serializable (could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies). Applications must retry serialization failures — the level is unusable without retry loops. Predicates consume shared memory (max_pred_locks_per_transaction); overflow degrades to coarser tracking (more false aborts, never missed anomalies).

Level Snapshot scope Anomalies prevented Failure mode Read Committed per statement lost update (via recheck) non-repeatable reads, phantoms Repeatable Read per transaction + phantoms, non-repeatable concurrent-update abort Serializable (SSI) per transaction + predicates + serialization anomalies read/write-dependency abort (retry)

docs.title: Subtransactions / Savepoints / 2PC / Prepared Transactions
docs.text:
• Savepoints (SAVEPOINT s; ROLLBACK TO s): subtransactions with their own resource owners — partial rollback without aborting. Cost: each savepoint forces WAL/XID bookkeeping; thousands per transaction (ORM anti-patterns) bloat pg_xact and slow commit.
  • 2PC (PREPARE TRANSACTION 'gid'; COMMIT PREPARED): durable prepared state in pg_twophase/ surviving crashes, for distributed coordinators. Danger: forgotten prepared xacts pin xmin forever (wraparound/blocked vacuum) — monitor pg_prepared_xacts and alert.

docs.title: Wraparound / XID Consumption / Long Transactions / Idle-in-Transaction
docs.text:
Covered mechanically in MVCC Internals and VACUUM Internals; transaction-layer summary:

  • Read-only transactions consume no XID (lazy assignment) — safe to be long-ish.
  • Any write transaction, plus VACUUM-blocking snapshot holders, advances the danger: age(datfrozenxid) in pg_database is the cluster-wide countdown.
  • idle in transaction with prior writes holds XID + snapshot + locks — the worst combination; idle_in_transaction_session_timeout exists for exactly this.
SELECT datname, age(datfrozenxid) AS xid_age FROM pg_database;
SELECT pid, now()-xact_start AS age, query FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE xact_start IS NOT NULL ORDER BY xact_start LIMIT 10;

docs.title: What Actually Happens Internally?
docs.text:
RR transaction updating a concurrently-changed row:

  1. BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; SELECT — snapshot S taken.
  2. Concurrent txn commits a change to row R.
  3. UPDATE ... R — executor finds R's new version is invisible-to-S but committed-after-S → error could not serialize, transaction must roll back and retry (no EvalPlanQual escape hatch at RR+, unlike Read Committed).

docs.title: Hands-on Experiment
docs.text: T1: BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; SELECT * FROM t WHERE id=1; T2: UPDATE t SET v=2 WHERE id=1; COMMIT; T1: UPDATE t SET v=3 WHERE id=1; → serialization error. Repeat at Read Committed: T1's UPDATE succeeds (rechecks latest version). This contrast is the isolation implementation.

docs.title: Symptom: prepared transaction with identifier "x" has been prepared lingering for days
docs.text: Orphaned 2PC from a dead coordinator. Fix: verify with coordinator owner, then ROLLBACK PREPARED 'x' (or commit). Alert on count(*) FROM pg_prepared_xacts > 0.

docs.title: Intermediate
docs.text:
• Why do lazy XIDs matter? — Read-only traffic doesn't consume the 4B XID space or freeze work; only writers advance wraparound.
  • Read Committed vs Repeatable Read in one mechanism? — Snapshot scope: per-statement vs per-transaction.

docs.title: Advanced
docs.text:
• Why must serializable apps retry, and what happens without it? — SSI detects non-serializable orders by aborting; without retry the business operation silently never happens.
  • Savepoint abuse cost? — Each savepoint is a real subtransaction with resource-owner + WAL overhead; thousands per txn slows commit and bloats state.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Isolation = snapshot scope + conflict policy. Know both per level.
  • Long write transactions are a cluster-health hazard (vacuum, wraparound, bloat) — keep them short or read-only.
  • Prepared transactions need an owner and an alert; orphans are wraparound time-bombs.

Real-life scenario: Two concurrent booking transactions both read "1 seat left" under Read Committed and both insert — double booking. Serializable would abort one with 40001; the app retries the loser and the user sees "sold out" instead of two confirmations for one seat.

docs.title: Architecture Recap
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Txn[Transaction] --> Snap["Snapshot (xmin/xmax)"]
    Snap --> RC["Read Committed: fresh snapshot per statement"]
    Snap --> RR["Repeatable Read: one snapshot per txn"]
    Snap --> SSI["Serializable: snapshot + predicate tracking (abort on cycle)"]

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
PostgreSQL layers three lock systems: heavyweight table/row locks (multi-granularity, in shared memory), light LWLocks protecting internal structures, and spinlocks for single instructions. No lock escalation, MVCC eliminating read locks, and deadlock detection instead of prevention. This file maps modes, queues, and failure behavior.

See also:

  • MVCC Internals
  • Isolation and Transaction Internals
  • Monitoring PostgreSQL Internals

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text: "Query stuck" is almost always lock queueing; "deadlock found" is application ordering; "reporting blocks deploys" is lock-mode conflict. The compatibility matrix below answers all three.

docs.title: Locking Architecture / Lock Manager / Modes / Compatibility / Queues
docs.text:
src/backend/storage/lmgr/ implements heavyweight locks keyed by (type, database, relation, page, tuple). Main table modes:

Mode Taken by Conflicts with AccessShare SELECT AccessExclusive only RowShare SELECT FOR UPDATE/SHARE Exclusive, AccessExclusive RowExclusive INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE Share, ShareRowExclusive, Exclusive, AX Share CREATE INDEX (non-concurrent) RowExclusive+ ShareRowExclusive CREATE TRIGGER, FK checks RowExclusive+ Exclusive REFRESH MATVIEW CONCURRENTLY steps most writes AccessExclusive ALTER TABLE, DROP, VACUUM FULL, CLUSTER everything, including reads

Queues are FIFO-ish with priorities: a waiting AccessExclusive (e.g., migration) blocks new AccessShare grants behind it — which is how one ALTER TABLE freezes an entire app (lock pile-up, not just the alter waiting).

SELECT pid, locktype, relation::regclass, mode, granted,
       now() - query_start AS wait
FROM pg_locks JOIN pg_stat_activity USING (pid)
WHERE NOT granted ORDER BY query_start;

docs.title: Table / Row / Tuple / Predicate / Advisory Locks
docs.text:
• Row locks: stored in tuple xmax/MultiXact, not the lock table — SELECT FOR UPDATE marks the version; concurrent updaters get WriteConflict/serialization errors per isolation level.
  • Predicate locks (serializable): SIREAD locks in shared memory tracking read predicates for SSI conflict detection.
  • Advisory locks (pg_advisory_lock(key)): application-managed mutexes outside MVCC — session or transaction scoped. Coordination primitive (leader election, single-flight jobs) with no table involved. Must handle crash-release semantics explicitly.

docs.title: SELECT FOR UPDATE/SHARE / No Escalation / LWLocks / Spinlocks
docs.text:
• FOR UPDATE (write intent), FOR SHARE (read-stability intent), FOR NO KEY UPDATE/KEY SHARE (weaker, FK-friendly variants that reduce upgrade conflicts).
  • No lock escalation: PostgreSQL never upgrades many row locks to a table lock (unlike SQL Server). Memory stays bounded because row locks live in tuples/MultiXact, not RAM structures — at the cost of MultiXact pressure under extreme concurrent row-locking.
  • LWLocks (buffer_content, WALInsert, ProcArray, relation_extension…): sharded, short-held, visible in pg_stat_activity.wait_event_type = 'LWLock'.
  • Spinlocks: single-instruction atomic sections (PGPROC assignment). wait_event = 'SpinLock' + high CPU = pathological contention, usually a bug or extreme skew.

docs.title: Extension / XID / Buffer / WAL Locks
docs.text:
• Relation extension: serializes file growth — hot spot for append-only + sequence-PK inserts; partitioning or hash-distributed keys relieve it.
  • Transaction ID locks: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on in-flight XIDs waits on the owner's commit/abort.
  • Buffer/WAL insert locks: page- and WAL-segment-striping; WALInsert contention means tiny unbatched commits on many cores.

docs.title: Deadlocks / Detection / Timeout
docs.text:
Deadlock detector (deadlock.c) runs when lock_timeout/deadlock_timeout (1 s) expires on a waiter: builds wait-for graph, aborts a participant with deadlock detected, other retries. Design: detection (cheap, periodic) instead of prevention (ordering constraints on all apps).

SET deadlock_timeout = '1s';  -- keep default; raising it only delays detection
-- app code: always retry serialization/deadlock errors with backoff

ROW-level deadlocks need no table locks: T1 locks row A then wants B while T2 holds B wants A — same graph logic at tuple granularity.

docs.title: What Actually Happens Internally?
docs.text:
Migration ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN x during traffic:

  1. Requests AccessExclusive; queued behind running AccessShares.
  2. New SELECTs queue behind the alter (lock-queue ordering) — app appears frozen though the alter hasn't started.
  3. Alter runs in ms once granted; queue drains. Total outage = wait time, not work time. Fix: SET lock_timeout, ALTER ... WITH (false) patterns, or concurrent-safe rewrites (pg_repack, ALTER ... ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT is cheap since v11).

docs.title: Hands-on Experiment
docs.text: Terminal 1: BEGIN; SELECT * FROM t WHERE id=1 FOR UPDATE; (hold). Terminal 2: UPDATE t SET v=2 WHERE id=1; — blocks. SELECT * FROM pg_locks WHERE NOT granted; shows the waiter. Terminal 1: COMMIT; — Terminal 2 proceeds. Reverse the order on two rows across two terminals for a true deadlock; watch ERROR: deadlock detected.

docs.title: Symptom: all queries suddenly queue, CPU idle
docs.text: Lock pile-up behind DDL or VACUUM FULL/CLUSTER. Diagnose: non-granted AccessExclusive oldest in queue + granted AccessShares ahead. Fix: cancel the DDL (pg_cancel_backend), set lock_timeout = '5s' for migrations, use concurrent index builds.

docs.title: Intermediate
docs.text:
• Why does SELECT never block on row locks? — MVCC: readers use snapshots, not locks; only FOR UPDATE/SHARE takes row locks explicitly.
  • What is lock queue jumping, and why does one migration freeze reads? — Waiting exclusive-mode requests block later shared grants; the queue, not the work, causes the outage.

docs.title: Advanced
docs.text:
• Why no lock escalation, and what replaces it? — Row locks in tuple headers/MultiXact bound memory without coarsening; trade is multixact churn under mass concurrent locking.
  • Advisory locks vs SELECT FOR UPDATE? — Advisory: arbitrary app mutex, no row needed, manual lifecycle. Row locks: tied to tuple visibility and transaction scope.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Compatibility matrix + queue ordering explain nearly every "stuck database" page.
  • Migrations need lock_timeout and concurrent patterns — DDL queueing is the outage, not DDL speed.
  • Deadlocks are retried in app code, not prevented in schema.

Real-life scenario: A deploy runs ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN without lock_timeout; it queues behind a 30-second analytics query, and every new checkout SELECT queues behind the alter — the site freezes for 30 s though the alter itself takes 5 ms. The queue, not the work, was the outage.

docs.title: Architecture Recap
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    DDL["DDL (AccessExclusive)"] --> Queue["Lock queue (FIFO per mode)"]
    Reads["Reads (AccessShare)"] --> Queue
    Queue -->|grants in order| Grant["Execute"]

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Logical decoding turns WAL records into ordered row-change streams consumed via replication slots — the foundation of CDC pipelines (Debezium → Kafka → warehouse). This file explains slots, plugins, streaming, ordering, and the WAL-retention economics that make CDC an operational commitment.

See also:

  • Logical Replication
  • WAL: Write-Ahead Logging
  • Replication Internals

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text: CDC looks like "just reading changes" but pins WAL, adds primary decoding CPU, and reorders failure domains: a stalled Kafka consumer can fill the database disk. Design the retention and lag budget first.

docs.title: What Decoding Does / WAL→Changes / Slots / Plugins / Streaming
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Txn[Committed txns in WAL] --> Decode[Decoding: reorder + filter]
    Decode --> Slot[Logical slot: confirmed_flush_lsn]
    Slot --> Consumer[pgoutput / Debezium / wal2json]
    Consumer --> Kafka[Kafka / sink]
  • Decoding (src/backend/replication/logical/): reassembles committed transactions from WAL in commit order, filters by publication/row-filter, emits BEGIN/COMMIT-framed changes.
  • Slots (pg_create_logical_replication_slot): durable consumer cursor (confirmed_flush_lsn); unacked changes pin WAL from restart_lsn.
  • Plugins: pgoutput (native protocol), wal2json (JSON over SQL interface), decoderbufs (protobuf), Debezium (Kafka Connect source with schema history + SMTs).
  • Streaming (v14+ streaming = on): large in-progress transactions stream before commit (with abort markers) instead of buffering whole txns in memory — essential for bulk loads.

docs.title: Retention / pgoutput / Transactions / Ordering / Exactly-Once
docs.text:
• Retention: slot lag = unconsumed WAL on primary disk. Alert on pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn) per slot.
  • Ordering: commit order per database; row order within txn preserved. No global order across databases.
  • Exactly-once: not provided end-to-end. At-least-once delivery + idempotent sinks (upsert on PK, transactional outbox) is the workable contract. Debezium + Kafka transactions narrow but don't eliminate duplicates across restarts.

docs.title: Architectures: Postgres→Kafka / Debezium / Consistency / Consumer Lag
docs.text:
Standard pipeline: logical slot → Debezium server/Connect → Kafka topics (one per table, keyed by PK) → sink connectors (warehouse, cache invalidation, search index). Consumers lag → slot retains → disk fills: backpressure must propagate (pause source, scale consumers, expire with eyes open — dropping a slot means full re-snapshot).

Transactional outbox alternative: app writes business row + outbox row in one txn; relay publishes outbox (via decoding or polling). Atomic publish without dual-write anomalies.

docs.title: What Actually Happens Internally?
docs.text: INSERT commits → WAL → reorder buffer holds txn → commit LSN → decoder emits change with LSN → consumer acks → confirmed_flush_lsn advances → WAL before it becomes recyclable. Consumer stall freezes the last step; everything upstream accumulates.

docs.title: Hands-on Experiment
docs.text:
SELECT pg_create_logical_replication_slot('cdc_test', 'pgoutput');
-- run writes; watch restart_lsn lag:
SELECT slot_name, pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS retained
FROM pg_replication_slots WHERE slot_name='cdc_test';
