SELECT date_trunc('month', observation_timestamp) AS month,
       sum(num_animals) AS total
FROM observations
WHERE family = 'Sharks'
GROUP BY month;

db.observations.aggregate([
  { $match: { family: "Sharks" } },
  { $group: {
      _id: { year: { $year: "$observationTimestamp" },
             month: { $month: "$observationTimestamp" } },
      totalAnimals: { $sum: "$numAnimals" }
  } }
]);

MATCH (person)-[:BORN_IN]->()-[:WITHIN*0..]->(us:Location {name: 'United States'}),
      (person)-[:LIVES_IN]->()-[:WITHIN*0..]->(eu:Location {name: 'Europe'})
RETURN person.name

WITH RECURSIVE in_usa(vertex_id) AS (
  SELECT vertex_id FROM vertices WHERE properties->>'name' = 'United States'
  UNION
  SELECT edges.tail_vertex FROM edges
  JOIN in_usa ON edges.head_vertex = in_usa.vertex_id
  WHERE edges.label = 'within'
)
SELECT properties->>'name' FROM vertices JOIN in_usa USING (vertex_id);

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Relational: joins + many-to-many strength, schema-on-write, optimizer hides access path.
  2. Document: locality + schema flexibility for tree data; weak joins, keep docs small.
  3. Declarative (SQL/Cypher/pipeline) beats imperative for optimizer freedom + parallelism.
  4. Graph property vs triple-store for dense relationships; Cypher/SPARQL/Datalog for traversal.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Databases do two things: store data and give it back. This chapter covers the index structures that power them — hash indexes, SSTables/LSM-trees, B-trees — then OLTP vs OLAP and column storage.

docs.title: Section 1: Hash Indexes
docs.text:
Simplest DB: append key,value to file, scan for lookup (O(n)). Add index — derived metadata mapping key to byte offset — for fast reads. Every index slows writes, so don't index everything; pick with query patterns in mind.

Bitcask-style hash index: in-memory hash map key → file offset. Append-only writes.

Scaling past one file: break log into segments, close when full, compact + merge in background (throw away duplicates, keep latest per key). Segments immutable after write, so merging is safe offline; switch reads to merged file, delete olds.

Real-implementation issues: - File format: binary, not CSV. - Deletes: append tombstone marker. - Crash recovery: snapshot hash maps to disk, replay log. - Partial writes: checksums to detect torn records. - Concurrency: single writer thread (sequential appends), many readers (immutable segments).

Pros: sequential writes (fast on spinning disk), simple concurrency/crash recovery, no fragmentation. Cons: hash table must fit RAM, no range queries.

docs.title: Section 2: SSTables and LSM-Trees
docs.text:
Require segments sorted by key: SSTable (Sorted String Table). Each key appears once per merged file.

Wins over hash segments: 1. Merging is a simple mergesort; keep newest on duplicate. 2. Sparse in-memory index suffices (e.g. one key per few KB) — binary-search to nearest offset, scan forward. 3. Group records into blocks + compress before writing.

Write path with memtable (in-memory balanced tree: red-black/AVL): 1. Write → memtable. 2. Memtable over threshold (MBs) → flush to SSTable on disk. 3. Read → memtable, then newest segment → older. 4. Background merge/compaction discards overwritten/deleted values.

Crash loses memtable → keep separate append-only log (not sorted) only for recovery; discard on flush. This family is LSM-tree (Log-Structured Merge-Tree): LevelDB, RocksDB, Cassandra, HBase, Lucene term dictionary.

Speed non-existent-key lookups with Bloom filters. Compaction strategies: size-tiered (merge small into larger; HBase, Cassandra option) vs leveled (key range split into levels; LevelDB, RocksDB, Cassandra option). Leveled uses less disk; size-tiered needs less compaction IO tuning.

Size-tiered vs leveled and unchecked compaction growth can eat disk and interfere with live reads/writes — tune and monitor.

docs.title: Section 3: B-Trees
docs.text:
Standard in almost all relational DBs. Like SSTables keep keys sorted (range queries easy), but break data into fixed pages/blocks (traditionally 4 KB) instead of variable segments. Root page → child refs; depth O(log n); branching factor in hundreds; 3–4 levels hold 100s of TB.

Writes overwrite pages in place: find leaf, update, write back. Full page → split in two half-full, update parent. Overwrites never move page location (vs LSM append-only).

Crash: torn multi-page writes corrupt index → write-ahead log (WAL / redo log) records intent before pages. Concurrency: latches (lightweight locks) on tree internals. Optimizations: copy-on-write pages, key-prefix abbreviation, sibling pointers.

docs.title: LSM vs B-Tree
docs.text:
• LSM faster writes: sequential appends, lower write amplification, better compression, smaller files.
  • B-tree faster reads: one place per key; LSM checks memtable + many SSTables.
  • LSM compaction can spike and stall reads/writes; B-trees more predictable latency.
  • B-tree exactly-one-location gives strong transactional semantics (range locks attach directly).

docs.title: Section 4: Other Indexes
docs.text:
• Secondary index: non-unique values; either list of row IDs per value or make entries unique by appending row ID. Built on B-tree or LSM.
  • Clustered index: store row inside index (InnoDB primary). Covering index answers queries from index alone. Heap files otherwise hold rows with index → pointer.
  • Multi-column/concatenated: (lastname, firstname) — order matters; good for left-prefix, useless for first-name-only. Geospatial uses same trick (lat+lon) but true 2-D needs special trees (R-tree/PostGIS).
  • Full-text/fuzzy: normalization, stemming, proximity. Lucene uses SSTable-like term dictionary + finite-state automaton (trie-like) in-memory map.

docs.title: In-Memory
docs.text: Durability vs cost tradeoff. Memcached = cache only. VoltDB/MemSQL/TimesTen = relational in-memory with logs/snapshots/replication for durability; Redis/Couchbase = async weak durability. Wins: no encode-to-disk overhead, exotic structures (queues, sets) easy. Serve reads from RAM, reload from disk/replica on restart.

docs.title: Section 5: OLTP vs OLAP
docs.text:
• OLTP: small low-latency random reads/writes (MySQL, Postgres, Oracle). Bottleneck: disk seeks.
  • OLAP: scan millions of rows, few columns, aggregates (Hive, Presto, Spark, Redshift). Bottleneck: disk bandwidth.

Early 90s split: don't run analytics on OLTP. Data warehouse = read-only copy of all OLTP systems via ETL (extract-transform-load): periodic dump or continuous stream, cleaned into analysis schema. Often relational (SQL good for analytics) but internals differ.

Star schema: central fact table (events: transactions/sales, 100s of columns) + dimension tables (who/what/where/when). Snowflake = normalized dimensions.

docs.title: Section 6: Column-Oriented Storage
docs.text:
Row stores load whole rows even for 4-column queries. Column stores keep each column together — read only needed columns.

Wins: compression (repeated values + bitmap + run-length encoding; bitmaps answer IN/AND/OR fast), vectorized/SIMD CPU processing, same sort order across columns (often by date).

Cost: writes hard — no in-place update into compressed columns. Solution: buffer in memory like LSM, merge later. Materialized aggregates/views and OLAP cubes precompute common counts/sums; DB maintains them, writes pay the price.

docs.title: LSM write and read path
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    W[Writes] --> WAL["WAL (append, fsync)"]
    WAL --> Mem["MemTable (sorted, in memory)"]
    Mem -->|flush threshold| S0["SSTable segment (sorted)"]
    S0 -->|merge + compact| S1["Merged SSTable"]
    R[Reads] --> Mem
    R --> BF["Bloom filter"]
    BF --> S0
    BF --> S1

docs.title: B-tree page split
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    Root["Root page"] --> A["Page A: keys 1-100"]
    Root --> B["Page B: keys 101-200"]
    B -->|split full page| B1["Page B1: 101-150"]
    B --> B2["Page B2: 151-200+"]

docs.title: Code: minimal SSTable-style store
docs.text:
import bisect

class MemTable:
    def __init__(self, threshold=3):
        self.keys = []
        self.vals = {}
        self.threshold = threshold
        self.segments = []

    def put(self, k, v):
        if k not in self.vals:
            bisect.insort(self.keys, k)
        self.vals[k] = v
        if len(self.keys) >= self.threshold:
            self.flush()

    def flush(self):
        self.segments.append({k: self.vals[k] for k in self.keys})
        self.keys = []
        self.vals = {}

    def get(self, k):
        if k in self.vals:
            return self.vals[k]
        for seg in reversed(self.segments):
            if k in seg:
                return seg[k]
        return None

store = MemTable(threshold=3)
for k, v in [("a", 1), ("b", 2), ("c", 3), ("d", 4)]:
    store.put(k, v)
print(store.get("b"))
print(store.segments)

SELECT dim_date.weekday, dim_product.category,
       SUM(fact_sales.quantity) AS quantity_sold
FROM fact_sales
JOIN dim_date ON fact_sales.date_key = dim_date.date_key
JOIN dim_product ON fact_sales.product_sk = dim_product.product_sk
WHERE dim_date.year = 2013
  AND dim_product.category IN ('Fresh fruit', 'Candy')
GROUP BY dim_date.weekday, dim_product.category;

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Hash index: RAM map + segmented append log + compaction; fast writes, no ranges.
  2. LSM/SSTable: sorted + memtable + WAL; write-optimized, Bloom filters, leveled vs size-tiered.
  3. B-tree: fixed pages + WAL + latches; read-optimized, O(log n), exactly-once key location.
  4. OLTP (rows, seeks) vs warehouse/OLAP (columns, bandwidth, star schema, ETL).

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: App features change, so stored data must change too. Old and new code plus old and new formats coexist — rolling upgrades, mobile clients lagging, five-year-old rows still on disk. Data outlives code. Maintain both directions: - Backward compatibility: new code reads old data. - Forward compatibility: old code reads new data (ignore unknown fields).

docs.title: Section 1: Formats for Encoding Data
docs.text:
In-memory (pointers, objects) vs bytes on disk/wire. Translation = encode/serialize/marshal and decode/parse/deserialize.

Avoid language built-ins: tied to one language, instantiate-arbitrary-class security holes, bad versioning, poor efficiency.

Textual (JSON, XML, CSV): human-readable, good for interchange, but ambiguous numbers/large ints, no binary (Base64 +33%), optional schema (XML/JSON) or none (CSV).

Binary: MessagePack/BSON/BJSON (JSON-like, ~20-30% smaller — often not worth losing readability for small payloads), WBXML/Fast Infoset (XML-like).

docs.title: Thrift and Protocol Buffers
docs.text:
Schema-driven with codegen. Field tags (numbers) replace names on wire. Thrift BinaryProtocol vs CompactProtocol (type+tag in one byte); Protobuf similar with different bit-packing.

Schema evolution rules: - Add only optional/defaulted fields, never reuse a tag. - Remove only optional fields, never reuse tag. - Forward compat: old code ignores unknown tags. - Backward compat: new code reads old data (missing fields get defaults). - Changing a type risks truncation/precision loss.

Properties: compact (omit names), schema doubles as up-to-date docs, schema registry checks compat, codegen gives compile-time types.

docs.title: Avro
docs.text:
Hadoop subproject, 2009. Two schema languages (Avro IDL for humans, JSON for machines). No tags — decode by field order, so reader needs schema. Ships writer schema with data (file header) or negotiates per connection; per-record version when schemas vary.

Resolution uses writer schema + reader schema: forward = new writer/old reader; backward = new reader/old writer. Only add/remove fields with defaults. Renames break forward compat; type changes allowed only if Avro can convert. Friendly to dynamically generated schemas (dump DB → generate Avro JSON automatically vs hand-maintaining Thrift tag maps).

docs.title: Via Databases
docs.text: Writer encodes, reader decodes — possibly years apart. Needs both compat directions. Migrations (rewrite whole DB) expensive; most relational DBs allow cheap adds (nullable column backfilled with NULL on read). Caution: old code overwriting new-shaped rows can silently drop new fields.

docs.title: Via Service Calls
docs.text:
Each service owned by one team, independently deployable — old and new versions coexist, so expect mixed traffic. Client/server, SOA/microservices.

  • REST: design philosophy on HTTP (verbs, caching, content negotiation), URLs for resources, OpenAPI/Swagger docs, great for public APIs and debugging.
  • SOAP: XML protocol with WSDL codegen, heavier.
  • RPC (Thrift, Avro RPC, gRPC/Protobuf, Finagle, Rest.li): makes remote look like local call — flawed idea. Network vs local: unpredictable, timeouts with no result, retries cause duplicates without idempotence, wildly variable latency, no shared pointers, cross-language type mapping. Modern frameworks admit remoteness (futures/promises). Assume servers update first, clients second → need backward compat on requests, forward on responses.

docs.title: Via Asynchronous Message Passing
docs.text:
Producer → broker/queue (RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ, HornetQ, NATS, Kafka) → consumers. Advantages over direct RPC: buffers unavailable recipients, auto-redelivery, no need to know recipient IP, fan-out to many, sender/receiver decoupled. One-way (reply needs second channel). Any encoding works if it stays compat.

Actor model: per-entity actors + async messages instead of threads (single message at a time, no locks). Distributed actors = broker + actors fused. Akka (Java serialization default — swap for Protobuf for rolling upgrades), Orleans (custom format, same caveat), Erlang OTP (record-schema changes hard).

flowchart LR
    OW[Old writer] --> NR[New reader]
    NW[New writer] --> OR[Old reader]

    NW -- forward compatible --> OR

docs.title: Code: schemas and evolution
docs.text:
syntax = "proto3";

message Person {
  string user_name = 1;
  int64 favorite_number = 2;
  repeated string interests = 3;
}

{
  "type": "record",
  "name": "Person",
  "fields": [
    {"name": "userName", "type": "string"},
    {"name": "favoriteNumber", "type": ["null", "long"], "default": null},
    {"name": "interests", "type": {"type": "array", "items": "string"}}
  ]
}

def reader_view(record, known_fields):
    return {k: record[k] for k in known_fields if k in record}

new_data = {"user_name": "Martin", "favorite_number": 1337, "interests": ["hacking"], "nickname": "mk"}
print(reader_view(new_data, {"user_name", "favorite_number", "interests"}))

old_data = {"user_name": "Ada"}
print({**{"favorite_number": None, "interests": []}, **old_data})

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Support both compat directions; data outlives code, avoid full rewrites.
  2. Thrift/Protobuf: tags, optional-only adds. Avro: order-based, writer+reader resolution, default-required changes.
  3. DB flow needs both directions; RPC assumes servers-first; async via broker decouples + buffers.
  4. RPC ≠ local call: timeouts, retries, idempotence, encoding costs are fundamental.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Keep copies on multiple machines to stay close to users (latency), survive failures (availability), and scale reads (throughput). Hard part is handling changes: single-leader, multi-leader, leaderless.

docs.title: Section 1: Leaders and Followers
docs.text: One leader (master/primary) accepts writes, streams changes via replication log / change stream; followers (read replicas, slaves, hot standbys) apply it. Reads go anywhere, writes only to leader. Used by Postgres, MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server, MongoDB, RethinkDB, Espresso, Kafka, RabbitMQ.

docs.title: Synchronous vs Asynchronous
docs.text:
• Sync: follower confirms before success. Guaranteed up-to-date copy, but one slow/dead follower blocks writes.
  • Async: leader replies immediately. Leader never blocks, but writes can be lost on failover.

Practice: semi-sync — one sync follower, rest async.

docs.title: Setting Up New Followers
docs.text: Files copy insufficient (DB keeps writing). Without downtime: snapshot leader → copy to follower → follower replays changes since snapshot → caught up.

docs.title: Node Outages
docs.text:
• Follower fails: catch-up recovery — replays log gap from last processed transaction.
  • Leader fails (failover): detect dead (timeout) → elect most-up-to-date replica → repoint clients + followers. Risks with async: new leader missing writes (must discard → dangerous for external systems), split brain (two leaders), when to declare dead. Many teams fail over manually.

docs.title: Replication Log Implementations
docs.text:
• Statement-based: ship SQL (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE). Breaks on nondeterminism (NOW(), RAND(), auto-increment order, triggers/side effects). Fix nondeterminism by substituting leader's fixed values — generally avoid.
  • WAL shipping: ship byte-level storage logs (Postgres, Oracle). Fast but coupled to engine version — no mixed-version rolling upgrade, downtime required.
  • Logical/row-based: rows changed (insert values, delete keys, update old+new + commit marker). Decoupled, backward-compatible, parseable for CDC (warehouses, caches). MySQL binlog style.
  • Trigger-based: app code logs changes to table for external reader. Flexible, but overhead + bug-prone.

docs.title: Section 2: Problems With Replication Lag
docs.text: Read-scaling needs async followers → eventual consistency. Lag from milliseconds to minutes. Three anomalies + fixes:

docs.title: Reading Your Own Writes (read-after-write)
docs.text: User writes via leader, reads from lagging follower, misses own write. Fix: read own-modifiable data from leader (e.g. own profile); or route all reads to leader for N seconds after update (track timestamp — hard cross-device, needs central metadata + same-DC routing).

docs.title: Monotonic Reads
docs.text: User sees time move backward (first read hits fresh replica, refresh hits lagging one). Fix: sticky sessions — hash user ID to one replica; reroute only on failure.

docs.title: Consistent Prefix Reads
docs.text:
Causally ordered writes read out of order (question appears after answer) — acute in partitioned DBs with no global order. Fix: co-locate causally related writes on same partition, written in order.

If lag to minutes is unacceptable, use transactions/stronger guarantees (Ch. 7).

docs.title: Section 3: Multi-Leader Replication
docs.text:
Every node is leader for its writes, follower for others'. Only sensible across datacenters or offline devices, rarely inside one DC.

Use cases: per-DC leader (local writes hide cross-ocean latency, DCs survive independently — Tungsten/MySQL, BDR/Postgres, GoldenGate/Oracle), offline clients (device = leader, sync later — CouchDB/calendar), collaborative editing (keystroke-granularity, no locking — Google Docs/Etherpad).

Retrofitted auto-increment/triggers/constraints break — often considered dangerous, avoid if possible.

docs.title: Handling Write Conflicts
docs.text: Async detection only (sync detection = just use single-leader). Strategies: 1. Avoid: route each record's writes through one leader (e.g. user → home DC). 2. Converge: unique write IDs, highest wins (LWW — simple, loses data); per-replica IDs, higher wins (also lossy); merge values; record conflict for later resolution. 3. Custom: on-write handler (must be fast) or on-read multi-version return (CouchDB siblings; app/user merges).

docs.title: Topologies
docs.text:
• All-to-all: every leader → every leader. Best fault tolerance, but fast links overtake slow (causality breaks; needs version vectors). No causal order in BDR; Tungsten doesn't even detect.
  • Circular (MySQL default) / Star: write passes through intermediaries; each node has ID + seen-list to stop loops. One node failure stalls flow.

docs.title: Section 4: Leaderless Replication (Dynamo-style)
docs.text:
No failover — client (or coordinator) writes/reads several replicas in parallel (Riak, Cassandra, Voldemort, Dynamo). Version numbers pick newest on read.

Catch-up: read repair (client writes back fresher value to stale replica) + anti-entropy (background diff + copy, unordered).

docs.title: Quorums
docs.text: n replicas, w confirm writes, r queried on reads. w + r > n → read overlaps a fresh node. Odd n (3/5), w = r = majority typical. Smaller w/r = lower latency + higher availability, staler reads. Breaks when: sloppy quorum places w/r on different nodes, concurrent writes (merge needed), read/write races, partial-write failures unrolled back, failed-node restore breaks quorum. Optimized for tolerable eventual consistency.

docs.title: Sloppy Quorums and Hinted Handoff
docs.text: During partition, accept writes on any w reachable nodes (outside home n), hand off to home nodes later. Increases write availability, sacrifices read freshness. Multi-DC: wait only for local quorum, async cross-DC.

docs.title: Detecting Concurrent Writes
docs.text: Overwriting by arrival order diverges replicas. Options: - LWW by timestamp: converges, drops data. OK for caches, bad where loss matters. - Happens-before: track causality; concurrent = neither happened-before other. - Version vectors (per-key per-replica counters, Riak causal context): client sends read versions back on write; server overwrites ≤ version, keeps higher as siblings. App merges siblings; deletes need tombstones or resurrection. CRDTs auto-merge to avoid hand-rolled merge bugs.

docs.title: Code: quorum check and version vectors
docs.text:
def quorum_ok(n, w, r):
    return w + r > n and w > 0 and r > 0 and w <= n and r <= n

for n, w, r in [(3, 2, 2), (3, 1, 1), (5, 3, 3), (5, 1, 5)]:
    print(n, w, r, quorum_ok(n, w, r))

def merge_siblings(values):
    out = set()
    for v in values:
        out.update(v if isinstance(v, (set, list, tuple)) else [v])
    return sorted(out)

print(quorum_ok(3, 2, 2))
print(merge_siblings([{"a", "b"}, {"b", "c"}]))

class VersionVector(dict):
    def increment(self, node):
        self[node] = self.get(node, 0) + 1
        return self

    def concurrent_with(self, other):
        a_gt = any(self.get(k, 0) > other.get(k, 0) for k in self)
        b_gt = any(other.get(k, 0) > self.get(k, 0) for k in other)
        return a_gt and b_gt

v1 = VersionVector({"a": 2, "b": 1})
v2 = VersionVector({"a": 2, "b": 2})
print(v1.concurrent_with(v2))
print(v2.increment("a"))

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Single-leader: one sync + rest async; failover risks split brain + lost async writes.
  2. Lag anomalies: read-your-writes (leader reads), monotonic (sticky replica), prefix (same-partition causal order).
  3. Multi-leader only for multi-DC/offline/collab; conflicts need avoid/LWW/merge handlers.
  4. Leaderless: w + r > n, read repair + anti-entropy, version vectors over LWW when loss matters.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Replication isn't enough for huge data or query load — split into partitions (shards), each a small DB. Replication (availability/latency) and partitioning (scalability) combine: each node leads some partitions, follows others.

docs.title: Section 1: Partitioning of Key-Valve Data
docs.text:
Goal: spread data + load evenly. Skew = unfair split; hot spot = overloaded partition.

Random assignment spreads well but forces querying all nodes for any key.

docs.title: Partition by Key Range
docs.text: Sort keys, cut continuous ranges (encyclopedia volumes A–B, C–D). Boundaries manual or auto. Keys sorted per partition → range scans easy. Downside: access-pattern hot spots (e.g. today's dates). Used by HBase, RethinkDB, MongoDB pre-2.4.

docs.title: Partition by Hash of Key
docs.text:
Hash (MD5, Murmur3, Fowler-Noll-Vo — non-crypto fine) → partition by hash range (consistent hashing for even boundaries). Skew disappears, but adjacent keys scatter → range queries fan out to all partitions (Riak, Couchbase, Voldemort limitation; Mongo hash-sharding same).

Compromise: compound key — hash first part for partition, sort rest inside (Cassandra: (zipcode, user, timestamp) — all of one zipcode's users together, ordered by time).

docs.title: Skewed Workloads and Hot Spots
docs.text: Celebrity key (millions of reads/writes) still overloads one partition. App-level fix: prepend/append random salt to spread writes — pays back with scatter reads + bookkeeping.

docs.title: Section 2: Partitioning and Secondary Indexes
docs.text:
Secondaries don't map neatly to partitions. Two choices:

  • By document (local index): each partition indexes its own docs. Writes touch one partition (fast writes), reads scatter/gather all partitions (tail-latency risk). MongoDB, Riak, Cassandra, Elasticsearch, SolrCloud, VoltDB.
  • By term (global index): partition index by indexed term, not document. Reads hit one partition (fast reads), writes fan out + complex (usually async). Hash term for balance, range-split term for range scans.

docs.title: Section 3: Rebalancing Partitions
docs.text:
Move load as throughput/storage/failures shift. Requirements: fair after, live reads/writes during, minimal movement.

  • Hash mod N: hash(key) mod N. N change → almost everything moves. Never use.
  • Fixed partitions: many more partitions than nodes (e.g. 1000/10 nodes), steal some per new node. Key→partition stable, only assignment moves. Riak, Elasticsearch, Couchbase, Voldemort. Risk: fixed count too big (overhead) or too small (giant partitions, slow rebalance/recovery).
  • Dynamic (B-tree-like): split over-size, merge under-size. Count follows volume. HBase, MongoDB 2.4+ (pre-split to avoid cold single-partition start).
  • Proportional to nodes: fixed partitions-per-node (Cassandra 256/node). Random split choice can unbalance.

Fully automatic rebalance can saturate network/nodes — keep a human in the loop.

docs.title: Section 4: Request Routing (Service Discovery)
docs.text:
Client needs key → node mapping. Options: 1. Any node + forward. 2. Routing tier (partition-aware load balancer). 3. Smart client with partition map.

Map changes must propagate: ZooKeeper authoritative mapping (HBase, SolrCloud, Kafka; MongoDB uses config servers + mongos), or gossip protocol (Cassandra, Riak), or fixed tier (Couchbase moxi). MPP databases add sophisticated parallel query planning on top.

docs.title: Code: consistent hashing ring
docs.text:
import hashlib
import bisect

class HashRing:
    def __init__(self, nodes, replicas=100):
        self.ring = []
        self.nodes = {}
        for n in nodes:
            for i in range(replicas):
                h = int(hashlib.md5(f"{n}:{i}".encode()).hexdigest(), 16)
                self.ring.append(h)
                self.nodes[h] = n
        self.ring.sort()

    def get(self, key):
        h = int(hashlib.md5(key.encode()).hexdigest(), 16)
        i = bisect.bisect(self.ring, h) % len(self.ring)
        return self.nodes[self.ring[i]]

ring = HashRing(["n1", "n2", "n3"])
print([ring.get(f"user:{i}") for i in range(5)])
print(ring.get("celebrity:alice"))

def salted_key(hot_key, salt):
    return f"{hot_key}#{salt}"

print(salted_key("celebrity:alice", 7))

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Range = scans, hot spots. Hash = balance, no ranges. Compound = middle ground.
  2. Local index: fast writes, scatter reads. Global: fast reads, slow/async writes.
  3. Rebalance: fixed/dynamic/proportional — never mod N; human-gated.
  4. Routing via ZooKeeper/gossip/routing tier; keep mapping fresh.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Apps fail mid-write, networks cut off, concurrent clients overwrite each other, readers see half-updated state. Transaction groups reads/writes into one logical unit: all commit or all abort/rollback. DB handles safety guarantees so app ignores many error paths.

docs.title: Section 1: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction
docs.text: "Abandon transactions for scale" and "transactions are vendor lock-in" are both hyperbole. Safety model is ACID; non-ACID is BASE (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent — effectively "not ACID").

docs.title: ACID
docs.text:
• Atomicity: all-or-nothing; fault → abort + safe retry. Prefer "abortability". Crash recovery via log.
  • Consistency: app invariants hold (bank balance, foreign keys). App property, not DB's.
  • Isolation: concurrent txns act as if serial. Locks per object.
  • Durability: committed = never forgotten. Single node: fsync to disk. Replicated: copied to N nodes.

Single-object atomicity/isolation is universal; multi-object across partitions is what distributed stores drop. Leaderless stores won't undo — app must recover. Retry hazard: network succeeds but ack lost → double-apply; overload retries amplify; only retry transient errors (deadlock, failover), never permanent (constraint violation). Use backoff + limits.

docs.title: Section 2: Weak Isolation Levels
docs.text: Serializable is expensive, so production uses weaker levels that stop some races. Read committed is default in Postgres, Oracle, SQL Server, MemSQL.

docs.title: Read Committed
docs.text:
1. No dirty reads (only committed visible). Impl: keep old + new value, readers get old — no read locks stalling writers.
  2. No dirty writes (only overwrite committed). Impl: row-level write locks.

Still allows read skew, lost update, write skew, phantoms.

docs.title: Snapshot Isolation (Repeatable Read)
docs.text:
Each txn reads consistent snapshot frozen at start — fixes read skew/nonrepeatable read (Alice sees \(500+\)400=$900 vanishing; backups/analytics/integrity checks inconsistent). Readers never block writers and vice versa.

Impl: MVCC — multiple versions per object with timestamps; index points to all versions (or copy-on-write tree like CouchDB). Garbage-collect versions no txn can see. Called serializable in Oracle, repeatable read in Postgres/MySQL.

docs.title: Preventing Lost Updates
docs.text: Read-modify-write race: two counters increment from same base, one clobbered. Fixes: - Atomic ops: UPDATE counters SET value = value + 1 (Mongo/Redis have equivalents). Best when expressible; ORMs often hide unsafe cycles. - Explicit locking: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE. - Auto-detect: DB aborts loser under snapshot (Postgres repeatable read, Oracle serializable, SQL Server snapshot). MySQL InnoDB repeatable read does NOT. - Compare-and-set: UPDATE ... WHERE content = 'old' — fails if changed. - Conflict resolution: replicated DBs keep siblings, app merges / LWW (Ch. 5).

docs.title: Write Skew and Phantoms
docs.text:
Write skew: two txns read same set (2 doctors on call), each updates different row (self off-call), both commit → invariant broken (0 doctors). Needs serializable, DB constraints/triggers/materialized views, or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on depended rows.

Phantom: write in one txn changes another's search result (rows added/removed mid-txn, no lockable rows yet). Fix with materialized conflicts (artificial lock rows) or serializable.

docs.title: Section 3: Serializability
docs.text: Strongest: parallel txns end as if serial. Three implementations:

docs.title: Actual Serial Execution
docs.text:
One thread, one txn at a time (VoltDB/H-Store, Redis, Datomic). Feasible now: RAM cheap, OLTP txns tiny (analytics use snapshot instead). Sometimes beats concurrent engines; capped at single-CPU throughput.

Scale via stored procedures (submit whole txn upfront, no network round-trips) + partitioning (one thread per partition; cross-partition slow). Modern procs use Java/Groovy (VoltDB), Clojure (Datomic), Lua (Redis) — not PL/SQL. VoltDB replicates by re-executing deterministic procs.

docs.title: Two-Phase Locking (2PL)
docs.text:
Pessimistic: shared lock for read, exclusive for write, hold to commit/abort; writers block readers and reverse. Deadlock → detect + abort one. MySQL InnoDB + SQL Server serializable. Predictable correctness, worst throughput/latency: one slow txn stalls all; p99 suffers. Predicate locks (match search condition, incl. not-yet-existing rows) stop phantoms but costly → index-range locks approximate by locking larger range.

NOTE: 2PL (locking) ≠ 2PC (commit) — different chapters.

docs.title: Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)
docs.text: Optimistic (2008): run on snapshot, track stale reads (MVCC visibility ignored committed writes) + writes affecting prior reads (non-blocking index-range notices); abort on commit if premise violated. Writers never block readers. Beats 2PL when contention low; abort rate kills it under high contention (keep read-write txns short; long read-only OK). Distributable across partitions/cores, unlike single-thread serial.

docs.title: Transaction lifecycle and isolation ladder
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Active
    Active --> Committed: commit
    Active --> Aborted: abort / error
    Aborted --> Active: retry transient errors
    Committed --> [*]

flowchart TB
    RC[Read Committed] --> SI[Snapshot Isolation]
    SI --> SR[Serializable]
    RC -->|prevents| DR[dirty reads/writes]
    SI -->|adds| RS[no read skew / lost update with checks]
    SR -->|adds| WS[no write skew / phantoms]

docs.title: Code: atomic transfer and retry on serialization failure
docs.text:
BEGIN;
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;

UPDATE counters SET value = value + 1 WHERE key = 'foo';

UPDATE wiki_pages SET content = 'new content'
WHERE id = 1234 AND content = 'old content';

import time
import random

class SerializationFailure(Exception):
    pass

def transfer(db, retries=5):
    for attempt in range(retries):
        try:
            db.begin()
            db.execute("SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE")
            db.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1")
            db.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2")
            db.commit()
            return True
        except SerializationFailure:
            db.rollback()
            time.sleep((2 ** attempt) * 0.01 + random.random() * 0.01)
    return False

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. ACID: abortability + app invariants + serial illusion + fsync/replication. BASE = not-ACID.
  2. Read committed stops dirty R/W; snapshot stops skew via MVCC; neither stops write skew/phantoms.
  3. Lost update: atomic > FOR UPDATE > auto-abort > CAS > merge.
  4. Serializable via serial thread, 2PL (pessimistic, slow), or SSI (optimistic, aborts on contention).

docs.title: Chapter 8: The Trouble with Distributed Systems
Introduction
docs.text: Single-computer programs are deterministic — same input, same result. Distributed systems are nondeterministic: parts fail unpredictably while others work. Accept partial failure and build fault-tolerance in; test by injecting faults.

docs.title: Section 1: Faults and Partial Failures
docs.text: No total failure vs total success — gray states. Know expected behavior under fault, enumerate possibilities, chaos-test (kill nodes, partition network, pause processes) before prod does it for you.

docs.title: Section 2: Unreliable Networks
docs.text:
Shared-nothing systems talk only via network — async packet network with no delivery or timing guarantees. Send request, possible outcomes: lost, queued, remote dead, remote paused, response lost, response delayed. No response tells you nothing about what happened.

If you need certainty, need positive app-level reply — TCP ACK or RST/FIN only proves packet arrived, not processed.

docs.title: Timeouts and Unbounded Delays
docs.text:
• Long timeout: slow detection, idle capacity.
  • Short timeout: fast detection, false positives — double-execution, cascading failover load.

Theory says 2d + r (max delay + processing), but d unbounded in practice. Measure distribution + jitter experimentally (AWS, Akka, Cassandra style), adapt timeouts continuously. Some latency-sensitive paths use UDP (VoIP, live stream) where stale data worthless.

Queue sources: switch buffers, OS runqueues, hypervisor steal, TCP flow control, GC pauses. Ethernet/IP are packet-switched (queue → unbounded) vs telephone circuits (reserved bandwidth → bounded but wasteful for bursty data). TCP adapts to available bandwidth; circuits waste it.

docs.title: Section 3: Unreliable Clocks
docs.text:
Every machine's clock drifts. NTP syncs wall clocks via server hierarchy (GPS-backed), but still tens-of-ms uncertainty; jumps possible.

  • Time-of-day (wall): date/time for humans, NTP-synced, can jump backward — never measure durations.
  • Monotonic: always forward, meaningless absolute value, NTP only slews rate — right for timeouts.
  • Logical: counters (Lamport, version vectors) for ordering — no wall time at all.

Don't order cross-node events by wall clock — LWW on timestamps loses data in multi-leader/leaderless stores. Track causality explicitly.

Confidence intervals: treat reading as range [earliest, latest], not point. Spanner waits out uncertainty before committing to get externally-consistent snapshots; Google deploys GPS/atomic clocks per DC to shrink interval.

docs.title: Process Pauses
docs.text: Leader lease ≠ guarantee: GC stop-the-world, VM suspend, laptop sleep, context switch, sync disk, swap, SIGSTOP can pause a holder past expiry while it believes it still holds lock. Fencing (Ch. 9) required. Real-time (RTOS) deadlines need bare-metal testing, no dynamic alloc, documented worst-case — not typical servers.

docs.title: Section 4: Knowledge, Truth, and Lies
docs.text:
No node sees global truth — only system model assumptions algorithms are proved against. Don't trust self-judgment; decide by quorum (majority vote).

  • Fencing tokens: lock service returns increasing number per grant (ZooKeeper zxid/cversion); storage rejects writes with older token — blocks paused ex-leader.
  • Byzantine faults: nodes lie/attack. BFT algorithms costly, impractical inside own DCs; relevant for multi-org/P2P. Weak lying (bad disk, bug, misconfig) handled by checksums + validation.

Models: - Timing: synchronous (bounded delay — unrealistic), partially synchronous (sync mostly — realistic), asynchronous (no timing — very restrictive, FLP impossibility). - Failure: crash-stop (gone forever), crash-recovery (may return — most useful + partial-sync), Byzantine (anything). - Properties: safety (once broken, irreversible) must always hold; liveness (eventually restored) may caveat.

Handle even "impossible" cases — at least with explicit error.

    C->>S: request
    Note over C,S: response lost OR server paused OR server dead
    C->>C: timeout fires
    Note over C: did it happen? retry may double-execute

docs.title: Code: monotonic timeouts with jitter
docs.text:
import time
import random

start = time.monotonic()
deadline = start + 2.0

def timed_out():
    return time.monotonic() > deadline

def backoff_with_jitter(attempt, base=0.05, cap=2.0):
    return min(cap, base * (2 ** attempt)) + random.uniform(0, 0.05)

print(timed_out())
print([round(backoff_with_jitter(i), 3) for i in range(4)])
print(time.monotonic() - start >= 0)

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Design for partial failure; app-level replies only truth.
  2. No correct timeout — measure, adapt; packet networks queue unboundedly.
  3. Wall for humans, monotonic for durations, logical for order. Pause-aware leases + fencing.
  4. Quorums over self-belief; partial-sync + crash-recovery is practical model.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Letting the whole service fail is simple; better is a reusable abstraction with useful guarantees. Core one: consensus — getting all nodes to agree (leader election, atomic commit). Prevents split brain where two nodes both think they're leader.

docs.title: Section 1: Consistency Guarantees
docs.text:
Most replicated DBs give at least eventual consistency — temporary divergence, eventual convergence. Weak = fast/available but app must handle quirks; strong = easy to reason, slower/less fault-tolerant.

Isolation (Ch. 7) = avoid races among concurrent txns. Distributed consistency = recency/ordering of replicas under faults/delays.

docs.title: Section 2: Linearizability
docs.text:
Makes system look like single copy, every operation atomic. Once any client reads new value, all later reads return it. Test by recording request/response timings and checking sequential validity. cas(x, old, new) is canonical linearizable op.

  • Serializability: txns behave as if in some serial order (isolation).
  • Linearizability: reads/writes have recency on single register.
  • Both = strict serializability. 2PL/serial execution typically linearizable; SSI is not by design.

When you need it: 1. Lock/leader election: only one leader — ZooKeeper/etcd via consensus. 2. Uniqueness constraints: username, email, seat, stock — check-and-set or lock; foreign-key checks don't need it. 3. Cross-channel timing: uploader → storage → queue → resizer race; linearizable storage removes it.

Implementations: single copy (not fault-tolerant), single-leader replication (potentially), consensus algorithms (yes). Multi-leader no, leaderless (Dynamo-style) probably no — and slow if forced.

CAP: only linearizability + one network fault considered (Consistent-or-Available-under-Partition). Delays, dead nodes, other tradeoffs ignored — historically influential, little design value now. Main cost of linearizability is performance always, not just during partitions. If you don't need it, replicas stay available under partition.

docs.title: Section 3: Ordering Guarantees
docs.text:
Causality: cause before effect (question before answer). Causally consistent = you see causes before effects (snapshot isolation qualifies). Partial order (concurrent ops any order) vs linearizable total order (any two comparable). Linearizability preserves causality but costs; causal is strongest model that stays fast + available under network trouble.

Track dependencies: - Version vectors distinguish concurrent vs causal — precise but heavy. - Sequence numbers / Lamport timestamps (counter, nodeID): each node/client tracks max seen, bumps own on receive. Compact total order consistent with causality, but forces order on concurrent ops.

Total order broadcast = reliable + same-order delivery to all nodes (ZooKeeper/etcd). Equivalent to repeated consensus; basis for state machine replication (same writes same order → same state). Fixed at delivery — no retroactive inserts. Use: replication, serializable txns, log, fencing.

Build linearizable storage on total-order log: append claim (e.g. username), read log, first claim wins. Reads linearizable via log-append-then-read, sync()-style position wait (ZooKeeper), or sync-updated replica. Reverse (total order from linearizable register): increment-and-get sequence, attach, deliver in order.

docs.title: Section 4: Distributed Transactions and Consensus
docs.text: Agree on leader + agree on commit/abort. Impossible in pure async with crashes (FLP) — timeouts/crash detection make it practical.

docs.title: Atomic Commit and 2PC
docs.text:
Single node: order of disk writes decides. Multi-node: sending commit independently breaks atomicity. 2PC (prepare → commit/abort) via coordinator: 1. App reads/writes participants, gets txn ID. 2. Coordinator sends prepare; participant fsyncs + votes yes (point of no return) or no. 3. All yes → commit, else abort; coordinator fsyncs decision first, retries sends forever.

Failure: coordinator dead before prepare → safe abort. After yes-vote → participant blocked (in doubt) until coordinator recovers via log. 3PC needs perfect failure detector — not practical. XA standardizes 2PC across Postgres/MySQL/Oracle + ActiveMQ/MQ (C API, not wire protocol). Costs: fsync + round-trips (~10x slower), locks held while in doubt stall app, coordinator log = stateful single point, lowest-common-denominator (no cross-system deadlock detection). Exactly-once queue+DB processing is the payoff use.

docs.title: Fault-Tolerant Consensus
docs.text:
Properties: uniform agreement, integrity (no double-decide), validity (decided value was proposed), termination (non-crashed eventually decide — needs majority up). Algorithms: Viewstamped Replication, Paxos, Raft, Zab — all but Paxos give total-order broadcast directly.

Internally all use leader + epochs (Paxos ballot, VSR view, Raft term): unique leader per epoch, higher epoch wins. Two votes: elect leader, then approve proposal — quorums must overlap (vs 2PC needing every yes). Limits: strict majority required, fixed voter set (dynamic membership hard), timeout-based failure detection flaps across DCs.

docs.title: Membership and Coordination Services
docs.text: ZooKeeper/etcd/Consul: tiny in-memory dataset, replicated via total-order broadcast. Not general DBs — used indirectly (HBase, YARN, Kafka). Provide linearizable CAS, total-order fencing tokens (zxid/cversion), session failure detection + ephemeral lock release, watch notifications, service discovery (though DNS + cache often suffices).

docs.text:
sequenceDiagram

    participant C as Coordinator
    participant P1 as Participant 1
    participant P2 as Participant 2
    A->>C: commit request
    C->>P1: prepare
    C->>P2: prepare
    P1-->>C: yes
    P2-->>C: yes
    C->>C: fsync decision = commit
    C->>P1: commit
    C->>P2: commit

flowchart TB
    SER[Serializableisolation] --> SS[Strict serializable]
    LIN[Linearizablerecency] --> SS

docs.title: Code: Lamport clock and 2PC sketch
docs.text:
class Lamport:
    def __init__(self, node):
        self.node = node
        self.counter = 0

    def tick(self):
        self.counter += 1
        return (self.counter, self.node)

    def receive(self, remote):
        self.counter = max(self.counter, remote[0]) + 1
        return (self.counter, self.node)

a = Lamport("a")
b = Lamport("b")
t1 = a.tick()
t2 = b.receive(t1)
print(t1, t2, t2 > t1)

class Coordinator:
    def __init__(self, parts):
        self.parts = parts
        self.log = []

    def commit(self, txn):
        votes = [p.prepare(txn) for p in self.parts]
        decision = "commit" if all(v == "yes" for v in votes) else "abort"
        self.log.append((txn, decision))
        for p in self.parts:
            p.send(decision, txn)
        return decision

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Eventual always; linearizable when recency matters (leader, uniqueness, cross-channel).
  2. Causal = fast + available; Lamport for compact order, vectors for concurrency detection.
  3. Total-order broadcast ⇔ consensus; state-machine replication keeps replicas identical.
  4. 2PC for atomic commit but blocking + slow; Raft/Paxos/Zab + ZooKeeper for leader/coordination.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Three system kinds: - Services (online): wait for request, reply fast. - Batch (offline): run job over large bounded input, produce output. Scheduled, may take days, no user waiting. - Stream (near-real-time): consume unbounded input shortly after arrival (Ch. 11).

This chapter: Unix tools → MapReduce/HDFS → dataflow engines.

docs.title: Section 1: Batch Processing With Unix Tools
docs.text:
Log analysis in minutes: awk/sed/grep/sort/uniq/xargs.

Top-5 pages example: 

cat access.log | awk '{print $7}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -r -n | head -n 5
Split by whitespace ($7 = URL), sort, count uniques, numeric reverse sort, top 5.

Why Unix wins: - Uniform interface: everything is a file/byte stream via stdin/stdout. Any output plugs into any input; write your own tool by obeying the convention. - Immutability-friendly: inputs untouched, pipeline stoppable anytime, intermediate stages dumpable to files for fault tolerance; auto-sorts across cores, handles larger-than-RAM. - Limitation: single machine only → Hadoop.

docs.title: Section 2: MapReduce and Distributed Filesystems
docs.text:
MapReduce = Unix tools across thousands of machines. stdin/stdout replaced by distributed filesystem files (HDFS). HDFS = shared-nothing: per-machine daemon + central NameNode tracking block placement; blocks replicated or erasure-coded (Reed-Solomon).

Job = mapper + reducer callbacks: 1. Split input files into records (e.g. log line). 2. Mapper per record → key-value (e.g. URL → count). 3. Shuffle: partition by reducer (hash of key), sort, copy partitions to reducers — sorted merge across mappers. 4. Reducer per key → iterate values, emit output.

Mapper/reducer see one record at a time, no placement knowledge. Scheduler puts computation near data; reducer count configured by author. No randomness allowed. Single job limited → chain into workflows via directory names (output dir = next input).

docs.title: Joins in Batch Processing
docs.text:
No indexes — full table scans. Copy needed DB into HDFS via ETL (remote per-record queries too slow + inconsistent mid-round-trip).

  • Sort-merge join: mappers emit (userID, event) + (userID, profile); reducers get both adjacent, join in one pass (e.g. age-at-click per URL). Only one user record in RAM, no network. Handles grouping too. Hot/linchpin keys skew one reducer (celebrity) → stall whole workflow; fix by sampling + replicating hot key to many reducers (skewed/shared join in Pig/Crunch, Hive needs explicit keys).
  • Map-side (no reducers/sort): broadcast hash (small side in memory) or partitioned hash (both pre-partitioned same way). Faster, needs assumptions.

docs.title: Output of Batch Workflows
docs.text:
Often not a report but a structure: search indexes (Google's original 5–10 job MapReduce pipeline; still good for Lucene/Solr), ML classifiers/recommenders (user→friends, product→related).

Don't write per-record to live DB from mappers (per-request latency, overwhelm, partial-job visibility). Instead build new DB inside job as files on HDFS (Voldemort, Terrapin, ElephantDB, HBase bulk load), then atomic switch: copy files to servers, flip to new version, rollback by flipping back.

Unix philosophy pays off: immutable inputs, rerunnable same-output, fast feature iteration, transparent task retry, separation of concerns, same files feed many jobs. Hadoop = distributed Unix (HDFS = FS, MapReduce = process). Dump raw to HDFS first, interpret later (consumer's problem) — MPPs instead demand upfront modeling but give SQL elegance. MPP aborts whole query on node crash; MapReduce retries single task, loves disk (fault tolerance + bigger-than-RAM). 1-hour task ~5% preemption at Google — design for it.

docs.title: Section 3: Beyond MapReduce
docs.text:
Higher layers (Pig, Hive, Cascading, Crunch) cut code + enable interactive use. MapReduce robust but slow for some shapes.

Core flaw: full materialization — every job writes intermediate state to replicated HDFS. No next job starts until all prior tasks done, redundant mappers re-read reducer output, temp replication wastes resources.

Dataflow engines (Spark, Tez, Flink/Dryad/Nephele): whole workflow = one job, flexible operators (not just map/reduce), in-place sort only when needed, no forced HDFS writes. Same logic runs far faster. Fault tolerance flips: track lineage (RDD) or checkpoint operator state, recompute lost partitions. Recompute hurts for tiny data/CPU-heavy jobs — materialization cheaper there.

Graphs/iteration ("repeat until done") can't do single-pass MapReduce → BSP/Pregel (Giraph, GraphX, Gelly): vertices hold state in RAM across supersteps, message along edges, batch messages, checkpoint per iteration. Cross-machine overhead huge — if graph fits one machine, stay there.

import sys
from collections import defaultdict

def mapper():
    for line in sys.stdin:
        parts = line.split()
        if len(parts) >= 7:
            print(f"{parts[6]}\t1")

def reducer():
    counts = defaultdict(int)
    for line in sys.stdin:
        url, n = line.rsplit("\t", 1)
        counts[url] += int(n)
    for url, c in sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1], reverse=True)[:5]:
        print(f"{c}\t{url}")

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Unix pipes: uniform byte interface + immutability; single-machine limit.
  2. MapReduce: mapper → shuffle/sort → reducer; sort-merge vs map-side joins; build DB files, atomic swap.
  3. Materialization cost vs recompute cost; dataflow engines + Pregel for iterative/graph work.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Batch waits for bounded input to finish; stream processes unbounded events as they arrive — sub-second latency vs days. Event = small immutable record with timestamp, grouped into topic/stream. Polling a DB for new events is expensive → messaging systems notify consumers.

docs.title: Section 1: Transmitting Event Streams
docs.text:
Two questions per pub/sub design: 1. Producers faster than consumers? Drop, buffer/queue, or backpressure (block producer). 2. Node crash? Lose messages or pay durability cost (disk + replication, lower throughput, higher latency).

  • Direct: UDP multicast, ZeroMQ, StatsD/Brubeck metrics, webhooks (HTTP/RPC push). No intermediary, but app handles loss; offline consumer misses data; crashed producer loses buffer.
  • Broker/queue: server both sides connect to (RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ, HornetQ, JMS/AMQP, TIBCO, IBM MQ, Pub/Sub). Producer waits only for broker-buffer ack (asynchronous consumers). Broker deletes on successful delivery (no long storage), assumes small working set, supports topic-pattern subscription + change notifications. Patterns: load balancing (each message → one consumer) vs fan-out (each → all). Acknowledgements drive redelivery (crashed consumer's message → another), but load-balance + redelivery reorders — use per-consumer queues to preserve order.

docs.title: Partitioned (Log-Based) Logs
docs.text:
AMQP/JMS delete on consume — new consumer can't replay history. Fix: append-only log on disk (like tail -f). Producer appends; consumer reads sequentially + waits for new tail. Partition for scale; topic = group of partitions; each partition assigns monotonic offset per message.

Kafka, Kinesis, DistributedLog work this way. Fan-out free (independent readers, no deletion); load balance by assigning whole partitions to consumer-group members (limits: consumers ≤ partitions, slow message blocks its partition). Prefer JMS/AMQP when per-message cost high + order unimportant (fine-grained parallelism); prefer logs when throughput high + messages cheap + order matters. Offsets mirror DB log sequence numbers (broker = leader, consumer = follower); restart resumes at recorded offset (unrecorded tail replays). Retention by time/size — lagging past deleted segment loses data. Offset is consumer-controlled → replay by rewinding.

docs.title: Section 2: Databases and Streams
docs.text: Replication log = stream of write events. Dual writes (app writes DB + index + cache) race (DB: A→B, index: B→A order flipped) and lack atomic commit (one succeeds, other fails). Better: Change Data Capture (CDC) — observe DB changes, replay in order to followers. Log-based broker preserves order. Impl: parse replication log (Databus, Wormhole, Sherpa, Bottled Water/Postgres WAL, Maxwell/Debezium MySQL binlog, Mongoriver oplog, GoldenGate/Oracle) + snapshot at known offset + log compaction (keep latest per key, tombstone = delete) for rebuilds. Kafka log compaction + Kafka Connect generalize this. RethinkDB/Firebase/CouchDB changefeeds similar.

docs.title: Event Sourcing
docs.text:
CDC extracts mutable-DB changes at storage layer; event sourcing writes immutable command events at app layer (append-only event store, updates discouraged). Store intent ("student cancelled enrollment"), not side effects — new features chain off old events, debugging explains why, bugs don't destroy history. Transform log → read views deterministically; snapshot to truncate replay.

CQRS insight: write form need not equal read form (Druid/Kafka, Pistachio/Kafka commit log, Connect sinks). Costs: async consumers break read-your-writes (fix: sync view update for own writes, total-order broadcast, or same-partition single-threaded consumer needing no locks); immutable history fragments under heavy update/delete (compaction/GC cost) + admin deletes hard (Datomic excision).

docs.title: Section 3: Processing Streams
docs.text:
Per event, three sinks: write to store (DB/cache/index), push to user (alerts/dashboards), emit to another stream (operator job — never ends, unlike batch).

Uses: fraud, trading rules, factory monitoring, intel/attack detection.

  • CEP (Esper, InfoSphere, Apama, StreamBase, SQLstream): long-lived declarative/SQL-pattern queries; input flows past; match emits complex event.
  • Analytics (Storm, Spark Streaming, Flink, Concord, Samza, Kafka Streams, Dataflow, Azure Stream Analytics): rates, rolling averages, week-over-week comparisons — less sequence-matching, more aggregation.
  • Search streams: invert engine — store + index queries, stream events past them (vs index data, query once).
  • RPC crossover: Storm distributed RPC.

docs.title: Time and Windows
docs.text: Batch time ≠ event time. Frameworks defaulting to processing time (local clock) break under queue/restart lag. Log three stamps (occur/device-send/server-receive) to estimate clock offset. Windows never provably complete — timeout after silence, then ignore stragglers (count drops) or publish correction (retract prior). Types: tumbling (fixed, disjoint, e.g. 1-min), hopping (fixed, overlapping for smoothing, e.g. 5-min/1-min hop), sliding (event-anchored interval), session (activity burst until 30-min idle; web analytics).

docs.title: Joins
docs.text:
• Stream-stream: keep hour-indexed state per session ID; on search or click, probe other index, emit matched pair.
  • Stream-table (enrich): per activity event, need profile — remote lookup slow/risky; replicate table locally via CDC.
  • Table-table: maintain follower sets to know which timelines update per tweet.
  • Time-dependence (SCD): joining against changing state is nondeterministic unless versioned (embed tax-rate ID in invoice → deterministic, but kills log compaction).

docs.title: Fault Tolerance
docs.text: Batch retries task → exactly-once appearance. Streams can't hide output until end (infinite). Fixes: microbatching (Spark Streaming ~1s blocks as mini-batches; small = overhead, large = latency) or checkpointing (Flink rolling state snapshots to HDFS). Once output leaves processor, redelivery duplicates side effects → need atomic commit across systems (Dataflow, VoltDB, Kafka plans amortize 2PC over many messages) or idempotence (same effect once or many times; add metadata/operation IDs). State recovery: remote replicated store (slow) vs local + periodic replication (Flink snapshots, Samza/Kafka Streams changelog topics with compaction, VoltDB redundant multi-node execution).

docs.text:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

def tumbling_window(ts, size_minutes=1):
    epoch = datetime(1970, 1, 1)
    n = int((ts - epoch).total_seconds() // (size_minutes * 60))
    start = epoch + timedelta(minutes=n * size_minutes)
    return start, start + timedelta(minutes=size_minutes)

def hopping_window(ts, size_minutes=5, hop_minutes=1):
    epoch = datetime(1970, 1, 1)
    secs = int((ts - epoch).total_seconds())
    latest = (secs // (hop_minutes * 60)) * hop_minutes
    return [(epoch + timedelta(minutes=s),
             epoch + timedelta(minutes=s + size_minutes))
            for s in range(latest - size_minutes + hop_minutes, latest + 1, hop_minutes)
            if s >= 0]

now = datetime(2024, 1, 1, 10, 3, 30)
print(tumbling_window(now))
print(hopping_window(now)[-1])

SELECT window_start, count(*) AS events
FROM TABLE(TUMBLE(TABLE events, DESCRIPTOR(event_time), INTERVAL '1' MINUTE));

seen = set()

def sink(event_id, apply):
    if event_id in seen:
        return False
    apply()
    seen.add(event_id)
    return True

sink("req-1", lambda: print("applied"))
print(sink("req-1", lambda: print("applied")))

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Broker vs log: delete-on-read + per-message parallelism vs replayable offsets + order.
  2. CDC/event sourcing replace dual writes; compaction + snapshots bound history.
  3. Event time over processing time; tumbling/hopping/sliding/session; version IDs for deterministic joins.
  4. Microbatch vs checkpoint; atomic commit or idempotence for exactly-once.

docs.title: Chapter 12: The Future of Data Systems
Introduction
docs.text: No single tool fits all patterns. This chapter combines specialized tools via derived data, unbundles the database, aims for correctness without heavy coordination, and closes with ethics.

docs.title: Section 1: Data Integration
docs.text:
Every product — even "general-purpose" DB — targets a usage pattern. Real apps compose many: OLTP for requests, search index for keywords, warehouse/batch/stream for analytics, caches/denormalized views, ML/ranking, notifications. Keeping copies in sync is the hard part.

Distributed transactions order writes with locks (2PL) + atomic commit — linearizable but poor fault tolerance/performance (XA). CDC/event sourcing order with log + ensure once via deterministic retry + idempotence — async, robust. Without good distributed-txn protocol, log-based derived data is most promising; keep read-your-writes where needed.

Open problems: total order needs single leader (throughput cap); cross-DC / cross-service event order undefined; client-side state sees different order than server. Total-order broadcast beyond single node still research.

docs.title: Batch and Stream Processing
docs.text:
Both have functional flavor (output depends only on input, managed state) — good for fault tolerance + reasoning as pipelines. Spark = streaming atop batch (microbatches); Flink = batch atop streaming.

  • Stream: low-delay view updates.
  • Batch: reprocess history for new views.
  • Gradual evolution: keep old + new schema as side-by-side derived views, drop old when safe — no flag-day migration.
  • Lambda architecture: immutable event log + both engines in parallel; stream gives approximate fast view, batch corrects later. Cost: run/debug two systems.

docs.title: Section 2: Unbundling Databases
docs.text: One DB bundles secondary indexes, materialized views, replication logs, full-text indexes — synchronously maintained via distributed txns. Async event log + idempotent writers unbundles this into loosely coupled components that act like a database together. Advantage: outage in one part doesn't take all; teams evolve pieces independently. Only do it when no single product covers needs.

docs.title: Designing Applications Around Dataflow
docs.text:
Run app code on Mesos/YARN/Docker/Kubernetes (does it better than in-DB UDFs). Keep stateless logic separate from state (no logic in DB, no state in app — "separation of Church and state"). SOA wins via loose coupling + independent deploys.

Dataflow vs microservices: one-way async stream joins vs sync RPC. Example — currency conversion on purchase: microservice queries rate service per purchase (network per request); dataflow subscribes to rate stream, caches locally, joins on read (no network on hot path — fastest request is none).

Push to edge: Server-Sent Events/WebSockets + Elm/React-Redux event streams extend dataflow to browsers (chat, games, live dashboards). Materialized views/caches = precomputed common queries (write pays, read fast). Even reads can be events through the processor (reconstruct what user saw, track causality).

docs.title: Section 3: Aiming for Correctness
docs.text:
Transactions aren't leaving, but correctness works in dataflow too. Serializability doesn't prevent bugs — favor immutable append-only (don't let bad code destroy good data) + idempotence + end-to-end operation IDs.

2PC doesn't guarantee once: browser double-POST after timeout commits twice. Fix: UUID/request hash from client through all layers (UNIQUE(request_id) + conditional balance updates), immutable messages, deterministic derivations, duplicate suppression. TCP covers low level; remaining faults rare but need app-level IDs.

Constraints without coordination: - Uniqueness needs consensus (single leader or partitioned log). Partition by constrained value (hash username) to scale; async multi-master can't reject immediately. - Log approach: client appends request to ID-partitioned log; single-threaded processor per partition decides first-wins deterministically; emits success/reject. Money transfer: request log → debit stream (payer partition) + credit stream (payee partition) → dedup by request ID. Same as linearizable-log algorithm, scales with partitions.

Timeliness vs integrity: consistency conflates both. Timeliness violation = eventual consistency (stale bank lag OK). Integrity violation = perpetual inconsistency (wrong sums, disappearing money — catastrophic). ACID gives both; dataflow guarantees integrity (single-message atomic writes, deterministic fns, request IDs, immutability) without timeliness. Many domains accept temporary constraint breach + apology (oversell → refund) to avoid sync cost. Run serializable only in small scopes needing it; skip XA everywhere.

Trust but verify (auditing): never blindly trust guarantees — continually check integrity end-to-end (restore backups, checksums, Merkle trees, certificate transparency, blockchains). Event sourcing audits better (why, not just what); deterministic pipelines trace easily. Auditing lets you ship faster, like tests.

docs.title: Section 4: Doing the Right Thing
docs.text:
Systems have intended + unintended consequences — ethics is ours to bear (ACM Code). Predictive analytics amplifies input bias (past behavior → stereotype, feedback loops, echo chambers). Needs systems thinking + moral imagination — data as tool, not master; humans accountable.

Privacy/tracking: storing explicit user input = service (user is customer). Side-effect logging for advertisers = surveillance (advertisers are customers). Privacy = freedom to choose what to reveal, not total secrecy. Collection transfers that right to company; consent meaningless without understanding + network-effect lock-in; future regimes may abuse retained data ("poor civic hygiene to build police-state-ready tech"). Don't treat users as metrics; self-regulate collection, educate users, purge when unneeded. Like industrial pollution controls, constraints benefit society long-term.

def fold(events, state):
    for e in events:
        t = e["type"]
        if t == "credited":
            state["balance"] += e["amount"]
        elif t == "debited":
            state["balance"] -= e["amount"]
    return state

ledger = [
    {"type": "credited", "amount": 100},
    {"type": "debited", "amount": 11},
]
print(fold(ledger, {"balance": 0}))

processed = set()

def handle(request_id, effect):
    if request_id in processed:
        return False
    effect()
    processed.add(request_id)
    return True

docs.text:

  2. Unbundle with async idempotent logs; dataflow joins beat RPC on hot paths.
  3. Integrity via immutability + request IDs + deterministic replay; audit continuously.
  4. Bias amplifies; surveillance ≠ service — purge, consent, dignity by design.

docs.title: Chapter 1: Scale from Zero to Millions of Users
Introduction
docs.text: Scaling a system to support millions of users is a complex, iterative journey requiring refinement and optimization. This chapter outlines how to begin with a single server setup and scale the architecture step by step to handle millions of users.

docs.title: Section 1: Single Server Setup
docs.text: Initially, all components (web app, database, cache) run on a single server.

docs.title: Request Flow
docs.text:
1. Users access the application via domain names (e.g., api.mysite.com), resolved to IP addresses using DNS.
  2. IP address of the web-server is returned to the browser or mobile app.
  3. HTTP requests are sent to the web server, which returns HTML or JSON responses.

docs.title: Traffic Sources
docs.text:
1. Web Applications: Use server-side languages (e.g., Python, Java) for business logic and client-side languages (e.g., JavaScript, HTML) for presentation.
  2. Mobile Applications: Communicate with the web server using HTTP and JSON for lightweight data exchange.

docs.title: Section 2: Database Separation
docs.text: As the user base grows, the database is moved to a dedicated server to allow independent scaling of web and database tiers.

docs.title: Database Choices
docs.text:
1. Relational Databases (SQL): Structured data stored in tables. Examples: MySQL, PostgreSQL.
  2. Non-Relational Databases (NoSQL): Suitable for unstructured data or low-latency requirements. Categories include:
  3. Key-Value Stores
  4. Graph Databases
  5. Column Stores

  6. Document Stores

  7. Non-relational databases might be the right choice if:

  8. application requires super-low latency.
  9. data is unstructured, or there is no relational data.
  10. only need to serialize and deserialize data (JSON, XML, YAML, etc.).
  11. need to store a massive amount of data.

docs.title: Vertical Scaling
docs.text:
• Adds more resources (CPU, RAM) to existing servers.
  • Limited by hardware constraints and lacks redundancy.

docs.title: Horizontal Scaling
docs.text:
• Adds more servers to the pool, making it more suitable for large-scale systems.
  • A load balancer is used to handle the request routing between the servers.

docs.title: Section 4: Load Balancer
docs.text: A load balancer distributes traffic among multiple servers. Benefits include: 1. Redundancy: If a server goes offline, traffic is rerouted. - If server 1 goes offline, all the traffic will be routed to server 2. 2. Scalability: Easily add servers to handle traffic spikes. - If the website traffic grows rapidly, subsequent servers can be added to handle the additional traffic.

docs.title: Master-Slave Model
docs.text:
• Master Database: Handles write operations.
  • All the data-modifying commands like insert, delete, or update must be sent to the master database.
  • Slave Databases: Handle read operations, improving performance and reliability.
  • Since the ratio of reads to writes is higher in most applications; thus, the number of slave databases in a system is usually larger than the number of master databases.

docs.title: Benefits
docs.text:
1. Improved performance through parallel read operations.
  2. High availability and data reliability through redundancy.

docs.title: Failure Handling
docs.text:
• If only one slave database is available and it goes offline, read operations will be directed to the master database temporarily.
  • In case multiple slave databases are available, read operations are redirected to other healthy slave databases and a new server will replace the old one.
  • If the master database goes offline, a slave database will be promoted to be the new master.
  • In production system the chosen slave database might not be up to date, hence data needs to be updated by running data recovery scripts (methods like multi-masters and circular replication could help).

docs.title: Section 6: Caching
docs.text: A cache stores frequently accessed data in memory to reduce database load. The cache tier is a temporary data store layer, much faster than the database.

docs.title: Caching considerations
docs.text:
1. Use case: Consider using cache when data is read frequently but modified infrequently.
  2. Expiration Policies: Once cached data is expired, it is removed from the cache. When there is no expiration policy, cached data will be stored in the memory permanently.
  3. Consistency: This means keeping the data store and the cache in sync. Inconsistency can happen because data-modifying operations on the data store and cache are not in a single transaction.
  4. Mitigating failures: A single cache server represents a potential single point of failure, multiple cache servers across different data centers are recommended to avoid SPOF.
  5. Eviction Policies:: Once the cache is full, items need to be evicted to free up memory. LRU is the most popular cache eviction policy.

docs.title: Section 7: Content Delivery Network (CDN)
docs.text: A CDN improves load times by caching static content (images, CSS, JavaScript) on geographically distributed servers.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. User requests content from the nearest CDN server.
  2. If unavailable, content is fetched from the origin server and cached.

docs.title: CDN considerations
docs.text:
1. Cost: CDNs are run by third-party providers which charge for data transfers in and out of the CDN.
  2. Cache Expiry: The cache expiry time should neither be too long nor too short.
  3. CDN fallback: If there is a temporary CDN outage, clients should be able to detect the problem and request resources from the origin.
  4. Invalidating files: If files are updated the cache should be invalidated to point to the updated files.

docs.title: Section 8: Stateless Web Tier
docs.text: By moving session data to a shared datastore, web servers become stateless. This allows: 1. Easier horizontal scaling. 2. Auto-scaling based on traffic.

docs.title: Section 9: Multi-Data Center Setup
docs.text:
Deploying across multiple data centers improves availability and reduces latency. Strategies include:

  1. GeoDNS Routing: Direct users to the nearest data center.
  2. Data Replication: Synchronize data across centers to prevent inconsistencies.

docs.title: Key considerations
docs.text:
• Traffic redirection: Effective tools are needed to direct traffic to the correct data center.
  • Data synchronization: A common strategy is to replicate data across multiple data centers.
  • Test and deployment: Automated deployment tools are vital to keep services consistent through all the data centers.

docs.title: Section 10: Message Queue
docs.text:
A message queue is a durable component, stored in memory, that supports asynchronous communication. It serves as a buffer and distributes asynchronous requests.

  • Input services, called producers/publishers, create messages, and publish them to a message queue.
  • Other services called consumers/subscribers, connect to the queue, and perform actions defined by the messages.

docs.title: Importance
docs.text:
1. Logging: Tracks errors and system health.
  2. Metrics: Provides insights into performance and user activity.
  3. Automation: Streamlines testing, deployment, and scaling.

docs.title: Vertical Scaling
docs.text:
• Adds hardware resources but has physical and cost limitations.
  • Has multiple drawbacks:
  • Greater risk of single point of failures.
  • Overall cost of vertical scaling is high

docs.title: Horizontal Scaling (Sharding)
docs.text:
• Divides data across multiple shards using keys (e.g., user_id).
  • Sharding separates large databases into smaller, more easily managed parts called shards.
  • Each shard shares the same schema, though the actual data on each shard is unique to the shard.
  • Sharding key is critical when implementing a sharding strategy. When choosing a sharding key it is important to choose a key that can evenly distribute data.

docs.title: Challenges
docs.text:
1. Resharding data: Resharding data is needed when:
  2. Single shard could no longer hold more data due to rapid growth.
  3. Certain shards might experience shard exhaustion faster than others due to uneven data distribution.

  4. Consistent Hashing is used to overcome these problems

  5. Celebrity problem: Excessive access to a specific shard could cause server overload.

  6. To solve this problem, we may need to allocate a shard for each celebrity.

  7. Join and de-normalization: Once a database has been sharded across multiple servers, it is hard to perform join operations across database shards.

  8. A common workaround is to de-normalize the database so that queries can be performed in a single table.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Keep the web tier stateless.
  2. Build redundancy at every tier.
  3. Use caching and CDNs to optimize performance.
  4. Scale the data tier with sharding.
  5. Decouple components for flexibility.

This chapter provides a solid foundation for building scalable systems that can handle millions of users.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Back-of-the-envelope estimation is a crucial skill in system design interviews. It involves making quick, rough calculations to assess system capacity or performance. According to Jeff Dean, Google Senior Fellow, these estimates help evaluate whether designs meet requirements through thought experiments and common performance benchmarks.

This chapter covers key concepts, methodologies, and examples to build proficiency in scalability and estimation.

docs.title: Power of Two
docs.text:
Understanding data volume in terms of powers of two is fundamental:

This knowledge helps in performing accurate storage and bandwidth calculations.

docs.title: Latency Numbers Every Programmer Should Know
docs.text:
Latency numbers represent the time taken for various operations in computing systems. These provide insights into relative performance:

Operation Latency (2020) L1 Cache Access 0.5 ns L2 Cache Access 7 ns Main Memory Access 100 ns SSD Random Read 150 µs HDD Random Seek 10 ms Round-Trip in Data Center 500 µs Inter-Region Data Center 150 ms

Key Insights: - Memory is fast, disk is slow. - Avoid disk seeks whenever possible. - Compress data before transmitting over the internet to save bandwidth.

docs.title: Availability Numbers
docs.text:
High availability (HA) ensures minimal downtime. Availability is expressed in nines: - 99% (Two Nines): ~3.65 days/year of downtime - 99.9% (Three Nines): ~8.8 hours/year of downtime - 99.99% (Four Nines): ~52 minutes/year of downtime - 99.999% (Five Nines): ~5.3 minutes/year of downtime - 99.9999% (Six Nines): ~31.56 seconds/year of downtime

Cloud providers like Amazon, Google, and Microsoft aim for SLAs (Service Level Agreements) of 99.9% or higher.

docs.title: Section 2: Example Estimation - Twitter QPS and Storage Requirements
Assumptions
docs.text:
• 300 million monthly active users (MAU).
  • 50% daily active users (DAU).
  • Average tweets/user/day: 2.
  • 10% of tweets contain media.
  • Data retention: 5 years.

docs.title: Estimations
docs.text:
1. Query Per Second (QPS):
  2. DAU = \( 300M x 50\% = 150M \)
  3. Tweets QPS = ( 150M x 2 tweets / 24 hour / 3600 seconds = ~3500 )

  4. Peak QPS = \( 2 x 3500 = ~7000 \)

  5. Media Storage:

  6. Tweet Size Components:
    • tweet_id: 64 bytes
    • text: 140 bytes
    • media: 1 MB
  7. Daily Media Storage: \( 150M x 2 x 10\% x 1MB = 30TB per day \)
  8. 5-Year Storage: \( 30TB x 365 x 5 = ~55PB \)

docs.title: 1. Rounding and Approximation
docs.text: Precision is not critical; focus on the process. Simplify complex calculations using round numbers. For example: - \( 99987 / 9.1 \) can be approximated as \( 100,000 / 10 = 10,000 \).

docs.title: 2. Write Down Assumptions
docs.text: Document assumptions clearly for future reference.

docs.title: 3. Label Units
docs.text: Avoid ambiguity by labeling units (e.g., 5 MB instead of 5).

docs.title: 4. Common Estimation Scenarios
docs.text:
• QPS (Queries Per Second): Measure traffic intensity.
  • Peak QPS: Account for traffic spikes.
  • Storage Requirements: Estimate total data needs.
  • Cache Requirements: Evaluate memory requirements for caching.
  • Number of Servers: Calculate hardware needs based on workload.

docs.title: Chapter 3: A Framework for System Design Interviews
Introduction
docs.text:
System design interviews are a key part of the hiring process, simulating real-life problem-solving scenarios. These interviews evaluate not just technical skills but also collaboration, communication, and the ability to handle ambiguous requirements.

This chapter introduces a 4-step framework for navigating system design interviews effectively.
