docs.title: Chain of Responsibility Design Pattern
docs.text: Youtube: 10. Design Logging System (Hindi) | Chain of Responsibility Design Pattern | System Design interview

docs.title: 1. Overview and Fundamentals
docs.text:
Chain of Responsibility is a behavioral design pattern that lets a request travel along a chain of potential handlers until one of them handles it. The sender knows only the head of the chain, not which object will ultimately process the request.

  • GoF classification: Behavioral — concerned with how objects communicate and distribute responsibility.
  • Intent (GoF): "Avoid coupling the sender of a request to its receiver by giving more than one object a chance to handle the request. Chain the receiving objects and pass the request along the chain until an object handles it."
  • Core idea: Decouple Client → Receiver into Client → Chain Head → … → Handler N. Each handler either processes the request or forwards it.
  • Everyday analogy: A customer support escalation: L1 → L2 → L3. You submit one ticket; you do not choose who resolves it. Each level handles what it can and escalates the rest.
  • Key participants:
  • Handler (abstract): Defines handle(request) and holds a reference to next.
  • ConcreteHandler: Checks canHandle(request); processes or forwards.
  • Client: Builds the chain once and sends requests to the head.
  • Request: Value object carrying data plus context (severity, headers, credentials).
  • Success conditions: Handlers are ordered deliberately (cheap/specific first), the chain always terminates (default handler), and each handler has a single, testable responsibility.
  • What it is not: It is not a broadcast (only one handler normally acts), not a decorator stack (not every layer acts), and not an if-else ladder hidden in one method (responsibilities are distributed objects).

docs.title: How the mechanism works
docs.text:
1. Client composes handlers: h1.setNext(h2); h2.setNext(h3).
  2. Client calls h1.handle(request).
  3. Each handler runs: if canHandle → process + stop (or process + continue); else → next?.handle(request).
  4. If the tail is reached with no match, a default handler logs, rejects, or raises an error — never silently drops.

docs.title: Pure vs impure chains
docs.text:
Variant Behavior Example Pure chain Exactly one handler processes; request stops there Support escalation, approval workflow Impure / filtering chain Every handler gets a chance; each may enrich, log, or veto Servlet filters, Express middleware, logging pipeline Short-circuit chain Any handler can abort the chain early Auth filter rejecting unauthenticated requests

Most production chains are impure: logging + auth + validation + business handler + audit.

docs.title: Design dynamics
docs.text:
• Ordering is semantics. Put cheap, high-volume handlers first (cache, validation) and expensive, rare handlers last (expert team, DB fallback). Reordering changes behavior — document and test the order.
  • Request object design matters. Make it immutable where possible, carry a correlation ID, and allow handlers to attach diagnostics (handledBy, attempts) without mutating core fields.
  • Dynamic reconfiguration. Chains can be rebuilt at runtime from config: add/remove handlers, reorder by feature flag, or build per-tenant chains. This is the main advantage over static if-else.
  • Termination guarantees. Always install a catch-all tail handler (UnhandledRequestHandler, DefaultLogger, 404Handler). Validate non-empty chain at startup and fail fast if misconfigured.
  • SOLID alignment: Single Responsibility (one reason to change per handler), Open/Closed (new handler = new class, no client edit), Dependency Inversion (client depends on Handler abstraction).
  • Failure modes: Unhandled requests, over-long chains (latency, stack depth), implicit control flow that is hard to trace, and handlers with hidden side effects that make order fragile.

docs.title: Variants and extensions
docs.text:
• Builder-assembled chains: A ChainBuilder reads YAML/config and wires handlers — common in API gateways.
  • Composite + Chain: A handler that fans out to a sub-chain (e.g., fraud checks running risk rules).
  • Chain + Command: Each link executes a Command object, giving queueing + undo per step.
  • Async chains: Handlers return futures/promises; forwarding becomes await next.handle(req). Requires timeout and cancellation policy.

docs.title: 3.1 Static structure — who holds whom
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Client {
        +send(request: Request)
    }
    class Handler {
        <>
        #next: Handler
        +setNext(next: Handler) Handler
        +handle(request: Request) void
        #canHandle(request: Request) bool
        #process(request: Request) void
    }
    class ConcreteHandlerA {
        #canHandle(request: Request) bool
        #process(request: Request) void
    }
    class ConcreteHandlerB {
        #canHandle(request: Request) bool
        #process(request: Request) void
    }
    class DefaultHandler {
        #canHandle(request: Request) bool
        #process(request: Request) void
    }
    class Request {
        +severity: String
        +payload: String
        +correlationId: String
    }
    Client --> Handler : sends to head
    Handler --> Handler : next
    Handler ..> Request : handles
    ConcreteHandlerA --|> Handler
    ConcreteHandlerB --|> Handler
    DefaultHandler --|> Handler

Explanation: Client depends only on the Handler abstraction. Each Handler holds at most one next reference, forming a singly linked list. ConcreteHandlerA/B implement the guard (canHandle) and action (process). DefaultHandler always returns true from canHandle so the chain provably terminates. Request is a dumb data carrier shared by all links.

docs.title: 3.2 Dynamic flow — how a request travels
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant L1 as L1Support
    participant L2 as L2Support
    participant L3 as L3Support
    participant Tail as DefaultHandler
    Client->>L1: handle(ticket CRITICAL)
    L1->>L1: canHandle? No
    L1->>L2: handle(ticket)
    L2->>L2: canHandle? No
    L2->>L3: handle(ticket)
    L3->>L3: canHandle? Yes
    L3->>L3: process (resolve)
    L3-->>Client: resolved by L3

Explanation: The sender makes one call. Responsibility propagates until a guard matches. Note the two self-checks that miss before the hit — this is why per-handler logging (handler=L2 decision=pass) and a correlation ID are essential for observability. If L3 also missed, the call would continue to DefaultHandler, which logs unhandled ticket and alerts instead of dropping silently. A second scenario worth tracing is an impure filter chain where every participant runs (auth → validation → business logic) rather than stopping at the first match.

docs.title: 4. Implementation Examples in Java, Python, and Go
docs.text: All three examples model a support-escalation chain (LOW → MEDIUM → CRITICAL → default). Build the chain once, send requests to the head, observe which handler acts.

docs.title: 4.1 Java (OOP, classic GoF style)
docs.text:
Explanation: Abstract SupportHandler owns the next link and the template method handle(). Subclasses implement only canHandle/process. HelpdeskDemo wires L1 → L2 → L3 → Default and sends four tickets.

abstract class SupportHandler {
    protected SupportHandler next;

    SupportHandler setNext(SupportHandler next) {
        this.next = next;
        return next;
    }

    void handle(Ticket ticket) {
        if (canHandle(ticket)) {
            process(ticket);
        } else if (next != null) {
            next.handle(ticket);
        } else {
            System.out.println("[unhandled] " + ticket);
        }
    }

    protected abstract boolean canHandle(Ticket ticket);
    protected abstract void process(Ticket ticket);
}

final class Ticket {
    final String severity;
    final String description;
    Ticket(String severity, String description) {
        this.severity = severity;
        this.description = description;
    }
    @Override public String toString() { return severity + ": " + description; }
}

final class Level1Support extends SupportHandler {
    @Override protected boolean canHandle(Ticket t) { return "LOW".equals(t.severity); }
    @Override protected void process(Ticket t) { System.out.println("[L1 resolved] " + t.description); }
}

final class Level2Support extends SupportHandler {
    @Override protected boolean canHandle(Ticket t) { return "MEDIUM".equals(t.severity); }
    @Override protected void process(Ticket t) { System.out.println("[L2 resolved] " + t.description); }
}

final class Level3Support extends SupportHandler {
    @Override protected boolean canHandle(Ticket t) { return "CRITICAL".equals(t.severity); }
    @Override protected void process(Ticket t) { System.out.println("[L3 expert resolved] " + t.description); }
}

final class DefaultHandler extends SupportHandler {
    @Override protected boolean canHandle(Ticket t) { return true; }
    @Override protected void process(Ticket t) { System.out.println("[default] escalated to on-call: " + t.description); }
}

public class HelpdeskDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SupportHandler chain = new Level1Support();
        chain.setNext(new Level2Support())
             .setNext(new Level3Support())
             .setNext(new DefaultHandler());
        chain.handle(new Ticket("LOW", "Password reset"));
        chain.handle(new Ticket("MEDIUM", "VPN flaky"));
        chain.handle(new Ticket("CRITICAL", "Prod DB down"));
        chain.handle(new Ticket("UNKNOWN", "Mystery bug"));
    }
}

Sample I/O:

[L1 resolved] Password reset
[L2 resolved] VPN flaky
[L3 expert resolved] Prod DB down
[default] escalated to on-call: Mystery bug

docs.title: 4.2 Python (pythonic, PEP 8)
docs.text:
Explanation: Uses abc.ABC for the handler contract, @dataclass for the immutable request, and fluent set_next returning the next link for one-line chain building. Follows PEP 8 naming and type hints.

from __future__ import annotations
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Ticket:
    severity: str
    description: str


class SupportHandler(ABC):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._next: SupportHandler | None = None

    def set_next(self, nxt: SupportHandler) -> SupportHandler:
        self._next = nxt
        return nxt

    def handle(self, ticket: Ticket) -> str:
        if self.can_handle(ticket):
            return self.process(ticket)
        if self._next is not None:
            return self._next.handle(ticket)
        return f"[unhandled] {ticket.description}"

    @abstractmethod
    def can_handle(self, ticket: Ticket) -> bool: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def process(self, ticket: Ticket) -> str: ...


class Level1Support(SupportHandler):
    def can_handle(self, ticket: Ticket) -> bool:
        return ticket.severity == "LOW"

    def process(self, ticket: Ticket) -> str:
        return f"[L1 resolved] {ticket.description}"


class Level2Support(SupportHandler):
    def can_handle(self, ticket: Ticket) -> bool:
        return ticket.severity == "MEDIUM"

    def process(self, ticket: Ticket) -> str:
        return f"[L2 resolved] {ticket.description}"


class Level3Support(SupportHandler):
    def can_handle(self, ticket: Ticket) -> bool:
        return ticket.severity == "CRITICAL"

    def process(self, ticket: Ticket) -> str:
        return f"[L3 expert resolved] {ticket.description}"


class DefaultHandler(SupportHandler):
    def can_handle(self, ticket: Ticket) -> bool:
        return True

    def process(self, ticket: Ticket) -> str:
        return f"[default] escalated to on-call: {ticket.description}"


def build_chain() -> SupportHandler:
    head = Level1Support()
    head.set_next(Level2Support()).set_next(Level3Support()).set_next(DefaultHandler())
    return head


if __name__ == "__main__":
    chain = build_chain()
    for ticket in [
        Ticket("LOW", "Password reset"),
        Ticket("MEDIUM", "VPN flaky"),
        Ticket("CRITICAL", "Prod DB down"),
        Ticket("UNKNOWN", "Mystery bug"),
    ]:
        print(chain.handle(ticket))

Sample I/O:

[L1 resolved] Password reset
[L2 resolved] VPN flaky
[L3 expert resolved] Prod DB down
[default] escalated to on-call: Mystery bug

docs.title: 4.3 Go (idiomatic)
docs.text:
Explanation: Handler is a small interface; baseHandler embeds the next pointer to avoid repetition. Each level is a struct embedding baseHandler. Chain is wired with setters; Handle returns a string so it is trivially testable.

package main

import "fmt"

type Ticket struct {
    Severity    string
    Description string
}

type Handler interface {
    SetNext(next Handler) Handler
    Handle(t Ticket) string
}

type baseHandler struct{ next Handler }

func (b *baseHandler) SetNext(next Handler) Handler {
    b.next = next
    return next
}

func forward(b *baseHandler, t Ticket) string {
    if b.next != nil {
        return b.next.Handle(t)
    }
    return "[unhandled] " + t.Description
}

type Level1 struct{ baseHandler }

func (h *Level1) Handle(t Ticket) string {
    if t.Severity == "LOW" {
        return "[L1 resolved] " + t.Description
    }
    return forward(&h.baseHandler, t)
}

type Level2 struct{ baseHandler }

func (h *Level2) Handle(t Ticket) string {
    if t.Severity == "MEDIUM" {
        return "[L2 resolved] " + t.Description
    }
    return forward(&h.baseHandler, t)
}

type Level3 struct{ baseHandler }

func (h *Level3) Handle(t Ticket) string {
    if t.Severity == "CRITICAL" {
        return "[L3 expert resolved] " + t.Description
    }
    return forward(&h.baseHandler, t)
}

type DefaultHandler struct{ baseHandler }

func (h *DefaultHandler) Handle(t Ticket) string {
    return "[default] escalated to on-call: " + t.Description
}

func main() {
    head := &Level1{}
    head.SetNext(&Level2{}).SetNext(&Level3{}).SetNext(&DefaultHandler{})
    tickets := []Ticket{
        {"LOW", "Password reset"},
        {"MEDIUM", "VPN flaky"},
        {"CRITICAL", "Prod DB down"},
        {"UNKNOWN", "Mystery bug"},
    }
    for _, t := range tickets {
        fmt.Println(head.Handle(t))
    }
}

Sample I/O:

[L1 resolved] Password reset
[L2 resolved] VPN flaky
[L3 expert resolved] Prod DB down
[default] escalated to on-call: Mystery bug

docs.title: 5. Real-World Industry Applications
docs.text:
• Logging frameworks (Log4j, SLF4J, Python logging): Loggers form a level-filtered chain (DEBUG → INFO → WARN → ERROR). Each appender decides to record or forward; a root logger acts as the default handler.
  • Servlet / web filter chains (Jakarta Filters, Django middleware, Express): Authentication → rate limiting → validation → routing. Each filter may short-circuit (401) or enrich the request and call chain.doFilter().
  • API gateways (Kong, AWS API Gateway, Envoy): Request passes through auth, quota, transformation, and routing handlers assembled from config per route.
  • Customer support platforms (Zendesk, Freshdesk, Intercom): Ticket triage rules escalate L1 → L2 → L3 based on keywords, SLA, and sentiment; unmatched tickets hit an on-call default queue.
  • Approval workflows (Workday, SAP, ServiceNow): Expense or access requests flow Manager → Director → VP → Finance, each with an approval limit; amounts above the limit auto-forward.
  • Payment fraud screening (Stripe Radar, Adyen): Transactions traverse velocity checks → geolocation → ML risk score → manual review; any link can approve, flag, or block.
  • Exception handling in layered backends: Controller → Service → DAO catch blocks each handle what they understand and rethrow the rest, ending in a global exception handler (the default tail).
  • Game input pipelines (Unity, Unreal): Key events propagate UI → player controller → camera → debug console until consumed, mirroring a pure chain.

docs.title: 6. Practical Use Cases and Scenarios
docs.text:
• Logging pipeline: ConsoleHandler(INFO) → FileHandler(WARN) → PagerDutyHandler(ERROR). An INFO record stops at console; an ERROR traverses all three and pages. Adding a Slack handler means one insertion, zero client changes.
  • HTTP middleware: Auth → RateLimit → Validation → Controller. Unauthenticated requests stop at Auth with 401; valid requests accumulate request.user and request.id as they travel. Order matters: rate-limit after auth so you can key by user.
  • Helpdesk escalation (Section 4): Cheap generalists first, experts last. Metrics per link (l1_resolved_total, escalated_to_l2_total) reveal staffing needs.
  • Document approval: Amounts ≤ $1k stop at manager; ≤ $10k stop at director; above that reach CFO. Each approver stamps approvedBy; auditors replay the chain from the stamps.
  • Chat moderation: Profanity filter → spam detector → hate-speech model → human review. Fast regexes run first; expensive ML models run only on survivors, saving cost.
  • IoT sensor pipeline: Calibrate → debounce → threshold-alert → cloud-upload. Faulty readings are dropped early; only meaningful events pay the network cost.

docs.title: 7. When to Use and When Not to Use
docs.text:
Use Chain of Responsibility when:

  • More than one object may handle a request and the handler is not known at compile time.
  • You want to decouple sender from receivers and rewire handlers from config.
  • Requests naturally form a pipeline: validate → authenticate → authorize → execute → audit.
  • Handling priority matters and can be expressed as chain order.

Do NOT use when:

Situation Prefer instead Every layer must run (enrichment, not selection) Decorator or explicit pipeline stages Exactly one receiver is known statically Direct call or Strategy/Map dispatch Deterministic audit trail is mandatory and implicit routing is risky Explicit router with logged switch + metrics Chain would be 1–2 trivial branches Simple if-else / polymorphism Ultra-low-latency path where traversal cost matters Indexed dispatch (map, jump table)

docs.title: 8. Do's and Don'ts
docs.text:
Do:

  • Always terminate with a default handler that logs, metrics, and alerts on unhandled requests.
  • Keep handlers stateless or request-scoped; never stash mutable conversation state in the link.
  • Log handler name + decision (handled/passed) with a correlation ID at each step.
  • Keep chains short (3–5 links); extract sub-chains when a handler grows its own pipeline.
  • Validate chain construction at startup (non-empty, tail is default, no cycles).
  • Make the request object carry everything handlers need — avoid hidden service-locator calls.

Don't:

  • Don't let handlers secretly depend on execution order beyond their guard (fragile coupling).
  • Don't swallow requests silently when nothing matches — that is a production incident waiting to happen.
  • Don't put heavy I/O in early links that run for every request; defer cost to later links.
  • Don't share one handler instance across threads if it holds mutable per-request fields.
  • Don't use a chain to hide business rules that belong in an explicit, reviewable policy table.
  • Don't recurse without bound — deep chains over large inputs risk stack overflow; iterate instead.

docs.title: 9.1 Chain of Responsibility vs Decorator vs Command
docs.text:
Aspect Chain of Responsibility Decorator Command Purpose Route one request to one anonymous handler Add behavior by wrapping every layer Encapsulate a request as an object for queuing/undo Flow Stops at first matching handler (pure) or filters through (impure) Always passes through all wrappers Invoker executes a stored command later Link knowledge Knows only next Wraps an inner component Knows receiver + parameters + inverse Undo No built-in undo No undo First-class undo/redo via history stacks Typical use Filters, escalation, middleware BufferedInputStream, UI borders, enrichment Job queues, macros, editor undo

Rule of thumb: One handler should act → Chain. Every layer should contribute → Decorator. The request itself must be stored, queued, or undone → Command (a chain link can hold a Command).

docs.title: 9.2 Chain vs Mediator vs Observer
docs.text: Aspect Chain Mediator Observer Topology Linear pipeline Star (peers via hub) Fan-out (subject → many listeners) Who talks to whom Each link calls only next Peers call hub, hub coordinates Subject broadcasts, listeners react Decision Handler decides handle-or-forward Hub decides routing/rules Each observer decides its own reaction Use when Ordered selection/filtering Complex many-to-many coordination One-to-many state notification

docs.title: Q&A
docs.text:
Q1. What is Chain of Responsibility in one sentence? A: A request travels down an ordered list of handlers until one handles it, so the sender knows only the chain head, not the final receiver.

Q2. What happens if no handler matches? A: Without a tail guard the request is silently dropped. Always install a default handler that logs with correlation ID, emits a metric, and either rejects gracefully or pages on-call.

Q3. How is it different from if-else or switch dispatch? A: Behaviorally similar for pure selection, but the chain distributes each branch into its own class (SRP), allows runtime reordering/insertion, and decouples the sender. If-else concentrates all branches in one method that must be edited per new case.

Q4. Chain vs Decorator — how do you choose on the spot? A: Ask "should exactly one link act, or every layer contribute?" One actor → Chain (auth chain stops at first failure). Every layer contributes → Decorator (compression + encryption + buffering all apply).

Q5. How do you debug "which handler processed my request"? A: Structured log per link (handler, decision, correlationId), a handledBy field stamped on the request, per-handler counters, and short chains. Add integration tests asserting order and handler identity.

Q6. How do you make chains configurable at runtime? A: A builder/factory reads handler names + order from config or DI container and wires setNext. Validate at startup; support per-tenant chains by building once per tenant and caching.

Q7. What are the performance and reliability risks? A: Traversal overhead per request, worst case O(n) with I/O in early links, no compile-time guarantee of handling, and implicit flow that complicates tracing. Mitigate with short chains, cheap guards first, tail defaults, timeouts, and metrics.

Q8. How do you test a chain thoroughly? A: Unit-test each handler's guard + action in isolation (mock next); integration-test full order including tail; test empty chain, no-match, multi-match (first wins), exception in a middle link, and concurrent requests for shared handler instances.

Q9. Can handlers run in parallel or async? A: Yes with care: fan out to sub-chains and join, or await next.handle(). You then need timeout, cancellation, and a deterministic merge policy (first match wins vs collect-all). Keep the common case sequential for readability.

docs.title: LLD scenarios
docs.text:
S1. Design a logging system (classic interview prompt). Requirements: levels DEBUG/INFO/WARN/ERROR, destinations console/file/pager, runtime reconfiguration. Solution: AbstractLogger(level, next) chain ordered by severity; each link writes if record.level >= ownLevel then forwards (impure chain). Tail NullLogger drops below-threshold noise with a counter. Discuss fallback when file handler fails (forward vs buffer-and-retry) and bounding I/O cost.

S2. Design an expense-approval workflow. Requirements: manager ≤ $1k, director ≤ $10k, CFO above, audit trail, delegation when approver is OOO. Solution: Approver(limit, next) pure chain; request carries amount + approvedBy[]; each link stamps or forwards. OOO handled by decorator around a link or temporary rewiring. Discuss persistence of approvals and exactly-once semantics on retry.

S3. Design API gateway middleware. Requirements: auth → rate limit → schema validation → routing → audit, per-route chains, short-circuit with proper status codes. Solution: filter-style chain where each link returns CONTINUE or a response; builder assembles per-route chains from config. Discuss ordering (auth before rate-limit for user-keyed quotas), timeouts, and how to unit-test each filter with a fake next.

docs.title: 11. Testing and Best Practices
docs.text:
• Unit tests per handler: Table-drive canHandle true/false cases; verify process side effects; mock next to assert forward-vs-stop. Example (Python/pytest): assert Level2().can_handle(Ticket("MEDIUM","x")) is True.
  • Order tests: Build the real chain and assert handledBy for representative requests, including tail fallback. Any reorder should break exactly one intentional test.
  • Edge cases: Empty chain (constructor should reject), null request, unknown severity, exception thrown mid-chain (wrap with try/finally that logs handler name), extremely long chain (depth guard).
  • Concurrency: Handlers must be stateless or use request-scoped state only; stress-test shared chain instances with parallel requests; use immutable Ticket to avoid races.
  • Observability: Correlation ID from ingress propagated through every link; per-handler latency histogram; unhandled_total alert. In interviews, mention OpenTelemetry spans per handler.
  • Best practices: Builder/factory for assembly; fail-fast startup validation; default tail; keep handle() template method final/non-overridable so subclasses cannot break forwarding; document ordering rationale next to wiring code; bound chain length and per-link timeouts for I/O links.

docs.title: 12. Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Chain of Responsibility routes one request to one anonymous handler through an ordered pipeline, decoupling sender from receiver.
  • Prefer it for filters, middleware, escalation, and approval workflows where handlers are dynamic and ordered.
  • Distinguish from Decorator (every layer acts) and Command (requests become storable objects); chains and commands compose well.
  • Always provide a default tail handler, keep chains short and stateless, log every decision with correlation ID, and test guards, order, and tail explicitly.
  • In LLD interviews, reach for it when you hear "multiple handlers, unknown at compile time, dynamic ordering, pass-or-process" — then immediately discuss termination, ordering, and observability to show production maturity.

docs.title: Command Design Pattern
docs.text: Youtube: 31. Design Undo, Redo feature with Command Pattern | Command Design Pattern| Low Level System Design

docs.title: 1. Overview and Fundamentals
docs.text:
Command is a behavioral design pattern that turns a request into a standalone object containing everything needed to execute it: the receiver, the method, and the parameters. The sender (invoker) triggers commands without knowing what they do or what they operate on.

  • GoF classification: Behavioral — encapsulates interaction between invoking and performing objects.
  • Intent (GoF): "Encapsulate a request as an object, thereby letting you parameterize clients with different requests, queue or log requests, and support undoable operations."
  • Core idea: Replace a direct method call light.on() with an object new LightOnCommand(light) that can be stored, passed, queued, logged, and undone.
  • Everyday analogy: A restaurant order slip. The customer (client) writes the order (command), the waiter (invoker) carries it, and the kitchen (receiver) executes it. The waiter never cooks; the slip decouples who asks from who acts, and slips can be queued, reordered, or cancelled.
  • Key participants:
  • Command (interface): Declares execute() and usually undo().
  • ConcreteCommand: Binds a receiver, parameters, and the inverse operation.
  • Receiver: The domain object that does the real work (Light, Document).
  • Invoker: Holds/executes commands (button, scheduler, editor history) without knowing receivers.
  • Client: Creates commands and assigns them to invokers.
  • Success conditions: Commands are self-contained (receiver + args + undo state), invokers depend only on the Command interface, and history is bounded.
  • What it is not: It is not just a callback — commands carry state and support undo, persistence, and composition (macros). It is not Strategy — Strategy swaps how something is computed; Command defers and records a request to do something.

docs.title: How the mechanism works
docs.text:
1. Client creates a receiver (Document doc = new Document()).
  2. Client wraps each action in a command (new InsertCommand(doc, 5, " world")).
  3. Client hands commands to an invoker (editor.run(cmd), button.setCommand(cmd), queue.submit(cmd)).
  4. Invoker calls execute() now or later; for undoable commands it pushes them onto a history stack.
  5. undo() reverses the effect using state captured at execute time; redo() re-executes.

docs.title: Command lifecycle and state
docs.text:
• Parameter capture: Commands snapshot everything needed at creation (positions, payloads). Never let a command read mutable global state at execute time — that breaks replay and remote execution.
  • Undo models: (a) Inverse operation — store minimal delta (insert ↔ delete); memory-light but each command must implement a correct inverse. (b) State snapshot — store a Memento before executing; simpler but heavier. Most editors use (a); most game checkpoints use (b).
  • Redo invalidation: Any new command after undo clears the redo stack — otherwise history branches ambiguously. This single rule prevents an entire class of bugs.
  • Composition (Macro/CompositeCommand): A MacroCommand holds a list of commands and executes/undoes them in order/reverse order. Enables one-click "format + save + commit" actions.
  • Queueing and persistence: Because commands are objects, they can be serialized to a queue (Celery, RabbitMQ), a write-ahead log, or a network socket. The receiver may live on another machine entirely.
  • SOLID alignment: Single Responsibility (one action per class), Open/Closed (new command = new class), Dependency Inversion (invoker depends on abstraction).
  • Costs: Class proliferation (one class per action), memory for history, and the discipline to implement correct inverses (off-by-one in DeleteCommand undo is the classic bug).

docs.title: Variants and extensions
docs.text:
• Lambda commands: For one-shot, non-undoable actions, a lambda/Runnable/Callable is a sufficient command — avoid ceremony.
  • Transactional commands: execute() returns success/failure; a transaction manager rolls back completed commands in reverse on failure (Saga pattern).
  • Two-phase commands: validate() then execute(); the invoker rejects invalid commands before mutating anything.
  • Command + Memento: Command stores a Memento instead of hand-rolled inverse state — cleaner when receiver state is complex.

docs.title: 3.1 Static structure — who holds whom
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Client {
        +createCommands()
    }
    class Command {
        <>
        +execute() void
        +undo() void
    }
    class InsertCommand {
        -receiver: Document
        -pos: int
        -chunk: String
        +execute() void
        +undo() void
    }
    class DeleteCommand {
        -receiver: Document
        -pos: int
        -len: int
        -removed: String
        +execute() void
        +undo() void
    }
    class Document {
        -text: StringBuilder
        +insert(pos: int, s: String) void
        +delete(pos: int, len: int) void
        +content() String
    }
    class Editor {
        -undoStack: Deque~Command~
        -redoStack: Deque~Command~
        +run(cmd: Command) void
        +undo() void
        +redo() void
    }
    Client ..> InsertCommand : creates
    Client ..> DeleteCommand : creates
    Client --> Editor : uses
    InsertCommand ..|> Command
    DeleteCommand ..|> Command
    InsertCommand --> Document : invokes
    DeleteCommand --> Document : invokes
    Editor --> Command : stores & executes

Explanation: Client wires receivers into commands but never executes domain logic directly. InsertCommand/DeleteCommand each hold a Document reference plus the parameters and undo state. Editor (invoker) depends only on the Command interface and owns both history stacks — this is what decouples toolbar buttons and shortcuts from the text buffer. Adding a ReplaceCommand touches nothing except the new class.

docs.title: 3.2 Dynamic flow — execute, undo, redo
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Editor as Editor (Invoker)
    participant Insert as InsertCommand
    participant Doc as Document (Receiver)
    Client->>Insert: new InsertCommand(doc, 5, " world")
    Client->>Editor: run(insert)
    Editor->>Insert: execute()
    Insert->>Doc: insert(5, " world")
    Editor->>Editor: undoStack.push(insert); redoStack.clear()
    Client->>Editor: undo()
    Editor->>Insert: undo()
    Insert->>Doc: delete(5, 6)
    Editor->>Editor: redoStack.push(insert)
    Client->>Editor: redo()
    Editor->>Insert: execute()
    Insert->>Doc: insert(5, " world")

Explanation: Execution and inversion both flow through the command, never directly to the receiver. Note the redoStack.clear() on every fresh run() — this enforces linear history. The receiver (Document) is deliberately dumb: it knows insert/delete but nothing about undo, stacks, or buttons. All orchestration intelligence lives in the command + invoker pair.

docs.title: 4. Implementation Examples in Java, Python, and Go
docs.text: All three examples model a text editor with undo/redo. Each keystroke is a command; the editor keeps undo/redo stacks.

docs.title: 4.1 Java (OOP, classic GoF style)
docs.text:
Explanation: EditCommand declares execute()/undo(). Document is the receiver. InsertCommand stores position + chunk; DeleteCommand snapshots removed text so undo can restore it. Editor is the invoker owning both stacks.

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

interface EditCommand {
    void execute();
    void undo();
}

class Document {
    private final StringBuilder text = new StringBuilder();
    void insert(int pos, String s) { text.insert(pos, s); }
    void delete(int pos, int len) { text.delete(pos, pos + len); }
    String content() { return text.toString(); }
}

class InsertCommand implements EditCommand {
    private final Document doc;
    private final int pos;
    private final String chunk;
    InsertCommand(Document doc, int pos, String chunk) {
        this.doc = doc; this.pos = pos; this.chunk = chunk;
    }
    public void execute() { doc.insert(pos, chunk); }
    public void undo() { doc.delete(pos, chunk.length()); }
}

class DeleteCommand implements EditCommand {
    private final Document doc;
    private final int pos;
    private final int len;
    private String removed = "";
    DeleteCommand(Document doc, int pos, int len) {
        this.doc = doc; this.pos = pos; this.len = len;
    }
    public void execute() {
        removed = doc.content().substring(pos, pos + len);
        doc.delete(pos, len);
    }
    public void undo() { doc.insert(pos, removed); }
}

class Editor {
    private final Deque<EditCommand> undo = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final Deque<EditCommand> redo = new ArrayDeque<>();
    void run(EditCommand cmd) {
        cmd.execute();
        undo.push(cmd);
        redo.clear();
    }
    void undo() {
        if (!undo.isEmpty()) {
            EditCommand cmd = undo.pop();
            cmd.undo();
            redo.push(cmd);
        }
    }
    void redo() {
        if (!redo.isEmpty()) {
            EditCommand cmd = redo.pop();
            cmd.execute();
            undo.push(cmd);
        }
    }
}

public class EditorDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Document doc = new Document();
        Editor editor = new Editor();
        editor.run(new InsertCommand(doc, 0, "hello"));
        System.out.println(doc.content());
        editor.run(new InsertCommand(doc, 5, " world"));
        System.out.println(doc.content());
        editor.undo();
        System.out.println(doc.content());
        editor.redo();
        System.out.println(doc.content());
        editor.run(new DeleteCommand(doc, 5, 6));
        System.out.println(doc.content());
        editor.undo();
        System.out.println(doc.content());
    }
}

docs.title: 4.2 Python (pythonic, PEP 8)
docs.text:
Explanation: EditCommand is an ABC; Document wraps a list of characters; Editor owns deque stacks. Type hints + snake_case throughout. A MacroCommand bonus shows composition.

from __future__ import annotations
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from collections import deque


class Document:
    """Receiver: the text buffer. Knows nothing about undo."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._chars: list[str] = []

    def insert(self, pos: int, chunk: str) -> None:
        self._chars[pos:pos] = list(chunk)

    def delete(self, pos: int, length: int) -> None:
        del self._chars[pos:pos + length]

    @property
    def content(self) -> str:
        return "".join(self._chars)


class EditCommand(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def execute(self) -> None: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def undo(self) -> None: ...


class InsertCommand(EditCommand):
    def __init__(self, doc: Document, pos: int, chunk: str) -> None:
        self._doc = doc
        self._pos = pos
        self._chunk = chunk

    def execute(self) -> None:
        self._doc.insert(self._pos, self._chunk)

    def undo(self) -> None:
        self._doc.delete(self._pos, len(self._chunk))


class DeleteCommand(EditCommand):
    def __init__(self, doc: Document, pos: int, length: int) -> None:
        self._doc = doc
        self._pos = pos
        self._length = length
        self._removed = ""

    def execute(self) -> None:
        self._removed = self._doc.content[self._pos:self._pos + self._length]
        self._doc.delete(self._pos, self._length)

    def undo(self) -> None:
        self._doc.insert(self._pos, self._removed)


class MacroCommand(EditCommand):
    """Composite: run/undo a batch of commands as one unit."""

    def __init__(self, commands: list[EditCommand]) -> None:
        self._commands = commands

    def execute(self) -> None:
        for cmd in self._commands:
            cmd.execute()

    def undo(self) -> None:
        for cmd in reversed(self._commands):
            cmd.undo()


class Editor:
    """Invoker: owns history, knows nothing about document internals."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._undo: deque[EditCommand] = deque()
        self._redo: deque[EditCommand] = deque()

    def run(self, cmd: EditCommand) -> None:
        cmd.execute()
        self._undo.append(cmd)
        self._redo.clear()

    def undo(self) -> None:
        if self._undo:
            cmd = self._undo.pop()
            cmd.undo()
            self._redo.append(cmd)

    def redo(self) -> None:
        if self._redo:
            cmd = self._redo.pop()
            cmd.execute()
            self._undo.append(cmd)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    doc = Document()
    editor = Editor()
    editor.run(InsertCommand(doc, 0, "hello"))
    print(doc.content)
    editor.run(InsertCommand(doc, 5, " world"))
    print(doc.content)
    editor.undo()
    print(doc.content)
    editor.redo()
    print(doc.content)
    editor.run(DeleteCommand(doc, 5, 6))
    print(doc.content)
    editor.undo()
    print(doc.content)

docs.title: 4.3 Go (idiomatic)
docs.text:
Explanation: Command is a two-method interface. Receivers are passed as pointers. Editor uses slices as stacks. Constructors (NewInsertCommand) keep wiring explicit — idiomatic Go.

package main

import "fmt"

type Document struct{ text []rune }

func (d *Document) Insert(pos int, s string) {
    r := []rune(s)
    d.text = append(d.text[:pos], append(r, d.text[pos:]...)...)
}

func (d *Document) Delete(pos, length int) {
    d.text = append(d.text[:pos], d.text[pos+length:]...)
}

func (d *Document) Content() string { return string(d.text) }

type Command interface {
    Execute()
    Undo()
}

type InsertCommand struct {
    doc   *Document
    pos   int
    chunk string
}

func NewInsertCommand(doc *Document, pos int, chunk string) *InsertCommand {
    return &InsertCommand{doc: doc, pos: pos, chunk: chunk}
}

func (c *InsertCommand) Execute() { c.doc.Insert(c.pos, c.chunk) }
func (c *InsertCommand) Undo()    { c.doc.Delete(c.pos, len([]rune(c.chunk))) }

type DeleteCommand struct {
    doc     *Document
    pos     int
    length  int
    removed string
}

func NewDeleteCommand(doc *Document, pos, length int) *DeleteCommand {
    return &DeleteCommand{doc: doc, pos: pos, length: length}
}

func (c *DeleteCommand) Execute() {
    c.removed = string([]rune(c.doc.Content())[c.pos : c.pos+c.length])
    c.doc.Delete(c.pos, c.length)
}

func (c *DeleteCommand) Undo() { c.doc.Insert(c.pos, c.removed) }

type Editor struct {
    undo []Command
    redo []Command
}

func (e *Editor) Run(cmd Command) {
    cmd.Execute()
    e.undo = append(e.undo, cmd)
    e.redo = nil // new branch invalidates redo
}

func (e *Editor) Undo() {
    if len(e.undo) == 0 {
        return
    }
    cmd := e.undo[len(e.undo)-1]
    e.undo = e.undo[:len(e.undo)-1]
    cmd.Undo()
    e.redo = append(e.redo, cmd)
}

func (e *Editor) Redo() {
    if len(e.redo) == 0 {
        return
    }
    cmd := e.redo[len(e.redo)-1]
    e.redo = e.redo[:len(e.redo)-1]
    cmd.Execute()
    e.undo = append(e.undo, cmd)
}

func main() {
    doc := &Document{}
    editor := &Editor{}
    editor.Run(NewInsertCommand(doc, 0, "hello"))
    fmt.Println(doc.Content())
    editor.Run(NewInsertCommand(doc, 5, " world"))
    fmt.Println(doc.Content())
    editor.Undo()
    fmt.Println(doc.Content())
    editor.Redo()
    fmt.Println(doc.Content())
    editor.Run(NewDeleteCommand(doc, 5, 6))
    fmt.Println(doc.Content())
    editor.Undo()
    fmt.Println(doc.Content())
}

docs.title: 5. Real-World Industry Applications
docs.text:
• Text and design editors (VS Code, Google Docs, Figma, Photoshop): Every keystroke, stroke, or layer op is a command on undo/redo stacks; collaborative editing replays remote commands in order.
  • GUI toolkits (Qt, Swing, JavaFX, web menus): Buttons and menu items hold command objects, enabling shortcuts, rebindable keys, and disabled-state logic without touching receivers.
  • Job queues and schedulers (Celery, Sidekiq, RabbitMQ, cron): Tasks are serialized commands with parameters, retries, and dead-letter handling; workers execute without knowing producers.
  • Database transactions and Sagas: Each step is a command with a compensating action; orchestrators roll back completed steps in reverse on failure (booking: reserve flight → hotel → car).
  • Remote controls and IoT (TV remotes, Home Assistant): Physical buttons map to command objects; macros ("movie night" dims lights + lowers screen) compose them.
  • API gateways and CLI frameworks (kubectl, git): Each subcommand is a Command object with validate + execute + undo/dry-run, giving uniform help, logging, and audit.
  • Game engines (Unity, Unreal): Player inputs become commands for replay systems, netcode prediction/rollback, and AI action queues.
  • Financial ledgers: Postings are immutable commands; reversals are new compensating commands, never edits — yielding a complete audit trail.

docs.title: 6. Practical Use Cases and Scenarios
docs.text:
• Undo/redo editor (Section 4): Toolbar, shortcuts, and scripts all call editor.run(cmd). Bounded stacks (e.g., last 100) cap memory; MacroCommand implements "repeat last action".
  • Smart-home remote: LightOnCommand, ThermostatSetCommand, LockDoorCommand assigned to buttons and schedules. A PartyModeMacro composes five commands; undo restores prior state.
  • Background job queue: SendEmailCommand(to, template), ResizeImageCommand(path) serialized to Redis. Workers pop, execute with retries, and move failures to a dead-letter queue — producers never block.
  • Bank transfer saga: DebitCommand + CreditCommand each with compensating inverses. Coordinator executes in order; on credit failure it undoes debit. Every step is logged for audit.
  • Collaborative drawing: Local strokes execute immediately and broadcast as commands; remote clients replay them in sequence-number order, giving eventual consistency without shared memory.
  • CLI with dry-run: Each subcommand implements plan() (print what would happen) plus execute(). --dry-run runs only plan(), reusing validation and making dangerous ops reviewable.

docs.title: 7. When to Use and When Not to Use
docs.text:
Use Command when:

  • You need to parameterize invokers with actions (buttons, shortcuts, scheduled jobs).
  • You need to queue, log, serialize, retry, or send requests across processes/machines.
  • You need undo/redo, macros, or transactional compensation.
  • Senders and receivers must evolve independently (UI vs domain logic).

Do NOT use when:

Situation Prefer instead Single immediate call, never queued/logged/undone Direct method call or function Swapping algorithms at runtime with no history Strategy pattern One handler must be selected from a chain Chain of Responsibility State snapshots are simpler than inverses Memento (whole-state restore) Fire-and-forget events to many listeners Observer / event bus

docs.title: 8. Do's and Don'ts
docs.text:
Do:

  • Make commands self-contained: capture receiver + all parameters at construction; no hidden globals at execute time.
  • Implement undo() alongside execute() from day one — retrofitting inverses is error-prone.
  • Clear redo on every new command and bound history size (count or bytes) with a documented eviction policy.
  • Validate before mutating: validate() first, then execute(), so failed commands leave no partial state.
  • Log command name + parameters + result for audit; assign each command a stable ID for tracing across queues.
  • Compose with MacroCommand instead of writing mega-commands; keep each command focused on one action.

Don't:

  • Don't let commands reach into each other's state or into invoker internals — they should know only their receiver.
  • Don't store unbounded history (memory leak); don't keep removed snapshots larger than needed (store diffs).
  • Don't execute partially and report success — make execute() atomic or return explicit failure for saga rollback.
  • Don't create a full class for trivial one-shot actions; a lambda is a legitimate command.
  • Don't share a stateful command instance across threads; create one command per request.
  • Don't forget idempotency for queued/retried commands — workers may execute twice after a crash.

docs.title: 9.1 Command vs Strategy vs Memento
docs.text:
Aspect Command Strategy Memento (+ Serialization) Purpose Encapsulate a request + receiver for deferral/undo Encapsulate interchangeable algorithms Capture and restore whole object state Carries Receiver reference, args, inverse state Algorithm only (usually stateless) Opaque state snapshot, no behavior Invoker Stores, queues, logs, undoes commands Delegates immediately to chosen algorithm Caretaker stores; only originator restores Undo First-class via undo() / compensating action Not applicable Restore prior snapshot wholesale Typical use Undo stacks, job queues, macros, sagas Payment methods, sorting, pricing rules Game saves, checkpoints, form restore

Rule of thumb: Defer/queue/undo a request → Command. Swap how something is computed → Strategy. Restore whole state without inverting → Memento. In practice Command + Memento pair well: the command holds a memento as its undo state.

docs.title: 9.2 Command vs Chain of Responsibility vs Observer
docs.text: Aspect Command Chain of Responsibility Observer Direction Invoker → one command → one receiver Request travels link to link until handled Subject broadcasts → many observers Selection Client picks the exact command Chain picks handler dynamically All subscribers react Time Execution can be deferred/stored Handling is immediate traversal Notification is immediate fan-out Use when Actions must be objects Handler unknown at compile time Many parties need the same event

docs.title: Q&A
docs.text:
Q1. What is the Command pattern in one sentence? A: It turns a request (receiver + method + args) into an object so invokers can store, queue, log, and undo requests without knowing the receiver.

Q2. How does Command enable undo/redo? A: Each command captures enough state to invert itself. The invoker pushes executed commands onto an undo stack; undo() pops and inverts, redo() re-executes. New commands clear redo to keep history linear.

Q3. Why not just call receiver methods directly? A: Direct calls hardwire sender to receiver and lose queuing, logging, batching, retries, macros, and undo. Commands make calls first-class: serializable, schedulable, auditable, and composable.

Q4. How do you avoid an explosion of tiny command classes? A: Use lambdas for one-shot non-undoable actions, share an abstract base for related commands, and compose via MacroCommand. Reserve full classes for commands with state, undo, or reuse.

Q5. Command vs Strategy — how do you distinguish in an interview? A: Command encapsulates a request bound to a receiver (with history/undo); Strategy encapsulates an algorithm swapped at runtime (stateless). Commands are triggered by invokers and stored; strategies are delegated to immediately by a context.

Q6. How do you make queued commands reliable? A: Serialize commands with IDs, make execute() idempotent (dedupe by ID), persist before ack, retry with backoff, and route poison messages to a dead-letter queue after N attempts. Log every state transition.

Q7. How do you implement macros and transactions? A: MacroCommand executes children in order and undoes in reverse. For sagas, each step defines a compensating command; the coordinator runs forward and compensates backward on failure. Validate all steps before starting when possible.

Q8. What are the memory and complexity costs? A: One class per action plus history retention. Bound stacks (e.g., 100 entries or 10 MB), store deltas not full copies, compress/archive old entries, and measure snapshot size early for media-heavy receivers.

Q9. How do you test commands? A: Test execute() and undo() round-trip against a real receiver (assert state restored exactly), test invoker stacks (undo/redo/clear-on-new), and test macro ordering. Mock the receiver only for invoker-level tests.

docs.title: LLD scenarios
docs.text:
S1. Design undo/redo for a text editor. Requirements: insert/delete, unlimited undo with bounded memory, redo invalidation, macro replay. Solution: EditCommand + Document receiver + Editor invoker as in Section 4; bound stacks to 100; MacroCommand for replay. Discuss snapshot-vs-inverse tradeoff and how collaborative editing orders remote commands.

S2. Design a job queue with retries. Requirements: producers submit email/resize jobs, workers execute async, at-least-once delivery, poison-message handling. Solution: serializable command DTOs with IDs + idempotent execute(); broker persists; worker acks after success; exponential backoff; DLQ after 5 failures. Discuss deduplication and exactly-once illusions.

S3. Design a smart-home remote with scenes. Requirements: rebindable buttons, "movie night" scene, undo last action. Solution: buttons hold Command slots; scenes are MacroCommands; remote keeps one-level (or stacked) undo history. Discuss persistence of bindings and handling offline devices (queue + sync).

docs.title: 11. Testing and Best Practices
docs.text:
• Round-trip tests: For every command, assert execute(); undo() restores exact prior state, and undo(); redo() reproduces the post-execute state. Table-drive positions (0, middle, end) and empty-document edges.
  • Invoker tests: Assert undo on empty stack is a no-op, redo cleared after new command, macro executes in order and undoes in reverse, and history bound evicts oldest (not newest).
  • Isolation: Test command logic against a real receiver; test invoker with stub commands (no receiver). Never test both layers in one case — failures become ambiguous.
  • Concurrency: One command instance per request; stress shared invoker with parallel run() calls behind a lock or concurrent queue; assert history order under contention.
  • Reliability: For queued commands, test serialization round-trip, double-execution idempotency, and DLQ routing. Include command ID + version in every payload for forward compatibility.
  • Best practices: Keep execute() atomic (validate-then-mutate); name commands as verbs (InsertCommand, ChargeCardCommand); document the inverse next to each execute(); cap history by both count and bytes; never expose receiver mutators that bypass commands in undoable flows.

docs.title: 12. Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Command turns requests into objects — decoupling invokers from receivers and unlocking queues, macros, audit logs, and undo/redo.
  • Reach for it when actions must be stored, scheduled, retried, or reversed; prefer direct calls or Strategy when none of those apply.
  • Pair with Memento when inverses are complex (store snapshots) and with Chain when commands travel through handler pipelines.
  • Correctness hinges on self-contained commands, exact inverses, redo invalidation, and bounded history — test all four explicitly.
  • In LLD interviews, the editor-undo, job-queue, and remote-control scenarios are the canonical wins: draw the four roles (Command, ConcreteCommand, Receiver, Invoker) and immediately discuss undo state, idempotency, and history bounds to signal production experience.

docs.title: Interpreter Design Pattern
docs.text: Youtube: 40. Interpreter Design Pattern | LLD System Design | Design pattern explanation in Java

docs.title: 1. Overview and Fundamentals
docs.text:
Interpreter is a behavioral design pattern that defines a grammatical representation for a simple language and an interpreter that evaluates sentences in that language. Each grammar rule becomes a class; composing instances builds a parse tree that can be evaluated, printed, or translated.

  • GoF classification: Behavioral — models how sentences (composite requests) are evaluated.
  • Intent (GoF): "Given a language, define a representation for its grammar along with an interpreter that uses the representation to interpret sentences in the language."
  • Core idea: Map grammar productions to classes: terminal expressions hold values (Number, Equals), non-terminal expressions combine children (Add, And, Or). A sentence is just an object tree; interpret(context) walks it.
  • Everyday analogy: A recipe card system. Terminal cards say "200g flour" (values); non-terminal cards say "mix A with B" or "bake for 30 min" (combinations). Any recipe is a tree of cards, and any cook (interpreter) can execute it — or a translator could convert it to another language.
  • Key participants:
  • AbstractExpression: Declares interpret(context).
  • TerminalExpression: Leaf with no children (literal, variable lookup).
  • NonTerminalExpression: Holds child expressions and combines their results.
  • Context: Shared input state (variable map, environment, input string position).
  • Client: Builds (or parses into) the expression tree, then calls interpret.
  • Success conditions: Grammar is small, stable, and hierarchical; one tree serves multiple interpreters (evaluate, pretty-print, compile to SQL).
  • What it is not: It is not a full parser/compiler toolchain, not a regex engine, and not a business-rules UI — those may use an interpreter internally, but the pattern itself is only the expression-tree + evaluation discipline.

docs.title: How the mechanism works
docs.text:
1. Define the grammar: e.g., rule := rule AND rule | rule OR rule | NOT rule | key == value.
  2. Create one class per production (And, Or, Not, Equals).
  3. Parse input text into a tree (hand-rolled for tiny grammars; parser generators for larger ones).
  4. Call root.interpret(context); recursion evaluates leaves first, then combines.
  5. Reuse the same tree with different contexts, or different interpreters (evaluator vs SQL generator).

docs.title: Grammar-to-class mapping
docs.text:
• Terminals answer directly from context: Number(5).interpret() → 5; Equals("role","ADMIN").interpret(ctx) → ctx["role"] == "ADMIN".
  • Non-terminals delegate: And(l, r).interpret(ctx) → l.interpret(ctx) && r.interpret(ctx).
  • Shared nodes reduce class count: one BinaryOp(op, left, right) with an enum instead of Add/Subtract/Multiply classes; one Comparison(op, key, value) instead of per-operator classes.
  • Context design decides flexibility: a Map<String,String> suffices for equality rules; richer contexts carry types, scopes, and error collectors.

docs.title: Design dynamics
docs.text:
• Extensibility axis: Adding a new rule is easy (new class). Adding a new operation over all rules (type-check, optimize, pretty-print) requires touching every class — the classic Expression Problem. If you add operations often, pair with Visitor.
  • Performance profile: Tree interpretation is O(nodes) per evaluation with recursion overhead. Mitigations: parse once and cache the tree, short-circuit And/Or, share immutable subtrees (Flyweight), and compile hot paths to lambdas or bytecode.
  • Error handling: Fail at parse time with positions (ParseException: expected value at col 12), not at interpret time. At interpret time decide fail-open vs fail-closed for missing variables and document it.
  • SOLID alignment: Open/Closed for new rules (additive classes), Single Responsibility per production, but Interface Segregation suffers if one fat interpret must serve evaluation + printing + compilation — prefer separate interpreter interfaces per concern.
  • Scaling ceiling: Beyond ~20 productions, or once you need precedence, loops, functions, or good syntax errors, hand-rolled interpreters collapse under maintenance. Graduate to ANTLR, parser combinators, or an embedded script engine (GraalVM, Lua, Drools).

docs.title: Variants and extensions
docs.text:
• Parser + Interpreter split: A parser builds the tree; the pattern only evaluates it. Keep these separate so grammars can evolve without touching evaluation.
  • Compiling interpreter: Instead of walking the tree per evaluation, generate SQL, a predicate lambda, or bytecode once — same tree, faster repeated use.
  • Validating interpreter: A second pass that type-checks or authorizes rules before they run in production.
  • Musical notation, regex, SpEL: All classic GoF examples — small, stable, hierarchical languages where tree evaluation is the natural model.

docs.title: 3.1 Static structure — grammar as classes
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Client {
        +buildRule() Rule
    }
    class Rule {
        <>
        +interpret(ctx: Context) bool
    }
    class Equals {
        -key: String
        -expected: String
        +interpret(ctx: Context) bool
    }
    class And {
        -left: Rule
        -right: Rule
        +interpret(ctx: Context) bool
    }
    class Or {
        -left: Rule
        -right: Rule
        +interpret(ctx: Context) bool
    }
    class Not {
        -inner: Rule
        +interpret(ctx: Context) bool
    }
    class Context {
        +values: Map~String,String~
        +lookup(key: String) String
    }
    Client ..> Rule : builds tree
    Rule ..> Context : reads
    Equals ..|> Rule
    And ..|> Rule
    Or ..|> Rule
    Not ..|> Rule
    And --> Rule : left/right
    Or --> Rule : left/right
    Not --> Rule : inner

Explanation: Each grammar production is a class implementing Rule. Terminal Equals holds data and reads the Context; non-terminals And/Or/Not hold child Rule references and combine results. Client assembles the tree once (manually or via a parser) and re-evaluates it against many contexts. Adding GreaterThan means adding one leaf class — no existing code changes.

docs.title: 3.2 Dynamic flow — evaluating one sentence
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant OrRule as Or
    participant EqAdmin as Equals(role==ADMIN)
    participant AndRule as And
    participant Ctx as Context
    Client->>OrRule: interpret(ctx role=EDITOR owner=true)
    OrRule->>EqAdmin: interpret(ctx)
    EqAdmin->>Ctx: lookup(role)
    Ctx-->>EqAdmin: EDITOR
    EqAdmin-->>OrRule: false
    OrRule->>AndRule: interpret(ctx)
    AndRule->>Ctx: lookup(role) → EDITOR == EDITOR → true
    AndRule->>Ctx: lookup(owner) → true == true → true
    AndRule-->>OrRule: true AND true = true
    OrRule-->>Client: false OR true = true

Explanation: Evaluation is depth-first recursion with short-circuit potential (Or could skip the right side if the left were true). Every leaf read goes through the Context, which is why missing-key policy (return false vs throw) must be decided up front. The same tree evaluated against {role: VIEWER} takes the identical path but returns false — parse once, interpret many times.

docs.title: 4. Implementation Examples in Java, Python, and Go
docs.text: All three examples model an access-control rule engine: ADMIN, or (EDITOR who owns the document). The rule tree is built once and evaluated against multiple user contexts.

docs.title: 4.1 Java (OOP, classic GoF style)
docs.text:
Explanation: Rule is the abstract expression; Equals is terminal; And/Or/Not are non-terminal. Context is a Map<String,String>. AccessDemo builds the tree and interprets it twice.

import java.util.Map;

interface Rule {
    boolean interpret(Map<String, String> ctx);
}

final class Equals implements Rule {
    private final String key;
    private final String expected;
    Equals(String key, String expected) {
        this.key = key;
        this.expected = expected;
    }
    public boolean interpret(Map<String, String> ctx) {
        return expected.equals(ctx.get(key));
    }
}

final class And implements Rule {
    private final Rule left;
    private final Rule right;
    And(Rule left, Rule right) { this.left = left; this.right = right; }
    public boolean interpret(Map<String, String> ctx) {
        return left.interpret(ctx) && right.interpret(ctx);
    }
}

final class Or implements Rule {
    private final Rule left;
    private final Rule right;
    Or(Rule left, Rule right) { this.left = left; this.right = right; }
    public boolean interpret(Map<String, String> ctx) {
        return left.interpret(ctx) || right.interpret(ctx);
    }
}

final class Not implements Rule {
    private final Rule inner;
    Not(Rule inner) { this.inner = inner; }
    public boolean interpret(Map<String, String> ctx) {
        return !inner.interpret(ctx);
    }
}

public class AccessDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Rule canEdit = new Or(
            new Equals("role", "ADMIN"),
            new And(new Equals("role", "EDITOR"), new Equals("owner", "true"))
        );
        System.out.println(canEdit.interpret(Map.of("role", "EDITOR", "owner", "true")));
        System.out.println(canEdit.interpret(Map.of("role", "VIEWER", "owner", "false")));
        System.out.println(new Not(new Equals("role", "BANNED"))
            .interpret(Map.of("role", "EDITOR")));
    }
}

true
false
true

docs.title: 4.2 Python (pythonic, PEP 8)
docs.text:
Explanation: ABC Rule with interpret(ctx); frozen dataclasses for terminals; short-circuit and/or. Includes a tiny parse_equals helper hinting at the parser/interpreter split.

from __future__ import annotations
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Mapping


class Rule(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def interpret(self, ctx: Mapping[str, str]) -> bool: ...


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Equals(Rule):
    """Terminal: leaf comparison against the context."""

    key: str
    expected: str

    def interpret(self, ctx: Mapping[str, str]) -> bool:
        return ctx.get(self.key) == self.expected


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class And(Rule):
    """Non-terminal: both sides must hold (short-circuits)."""

    left: Rule
    right: Rule

    def interpret(self, ctx: Mapping[str, str]) -> bool:
        return self.left.interpret(ctx) and self.right.interpret(ctx)


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Or(Rule):
    """Non-terminal: either side holds (short-circuits)."""

    left: Rule
    right: Rule

    def interpret(self, ctx: Mapping[str, str]) -> bool:
        return self.left.interpret(ctx) or self.right.interpret(ctx)


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Not(Rule):
    """Non-terminal: negation of one child."""

    inner: Rule

    def interpret(self, ctx: Mapping[str, str]) -> bool:
        return not self.inner.interpret(ctx)


def can_edit_rule() -> Rule:
    return Or(
        Equals("role", "ADMIN"),
        And(Equals("role", "EDITOR"), Equals("owner", "true")),
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    rule = can_edit_rule()
    print(rule.interpret({"role": "EDITOR", "owner": "true"}))
    print(rule.interpret({"role": "VIEWER", "owner": "false"}))
    print(Not(Equals("role", "BANNED")).interpret({"role": "EDITOR"}))

False
True

docs.title: 4.3 Go (idiomatic)
docs.text:
Explanation: Rule interface with Interpret(ctx map[string]string) bool. Structs per production; value receivers since expressions are immutable. main builds the tree once and evaluates three contexts.

package main

import "fmt"

type Context map[string]string

type Rule interface {
    Interpret(ctx Context) bool
}

type Equals struct {
    Key      string
    Expected string
}

func (e Equals) Interpret(ctx Context) bool { return ctx[e.Key] == e.Expected }

type And struct {
    Left  Rule
    Right Rule
}

func (a And) Interpret(ctx Context) bool {
    return a.Left.Interpret(ctx) && a.Right.Interpret(ctx)
}

type Or struct {
    Left  Rule
    Right Rule
}

func (o Or) Interpret(ctx Context) bool {
    return o.Left.Interpret(ctx) || o.Right.Interpret(ctx)
}

type Not struct{ Inner Rule }

func (n Not) Interpret(ctx Context) bool { return !n.Inner.Interpret(ctx) }

func main() {
    canEdit := Or{
        Left: Equals{Key: "role", Expected: "ADMIN"},
        Right: And{
            Left:  Equals{Key: "role", Expected: "EDITOR"},
            Right: Equals{Key: "owner", Expected: "true"},
        },
    }
    fmt.Println(canEdit.Interpret(Context{"role": "EDITOR", "owner": "true"}))
    fmt.Println(canEdit.Interpret(Context{"role": "VIEWER", "owner": "false"}))
    fmt.Println(Not{Inner: Equals{Key: "role", Expected: "BANNED"}}.Interpret(
        Context{"role": "EDITOR"}))
}

docs.title: 5. Real-World Industry Applications
docs.text:
• Expression languages (Spring SpEL, JSP EL, Jakarta EL): #{user.role == 'ADMIN'} in configs and templates is parsed into an expression tree and interpreted per request.
  • SQL and query planners (Postgres, MySQL): WHERE clauses become expression trees; the same tree is interpreted (row filter), optimized (predicate pushdown), and compiled — the multi-interpreter payoff.
  • Regex engines (Java Pattern, RE2): Patterns compile to state machines / expression trees; matching is interpretation against input strings.
  • Infrastructure as code (Terraform, OPA/Rego): Policy rules (allow if input.role == "admin") are interpreted against plan JSON on every apply.
  • Spreadsheet engines (Excel, Google Sheets): Formulas parse to ASTs re-interpreted on cell change, with dependency-ordered re-evaluation.
  • Feature-flag and targeting platforms (LaunchDarkly, Unleash): Targeting rules (country == US AND plan != free) are small DSLs interpreted per evaluation context.
  • Monitoring alerts (Prometheus, Datadog): Alert expressions and threshold rules are parsed once and interpreted against each scrape.
  • Search and filters (Elasticsearch, Jira JQL, Gmail): User filter strings compile to trees interpreted per document/ticket/email.

docs.title: 6. Practical Use Cases and Scenarios
docs.text:
• Access-control rules (Section 4): Product teams edit role == ADMIN OR (role == EDITOR AND owner == true) in a dashboard; backend parses to a Rule tree once and evaluates per request. New operators ship as new classes; audit logs print the tree.
  • Calculator / formula bar: 3 + 4 * (2 - 1) parses to Add(3, Multiply(4, Subtract(2,1))). Same tree powers evaluate, pretty-print, and "show steps" modes.
  • Email inbox filters: from:boss AND has:attachment OR subject:urgent becomes Or(And(...), ...). Users compose rules in plain text; the client parses and the server interprets per message.
  • Discount engine: cart.total > 100 AND coupon == SAVE10 AND NOT member.excluded decides checkout discounts. Marketing edits rules without deploys; finance replays the same tree to audit past orders.
  • Home automation: IF motion AND time AFTER 22:00 THEN dim lights — sensor contexts flow through small condition trees evaluated on every event.
  • Validation DSL: age >= 18 AND (country == US OR guardian == true) for signup forms. One tree drives server validation, client error messages (via a message-rendering interpreter), and generated documentation.

docs.title: 7. When to Use and When Not to Use
docs.text:
Use Interpreter when:

  • The language/grammar is small (a handful of productions), stable, and hierarchical.
  • Non-technical users or configs must express rules without code changes.
  • The same sentences need multiple treatments: evaluate, print, optimize, compile to SQL.
  • Efficiency is not critical and expressions evaluate frequently against varying contexts.

Do NOT use when:

Situation Prefer instead Full programming language, loops, functions, precedence Parser generator (ANTLR), parser combinators, embedded engine (Lua, GraalVM) Grammar changes weekly or has 20+ productions Rule engine (Drools), decision tables, scripting Hot-path parsing (regex, protocol decoders) Hand-optimized parsers, regex libraries, codegen One-off boolean logic with 2–3 conditions Plain predicates / Specification pattern Rules need versioning, audit, and UI at scale Dedicated policy engine (OPA) with storage and tooling

docs.title: 8. Do's and Don'ts
docs.text:
Do:

  • Separate parsing from interpretation: parser builds the tree (and reports syntax errors with positions); interpreter only evaluates.
  • Keep the grammar minimal; prefer generic nodes (BinaryOp, Comparison) over per-operator classes.
  • Parse once, interpret many times — cache trees keyed by rule text with invalidation on edit.
  • Short-circuit And/Or and order cheap checks first (equality before regex).
  • Decide and document missing-variable policy (fail-closed for auth, fail-open only with explicit reason).
  • Share immutable subtrees freely; expressions should be value objects safe for concurrent interpretation.

Don't:

  • Don't hand-roll precedence climbing, loops, or function calls — that is a compiler project, not a pattern.
  • Don't interpret untrusted rule text without sandboxing, timeouts, and resource limits (ReDoS-style blowups apply to trees too).
  • Don't let interpret() mutate the context or perform I/O; side effects make rules untestable and non-replayable.
  • Don't grow past ~20 productions without re-evaluating: class explosion and recursive debugging will dominate.
  • Don't return cryptic false for malformed input — throw typed parse errors at build time.
  • Don't conflate evaluation with rendering; write a second interpreter (printer/SQL emitter) instead of stuffing toSQL() into evaluation classes.

docs.title: 9.1 Interpreter vs Visitor vs Composite
docs.text:
Aspect Interpreter Visitor Composite Purpose Evaluate sentences of a small grammar Add operations over a stable object structure Treat part-whole hierarchies uniformly Tree meaning Tree is the language (productions) Tree is domain data; visitor carries the operation Tree is containment (folders, org charts) Adding rules/nodes Easy: new expression class Painful: every visitor breaks Easy: new leaf/composite Adding operations Painful: touch every expression class Easy: new visitor class Depends on design Typical use Filters, rules, calculators, SpEL AST linting, export, reporting File systems, UI trees, menus

Rule of thumb: Grammar evaluation is the goal and grammar is small → Interpreter. Structure is stable but operations keep coming → put a Visitor over the tree. Hierarchy is about containment, not language → Composite.

docs.title: 9.2 Interpreter vs Strategy vs Command
docs.text: Aspect Interpreter Strategy Command Encapsulates Grammar productions composed into sentences One interchangeable algorithm A request + receiver + undo Composition Trees of arbitrary depth Single selection, no composition Macros compose sequentially Input Sentence + context evaluated recursively Data passed to chosen algorithm Self-contained, executable anytime Use when Users write rule-like expressions Swapping how to compute Deferring/undoing a request

docs.title: Q&A
docs.text:
Q1. What is the Interpreter pattern in one sentence? A: Each grammar rule becomes a class; sentences are object trees whose interpret(context) recursively evaluates to a result.

Q2. When is Interpreter better than ANTLR or a script engine? A: For tiny, stable grammars (filters, permissions, calculators) where each rule maps to a class and trees are parsed once and evaluated often. Once you need precedence, loops, functions, or quality errors, a generator or engine wins on correctness and maintenance.

Q3. How do you avoid class explosion as the grammar grows? A: Generic nodes (BinaryOp with operator enum, Comparison with operator), Flyweight-shared terminals, and refusing to model non-essential syntax. Cap productions and graduate to a real parser past ~20 rules.

Q4. How do you handle invalid input and missing variables? A: Parse-time validation with position-aware errors (ParseException); interpret-time policy for missing keys — fail-closed (false or throw) for authorization, explicit default otherwise. Never silently coerce.

Q5. How do you make repeated evaluation fast? A: Cache parsed trees, short-circuit boolean nodes, order cheap predicates first, share immutable subtrees, and for hot rules compile the tree once to a lambda/predicate or SQL instead of re-walking.

Q6. Terminal vs non-terminal — give a concrete example. A: In role == ADMIN OR owner == true, the Equals comparisons are terminals (leaves reading context); Or is non-terminal (combines two children). Terminals answer; non-terminals combine.

Q7. How does Interpreter relate to Composite and Visitor? A: The tree is a Composite (uniform interpret across leaves and groups). Adding operations (print, type-check, compile) across all node types is exactly what Visitor solves — the two patterns are commonly layered.

Q8. How do you test an interpreter? A: Unit-test each production in isolation (truth tables for And/Or/Not, boundary values for comparisons); test parsing separately from evaluation; property-test with generated trees; fuzz invalid syntax for clean errors; benchmark deep trees for stack/recursion limits.

Q9. What are the security concerns? A: Untrusted rule text can DoS (deep nesting → stack overflow; expensive regex leaves). Enforce max tree depth, evaluation timeout, allowlisted operators, and context scoping so rules cannot reach unintended data.

docs.title: LLD scenarios
docs.text:
S1. Design a discount / promotion engine. Requirements: marketers author IF cart.total > 100 AND coupon == SAVE10 THEN 10% off, versioned rules, audit of past orders. Solution: rule DSL → parser → Rule tree stored with version; checkout interprets against cart context; a second interpreter renders human-readable descriptions for audit. Discuss rule versioning, staged rollout, and compiling hot rules to predicates.

S2. Design a feature-flag targeting system. Requirements: country == US AND (plan == pro OR beta == true), per-request evaluation at scale, no deploys for new flags. Solution: flag conditions as cached expression trees; evaluation service interprets against request context in microseconds; short-circuit ordering by selectivity. Discuss caching, fail-open vs fail-closed defaults, and observability per flag.

S3. Design spreadsheet formula evaluation. Requirements: =A1 + B2 * 3, dependency ordering, cycle detection. Solution: formulas parse to expression trees referencing cell contexts; topological evaluation with memoization; cycle → typed error, not infinite recursion. Discuss lazy vs eager recompute and how Visitor could add "list dependents" over the same trees.

docs.title: 11. Testing and Best Practices
docs.text:
• Per-production tests: Truth tables for boolean combinators; boundary/empty-string/unicode cases for comparisons; missing-key behavior per policy. Keep them as living grammar documentation.
  • Parser vs evaluator split: Test parsing (valid trees, precise syntax errors) independently from interpretation (tree + context → result). A parsing bug should never masquerade as an evaluation bug.
  • Round-trip tests: Parse → pretty-print → re-parse should yield an equivalent tree; catches printer/parser drift.
  • Fuzzing and limits: Feed malformed and deeply nested input; assert typed errors, depth caps, and timeouts — never hangs or stack overflows.
  • Performance: Benchmark representative rules at expected QPS; profile before optimizing; prefer tree caching and compile-to-predicate over micro-tuning recursion.
  • Best practices: Immutable expression nodes; context as read-only view; typed errors with positions; versioned rule storage; audit logging of rule text + version + outcome; depth/time budgets for untrusted input.

docs.title: 12. Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Interpreter turns grammar into composable expression objects — parse once, interpret many times, against many contexts.
  • It shines for small, stable DSLs: access rules, filters, formulas, alert conditions, feature flags.
  • Its axes are clear: new rules are cheap, new operations are expensive (pair with Visitor when operations multiply); past ~20 productions or real language features, graduate to a parser generator or engine.
  • Production-readiness means parse/interpret separation, cached trees, short-circuiting, typed errors, depth/timeout budgets, and multi-interpreter reuse (evaluate today, SQL/print tomorrow).
  • In LLD interviews, propose it when you hear "users write simple rules, grammar is tiny and stable" — then immediately discuss the scaling ceiling and error policy to show judgment, not just pattern recall.

docs.title: Iterator Design Pattern
docs.text: Youtube: 33. Iterator Design Pattern Explained with Example | Low Level Design

docs.title: 1. Overview and Fundamentals
docs.text:
Iterator is a behavioral design pattern that provides sequential access to elements of an aggregate (collection, tree, stream, paged API) without exposing its internal representation. Clients loop with a uniform interface while each iterator owns traversal state and order.

  • GoF classification: Behavioral — decouples traversal algorithms from aggregate structure.
  • Intent (GoF): "Provide a way to access the elements of an aggregate object sequentially without exposing its underlying representation."
  • Core idea: Move the cursor out of the collection. The aggregate knows what it stores; the iterator knows how to walk it (hasNext/next, or __iter__/__next__, or Next() bool).
  • Everyday analogy: A TV remote. Channels may come from cable, satellite, or streaming (different internals), but up/down buttons walk them identically. Multiple remotes (iterators) can browse independently without rewiring the TV.
  • Key participants:
  • Iterator (interface): hasNext(), next(), often remove()/fail-fast semantics.
  • ConcreteIterator: Holds cursor/stack/page token for one traversal.
  • Aggregate (interface): Declares iterator() / factory methods per order.
  • ConcreteAggregate: Stores elements; creates iterators on demand.
