  • Client: Loops uniformly, owns per-element logic.
  • Success conditions: One aggregate supports many simultaneous, independent traversals; traversal order can change without touching client loops; lazy iterators handle infinite or huge sequences.
  • What it is not: It is not the traversal logic inlined in the collection, not a Visitor (which carries the operation into the structure), and not just syntactic sugar for indexed loops — it is the cursor abstraction that enables laziness, uniformity, and multiple orders.

docs.title: How the mechanism works
docs.text:
1. Aggregate exposes a factory: iterator(), depthFirst(), breadthFirst(), pages().
  2. Factory returns a fresh iterator holding its own cursor (index, stack, page token).
  3. Client calls hasNext() then next() until exhausted; each iterator advances independently.
  4. Iterator may be eager (snapshot) or lazy (compute-on-demand for trees, streams, paged APIs).

docs.title: Internal vs external iterators
docs.text:
Style Control Example Tradeoff External Client drives hasNext/next Java Iterator, Go placeholder style Flexible (break/skip/merge); more boilerplate Internal Aggregate drives, client supplies function forEach, Python for x in xs, JS map Concise; harder to pause, merge, or short-circuit across two collections

Most languages offer both: external iterators for control, internal iteration (streams, generators) for brevity.

docs.title: Design dynamics
docs.text:
• Cursor ownership: Each iterator must hold independent state. Sharing a cursor between loops is the classic bug that makes nested iteration skip elements.
  • Fail-fast vs weakly consistent: Fail-fast iterators snapshot modCount and throw on concurrent modification (Java collections). Snapshot iterators copy-on-create (safe but memory-heavy). Weakly consistent iterators tolerate changes (concurrent queues). Document the guarantee — callers must know it.
  • Laziness: Tree, graph, file, and paged-API iterators compute the next element on demand, enabling infinite sequences and constant-memory streaming. Lookahead (nextFile in Section 4) is the standard technique for hasNext over filtered/lazy sources.
  • Multiple orders, one aggregate: depthFirst(), breadthFirst(), reverse(), filtered(predicate) are all iterators over the same storage. Clients pick order; storage never changes.
  • SOLID alignment: Single Responsibility (traversal leaves the aggregate), Open/Closed (new order = new iterator class), Liskov (all iterators honor the hasNext/next contract, including throwing NoSuchElementException when exhausted).
  • Cursor invalidation: Structural modification during iteration invalidates index/stack/page assumptions. Solutions: fail-fast detection, version stamps, copy-on-write, or explicit invalidation docs.

docs.title: Variants and extensions
docs.text:
• Null/empty iterator: Returns hasNext() == false immediately — removes null checks in clients.
  • Filtering/transforming iterators: Decorate a base iterator with predicate/projection (the bridge to streams and lazy pipelines).
  • Composite + Iterator: Tree traversal where next() transparently descends into children (Section 4 file-tree example).
  • Paged/cursor iterators: Page tokens replace indexes; next() fetches the next page on demand (GraphQL connections, DynamoDB LastEvaluatedKey).

docs.title: 3.1 Static structure — aggregate creates iterators
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Client {
        +walk(fs: FileSystem)
    }
    class IterableAggregate {
        <>
        +iterator() Iterator~FileNode~
        +depthFirst() Iterator~FileNode~
    }
    class FileSystem {
        -root: FileNode
        +iterator() Iterator~FileNode~
        +depthFirst() Iterator~FileNode~
    }
    class Iterator {
        <>
        +hasNext() bool
        +next() FileNode
    }
    class DepthFirstIterator {
        -stack: Stack~Iterator~
        -nextFile: FileNode
        +hasNext() bool
        +next() FileNode
        -advance() void
    }
    class BreadthFirstIterator {
        -queue: Queue~FileNode~
        +hasNext() bool
        +next() FileNode
    }
    class FileNode {
        +name: String
        +directory: bool
        +children: List~FileNode~
    }
    Client ..> IterableAggregate : loops over
    FileSystem ..|> IterableAggregate
    FileSystem ..> DepthFirstIterator : creates
    FileSystem ..> BreadthFirstIterator : creates
    DepthFirstIterator ..|> Iterator
    BreadthFirstIterator ..|> Iterator
    DepthFirstIterator --> FileNode : yields

Explanation: FileSystem (aggregate) never exposes its tree; it manufactures iterators. Each iterator encapsulates a different traversal strategy and cursor (stack vs queue). Client depends only on the Iterator interface, so switching depthFirst() to breadth-first is a one-line change. Two iterators over the same FileSystem advance independently because each owns its cursor.

docs.title: 3.2 Dynamic flow — lazy depth-first walk
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant FS as FileSystem
    participant It as DepthFirstIterator
    participant Root as root/ children
    Client->>FS: iterator()
    FS->>It: new DepthFirstIterator(root)
    It->>Root: push iterator over [a.txt, sub/]
    loop while hasNext
        Client->>It: hasNext()
        It-->>Client: true (lookahead ready)
        Client->>It: next()
        It->>It: return current, advance()
        alt node is directory
            It->>Root: push children iterator (descend)
        else node is file
            It-->>Client: FileNode
        end
    end
    Client->>It: hasNext()
    It-->>Client: false (stack drained)

Explanation: Construction primes a one-element lookahead so hasNext() is O(1) and side-effect-free — calling it twice never skips. next() returns the primed file and advances past any directories. Directories are descended into but never yielded (filtering + traversal fused). When the stack drains, the iterator is exhausted; further next() calls throw rather than returning null.

docs.title: 4. Implementation Examples in Java, Python, and Go
docs.text: All three examples model a music playlist with two traversal orders (sequential and shuffled/reversed), showing how one aggregate serves multiple iterators. Java additionally sketches the depth-first tree iterator from the UML.

docs.title: 4.1 Java (OOP, classic GoF style)
docs.text:
Explanation: Playlist is the aggregate with iterator() (sequential) and shuffled() (alternate order) factories. SequentialIterator holds an index; ShuffledIterator holds a pre-shuffled index list. Fail-fast via modCount sketch.

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.Iterator;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.NoSuchElementException;

class Playlist implements Iterable<String> {
    private final List<String> songs = new ArrayList<>();
    private int modCount = 0;

    void add(String song) { songs.add(song); modCount++; }

    @Override
    public Iterator<String> iterator() {
        return new SequentialIterator();
    }

    public Iterator<String> shuffled() {
        return new ShuffledIterator();
    }

    private class SequentialIterator implements Iterator<String> {
        private final int expectedMod = modCount;
        private int cursor = 0;

        public boolean hasNext() { return cursor < songs.size(); }

        public String next() {
            if (expectedMod != modCount) {
                throw new java.util.ConcurrentModificationException("playlist modified");
            }
            if (!hasNext()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
            return songs.get(cursor++);
        }
    }

    private class ShuffledIterator implements Iterator<String> {
        private final List<Integer> order = new ArrayList<>();
        private int cursor = 0;

        ShuffledIterator() {
            for (int i = 0; i < songs.size(); i++) order.add(i);
            Collections.shuffle(order);
        }

        public boolean hasNext() { return cursor < order.size(); }

        public String next() {
            if (!hasNext()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
            return songs.get(order.get(cursor++));
        }
    }
}

public class PlaylistDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Playlist playlist = new Playlist();
        playlist.add("song-A");
        playlist.add("song-B");
        playlist.add("song-C");
        System.out.print("sequential: ");
        for (String s : playlist) System.out.print(s + " ");
        System.out.println();
        System.out.print("shuffled:   ");
        Iterator<String> it = playlist.shuffled();
        while (it.hasNext()) System.out.print(it.next() + " ");
        System.out.println();
    }
}

Sample I/O:

sequential: song-A song-B song-C
shuffled:   song-B song-C song-A   (order varies)

docs.title: 4.2 Python (pythonic, PEP 8)
docs.text:
Explanation: Python's protocol is the pattern: __iter__ on the aggregate, __next__ on iterators. Playlist supports sequential iteration plus reversed() and a lazy matching() generator — generators are the idiomatic lazy iterator.

from __future__ import annotations
import random
from typing import Iterator


class Playlist:
    """Aggregate: owns songs, manufactures iterators."""

    def __init__(self, songs: list[str] | None = None) -> None:
        self._songs: list[str] = list(songs or [])

    def add(self, song: str) -> None:
        self._songs.append(song)

    def __iter__(self) -> Iterator[str]:
        return iter(self._songs)  # sequential external iterator

    def __reversed__(self) -> Iterator[str]:
        return reversed(self._songs)  # alternate order, same storage

    def shuffled(self) -> Iterator[str]:
        order = self._songs[:]
        random.shuffle(order)
        return iter(order)

    def matching(self, keyword: str) -> Iterator[str]:
        """Lazy filtering iterator: yields on demand via generator."""
        for song in self._songs:
            if keyword.lower() in song.lower():
                yield song


if __name__ == "__main__":
    playlist = Playlist(["song-A", "song-B", "love-song-C"])
    print("sequential:", " ".join(playlist))
    print("reversed:  ", " ".join(reversed(playlist)))
    print("filtered:  ", " ".join(playlist.matching("love")))
    it_a = iter(playlist)
    it_b = iter(playlist)  # independent cursor
    print("independent:", next(it_a), "+ " + next(it_b), "(separate cursors)")

Sample I/O:

sequential: song-A song-B love-song-C
reversed:   love-song-C song-B song-A
filtered:   love-song-C
independent: song-A + song-A (separate cursors)

docs.title: 4.3 Go (idiomatic)
docs.text:
Explanation: Go 1.23+ ranges over iter.Seq[T]; pre-1.23 code uses closure or index iterators. This example shows both: a pull-style Iterator struct and a push-style All() yielding an iter.Seq, plus a filtered view.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "iter"
    "strings"
)

type Playlist struct{ songs []string }

func (p *Playlist) Add(song string) { p.songs = append(p.songs, song) }

// All returns a push (range-over-func) iterator: for s := range p.All().
func (p *Playlist) All() iter.Seq[string] {
    return func(yield func(string) bool) {
        for _, s := range p.songs {
            if !yield(s) {
                return
            }
        }
    }
}

// Matching returns a lazy filtered sequence.
func (p *Playlist) Matching(keyword string) iter.Seq[string] {
    return func(yield func(string) bool) {
        for _, s := range p.songs {
            if strings.Contains(strings.ToLower(s), strings.ToLower(keyword)) {
                if !yield(s) {
                    return
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

// SongIterator is a classic pull-style external iterator.
type SongIterator struct {
    songs []string
    pos   int
}

func (p *Playlist) Iterator() *SongIterator { return &SongIterator{songs: p.songs} }

func (it *SongIterator) HasNext() bool { return it.pos < len(it.songs) }

func (it *SongIterator) Next() (string, bool) {
    if !it.HasNext() {
        return "", false
    }
    s := it.songs[it.pos]
    it.pos++
    return s, true
}

func main() {
    p := &Playlist{}
    p.Add("song-A")
    p.Add("song-B")
    p.Add("love-song-C")

    fmt.Print("sequential: ")
    for s := range p.All() {
        fmt.Print(s + " ")
    }
    fmt.Println()

    fmt.Print("filtered:   ")
    for s := range p.Matching("love") {
        fmt.Print(s + " ")
    }
    fmt.Println()

    a, b := p.Iterator(), p.Iterator() // independent cursors
    sa, _ := a.Next()
    sb, _ := b.Next()
    fmt.Println("independent:", sa, "+", sb, "(separate cursors)")
}

Sample I/O:

sequential: song-A song-B love-song-C
filtered:   love-song-C
independent: song-A + song-A (separate cursors)

docs.title: 5. Real-World Industry Applications
docs.text:
• Language collections (Java Iterator/Iterable, C# IEnumerable, Python iterables, Go iter.Seq): The canonical implementation — every for-each loop runs on this pattern.
  • Database cursors (JDBC ResultSet, MongoDB cursors, Postgres portals): Rows stream one at a time; the cursor holds position, fetch size, and server-side state so billion-row tables never load fully into memory.
  • Paginated APIs (GitHub, Stripe, GraphQL connections, DynamoDB): Page tokens are serialized cursors; each next() transparently fetches the following page with backoff and retry.
  • Streaming frameworks (Kafka consumers, Flink, Java Streams, RxJS): Potentially infinite sequences with lazy operators (map/filter fuse onto the iterator chain).
  • File systems and IDEs (VS Code search, find, TreeWalker): Directory trees walked depth- or breadth-first without materializing the whole tree.
  • Game engines (Unity IEnumerator coroutines, Unreal iterators): Frame-by-frame traversal of scene graphs and scripted sequences.
  • Spreadsheet and DOM traversal (POI row iterators, NodeIterator): Uniform walking over heterogeneous node types with filtering built in.
  • ML data loaders (PyTorch DataLoader, TF tf.data): Batched, shuffled, prefetched iteration over datasets larger than RAM — iterators plus background prefetch.

docs.title: 6. Practical Use Cases and Scenarios
docs.text:
• Playlist with multiple orders (Section 4): One song list, three traversals (sequential, shuffled, reversed). Shuffle state lives in the iterator, so replaying the same playlist twice yields different orders without mutating storage.
  • Paginated user directory: UserPager(pageSize) holds nextToken; next() returns one user, fetching pages lazily. Clients write a plain loop; retries and rate limits hide inside the iterator.
  • Log-file tail: Iterator over a growing file yields lines as appended (like tail -f). Lookahead buffers partial lines; hasNext() blocks or returns false on timeout — same interface, streaming semantics.
  • Tree search in an org chart: depthFirst() finds the first matching employee; breadthFirst() finds the closest to the CEO. Same nodes, different iterators, no duplicated traversal code.
  • Merging sorted feeds: Two iterators (news, notifications) merged by timestamp in client code — possible only because iteration is external and pausable. Internal forEach cannot express this.
  • Batch export with resume: Iterator checkpoints its cursor (offset/page token) to disk every N items; on crash, reconstruction resumes exactly where it stopped — cursors as durable progress markers.

docs.title: 7. When to Use and When Not to Use
docs.text:
Use Iterator when:

  • Clients need sequential access without seeing storage (lists today, trees/pages tomorrow).
  • Multiple simultaneous or alternative traversals must coexist over one aggregate.
  • Sequences are large, lazy, paged, or infinite — materializing them is impossible or wasteful.
  • Traversal order varies independently from the collection (DFS vs BFS, forward vs reverse, filtered views).

Do NOT use when:

Situation Prefer instead Simple fixed-size array with index access and no alternative orders Plain indexed loop The operation should travel into the structure (export, type-check) Visitor Random access / search by key dominates Map/index structures, not linear traversal One-shot pipeline with map/filter/reduce and no custom order Streams / comprehensions / generators Traversal and element logic are trivially fused Internal forEach for brevity

docs.title: 8. Do's and Don'ts
docs.text:
Do:

  • Give every iterator independent cursor state; nested loops over the same aggregate must never interfere.
  • Honor the contract exactly: hasNext() side-effect-free, next() throws/returns-false when exhausted (never null-silently).
  • Document the modification policy (fail-fast, snapshot, weakly consistent) on every public aggregate.
  • Prefer lookahead for lazy/filtered sources so hasNext() stays O(1) and repeatable.
  • Expose factory methods per order (depthFirst(), pages(), reversed()) rather than boolean flags on one iterator.
  • Checkpoint long-running cursors (page tokens, offsets) so batch jobs resume after crashes.

Don't:

  • Don't expose internal arrays/lists/nodes to "simplify" iteration — it leaks representation and invites mutation bugs.
  • Don't share cursors across threads; iterators are single-threaded by default — synchronize or copy for concurrent use.
  • Don't mutate the aggregate inside next() except for the defined removal operation; keep traversal pure.
  • Don't make hasNext() perform expensive I/O repeatedly — prefetch once and cache the lookahead.
  • Don't write a custom iterator when stdlib covers it (list.iterator(), generators, iter.Seq) — custom cursors pay off for trees, pages, and lazy streams.
  • Don't swallow exhaustion: returning null/empty instead of throwing (or false, ok) hides client bugs.

docs.title: 9.1 Iterator vs Visitor vs Composite
docs.text:
Aspect Iterator Visitor Composite Purpose Walk elements one by one; client owns per-element logic Carry an operation into every element of a structure Unify part-whole hierarchies behind one interface Control flow Client drives the loop (pull) Elements call back into visitor (push/double-dispatch) Recursive structure; traversal often manual Knows Traversal order + cursor Element types + operation Parent/child containment Adding behavior New iterator = new order New visitor = new operation, zero element changes New node type ripples to visitors/iterators Typical use Collections, cursors, pages, trees AST checks, export, pricing over carts File systems, org charts, UI trees

Rule of thumb: Clients need sequential access with their own logic → Iterator. The operation itself should travel across heterogeneous elements → Visitor. The hierarchy is about containment → Composite (iterators then walk it).

docs.title: 9.2 External vs Internal iteration (streams/generators)
docs.text:
Aspect External Iterator Internal (forEach / Stream / generator consumer) Pause/merge/zip two sequences Natural (two cursors) Awkward or impossible Boilerplate More (while hasNext) Minimal (for x in xs, .map().filter()) Laziness Explicit lookahead/prefetch Built into streams/generators Early exit with resources Client controls break + close Needs short-circuiting terminal ops

Modern guidance: expose external iterators from libraries (maximum client control), consume via internal syntax at call sites (maximum readability).

docs.title: Q&A
docs.text:
Q1. What is the Iterator pattern in one sentence? A: It moves traversal state into a cursor object so clients walk any aggregate uniformly via hasNext/next without seeing its internals.

Q2. Why not just expose the internal list? A: Exposure leaks representation (ArrayList today, tree tomorrow), permits uncontrolled mutation, and spreads traversal logic across callers. Iterators hide storage, allow multiple simultaneous traversals, and let order/laziness change without breaking clients.

Q3. How do you handle modification during iteration? A: Three policies: fail-fast (modCount check → ConcurrentModificationException), snapshot (copy-on-create, safe but heavy), weakly consistent (tolerate, e.g., concurrent queues). Choose per use case and document it; never leave it ambiguous.

Q4. External vs internal iterators — when does it matter? A: External (client-driven) is required for merging/zippping two sequences, manual pause/resume, and interleaved traversal. Internal (forEach, streams) is terser for single-pass transforms. Libraries should expose external; call sites may wrap them internally.

Q5. How do you support multiple traversal orders? A: One aggregate, many factories: iterator() (default), depthFirst(), breadthFirst(), reverse(), pages(). Each returns an independent iterator; the collection is untouched and each cursor is isolated.

Q6. How do you implement a lazy iterator over a tree or paged API? A: Hold minimal resume state (stack of child iterators, or page token + buffer) plus a one-element lookahead primed at construction. hasNext() reports the lookahead; next() returns it and advances. Fetch/block only inside advance().

Q7. What makes a good hasNext/next contract? A: hasNext() is idempotent and cheap; next() throws (NoSuchElementException) or returns (value, false) when exhausted; neither returns stale data after modification (fail-fast or documented tolerance).

Q8. How do iterators relate to generators and streams? A: Generators (yield) and streams are lazy iterator implementations with internal-consumption syntax. The pattern is the same cursor abstraction; the syntax differs. Know when to drop to external iterators (merge/zip, manual control).

Q9. How do you test iterators? A: Empty/single/multi-element cases; double-hasNext() idempotence; exhaustion behavior; independent cursors (interleaved loops); traversal-order assertions on trees; concurrent-modification policy; and resume-from-checkpoint for paged iterators.

docs.title: LLD scenarios
docs.text:
S1. Design a paginated API client. Requirements: millions of users, page tokens, retries, resume after crash. Solution: UserIterator(pageSize) encapsulating token + buffer + backoff; next() fetches lazily; checkpoint token to disk every page. Discuss page-size tuning, duplicate/missing rows on concurrent writes, and rate-limit handling inside advance().

S2. Design file-system search. Requirements: find all *.log over 10 MB, huge trees, cancellable. Solution: DepthFirstIterator with extension/size filter fused into advance(); BreadthFirstIterator alternative for shallow-first results; cancellation flag checked per node. Discuss symlink cycles (visited-set), permission errors (skip + log vs abort), and memory bounds.

S3. Design a merged notification feed. Requirements: interleave posts, ads, and alerts by timestamp; each source paged. Solution: one external iterator per source; k-way merge in client comparing lookaheads. Discuss why internal forEach cannot express this, clock skew across sources, and stable tie-breaking.

docs.title: 11. Testing and Best Practices
docs.text:
• Contract tests: hasNext idempotence (call twice, same result), exhaustion (expect throw/ok=false), single-element, empty-aggregate, and interleaved-cursor independence. Run the same suite against every iterator implementation.
  • Order tests: Fixture trees with known DFS/BFS sequences; shuffled iterators assert permutation (same multiset, any order); filtered iterators assert exactly the matching subset in stable order.
  • Mutation tests: Modify aggregate mid-iteration and assert the documented policy (exception, snapshot stability, or documented tolerance) — never undefined behavior.
  • Resource tests: Paged/file iterators must close handles on exhaustion and on early break; test with forced GC/file-handle counting. Lazy iterators must not prefetch the entire source (assert fetch count).
  • Concurrency: Stress shared aggregates with parallel iterators; assert no cross-talk. Document iterators as not-thread-safe unless explicitly designed otherwise.
  • Best practices: Factories per order, not flags; immutable snapshots for elements when traversal outlives mutations; checkpoint tokens for resumable jobs; lookahead for lazy sources; never expose internals; prefer stdlib iteration at call sites and custom iterators only for trees/pages/streams.

docs.title: 12. Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Iterator decouples what is stored from how it is walked: aggregates own storage, iterators own cursors and order, clients own per-element logic.
  • It enables uniform loops, multiple simultaneous traversals, alternative orders, and lazy/infinite sequences — from collections to DB cursors to paged APIs.
  • Distinguish from Visitor (operation travels inward) and Composite (containment hierarchy); iterators typically walk composites and are consumed via streams/generators syntax.
  • Production correctness rests on contract discipline (hasNext purity, exhaustion behavior), documented modification policy, independent cursors, and resumable checkpoints for long jobs.
  • In LLD interviews, reach for it when you hear "traverse without exposing internals, multiple orders, lazy/paged/infinite" — then immediately discuss fail-fast policy, laziness technique, and cursor independence to show depth.

docs.title: Mediator Design Pattern
docs.text: Youtube: 34. Design Online Auction System with Mediator Design Pattern | Low Level Design

docs.title: 1. Overview and Fundamentals
docs.text:
Mediator is a behavioral design pattern that centralizes complex many-to-many communication between objects into a single hub. Colleagues never reference each other directly; they talk only to the mediator, which routes messages, enforces shared rules, and owns interaction state.

  • GoF classification: Behavioral — encapsulates how a set of objects interact.
  • Intent (GoF): "Define an object that encapsulates how a set of objects interact. Mediator promotes loose coupling by keeping objects from referring to each other explicitly, and it lets you vary their interaction independently."
  • Core idea: Replace an N×N mesh of references with a star: N colleagues × 1 mediator reference. Interaction complexity moves from scattered peer code into one coordinator.
  • Everyday analogy: An air-traffic-control tower. Pilots never negotiate with each other mid-air; each talks only to the tower, which sequences takeoffs, landings, and holds. Add a runway and only the tower's rules change — aircraft procedures stay identical.
  • Key participants:
  • Mediator (interface): Declares send/placeBid/notify coordination operations.
  • ConcreteMediator: Holds colleague registry, routing logic, and shared rules (highest bid, turn order, validation).
  • Colleague (abstract/base): Holds a mediator reference; reports events and receives callbacks.
  • ConcreteColleague: Domain participant (Bidder, ChatUser, DialogField) with no peer references.
  • Success conditions: Colleagues are independently reusable (only depend on the mediator interface); all cross-object rules live in one reviewable place; message flow is traceable.
  • What it is not: It is not a Facade (one-way simplified front door), not an Observer broadcast (one-to-many notification), and not a message queue (though a broker can implement mediation) — it is the coordination object that owns peer-to-peer interaction logic.

docs.title: How the mechanism works
docs.text:
1. Colleagues register with the mediator (house.register(bidder)) or receive it at construction.
  2. A colleague reports an event to the mediator (house.placeBid(new Bid(...))) instead of calling peers.
  3. The mediator applies shared rules (minimum increment, turn validation, closing time) and decides who to notify.
  4. The mediator invokes callbacks on affected colleagues (onNewHighest, onMessage) — peers never call each other.
  5. Colleagues remain thin: local UI/state plus event reporting; all cross-cutting decisions live centrally.

docs.title: Centralization dynamics
docs.text:
• Coupling math: N peers with direct links need up to N×(N−1) references; with a mediator they need N. This is the entire economic argument — it compounds with every added participant.
  • God-object risk: The mediator naturally attracts logic. Containment strategy: mediator owns coordination (routing, ordering, shared rules); domain behavior stays in colleagues; complex rules extract into Strategy/Policy objects the mediator consults.
  • Reusability payoff: A Bidder written against AuctionHouse works in English, Dutch, and sealed-bid auctions by swapping mediators — impossible if it imported sibling bidders.
  • Testability payoff: Colleagues test against a fake mediator; mediator tests against stub colleagues. The interaction matrix becomes a unit-testable table instead of emergent peer behavior.
  • Ordering and state: Mediators often own turn order, session state, and sequencing (whose move, whose bid is highest, which field is focused). Make that state explicit and queryable for debugging.
  • SOLID alignment: Single Responsibility per colleague, Open/Closed for new participant types (register, no rewiring), Dependency Inversion (everyone depends on abstractions).
  • Failure modes: Mediator as single point of failure/coupling, hidden call flows (who notified whom requires reading the hub), and over-centralization where two peers could simply talk directly.

docs.title: Variants and extensions
docs.text:
• Interface-per-role: Colleagues depend on a narrow mediator interface (Bidding, Messaging) rather than a fat hub — limits blast radius.
  • Multiple mediators: One hub per concern (bidding vs payment vs shipping) instead of one global coordinator; composes better at scale.
  • Event-bus mediator: A typed pub/sub bus acts as a generic mediator; routing rules become subscriptions. Flexible but less explicit — prefer explicit mediators for auditable flows.
  • Mediator + Observer: Colleagues observe the mediator's state (highest bid) while reporting events to it — common in UI dialogs (fields observe form validity owned by the dialog mediator).
  • Saga orchestrator: A mediator variant coordinating distributed transaction steps (reserve → pay → ship) with compensation on failure.

docs.title: 3.1 Static structure — star topology
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class BiddingMediator {
        <>
        +register(bidder: Bidder) void
        +placeBid(bid: Bid) void
    }
    class AuctionHouse {
        -bidders: List~Bidder~
        -highest: Bid
        +register(bidder: Bidder) void
        +placeBid(bid: Bid) void
        -broadcastHighest(bid: Bid) void
        -notifyBidder(name: String, msg: String) void
    }
    class Bidder {
        -name: String
        -house: BiddingMediator
        +bid(amount: double) void
        +onNewHighest(bid: Bid) void
        +onMessage(msg: String) void
    }
    class Bid {
        +bidder: String
        +amount: double
    }
    class AuctionClient {
        +runAuction() void
    }
    BiddingMediator <|.. AuctionHouse
    AuctionHouse --> Bidder : notifies
    Bidder --> BiddingMediator : reports to
    AuctionHouse ..> Bid : tracks highest
    Bidder ..> Bid : sends via mediator
    AuctionClient --> AuctionHouse : drives
    AuctionClient --> Bidder : creates

Explanation: The dependency arrows tell the whole story: Bidder points only at the BiddingMediator interface, never at another Bidder. AuctionHouse is the only class with fan-out (registry + highest-bid state + routing methods). Bid is a dumb message object. Swapping AuctionHouse for a SealedBidHouse reuses Bidder untouched — the reusability payoff made structural.

docs.title: 3.2 Dynamic flow — one bid through the hub
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Alice as Alice (Bidder)
    participant House as AuctionHouse (Mediator)
    participant Bob as Bob (Bidder)
    participant Carol as Carol (Bidder)
    Alice->>House: placeBid(Alice, 100)
    House->>House: 100 > highest(0)? accept, highest=100
    House->>Alice: onNewHighest(100)
    House->>Bob: onNewHighest(100)
    House->>Carol: onNewHighest(100)
    Bob->>House: placeBid(Bob, 90)
    House->>House: 90 > 100? No — reject
    House->>Bob: onMessage("Bid too low. Highest is 100")
    Bob->>House: placeBid(Bob, 150)
    House->>House: accept, highest=150
    House->>Alice: onNewHighest(150)
    House->>Bob: onNewHighest(150)
    House->>Carol: onNewHighest(150)

Explanation: Every cross-bidder effect passes through the hub: acceptance, broadcast, and private rejection. Note the two notification shapes — broadcast (onNewHighest to all) and unicast (onMessage to one) — both owned by the mediator. Bidders never learn each other's identities; Bob's rejection is invisible to Alice and Carol. The bidding rule (must exceed highest) is enforced exactly once, so auditing the rule means reading one method.

docs.title: 4. Implementation Examples in Java, Python, and Go
docs.text: All three examples model an online auction house: bidders register once, place bids through the house, and receive broadcasts — never contacting each other.

docs.title: 4.1 Java (OOP, classic GoF style)
docs.text:
Explanation: AuctionHouse is the concrete mediator (registry + highest-bid rule + routing). Bidder colleagues hold only the mediator reference. AuctionDemo drives the exact scenario from the sequence diagram.

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

final class Bid {
    final String bidder;
    final double amount;
    Bid(String bidder, double amount) {
        this.bidder = bidder;
        this.amount = amount;
    }
}

class AuctionHouse {
    private final List<Bidder> bidders = new ArrayList<>();
    private Bid highest = new Bid("none", 0);

    void register(Bidder bidder) { bidders.add(bidder); }

    void placeBid(Bid bid) {
        if (bid.amount <= highest.amount) {
            notifyBidder(bid.bidder, "Bid too low. Highest is " + highest.amount);
            return;
        }
        highest = bid;
        for (Bidder b : bidders) {
            b.onNewHighest(bid);
        }
    }

    private void notifyBidder(String name, String msg) {
        for (Bidder b : bidders) {
            if (b.name().equals(name)) b.onMessage(msg);
        }
    }

    Bid highest() { return highest; }
}

class Bidder {
    private final String name;
    private final AuctionHouse house;
    Bidder(String name, AuctionHouse house) {
        this.name = name;
        this.house = house;
        house.register(this);
    }
    String name() { return name; }
    void bid(double amount) { house.placeBid(new Bid(name, amount)); }
    void onNewHighest(Bid bid) {
        System.out.println(name + " sees new highest: " + bid.amount + " by " + bid.bidder);
    }
    void onMessage(String msg) { System.out.println(name + " <- " + msg); }
}

public class AuctionDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        AuctionHouse house = new AuctionHouse();
        Bidder alice = new Bidder("Alice", house);
        Bidder bob = new Bidder("Bob", house);
        new Bidder("Carol", house);
        alice.bid(100);
        bob.bid(90);
        bob.bid(150);
        System.out.println("winner amount: " + house.highest().amount);
    }
}

Sample I/O:

Alice sees new highest: 100.0 by Alice
Bob sees new highest: 100.0 by Alice
Carol sees new highest: 100.0 by Alice
Bob <- Bid too low. Highest is 100.0
Alice sees new highest: 150.0 by Bob
Bob sees new highest: 150.0 by Bob
Carol sees new highest: 150.0 by Bob
winner amount: 150.0

docs.title: 4.2 Python (pythonic, PEP 8)
docs.text:
Explanation: AuctionHouse mediator with register/place_bid; Bidder dataclass holding the mediator; Bid frozen message. Private _notify mirrors the Java unicast path.

from __future__ import annotations
from dataclasses import dataclass, field


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Bid:
    bidder: str
    amount: float


class AuctionHouse:
    """Mediator: central bidding rules + routing. Peers never meet."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._bidders: list[Bidder] = []
        self.highest = Bid("none", 0.0)

    def register(self, bidder: Bidder) -> None:
        self._bidders.append(bidder)

    def place_bid(self, bid: Bid) -> None:
        if bid.amount <= self.highest.amount:
            self._notify(bid.bidder, f"Bid too low. Highest is {self.highest.amount}")
            return
        self.highest = bid
        for bidder in self._bidders:
            bidder.on_new_highest(bid)

    def _notify(self, name: str, msg: str) -> None:
        for bidder in self._bidders:
            if bidder.name == name:
                bidder.on_message(msg)


@dataclass
class Bidder:
    """Colleague: knows only the mediator."""

    name: str
    house: AuctionHouse = field(repr=False)

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        self.house.register(self)

    def bid(self, amount: float) -> None:
        self.house.place_bid(Bid(self.name, amount))

    def on_new_highest(self, bid: Bid) -> None:
        print(f"{self.name} sees new highest: {bid.amount} by {bid.bidder}")

    def on_message(self, msg: str) -> None:
        print(f"{self.name} <- {msg}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    house = AuctionHouse()
    alice = Bidder("Alice", house)
    bob = Bidder("Bob", house)
    Bidder("Carol", house)
    alice.bid(100)
    bob.bid(90)
    bob.bid(150)
    print(f"winner amount: {house.highest.amount}")

Sample I/O:

Alice sees new highest: 100 by Alice
Bob sees new highest: 100 by Alice
Carol sees new highest: 100 by Alice
Bob <- Bid too low. Highest is 100
Alice sees new highest: 150 by Bob
Bob sees new highest: 150 by Bob
Carol sees new highest: 150 by Bob
winner amount: 150

docs.title: 4.3 Go (idiomatic)
docs.text:
Explanation: Mediator interface keeps colleagues decoupled; AuctionHouse implements routing; Bidder holds the interface (not the concrete house), enabling test fakes and variant houses.

package main

import "fmt"

type Bid struct {
    Bidder string
    Amount float64
}

type Mediator interface {
    Register(b *Bidder)
    PlaceBid(bid Bid)
}

type AuctionHouse struct {
    bidders []*Bidder
    highest Bid
}

func NewAuctionHouse() *AuctionHouse {
    return &AuctionHouse{highest: Bid{Bidder: "none", Amount: 0}}
}

func (h *AuctionHouse) Register(b *Bidder) { h.bidders = append(h.bidders, b) }

func (h *AuctionHouse) PlaceBid(bid Bid) {
    if bid.Amount <= h.highest.Amount {
        h.notify(bid.Bidder, fmt.Sprintf("Bid too low. Highest is %.0f", h.highest.Amount))
        return
    }
    h.highest = bid
    for _, b := range h.bidders {
        b.OnNewHighest(bid)
    }
}

func (h *AuctionHouse) notify(name, msg string) {
    for _, b := range h.bidders {
        if b.Name == name {
            b.OnMessage(msg)
        }
    }
}

type Bidder struct {
    Name  string
    house Mediator
}

func NewBidder(name string, house Mediator) *Bidder {
    b := &Bidder{Name: name, house: house}
    house.Register(b)
    return b
}

func (b *Bidder) Bid(amount float64) { b.house.PlaceBid(Bid{Bidder: b.Name, Amount: amount}) }

func (b *Bidder) OnNewHighest(bid Bid) {
    fmt.Printf("%s sees new highest: %.0f by %s\n", b.Name, bid.Amount, bid.Bidder)
}

func (b *Bidder) OnMessage(msg string) { fmt.Printf("%s <- %s\n", b.Name, msg) }

func main() {
    house := NewAuctionHouse()
    alice := NewBidder("Alice", house)
    bob := NewBidder("Bob", house)
    NewBidder("Carol", house)
    alice.Bid(100)
    bob.Bid(90)
    bob.Bid(150)
    fmt.Printf("winner amount: %.0f\n", house.highest.Amount)
}

Sample I/O:

Alice sees new highest: 100 by Alice
Bob sees new highest: 100 by Alice
Carol sees new highest: 100 by Alice
Bob <- Bid too low. Highest is 100
Alice sees new highest: 150 by Bob
Bob sees new highest: 150 by Bob
Carol sees new highest: 150 by Bob
winner amount: 150

docs.title: 5. Real-World Industry Applications
docs.text:
• Chat systems (Slack, Discord, WhatsApp groups): The room/channel object is the mediator — members send to the room; the room fans out, enforces moderation, and stores history. Members hold no peer references.
  • Air traffic control: Controllers sequence takeoffs/landings/holds; aircraft report position and obey clearances. The canonical textbook example, still accurate.
  • UI dialogs and forms (flight booking, checkout): A dialog controller enables/disables fields based on cross-field rules (dates valid → search enabled). Fields emit events; the controller decides.
  • Message brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS): Producers and consumers never meet; topics/exchanges route, persist, and apply retention and ordering rules.
  • Backend mediators (MediatR in .NET, CQRS dispatchers): Controllers send IRequests to a mediator that routes to handlers plus cross-cutting pipelines (validation, logging, transactions).
  • Multiplayer game servers: The server/sim loop mediates player actions, physics, and broadcasts — clients never trust each other directly.
  • Microservice saga orchestrators: An orchestrator service drives reserve → pay → ship across services and compensates on failure — mediation at architecture scale.
  • Smart-home hubs (Home Assistant, HomeKit): Motion sensor triggers hub; hub evaluates rules and commands lights/locks — devices never address each other.

docs.title: 6. Practical Use Cases and Scenarios
docs.text:
• Online auction (Section 4): Bids, minimum increments, reserve prices, closing-time extensions, and winner notifications all live in AuctionHouse. Adding proxy bidding touches one class; bidders stay thin.
  • Team chat room: send(user, text) fans out to members, filters profanity, threads replies, and persists history. Moderation (mute/kick) is a mediator rule, not peer logic.
  • Flight-booking dialog: Date pickers, airport selectors, and passenger counts report to a BookingDialog mediator; it validates combinations (return after departure → error) and enables Search only when the whole form is coherent.
  • Multiplayer lobby: Players ready-up through the Lobby mediator; it starts the match at full capacity, balances teams, and broadcasts countdowns. Dropouts re-trigger balancing centrally.
  • Order saga: OrderOrchestrator mediates inventory → payment → shipment services; on payment failure it triggers inventory release. Services expose actions; only the orchestrator knows the sequence.
  • Smart home evening scene: Motion + sunset + presence flow into the Hub; it decides light levels and lock state. Devices expose capabilities; the hub owns the combination logic users actually experience.

docs.title: 7. When to Use and When Not to Use
docs.text:
Use Mediator when:

  • Many objects communicate in complex, many-to-many ways that are hard to follow or change.
  • Reusing a class is difficult because it references many peers directly.
  • Interaction rules are centralized business logic (bidding, turn-taking, validation) that should live in one auditable place.
  • You want to vary interaction independently from the participants (new auction type, new dialog flow, new orchestration).

Do NOT use when:

Situation Prefer instead Simple one-to-one or one-to-many notification Direct call or Observer / pub-sub Interaction graph is sparse and stable (2–3 objects) Direct references — a mediator hides the flow for no gain You only need a simplified entry point to a subsystem Facade Throughput-critical paths where hub latency dominates Choreography (events) or direct dispatch with care Colleagues need rich peer APIs, not just events Reconsider boundaries — mediator fits event-style coordination

docs.title: 8. Do's and Don'ts
docs.text:
Do:

  • Keep the mediator to coordination: routing, ordering, shared rules. Push domain behavior into colleagues or extracted Policy/Strategy objects.
  • Depend on narrow mediator interfaces per role so colleagues cannot reach unrelated hub powers.
  • Split by concern as you grow: one mediator per workflow (bidding, payment, shipping), not one global hub.
  • Make routing observable: log/event every decision (bid accepted/rejected + reason) with correlation IDs.
  • Design registration explicitly (constructor vs register, deregistration for leaving members) to avoid ghost callbacks and leaks.
  • Guard shared mediator state for concurrency (highest bid, turn) — serialize mutations or use atomics/channels.

Don't:

  • Don't let the mediator become a god object absorbing every feature — extract rules early and review hub size as a metric.
  • Don't let colleagues bypass the hub with secret peer references; one backdoor re-tangles the graph.
  • Don't hide complex flows without documentation: keep a sequence diagram of hub interactions next to the code.
  • Don't use a single mediator for unrelated workflows; unrelated rules in one class is accidental coupling.
  • Don't forget deregistration: chat members, game players, and dialog listeners must unregister or the hub leaks.
  • Don't make the hub a single point of failure without a plan — replicate, persist critical state, or scope blast radius per workflow.

docs.title: 9.1 Mediator vs Facade vs Observer
docs.text:
Aspect Mediator Facade Observer Purpose Coordinate many-to-many peer interaction through a hub Simplify one-way access to a subsystem Broadcast one-to-many state changes Direction Multi-directional: peers ↔ hub ↔ peers One-directional: client → facade → subsystem One-directional: subject → observers Knowledge Colleagues know only the mediator; mediator knows all Client knows facade; facade knows subsystem Observers know subject; subject knows only the interface Typical use Chat rooms, auctions, ATC, dialogs, saga orchestrator SDK entry points, subsystem wrappers Event listeners, stock tickers, MVC model→view Risk God object; hidden flows Leaky abstraction hiding needed power Notification storms; ordering surprises

Rule of thumb: Peers must interact richly → Mediator. Clients need a simpler front door → Facade. One source notifies many passive listeners → Observer. Mediator and Observer compose: colleagues often observe hub state while reporting events to it.

docs.title: 9.2 Mediator vs Chain of Responsibility
docs.text: Aspect Mediator Chain of Responsibility Topology Star (all through hub) Line (link to link) Decision locus Hub applies global rules Each link decides handle-or-forward Reuse story Colleagues reusable across hubs Handlers reorderable within a chain Use when Interaction rules span many peers Requests need ordered selection/filtering

docs.title: Q&A
docs.text:
Q1. What is the Mediator pattern in one sentence? A: Colleagues communicate only through a central hub that owns routing and shared rules, replacing an N×N peer mesh with a star.

Q2. How does it reduce coupling, concretely? A: Without it N components need up to N-squared links and each imports its peers. With it each holds one mediator reference, and interaction logic moves into the hub — components become independently reusable and the graph becomes a reviewable star.

Q3. Mediator vs Facade — are they the same? A: No. Facade simplifies one direction (client → subsystem) as a static front door. Mediator manages two-way traffic between peers that know the mediator. Facade hides complexity; Mediator coordinates colleagues that would otherwise be tangled.

Q4. Mediator vs Observer — when does each win? A: Observer fits one-to-many notification where listeners are passive (price ticks, model→view). Mediator fits many-to-many interaction where peers affect each other through shared rules (chat, auctions, dialogs). If listeners start influencing each other, you have outgrown Observer.

Q5. How do you stop the mediator from becoming a god object? A: Restrict it to coordination; push domain logic to colleagues; extract rules into Strategy/Policy objects; split hubs per workflow; depend on narrow role interfaces; and treat hub line-count as a reviewed metric.

Q6. How do you test mediated interactions? A: Test colleagues against a fake mediator (record received callbacks); test the mediator against stub colleagues with scripted events; then add thin integration tests for key flows (bid-accept, bid-reject, broadcast). Assert routing tables, not emergent peer behavior.

Q7. What about thread safety and failure? A: Serialize hub mutations (highest bid, turn) — the hub is a contention point. Persist critical state if the hub is a single point of failure, scope one hub per workflow/room to bound blast radius, and define deregistration so departed colleagues stop receiving callbacks.

Q8. When should you avoid Mediator? A: For 1:1 or 1:many notifications (Observer suffices), sparse stable graphs (direct calls are clearer), or latency-critical paths where hub hops cost too much. Introduce it when the interaction mesh actually hurts.

Q9. How does MediatR relate to this pattern? A: MediatR is a mediator implementation: controllers send requests/notifications to IMediator, which routes through pipelines (validation, logging) to handlers. It demonstrates the pattern's value — thin senders, centralized cross-cutting behavior, independently testable handlers.

docs.title: LLD scenarios
docs.text:
S1. Design an online auction system. Requirements: register bidders, place bids with minimum increment, broadcast highest, reject low bids privately, close at deadline. Solution: AuctionHouse mediator exactly as in Section 4 plus closing timer and reserve-price policy object. Discuss proxy bidding (hub-side), bid-history audit, and horizontal scaling (one hub per auction room).

S2. Design a team chat with moderation. Requirements: rooms, join/leave, broadcast, profanity filter, mute. Solution: ChatRoom mediator with member registry, message pipeline (filter → persist → fan-out), and moderation rules. Discuss deregistration leaks, history pagination (Iterator!), and backpressure on large rooms.

S3. Design a flight-booking dialog. Requirements: interdependent fields (dates, airports, passengers), coherent validation, enabled Search. Solution: BookingDialog mediator observing field events and pushing validity state back (Mediator + Observer). Discuss test matrix for field combinations and extracting date/airport rules into testable policies.

docs.title: 11. Testing and Best Practices
docs.text:
• Colleague tests: Fake the mediator; assert the colleague reports the right events and reacts correctly to callbacks. No real hub needed — fast and focused.
  • Mediator tests: Stub colleagues (record onNewHighest/onMessage); script event sequences (accept, reject, broadcast, member leaves mid-auction); assert routing and rule outcomes. Table-drive bid scenarios including ties and reserve prices.
  • Integration tests: A few end-to-end flows (full auction, chat session, dialog happy-path + one invalid combination) to lock the wiring that unit tests intentionally isolate.
  • Edge cases: Duplicate registration, bidding after close, empty room broadcast, deregistered member receiving callbacks (must not), concurrent bids (highest-bid atomicity), and hub restart (state recovery).
  • Observability: Structured hub logs per decision with correlation IDs; metrics per route (bids_accepted, bids_rejected, broadcast_fanout); trace the hub as a span in distributed flows.
  • Best practices: Narrow role interfaces; one hub per workflow; explicit register/deregister lifecycle; extracted policy objects for complex rules; sequence diagram checked in beside the hub; concurrency guard on shared hub state.

docs.title: 12. Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Mediator replaces a tangled peer mesh with a star: colleagues stay thin and reusable; one coordinator owns routing and shared rules.
  • Reach for it when many objects interact in complex, evolving ways — chat, auctions, dialogs, game servers, saga orchestrators, smart hubs.
  • Distinguish from Facade (one-way simplification) and Observer (one-to-many broadcast); expect to combine Mediator with Observer (state pushes) and Strategy (extracted rules).
  • The central discipline is containing the hub: coordination only, narrow interfaces, per-workflow splits, explicit lifecycles, and observable routing.
  • In LLD interviews, the auction house and chat room are canonical: draw the star, state the N×N → N argument, then immediately discuss god-object containment, deregistration, and concurrency to show production maturity.

docs.title: Memento Design Pattern
docs.text: Youtube: 38. Memento Design Pattern explanation | LLD System Design | Design pattern explanation in Java

docs.title: 1. Overview and Fundamentals
docs.text:
Memento is a behavioral design pattern that captures and externalizes an object's internal state without violating encapsulation, so the object can be restored to that state later. A caretaker stores opaque snapshots; only the originator can create or consume them.

  • GoF classification: Behavioral — manages state history and restoration.
  • Intent (GoF): "Without violating encapsulation, capture and externalize an object's internal state so that the object can be restored to this state later."
  • Core idea: Split responsibilities three ways — Originator owns live state and knows how to snapshot/restore; Memento is the opaque, immutable snapshot; Caretaker stores and returns mementos without ever inspecting them.
  • Everyday analogy: A game checkpoint. The player (originator) keeps playing; the save system (caretaker) holds checkpoint files (mementos) it cannot meaningfully read. Dying restores the last checkpoint — the save system never needs to understand health, ammo, or position.
  • Key participants:
  • Originator: Holds state; save() creates a memento, restore(m) reverts to it.
  • Memento: Immutable snapshot exposing (at most) a narrow interface to the caretaker and a wide interface to the originator.
  • Caretaker: Owns history (stack with bound, timeline, named slots); never reads snapshot contents.
  • Client: Decides when to checkpoint and restore, never how state is stored.
  • Success conditions: Snapshots are opaque to everyone but the originator, history is bounded, and save/restore round-trips are exact.
  • What it is not: It is not clone() alone (cloning is a mechanism; Memento is the custody discipline), not Command (which stores actions + inverses rather than state), and not event sourcing (which stores the log of changes, not snapshots).

docs.title: How the mechanism works
docs.text:
1. Client calls originator.save() at a meaningful moment (checkpoint, before risky edit, transaction savepoint).
  2. Originator copies its essential state into a new immutable Memento and hands it out as an opaque object.
  3. Caretaker pushes it onto history (stack, list, or named slots) with a size/eviction policy.
  4. To undo, client pops a memento and calls originator.restore(m); the originator copies snapshot fields back into live state.
  5. The caretaker never calls getters on the snapshot — in strict designs it cannot, because access is package-private or inner-class scoped.

docs.title: Encapsulation discipline (narrow vs wide interfaces)
docs.text:
• Wide interface (originator only): Full read access to restore state — implemented via private/package-private accessors, inner classes, or friendship.
  • Narrow interface (caretaker): Opaque handle — push, peek, pop, maybe a timestamp or label. No state visibility.
  • Java enforcement: Memento as a private inner class or with package-private getters; caretaker in the same package sees only Object-like opacity.
  • Python enforcement: Convention + @property-less snapshots, or __slots__ with name-mangled privates; true enforcement needs discipline since privacy is by convention.
  • Go enforcement: Unexported struct fields with methods only on the originator type; caretaker in another package literally cannot read them.

docs.title: Design dynamics
docs.text:
• Memory economics: Full snapshots cost O(state) each. Controls: bound history (count + bytes), store diffs/deltas for large state, compress or spill old snapshots to disk, drop redo branches on new edits.
  • Granularity choice: Snapshot the document, not the application: exclude caches, derived data, and UI selection where possible. Restoring derived state causes subtle staleness bugs.
  • Identity vs value: Decide whether restore mutates the originator in place (usual) or returns a new instance (functional style, easier reasoning, harder integration).
  • Cascade scope: For object graphs, a memento may need deep copies of referenced objects; shallow copies alias live state and corrupt history when the original mutates. Prefer immutable state or explicit deep-copy at save time.
  • Durability boundary: In-memory stacks vanish on restart. If history must survive crashes, serialize mementos (JSON/protobuf) — at which point versioning and schema migration enter the picture.
  • SOLID alignment: Single Responsibility (originator = behavior, caretaker = history custody), Encapsulation preserved by construction, Open/Closed (new checkpoint policies = new caretakers, originator untouched).
  • Failure modes: Memory bloat, stale derived state after restore, aliasing from shallow copies, and unbounded caretakers that never evict.

docs.title: Variants and extensions
docs.text:
• Stack caretaker: Classic undo (push/pop, redo cleared on new edit).
  • Timeline caretaker: Named checkpoints with jump-to-version (git-style, game save slots).
  • Transactional savepoints: Nested save/restore with partial rollback (DB SAVEPOINT semantics).
  • Memento + Command: Command stores a memento as its undo state — whole-state restore without hand-rolled inverses.
  • Memento + Prototype: Snapshots created via clone() of internal state aggregates.

docs.title: 3.1 Static structure — custody of opaque snapshots
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Originator {
        -level: int
        -health: int
        -position: String
        +save() GameMemento
        +restore(m: GameMemento) void
        +move(where: String) void
        +damage(hp: int) void
    }
    class GameMemento {
        -level: int
        -health: int
        -position: String
        +level() int
        +health() int
        +position() String
    }
    class Caretaker {
        -checkpoints: Stack~GameMemento~
        -maxSaves: int
        +checkpoint(m: GameMemento) void
        +lastCheckpoint() GameMemento
        +hasSave() bool
    }
    class Client {
        +play() void
    }
    Originator ..> GameMemento : creates & consumes
    Caretaker --> GameMemento : stores (opaque)
    Client --> Originator : save/restore
    Client --> Caretaker : checkpoint/retrieve
    note for GameMemento "Narrow to Caretaker:\nopaque handle only.\nWide to Originator:\nstate readers."

Explanation: The two arrows into GameMemento carry different meanings: the originator's is a wide dependency (creates and reads), the caretaker's is custody only (stores and returns, never reads). Access modifiers enforce this: in Java the readers are package-private; in Go the fields are unexported outside the originator's package. Client orchestrates timing but never touches snapshot contents. maxSaves on the caretaker is the memory bound made structural.

docs.title: 3.2 Dynamic flow — checkpoint, damage, respawn
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Player as Player (Originator)
    participant Saves as SaveManager (Caretaker)
    Client->>Player: move("forest")
    Client->>Player: save()
    Player-->>Client: m1 {L1,hp100,forest}
    Client->>Saves: checkpoint(m1)
    Client->>Player: damage(80)
    Client->>Player: move("cave")
    Client->>Player: save()
    Player-->>Client: m2 {L1,hp20,cave}
    Client->>Saves: checkpoint(m2)
    Client->>Player: damage(90)
    Player-->>Client: hp=0 (dead)
    Client->>Saves: lastCheckpoint()
    Saves-->>Client: m2 (opaque hand-back)
    Client->>Player: restore(m2)
    Player->>Player: level/health/position = m2 fields
    Player-->>Client: L1 hp=20 @ cave

Explanation: The caretaker handles m1/m2 as black boxes — it never reads level or health, only stores and evicts (oldest dropped past maxSaves). Restoration is a single restore() call that copies all fields atomically, so the player never sits in a half-restored state. Note the client decides policy (when to checkpoint, when to respawn from which slot) while originator and caretaker supply mechanism — a clean separation that keeps save-slot UI simple.

docs.title: 4. Implementation Examples in Java, Python, and Go
docs.text: All three examples model a game checkpoint system: the player snapshots position/health/level, the save manager stores bounded history, and death restores the last checkpoint.

docs.title: 4.1 Java (OOP, classic GoF style)
docs.text:
Explanation: GameMemento exposes state only via package-private readers (caretaker cannot meaningfully use them outside discipline). Player is the originator; SaveManager is the bounded caretaker; GameDemo checkpoints, dies, and respawns.

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

final class GameMemento {
    private final int level;
    private final int health;
    private final String position;
    GameMemento(int level, int health, String position) {
        this.level = level;
        this.health = health;
        this.position = position;
    }
    int level() { return level; }       // wide interface: originator (same package)
    int health() { return health; }
    String position() { return position; }
}

class Player {
    private int level = 1;
    private int health = 100;
    private String position = "spawn";

    void move(String where) { position = where; }
    void damage(int hp) { health = Math.max(0, health - hp); }
    void levelUp() { level++; health = 100; }

    GameMemento save() { return new GameMemento(level, health, position); }

    void restore(GameMemento m) {
        level = m.level();
        health = m.health();
        position = m.position();
    }

    @Override public String toString() { return "L" + level + " hp=" + health + " @ " + position; }
}

class SaveManager {
    private final Deque<GameMemento> checkpoints = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final int maxSaves;
    SaveManager(int maxSaves) { this.maxSaves = maxSaves; }

    void checkpoint(GameMemento m) {
        checkpoints.push(m);
        while (checkpoints.size() > maxSaves) checkpoints.removeLast();
    }
    GameMemento lastCheckpoint() { return checkpoints.peek(); }
    boolean hasSave() { return !checkpoints.isEmpty(); }
}

public class GameDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Player player = new Player();
        SaveManager saves = new SaveManager(3);
        player.move("forest");
        saves.checkpoint(player.save());
        System.out.println("checkpoint: " + player);
        player.damage(80);
        player.move("cave");
        saves.checkpoint(player.save());
        System.out.println("checkpoint: " + player);
        player.damage(90);
        System.out.println("after fatal hit: " + player);
        if (saves.hasSave()) player.restore(saves.lastCheckpoint());
        System.out.println("respawned: " + player);
    }
}

Sample I/O:

checkpoint: L1 hp=100 @ forest
checkpoint: L1 hp=20 @ cave
after fatal hit: L1 hp=0 @ cave
respawned: L1 hp=20 @ cave

docs.title: 4.2 Python (pythonic, PEP 8)
docs.text:
Explanation: Frozen dataclass memento (immutable snapshot); name-mangled privates are unnecessary — immutability + no readers for the caretaker is the discipline. SaveManager bounds history with deque(maxlen=...), the idiomatic bounded stack.

from __future__ import annotations
from collections import deque
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class GameMemento:
    """Opaque snapshot. Caretaker stores it; only Player reads it."""

    level: int
    health: int
    position: str


class Player:
    """Originator: owns live state, creates/consumes snapshots."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.level = 1
        self.health = 100
        self.position = "spawn"

    def move(self, where: str) -> None:
        self.position = where

    def damage(self, hp: int) -> None:
        self.health = max(0, self.health - hp)

    def level_up(self) -> None:
        self.level += 1
        self.health = 100

    def save(self) -> GameMemento:
        return GameMemento(self.level, self.health, self.position)

    def restore(self, memento: GameMemento) -> None:
        self.level, self.health, self.position = (
            memento.level,
            memento.health,
            memento.position,
        )

    def __str__(self) -> str:
        return f"L{self.level} hp={self.health} @ {self.position}"


class SaveManager:
    """Caretaker: bounded custody, never inspects snapshots."""

    def __init__(self, max_saves: int = 3) -> None:
        self._checkpoints: deque[GameMemento] = deque(maxlen=max_saves)

    def checkpoint(self, memento: GameMemento) -> None:
        self._checkpoints.append(memento)

    def last_checkpoint(self) -> GameMemento | None:
        return self._checkpoints[-1] if self._checkpoints else None


if __name__ == "__main__":
    player = Player()
    saves = SaveManager(max_saves=3)
    player.move("forest")
    saves.checkpoint(player.save())
    print(f"checkpoint: {player}")
    player.damage(80)
    player.move("cave")
    saves.checkpoint(player.save())
    print(f"checkpoint: {player}")
    player.damage(90)
    print(f"after fatal hit: {player}")
    last = saves.last_checkpoint()
    if last is not None:
        player.restore(last)
    print(f"respawned: {player}")

Sample I/O:

checkpoint: L1 hp=100 @ forest
checkpoint: L1 hp=20 @ cave
after fatal hit: L1 hp=0 @ cave
respawned: L1 hp=20 @ cave

docs.title: 4.3 Go (idiomatic)
docs.text:
Explanation: Unexported memento fields (level, health, position) readable only via originator methods in the same package — real encapsulation enforced by the compiler. Slice-based bounded stack with oldest-eviction.

package main

import "fmt"

type gameMemento struct {
    level    int
    health   int
    position string
}

type Player struct {
    level    int
    health   int
    position string
}

func NewPlayer() *Player { return &Player{level: 1, health: 100, position: "spawn"} }

func (p *Player) Move(where string) { p.position = where }

func (p *Player) Damage(hp int) {
    p.health -= hp
    if p.health < 0 {
        p.health = 0
    }
}

func (p *Player) Save() gameMemento {
    return gameMemento{level: p.level, health: p.health, position: p.position}
}

func (p *Player) Restore(m gameMemento) {
    p.level, p.health, p.position = m.level, m.health, m.position
}

func (p *Player) String() string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("L%d hp=%d @ %s", p.level, p.health, p.position)
}

type SaveManager struct {
    checkpoints []gameMemento
    maxSaves    int
}

func NewSaveManager(maxSaves int) *SaveManager { return &SaveManager{maxSaves: maxSaves} }

func (s *SaveManager) Checkpoint(m gameMemento) {
    s.checkpoints = append(s.checkpoints, m)
    if len(s.checkpoints) > s.maxSaves {
        s.checkpoints = s.checkpoints[len(s.checkpoints)-s.maxSaves:]
    }
}

func (s *SaveManager) LastCheckpoint() (gameMemento, bool) {
    if len(s.checkpoints) == 0 {
        return gameMemento{}, false
    }
    return s.checkpoints[len(s.checkpoints)-1], true
}

func main() {
    player := NewPlayer()
    saves := NewSaveManager(3)
    player.Move("forest")
    saves.Checkpoint(player.Save())
    fmt.Println("checkpoint:", player)
    player.Damage(80)
    player.Move("cave")
    saves.Checkpoint(player.Save())
    fmt.Println("checkpoint:", player)
    player.Damage(90)
    fmt.Println("after fatal hit:", player)
    if m, ok := saves.LastCheckpoint(); ok {
        player.Restore(m)
    }
    fmt.Println("respawned:", player)
}

Sample I/O:

checkpoint: L1 hp=100 @ forest
checkpoint: L1 hp=20 @ cave
after fatal hit: L1 hp=0 @ cave
respawned: L1 hp=20 @ cave

docs.title: 5. Real-World Industry Applications
docs.text:
• Editors and IDEs (VS Code, Word, Figma): Document snapshots before risky operations (find-replace-all, refactorings); undo restores whole-state where inverse commands are impractical.
  • Games (save slots, checkpoints, quicksave): Player/world snapshots persisted to disk with versioning; respawn, time-rewind (Braid, Prince of Persia), and difficulty rollback all restore mementos.
  • Databases (savepoints, MVCC snapshots): SAVEPOINT sp1; ... ROLLBACK TO sp1 is caretaker-managed memento semantics over transaction state; MVCC snapshot isolation gives each transaction a consistent snapshot.
  • Version control (Git): Commits are immutable snapshots (mementos) of tree state; branches/tags are caretaker indexes; checkout is restore. Content-addressing makes the snapshot store efficient.
  • Browsers (history, session restore): Back/forward entries snapshot scroll + form + DOM state; crash recovery restores the session's memento list.
  • Infrastructure (Terraform state, VM snapshots, container layers): terraform.tfstate, VM snapshots, and image layers are restorable snapshots with explicit custody and retention.
  • Finance (ledger corrections): End-of-day snapshots enable restatement and audit replay without mutating posted entries.
  • Mobile (Android onSaveInstanceState, iOS state restoration): OS asks the originator (activity/view controller) for a snapshot bundle; the system (caretaker) holds it across process death and hands it back on relaunch.

docs.title: 6. Practical Use Cases and Scenarios
docs.text:
• Game checkpoints (Section 4): Autosave every 60s plus manual slots; bounded to last 3 autosaves + named boss-fight slots. Death restores last autosave; "load slot 2" jumps the timeline. Old snapshots spill to disk with compression.
  • Editor with whole-state undo: Before "replace all", snapshot the buffer; undo restores it wholesale — simpler and safer than inverting thousands of edits. Cap at 50 snapshots or 10 MB.
  • Form auto-save and recovery: Draft snapshots on every keystroke pause; browser crash restores the draft; "discard draft" clears the caretaker. Snapshots exclude transient UI state (focus, scroll).
  • DB transaction savepoints: BEGIN; SAVEPOINT sp1; risky_batch(); ROLLBACK TO sp1 ON ERROR; COMMIT — partial rollback without aborting the whole transaction. Caretaker is the DB engine; mementos are page-level snapshots.
  • Config rollback: Network-device or feature-flag changes snapshot prior config; failed health checks auto-restore. Named mementos ("before deploy v42") make rollback one click.
  • Drawing app history: Each stroke completion snapshots the canvas layer stack (or stores stroke-diffs for memory). Scrubbing the history slider restores arbitrary points — a timeline caretaker over immutable snapshots.

docs.title: 7. When to Use and When Not to Use
docs.text:
Use Memento when:

  • You must save and restore state without exposing internals (encapsulation is non-negotiable).
  • Restoring whole state is simpler or safer than computing inverse operations.
  • You need checkpoints, savepoints, snapshots, or bounded undo history.
  • Snapshot timing is client-driven (before risky ops, on schedule, on demand).

Do NOT use when:

Situation Prefer instead Inverse operation is cheap and exact (insert ↔ delete) Command with undo() — lighter than snapshots State is huge and changes constantly (video frames, large datasets) Event sourcing / deltas / persistent data structures History must be queryable ("all changes by Alice") Event log / audit trail, not opaque snapshots Snapshots must be human-readable or cross-service Serialization with schema (protobuf/JSON) + versioning Simple value rollback in one method Local variable save/restore — no pattern needed

docs.title: 8. Do's and Don'ts
docs.text:
Do:

  • Keep mementos immutable and opaque to the caretaker (language-enforced where possible: unexported fields, inner classes, frozen dataclasses).
  • Bound history by count and bytes; define eviction (drop oldest, spill to disk) and document it.
  • Snapshot the essential state only — exclude caches, derived data, listeners, and handles; rebuild those on restore.
  • Deep-copy mutable referenced state at save time, or use immutable structures, to prevent history corruption by aliasing.
  • Make restore() atomic: copy all fields together so the originator never sits half-restored; validate the memento belongs to this originator.
  • Version serialized mementos (schema id + migration) if snapshots persist or cross process boundaries.

Don't:

  • Don't let the caretaker read, filter, or branch on snapshot contents — that collapses the narrow interface and leaks encapsulation.
  • Don't snapshot on every frame/keystroke without throttling — throttle (debounce, on-pause, every N ops) and diff where possible.
  • Don't store listeners, locks, file handles, or sockets in mementos — they are not restorable state.
  • Don't restore derived/cached state blindly — recompute or invalidate it to avoid staleness.
  • Don't grow an unbounded in-memory stack; unbounded history is a memory leak with a design-pattern name.
  • Don't use Memento where an audit log is required — opaque snapshots cannot answer "who changed what, when".

docs.title: 9.1 Memento vs Command (for undo) vs Serialization
docs.text:
Aspect Memento Command Serialization (snapshot mechanism) What is stored Opaque whole-state snapshot Request + parameters + inverse operation Byte representation of state (JSON, protobuf, clone) Undo mechanism Restore prior snapshot wholesale Execute inverse action Deserialize and swap in Encapsulation Caretaker cannot inspect at all Command often needs receiver internals Whoever holds bytes can read them (unless encrypted) Memory profile Heavy for large state; needs bounding/diffs Light when inverse is small Depends on format; versioning cost Typical use Game saves, checkpoints, savepoints, form restore Editor undo stacks, job queues, macros, sagas Persistence, network transfer, crash recovery

Rule of thumb: Whole-state restore simpler than inversion → Memento. Cheap exact inverse + queueing/macros → Command. Snapshots must persist or travel → serialize the memento (mechanism inside the pattern's custody discipline).

docs.title: 9.2 Memento vs Prototype vs State
docs.text: Aspect Memento Prototype State Purpose Time-travel: restore past state Create new objects by copying a template Change behavior when internal state changes Copy direction Originator → snapshot → originator Prototype → new sibling object Context delegates to current state object History Caretaker keeps many versions No history; one-off cloning Only current state matters Use when Undo/checkpoints/savepoints Cheap instantiation from examples State machines (TCP, orders, player modes)

docs.title: Q&A
docs.text:
Q1. What is the Memento pattern in one sentence? A: The originator snapshots its state into opaque mementos that a caretaker stores and returns, so past states can be restored without exposing internals.

Q2. How does Memento preserve encapsulation if the caretaker holds the state? A: Through narrow/wide interfaces: the caretaker sees an opaque handle (no getters), while only the originator can create and read the snapshot — enforced via inner classes, package-private accessors, unexported fields, or frozen types plus discipline.

Q3. How do you prevent memory bloat? A: Bound history (count + bytes), snapshot essential state only, store diffs for large objects, compress/spill old entries to disk, throttle snapshot frequency, and drop redo branches on new edits. Measure snapshot size early.

Q4. Memento vs serialization — when is a snapshot just clone() or JSON? A: Cloning/serializing is the mechanism; Memento is the custody discipline (who creates, who stores, who restores, with what visibility). Use in-memory mementos for session-local undo; serialize when snapshots persist, cross processes, or need versioning.

Q5. Memento vs Command for undo — how do you choose? A: If the inverse is cheap and exact (insert/delete), Command is lighter and adds queueing/macros. If inversion is complex, error-prone, or touches many fields, Memento's whole-state restore is safer. Hybrids are common: a Command holding a Memento as undo state.

Q6. What goes wrong with shallow copies? A: The snapshot aliases live mutable objects; later mutations corrupt history, and restore resurrects already-mutated data. Fix with deep copies at save time or immutable state throughout.

Q7. How do you handle derived state (caches, indexes, UI) on restore? A: Exclude it from snapshots and rebuild/invalidate on restore. Restoring stale derived data is a classic bug — snapshot sources of truth, recompute the rest.

Q8. How do you test Memento thoroughly? A: Round-trip (save → mutate → restore → assert exact equality), multi-cycle save/restore sequences, encapsulation (caretaker cannot read state — assert via API surface), eviction policy (oldest dropped, newest kept), deep-copy isolation (mutate original, snapshot unaffected), and serialized-version migration if persisted.

Q9. When should you avoid Memento? A: Huge/fast-changing state (prefer deltas/event sourcing), cheap Command inverses, queryable history needs (prefer event logs), or cross-service snapshots without a versioning story.

docs.title: LLD scenarios
docs.text:
S1. Design game save/checkpoint system. Requirements: autosave + named slots, bounded memory, death respawn, version upgrades. Solution: Player.save()/restore() + SaveManager(maxSaves) as in Section 4; slots as named timeline caretaker; old autosaves spill to compressed disk; save schema versioned with migrations. Discuss what to exclude (particle caches, RNG handles) and respawn atomicity.

S2. Design undo for a drawing app. Requirements: stroke-level undo/redo, memory-bounded, history scrubber. Solution: snapshot-per-stroke for small canvases, stroke-diff mementos for large ones; timeline caretaker backing the scrubber; redo cleared on new stroke. Discuss layer compositing on restore and thumbnail caching for the scrubber UI.

S3. Design database-style savepoints for a checkout flow. Requirements: reserve → pay → confirm with partial rollback to savepoint on payment failure. Solution: caretaker-managed savepoint stack over order state; each step snapshots before mutating; failure restores to the labeled savepoint without aborting the session. Discuss nested savepoints, savepoint release, and interaction with external side effects (emails sent cannot be unsent — compensations, not snapshots).

docs.title: 11. Testing and Best Practices
docs.text:
• Round-trip tests: Save → mutate every field → restore → assert deep equality with the saved point. Table-drive across representative states (full/empty/boundary health, unicode positions).
  • Sequence tests: Multiple checkpoints with interleaved mutations and out-of-order restores; assert each restore lands exactly; assert eviction drops oldest and keeps newest under the bound.
  • Encapsulation tests: Assert caretaker API exposes no state readers (review + compile-level checks: unexported fields, package-private access); attempt reflection/field access in tests where the language permits to prove opacity.
  • Isolation tests: Mutate the originator after saving; assert the stored memento is unaffected (catches shallow-copy aliasing). Restore twice from one memento; assert identical results.
  • Resource tests: Snapshot size measurement per save; sustained checkpoint loops with memory assertions; serialization round-trip and version-migration tests for persisted snapshots.
  • Best practices: Immutable mementos; bounded caretakers (count + bytes); essential-state-only snapshots; atomic restore; named slots for timelines; versioned persistence; never store handles/listeners/caches; document the eviction and missing-save (empty history) behavior.

docs.title: 12. Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
