• Memento externalizes state snapshots without breaking encapsulation: originator creates/consumes, memento stays opaque, caretaker only keeps custody.
  • Reach for it for checkpoints, savepoints, bounded undo, session restore, and config rollback — anywhere whole-state restore beats hand-rolled inverses.
  • Distinguish from Command (actions + inverses, queueable) and Serialization (the persistence mechanism mementos may use); the patterns compose (Command holding a Memento).
  • Production safety rests on opacity, immutability, bounded history, deep-copy isolation, essential-state-only snapshots, and atomic restore — test each explicitly.
  • In LLD interviews, the game-save and editor-undo scenarios are canonical: draw the three roles, state the narrow/wide interface split, then immediately discuss memory bounds, aliasing, and versioning to show production maturity.

docs.title: Observer Design Pattern
docs.text: Youtube: 3. Observer Design Pattern Explanation (Hindi) | Design Interview Question | LLD System Design

docs.title: 1. Overview and Fundamentals
docs.text:
The Observer pattern defines a one-to-many dependency between objects so that when one object (the Subject) changes state, all its dependents (Observers) are notified and updated automatically.

In one sentence: one subject broadcasts; many observers react — without the subject knowing who they are.

Core roles:

  • Subject (Observable): holds state, maintains a list of observers, provides subscribe(), unsubscribe(), and notify().
  • Observer: declares an update() callback the subject calls on change.
  • ConcreteSubject: stores real state (stock price, order status) and calls notify() after mutation.
  • ConcreteObserver: implements update() with reaction logic (refresh UI, send SMS, trigger warehouse pick).

Fundamental properties:

  • Push vs pull: subject can push the new data (update(price)) or push a "changed" hint and let observers pull (getState()).
  • Loose coupling: subject knows only the Observer interface, never concrete classes.
  • Dynamic membership: observers attach/detach at runtime.
  • Broadcast semantics: a single state change fans out to N dependents in one call.
  • Category: behavioral — it governs communication, not construction or structure.

Mental model: a YouTube channel (subject) with subscribers (observers). Uploading a video notifies every subscriber; the channel never hard-codes the subscriber list, and subscribers can join or leave freely.

Relationship to everyday code: DOM event listeners, useEffect on state change, Model→View updates in MVC, Redis Pub/Sub, Kafka consumers, and "follow" feeds are all Observer ideas at different scales.

docs.title: Intent and forces
docs.text:
Observer solves the consistency + decoupling tension: several objects must stay consistent with one source of truth, but the source should not be coupled to every consumer's type, count, or lifetime.

Without Observer, the subject either polls consumers (wasteful), hard-codes calls to each consumer (rigid, violates Open/Closed), or exposes state for everyone to poll (stale reads, chatty). Observer inverts this: consumers register interest once; the subject pushes changes.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Observers call subject.subscribe(this) at startup (UI mount, service init).
  2. Subject mutates state through a guarded method (e.g., setPrice(), advance()).
  3. That method calls notify(), iterating over a snapshot of the observer list and invoking observer.update(payload).
  4. Observers react independently; failures in one must not break the loop.
  5. On teardown, observers call unsubscribe() to avoid leaks and stale callbacks.

docs.title: Push, pull, and hybrid
docs.text: Model Subject sends Observer does Best when Push Full new state (price, status) Uses payload directly Small, stable payloads; dashboards, tickers Pull changed() hint + subject ref Queries subject.getState() for needed slice Rich state; observers need different projections Hybrid Version/sequence + minimal delta Pulls full state only on gap High-frequency streams where drops matter

docs.title: Design principles at play
docs.text:
• Open/Closed: add new observers without touching the subject.
  • Dependency Inversion: both sides depend on abstractions (Subject/Observer interfaces).
  • Hollywood Principle: "don't call us, we'll call you" — observers register and wait.
  • Single Responsibility: subject owns state + fan-out; each observer owns one reaction.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
• Synchronous in-process: method call loop (simplest, this page's focus).
  • Async/event-bus: notifications queued on an executor or bus.
  • Signal/reactive: RxJS Observable, Java Flow, Kotlin StateFlow — Observer with operators.
  • Distributed pub/sub: SNS/SQS/Kafka — durable Observer across processes.
  • Property-change: JavaBeans PropertyChangeSupport, C# INotifyPropertyChanged — per-field observers.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Benefits: loose coupling, broadcast, dynamic membership, testable reactions in isolation. Costs: notification order is unspecified unless designed, cascading updates (A notifies B which notifies C), debugging fan-out, and leak risk if unsubscribe is forgotten.

docs.title: 3. UML and Architecture Diagrams
docs.text:
Static structure: one subject interface with many attached observers; concrete subjects hold state and concrete observers hold reaction logic.

classDiagram
    class Subject {
        +subscribe(o: Observer)
        +unsubscribe(o: Observer)
        +notifyObservers()
    }
    class ConcreteSubject {
        -state: String
        -observers: List~Observer~
        +setState(state: String)
        +getState() String
    }
    class Observer {
        <>
        +update(state: String)
    }
    class ConcreteObserverA {
        +update(state: String)
    }
    class ConcreteObserverB {
        +update(state: String)
    }
    Subject <|.. ConcreteSubject
    Observer <|.. ConcreteObserverA
    Observer <|.. ConcreteObserverB
    ConcreteSubject o--> Observer : notifies

Explanation: ConcreteSubject aggregates Observer references through the interface only. setState() mutates state then calls notifyObservers(), which fans out to every update(). Adding ConcreteObserverC requires no change to the subject — the Open/Closed payoff.

Runtime flow: subscribe once, then every mutation triggers a fan-out loop. Observers may pull extra detail after the push hint.

sequenceDiagram
    participant App
    participant Order as Subject: Order
    participant Cust as Observer: CustomerApp
    participant Dash as Observer: SellerDashboard
    participant Wh as Observer: Warehouse
    App->>Order: subscribe(Cust)
    App->>Order: subscribe(Dash)
    App->>Order: subscribe(Wh)
    App->>Order: advance("PAID")
    Order->>Cust: onStatus(ORD-101, PAID)
    Order->>Dash: onStatus(ORD-101, PAID)
    Order->>Wh: onStatus(ORD-101, PAID)
    Note over Wh: picks items for ORD-101
    App->>Order: unsubscribe(Cust)
    App->>Order: advance("SHIPPED")
    Order->>Dash: onStatus(ORD-101, SHIPPED)
    Order->>Wh: onStatus(ORD-101, SHIPPED)

Explanation: subscription is explicit setup; each advance() produces one fan-out pass. After unsubscribe, the departed observer stops receiving events. In production, each arrow may be a queued task with try-catch isolation so one slow observer never blocks the rest.

Architecture note: keep notify() re-entrancy safe — iterate over a copy of the list so an observer that unsubscribes mid-loop does not cause ConcurrentModificationException. Never hold a lock while calling update(); a re-entrant subscribe from inside update would deadlock.

docs.title: 4. Implementation Examples in Java, Python, and Go
docs.text: The domain is order tracking: an Order subject pushes status changes; customer app, seller dashboard, and warehouse observe.

docs.title: Java (interface + ArrayList, unsubscribe discipline)
docs.text:
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

interface OrderObserver {
    void onStatus(String orderId, String status);
}

class Order {
    private final String orderId;
    private String status = "PLACED";
    private final List<OrderObserver> observers = new ArrayList<>();

    Order(String orderId) { this.orderId = orderId; }

    void subscribe(OrderObserver o) { observers.add(o); }
    void unsubscribe(OrderObserver o) { observers.remove(o); }

    void advance(String next) {
        status = next;
        // Snapshot + isolate: one bad observer cannot break the loop.
        for (OrderObserver o : List.copyOf(observers)) {
            try { o.onStatus(orderId, status); }
            catch (Exception e) { System.err.println("observer failed: " + e); }
        }
    }
    String status() { return status; }
}

class CustomerApp implements OrderObserver {
    public void onStatus(String id, String s) {
        System.out.println("SMS to customer: order " + id + " is " + s);
    }
}

class SellerDashboard implements OrderObserver {
    public void onStatus(String id, String s) {
        System.out.println("Dashboard refresh: " + id + " -> " + s);
    }
}

class WarehouseSystem implements OrderObserver {
    public void onStatus(String id, String s) {
        if ("PAID".equals(s)) System.out.println("Warehouse: pick items for " + id);
        if ("CANCELLED".equals(s)) System.out.println("Warehouse: restock " + id);
    }
}

public class OrderDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Order order = new Order("ORD-101");
        CustomerApp app = new CustomerApp();
        order.subscribe(app);
        order.subscribe(new SellerDashboard());
        order.subscribe(new WarehouseSystem());
        order.advance("PAID");
        order.advance("SHIPPED");
        order.unsubscribe(app);
        order.advance("DELIVERED");
    }
}

Explanation: List.copyOf snapshot avoids concurrent-modification; try-catch per observer provides failure isolation. unsubscribe is explicit to prevent leaks.

Sample I/O:

SMS to customer: order ORD-101 is PAID
Dashboard refresh: ORD-101 -> PAID
Warehouse: pick items for ORD-101
SMS to customer: order ORD-101 is SHIPPED
Dashboard refresh: ORD-101 -> SHIPPED
Dashboard refresh: ORD-101 -> DELIVERED

docs.title: Python (pythonic: protocol + weak-friendly list)
docs.text:
from __future__ import annotations
from typing import Protocol

class OrderObserver(Protocol):
    def on_status(self, order_id: str, status: str) -> None: ...

class Order:
    """Subject: pushes status changes to registered observers."""

    def __init__(self, order_id: str) -> None:
        self.order_id = order_id
        self.status = "PLACED"
        self._observers: list[OrderObserver] = []

    def subscribe(self, observer: OrderObserver) -> None:
        self._observers.append(observer)

    def unsubscribe(self, observer: OrderObserver) -> None:
        try:
            self._observers.remove(observer)
        except ValueError:
            pass

    def advance(self, status: str) -> None:
        self.status = status
        for observer in list(self._observers):  # snapshot: safe detach mid-loop
            try:
                observer.on_status(self.order_id, self.status)
            except Exception as exc:  # isolate one bad listener
                print(f"observer failed: {exc!r}")

class CustomerApp:
    def on_status(self, order_id: str, status: str) -> None:
        print(f"SMS to customer: order {order_id} is {status}")

class SellerDashboard:
    def on_status(self, order_id: str, status: str) -> None:
        print(f"Dashboard refresh: {order_id} -> {status}")

class WarehouseSystem:
    def on_status(self, order_id: str, status: str) -> None:
        if status == "PAID":
            print(f"Warehouse: pick items for {order_id}")
        elif status == "CANCELLED":
            print(f"Warehouse: restock {order_id}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    order = Order("ORD-101")
    app = CustomerApp()
    order.subscribe(app)
    order.subscribe(SellerDashboard())
    order.subscribe(WarehouseSystem())
    order.advance("PAID")
    order.advance("SHIPPED")
    order.unsubscribe(app)
    order.advance("DELIVERED")

Explanation: Protocol gives structural typing without forcing inheritance; list(...) snapshot and per-observer try/except mirror the Java discipline. For UI observers with short lifetimes, store weakref.ref entries to avoid leaks.

Sample I/O: identical to the Java output above.

docs.title: Go (idiomatic: interface + slice + mutex)
docs.text:
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "sync"
)

// Observer is the subscriber contract.
type Observer interface {
    OnStatus(orderID, status string)
}

// Order is the subject.
type Order struct {
    mu        sync.RWMutex
    id        string
    status    string
    observers []Observer
}

func NewOrder(id string) *Order { return &Order{id: id, status: "PLACED"} }

func (o *Order) Subscribe(obs Observer) {
    o.mu.Lock()
    defer o.mu.Unlock()
    o.observers = append(o.observers, obs)
}

func (o *Order) Unsubscribe(target Observer) {
    o.mu.Lock()
    defer o.mu.Unlock()
    kept := o.observers[:0]
    for _, obs := range o.observers {
        if obs != target {
            kept = append(kept, obs)
        }
    }
    o.observers = kept
}

func (o *Order) Advance(status string) {
    o.mu.Lock()
    o.status = status
    snapshot := append([]Observer(nil), o.observers...)
    id := o.id
    o.mu.Unlock() // never hold the lock while notifying

    for _, obs := range snapshot {
        func() {
            defer func() {
                if r := recover(); r != nil {
                    fmt.Println("observer failed:", r)
                }
            }()
            obs.OnStatus(id, status)
        }()
    }
}

type CustomerApp struct{}

func (CustomerApp) OnStatus(id, status string) {
    fmt.Println("SMS to customer: order " + id + " is " + status)
}

type SellerDashboard struct{}

func (SellerDashboard) OnStatus(id, status string) {
    fmt.Println("Dashboard refresh: " + id + " -> " + status)
}

type Warehouse struct{}

func (Warehouse) OnStatus(id, status string) {
    if status == "PAID" {
        fmt.Println("Warehouse: pick items for " + id)
    }
    if status == "CANCELLED" {
        fmt.Println("Warehouse: restock " + id)
    }
}

func main() {
    order := NewOrder("ORD-101")
    app := CustomerApp{}
    order.Subscribe(app)
    order.Subscribe(SellerDashboard{})
    order.Subscribe(Warehouse{})
    order.Advance("PAID")
    order.Advance("SHIPPED")
    order.Unsubscribe(app)
    order.Advance("DELIVERED")
}

Explanation: RWMutex guards subscribe/unsubscribe; Advance snapshots under lock then notifies without holding it, so an observer that re-subscribes cannot deadlock. Panic recovery per observer provides Go-idiomatic isolation.

Sample I/O: identical to the Java output above.

docs.title: 5. Real-World Industry Applications
docs.text:
• Frontend reactivity: React useState/useEffect, Vue refs, Angular Observable — view observers re-render on model change.
  • Spring Framework: ApplicationEvent + ApplicationListener for order-created, payment-succeeded domain events.
  • Android: LiveData/StateFlow observers bound to lifecycle owners; auto-unsubscribe on destroy.
  • Messaging: Redis Pub/Sub for cache invalidation, AWS SNS fan-out to SQS queues, Kafka consumer groups tailing order topics.
  • Stock/market data: one ticker subject fans price ticks to chart, alert, and portfolio observers (the classic interview example).
  • Social feeds: follow graph — a post notifies follower timelines, push service, and search indexer.
  • IoT: sensor subject notifies threshold-alert, dashboard, and persistence observers.
  • Databases: Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY, Firebase realtime listeners, CDC outbox publishers.

docs.title: 6. Practical Use Cases and Scenarios
docs.text:
1. Order tracking feed: PLACED → PAID → SHIPPED → DELIVERED pushes to customer SMS, seller dashboard, warehouse, fraud scoring. New consumers subscribe without touching Order.
  2. Stock ticker: exchange feed pushes ticks; chart, alert-rule, and P&L observers each keep their own projection.
  3. Form validation: each keystroke notifies validators, character counters, and submit-button enablers.
  4. Build pipelines: commit subject notifies test, lint, and deploy observers in parallel.
  5. Multiplayer lobby: player-ready changes notify matchmaking, chat roster, and countdown timer.
  6. Feature flags: flag-change subject pushes to every service instance holding a cached flag snapshot.
  7. Caching: write-through subject invalidates CDN, local, and query caches on entity change.

Scenario walkthrough (e-commerce): Order.advance("CANCELLED") notifies CustomerApp (refund SMS), Warehouse (restock), and AnalyticsObserver (funnel metric). Adding a FraudObserver later is one subscribe call — zero edits to Order.

docs.title: 7. When to Use and When Not to Use
docs.text:
Use Observer when:

  • One state change must reach many unknown dependents (events, feeds, model-view sync).
  • Dependents join/leave at runtime (UI mounts, plugin systems, feature subscriptions).
  • You need broadcast without polling (tickers, order feeds, sensor streams).
  • Cross-cutting reactions (logging, metrics, audit) must attach without touching core logic.

Do NOT use Observer when:

  • There is exactly one dependent — a direct callback or return value is clearer.
  • Publisher and subscribers span services with durability needs — use a queue/stream (SQS, Kafka) instead of in-memory fan-out.
  • Ordering guarantees matter strictly — Observer is unordered by default; use a chain or ordered bus.
  • The graph can cycle (A observes B observes A) — you will build an infinite notification storm; use a mediator or explicit orchestration.
  • Observers need request/response — Observer is one-way; use Command, Future, or RPC.

Rule of thumb: one source, many passive reactions, same process → Observer. Cross-process, durable, or ordered → broker/chain.

docs.title: 8. Do's and Don'ts
docs.text:
Do:

  • Provide unsubscribe (or scoped/auto-closeable subscriptions) and call it in lifecycle teardown.
  • Iterate over a snapshot copy; never mutate the list mid-notify without copying.
  • Isolate observer failures with per-observer try-catch so one crash cannot halt fan-out.
  • Never hold locks while notifying; snapshot under lock, notify outside it.
  • Document push payload versioning; treat the event shape as a public contract.
  • Consider async dispatch or batching for high-frequency subjects (price ticks).

Don't:

  • Don't notify from inside a constructor — half-built subjects leak this to observers.
  • Don't assume notification order — label any priority scheme explicitly or use a priority bus.
  • Don't let observers call back into mutating subject methods re-entrantly without a guard (storm risk).
  • Don't store strong references to short-lived UI observers without weak refs or lifecycle unsubscription.
  • Don't push huge object graphs — send IDs/deltas and let observers pull what they need.
  • Don't use Observer for request-reply; it has no return channel by design.

docs.title: 9. Comparison with Other Design Patterns
docs.text:
Aspect Observer Pub/Sub (broker) Mediator Topology Subject → known interface list, direct refs Publisher → topic → broker → subscribers Colleagues ↔ hub, hub owns rules Coupling Subject knows observer interface Neither side knows the other (topic only) Colleagues know hub; hub knows all Scope Usually in-process, synchronous Cross-process, durable, async In-process coordination with back-talk Ordering/durability None by default Ordered per partition, replayable Hub-defined sequencing Failure mode One throw breaks loop (guard it) Broker retries, DLQ Hub becomes god object Use when UI events, model-view, order feed Microservice events, Kafka/SNS fan-out Chat rooms, dialogs, ATC with two-way rules Aspect Observer Command Callback (single) Fan-out One-to-many One request object, one receiver (or queue) One-to-one function ref Reversibility No undo channel Supports undo/queue/replay No Lifetime Long-lived subscription One-shot execution Scoped to call Pick it when Ongoing interest in state changes Defer, queue, or undo work Single notification suffices

Observer vs Mediator (the classic confusion): Observer broadcasts one-way from a subject to passive listeners. Mediator orchestrates two-way conversations among peers with rules in the hub. If listeners never talk back, Observer wins. If peers negotiate (chat, auctions, dialog validation), Mediator wins.

docs.title: 10. Interview Preparation
docs.text:
Q1: Push vs pull — which do you choose? Push (subject sends data) is simpler and avoids extra queries but couples observers to the payload shape. Pull (subject sends "changed") lets each observer fetch its own slice. Use push for small stable payloads, pull for rich state, hybrid (version + delta) for streams.

Q2: How do you prevent memory leaks? Every subscribe needs a visible unsubscribe in lifecycle teardown; use weak references for UI listeners; scope subscriptions (try-with-resources, takeUntil(destroy)); bound the list and log its size. In review, grep for unmatched subscribes.

Q3: What if an observer throws or blocks? Isolate: try-catch per observer, log and optionally auto-unsubscribe repeat offenders. Never let one observer veto the loop. For slow observers, dispatch async with a bounded queue; never block the subject thread on I/O inside update().

Q4: How do you handle ordering and duplicate delivery? Observer gives no order guarantee — add explicit priorities or sequence numbers if needed, make observers idempotent (dedupe by event ID), and document at-least-once semantics for async variants.

Q5: Observer vs pub/sub vs mediator? Observer: direct in-process fan-out to an interface list. Pub/sub: decoupled via broker/topics across processes with durability. Mediator: hub with two-way rules among peers. Scale of distance and need for reply decide.

Q6: How do you avoid notification storms / cycles? Guard re-entrancy (dirty flag, version check — ignore setState with same value), batch coalesce rapid changes, and forbid observers from mutating the same subject synchronously; route follow-on changes through a queue. Detect cycles with event lineage IDs.

Q7: Is Observer thread-safe? Only if designed: guard the list with a mutex/RWMutex, snapshot before notifying, notify outside the lock, and make observers thread-safe or confine them to one executor. Test with concurrent subscribe/notify fuzz.

Q8: When do you replace Observer with polling or a queue? Poll when change frequency is low and staleness is tolerable (simpler, no leak surface). Queue when crossing processes, needing durability/replay, or scaling consumers independently. Keep in-process Observer for live UI/model sync.

LLD scenario 1 — Design a Stock Alert system. Expectation: StockTicker subject with subscribe(symbol, observer); PriceAlertObserver (threshold rule), DashboardObserver, AuditObserver. Discuss push tick vs pull quote, snapshot iteration, async dispatch for slow SMS, idempotency keys, and when to graduate to Kafka for multi-service fan-out.

LLD scenario 2 — Design an Order Tracking notification service. Expectation: Order subject, observers per channel (SMS, email, push) plus internal (warehouse, analytics). Show unsubscribe on delivery, per-observer try-catch, template-per-channel, rate limiting via decorator, and event versioning for out-of-order retries.

LLD scenario 3 — Design MVC live search. Expectation: keystroke subject notifies SuggestionObserver (debounced API), ResultCountObserver, HistoryObserver. Discuss coalescing (300 ms debounce), cancellation of stale requests, and pull-model for observers needing different query slices.

docs.title: 11. Testing and Best Practices
docs.text:
• Subscribe/unsubscribe: register two mocks, unsubscribe one, assert only the survivor receives the next event.
  • Fan-out completeness: attach N mocks, fire one change, verify all N update() calls with the exact payload.
  • Isolation: make one observer throw; assert the rest still receive the event and the subject stays usable.
  • Re-entrancy: observer that unsubscribes (or subscribes) inside update() must not throw ConcurrentModificationException.
  • No-op change: setting the same state twice should notify once or zero times per documented policy.
  • Leak check: destroy observer, force GC, assert subject list shrinks (weak-ref test) or explicit unsubscribe was called.
  • Concurrency: hammer subscribe/notify from threads; assert no deadlock and every notification delivers a consistent snapshot.
  • Contract test: payload schema versioned; old observers ignore unknown fields, new observers handle missing fields.
  • Best practice: mock observers for subject tests; use a recording fake subject for observer tests; keep observers stateless or inject clocks/IDs for determinism.

docs.title: 12. Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Observer = one subject, many loosely-coupled dependents, automatic push on change.
  • Prefer snapshots + per-observer isolation + explicit unsubscribe — the three disciplines that prevent 90% of Observer bugs.
  • Push for small payloads, pull for rich state, broker when crossing processes.
  • New reactions arrive as new observer classes; the subject never changes (Open/Closed).
  • Do not use it for request/reply, strict ordering, or durable cross-service events — reach for Command, Chain, or a queue.
  • Interview one-liner: "Observer keeps one source consistent with many dependents through interface-only fan-out; I snapshot the list, isolate failures, and unsubscribe on teardown — and graduate to pub/sub when delivery must cross processes."

docs.title: State Design Pattern
docs.text: Youtube: 16. Design Vending Machine (Hindi) | LLD of Vending Machine | State Design Pattern | LLD question

docs.title: 1. Overview and Fundamentals
docs.text:
The State pattern lets an object alter its behavior when its internal state changes — the object appears to change its class.

In one sentence: delegate every action to the current state object, and let state objects decide the next state.

Core roles:

  • Context: the stable facade clients call (Order, VendingMachine, TCPConnection). Holds a reference to the current State and delegates.
  • State interface: declares one method per event (pay(), ship(), insertCoin(), open()).
  • ConcreteState: implements valid events for that stage and rejects (or transitions) the rest (PendingState, PaidState, HasMoneyState).
  • Transition: a state method returns (or installs) the next state object.

Fundamental properties:

  • Behavioral: governs how behavior varies, not how objects are built.
  • Explicit machine: every (state, event) pair has an owner — no hidden if status == X spread across methods.
  • Self-driven switching: unlike Strategy, the state objects themselves trigger transitions.
  • Open/Closed: new stages arrive as new classes; the context stays untouched.

Mental model: a vending machine. Pressing the same "buy" button does different things when idle (ask for coins), when paid (dispense), or when out of stock (refund) — the button is fixed, the active state object answers.

docs.title: Intent and forces
docs.text:
State solves the conditional-explosion tension: behavior depends on lifecycle stage, so every method accumulates if/else or switch on a status field. Branches duplicate, invalid transitions slip through, and adding a stage means editing every method.

State replaces the status flag with polymorphism: each stage becomes an object owning its rules. The context shrinks to state = state.handle(event).

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Context starts in an initial state (new PendingState()).
  2. Client calls context.pay() — context delegates to state.pay(this).
  3. The state either returns the next state (PaidState), returns this (no-op with log), or rejects (log / exception).
  4. Context installs the returned state and optionally emits a transition event for audit.
  5. Terminal states (Delivered, Cancelled) reject everything.

docs.title: Where transition logic lives
docs.text:
Placement How Best when In state objects Each state returns the next Default — keeps context thin, rules co-located In context States return enums; context maps to next Auditors want one visible transition table In table/config (state, event) → next map or library 8+ states, compliance needs a printable graph

Prefer states-own-transitions until the graph needs centralized audit; then extract a transition table or a state-machine library (Spring StateMachine, XState, MassTransit sagas).

docs.title: Design principles at play
docs.text:
• Single Responsibility: each state class owns one stage's rules.
  • Open/Closed: add RefundedState without editing Order or sibling states.
  • Liskov: a shared base with default rejections keeps every state substitutable.
  • Explicitness: illegal transitions fail loudly instead of silently corrupting data.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
• Enum-state + behavior map: lighter for 2–3 trivial states.
  • Hierarchical states: nested machines (Payment sub-states inside Paid).
  • History states: remember sub-state on re-entry (media player pause/resume).
  • Table-driven: transition matrix data file for ops-visible workflows.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Benefits: no conditionals, illegal moves rejected, stages independently testable. Costs: more classes, transition logic can scatter, overkill for tiny machines — a 2-state toggle rarely earns the pattern.

docs.title: 3. UML and Architecture Diagrams
docs.text:
Static structure: context aggregates one state; every concrete state implements the same event interface.

classDiagram
    class Order {
        -state: OrderState
        +pay()
        +ship()
        +deliver()
        +cancel()
    }
    class OrderState {
        <>
        +pay(ctx) OrderState
        +ship(ctx) OrderState
        +deliver(ctx) OrderState
        +cancel(ctx) OrderState
        +name() String
    }
    class BaseState {
        +pay(ctx) OrderState
        +ship(ctx) OrderState
        +deliver(ctx) OrderState
        +cancel(ctx) OrderState
    }
    class PendingState
    class PaidState
    class ShippedState
    class DeliveredState
    class CancelledState
    OrderState <|.. BaseState
    BaseState <|-- PendingState
    BaseState <|-- PaidState
    BaseState <|-- ShippedState
    BaseState <|-- DeliveredState
    BaseState <|-- CancelledState
    Order o--> OrderState : delegates to current state

Explanation: BaseState supplies default rejections so each concrete state overrides only its valid events. Order never branches on status strings — it delegates and installs whatever state comes back. New stages subclass BaseState with zero edits to Order.

Runtime flow: events walk the machine; invalid events bounce with a log while valid ones advance.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Order as Context: Order
    participant Pending as State: PendingState
    participant Paid as State: PaidState
    participant Shipped as State: ShippedState
    Client->>Order: pay()
    Order->>Pending: pay(ctx)
    Pending-->>Order: PaidState
    Note over Order: PENDING -> PAID
    Client->>Order: deliver()
    Order->>Paid: deliver(ctx)
    Paid-->>Order: PaidState (rejected)
    Note over Order: Cannot deliver while PAID
    Client->>Order: ship()
    Order->>Paid: ship(ctx)
    Paid-->>Order: ShippedState
    Note over Order: PAID -> SHIPPED
    Client->>Order: deliver()
    Order->>Shipped: deliver(ctx)
    Shipped-->>Order: DeliveredState
    Note over Order: SHIPPED -> DELIVERED

Explanation: valid events return the next state; invalid ones return this plus a rejection log, so the context visibly stays put. Emitting OLD -> NEW per move gives an audit trail for support and metrics on rejected transitions.

docs.title: 4. Implementation Examples in Java, Python, and Go
docs.text: The domain is an order lifecycle: PENDING → PAID → SHIPPED → DELIVERED, with CANCELLED as an alternate terminal. Illegal moves are rejected loudly.

docs.title: Java (interface + rejecting base class)
docs.text:
interface OrderState {
    OrderState pay(Order ctx);
    OrderState ship(Order ctx);
    OrderState deliver(Order ctx);
    OrderState cancel(Order ctx);
    String name();
}

abstract class BaseState implements OrderState {
    public OrderState pay(Order ctx) { return reject("pay"); }
    public OrderState ship(Order ctx) { return reject("ship"); }
    public OrderState deliver(Order ctx) { return reject("deliver"); }
    public OrderState cancel(Order ctx) { return reject("cancel"); }
    private OrderState reject(String action) {
        System.out.println("Cannot " + action + " while " + name());
        return this;
    }
}

class PendingState extends BaseState {
    public String name() { return "PENDING"; }
    public OrderState pay(Order ctx) { return new PaidState(); }
    public OrderState cancel(Order ctx) { return new CancelledState(); }
}

class PaidState extends BaseState {
    public String name() { return "PAID"; }
    public OrderState ship(Order ctx) { return new ShippedState(); }
    public OrderState cancel(Order ctx) { return new CancelledState(); }
}

class ShippedState extends BaseState {
    public String name() { return "SHIPPED"; }
    public OrderState deliver(Order ctx) { return new DeliveredState(); }
}

class DeliveredState extends BaseState {
    public String name() { return "DELIVERED"; }
}

class CancelledState extends BaseState {
    public String name() { return "CANCELLED"; }
}

class Order {
    private OrderState state = new PendingState();
    private void move(OrderState next) {
        System.out.println(state.name() + " -> " + next.name());
        state = next;
    }
    void pay() { move(state.pay(this)); }
    void ship() { move(state.ship(this)); }
    void deliver() { move(state.deliver(this)); }
    void cancel() { move(state.cancel(this)); }
    String status() { return state.name(); }
}

class OrderDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Order order = new Order();
        order.pay();      // PENDING -> PAID
        order.deliver();  // rejected
        order.ship();     // PAID -> SHIPPED
        order.deliver();  // SHIPPED -> DELIVERED
        order.cancel();   // rejected: terminal
        System.out.println("Final: " + order.status());
    }
}

Explanation: BaseState centralizes rejection so concrete states declare only legal moves. The context logs every OLD -> NEW pair for audit.

Sample I/O:

PENDING -> PAID
Cannot deliver while PAID
PAID -> PAID
PAID -> SHIPPED
SHIPPED -> DELIVERED
Cannot cancel while DELIVERED
DELIVERED -> DELIVERED
Final: DELIVERED

docs.title: Python (pythonic: ABC + default rejections)
docs.text:
from __future__ import annotations
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class OrderState(ABC):
    """One method per event; default is loud rejection."""

    @abstractmethod
    def name(self) -> str: ...

    def _reject(self, action: str) -> OrderState:
        print(f"Cannot {action} while {self.name()}")
        return self

    def pay(self, ctx: Order) -> OrderState: return self._reject("pay")
    def ship(self, ctx: Order) -> OrderState: return self._reject("ship")
    def deliver(self, ctx: Order) -> OrderState: return self._reject("deliver")
    def cancel(self, ctx: Order) -> OrderState: return self._reject("cancel")

class PendingState(OrderState):
    def name(self) -> str: return "PENDING"
    def pay(self, ctx: Order) -> OrderState: return PaidState()
    def cancel(self, ctx: Order) -> OrderState: return CancelledState()

class PaidState(OrderState):
    def name(self) -> str: return "PAID"
    def ship(self, ctx: Order) -> OrderState: return ShippedState()
    def cancel(self, ctx: Order) -> OrderState: return CancelledState()

class ShippedState(OrderState):
    def name(self) -> str: return "SHIPPED"
    def deliver(self, ctx: Order) -> OrderState: return DeliveredState()

class DeliveredState(OrderState):
    def name(self) -> str: return "DELIVERED"

class CancelledState(OrderState):
    def name(self) -> str: return "CANCELLED"

class Order:
    """Context: delegates every event to the current state."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._state: OrderState = PendingState()

    def _move(self, nxt: OrderState) -> None:
        print(f"{self._state.name()} -> {nxt.name()}")
        self._state = nxt

    def pay(self) -> None: self._move(self._state.pay(self))
    def ship(self) -> None: self._move(self._state.ship(self))
    def deliver(self) -> None: self._move(self._state.deliver(self))
    def cancel(self) -> None: self._move(self._state.cancel(self))

    @property
    def status(self) -> str: return self._state.name()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    order = Order()
    order.pay()
    order.deliver()   # rejected
    order.ship()
    order.deliver()
    order.cancel()    # rejected: terminal
    print("Final:", order.status)

Explanation: the ABC supplies inherited rejections, so each state class stays tiny. Type hints + property keep the Python idiomatic; swapping in enum-keyed singletons is trivial if allocation matters.

Sample I/O: identical to the Java output above.

docs.title: Go (idiomatic: interface + small structs)
docs.text:
package main

import "fmt"

// OrderState declares one method per lifecycle event.
type OrderState interface {
    Name() string
    Pay(*Order) OrderState
    Ship(*Order) OrderState
    Deliver(*Order) OrderState
    Cancel(*Order) OrderState
}

func reject(s OrderState, action string) OrderState {
    fmt.Println("Cannot " + action + " while " + s.Name())
    return s
}

type Pending struct{}

func (Pending) Name() string                          { return "PENDING" }
func (s Pending) Pay(*Order) OrderState               { return Paid{} }
func (s Pending) Ship(*Order) OrderState              { return reject(s, "ship") }
func (s Pending) Deliver(*Order) OrderState           { return reject(s, "deliver") }
func (s Pending) Cancel(*Order) OrderState            { return Cancelled{} }

type Paid struct{}

func (Paid) Name() string                          { return "PAID" }
func (s Paid) Pay(*Order) OrderState               { return reject(s, "pay") }
func (s Paid) Ship(*Order) OrderState             { return Shipped{} }
func (s Paid) Deliver(*Order) OrderState          { return reject(s, "deliver") }
func (s Paid) Cancel(*Order) OrderState            { return Cancelled{} }

type Shipped struct{}

func (Shipped) Name() string                        { return "SHIPPED" }
func (s Shipped) Pay(*Order) OrderState             { return reject(s, "pay") }
func (s Shipped) Ship(*Order) OrderState            { return reject(s, "ship") }
func (s Shipped) Deliver(*Order) OrderState         { return Delivered{} }
func (s Shipped) Cancel(*Order) OrderState          { return reject(s, "cancel") }

type Delivered struct{}

func (Delivered) Name() string                    { return "DELIVERED" }
func (s Delivered) Pay(*Order) OrderState         { return reject(s, "pay") }
func (s Delivered) Ship(*Order) OrderState        { return reject(s, "ship") }
func (s Delivered) Deliver(*Order) OrderState     { return reject(s, "deliver") }
func (s Delivered) Cancel(*Order) OrderState      { return reject(s, "cancel") }

type Cancelled struct{}

func (Cancelled) Name() string                    { return "CANCELLED" }
func (s Cancelled) Pay(*Order) OrderState         { return reject(s, "pay") }
func (s Cancelled) Ship(*Order) OrderState        { return reject(s, "ship") }
func (s Cancelled) Deliver(*Order) OrderState     { return reject(s, "deliver") }
func (s Cancelled) Cancel(*Order) OrderState      { return reject(s, "cancel") }

// Order is the context.
type Order struct{ state OrderState }

func NewOrder() *Order { return &Order{state: Pending{}} }

func (o *Order) move(next OrderState) {
    fmt.Println(o.state.Name() + " -> " + next.Name())
    o.state = next
}

func (o *Order) Pay()     { o.move(o.state.Pay(o)) }
func (o *Order) Ship()    { o.move(o.state.Ship(o)) }
func (o *Order) Deliver() { o.move(o.state.Deliver(o)) }
func (o *Order) Cancel()  { o.move(o.state.Cancel(o)) }
func (o *Order) Status() string { return o.state.Name() }

func main() {
    order := NewOrder()
    order.Pay()
    order.Deliver() // rejected
    order.Ship()
    order.Deliver()
    order.Cancel() // rejected: terminal
    fmt.Println("Final:", order.Status())
}

Explanation: stateless struct states keep allocation trivial; the reject helper mirrors the Java/Python base class. Context methods are one-liners, and Status() exposes the current stage.

Sample I/O: identical to the Java output above.

docs.title: 5. Real-World Industry Applications
docs.text:
• E-commerce orders: PENDING → PAID → SHIPPED → DELIVERED / CANCELLED / RETURNED drives payment, warehouse, and refund logic.
  • Vending / parking machines: Idle → HasMoney → Dispensing → OutOfService, the textbook embedded use.
  • TCP connections: CLOSED → LISTEN → ESTABLISHED → FIN_WAIT → CLOSED in every network stack.
  • Media players: Playing / Paused / Stopped / Buffering gate which buttons are valid.
  • Auth sessions: Anonymous → Authenticated → Expired → Locked, with refresh and lockout transitions.
  • Document workflows: Draft → Review → Approved → Published in CMS and approval tools.
  • Game AI: Idle → Patrol → Chase → Attack finite-state machines for NPCs.
  • Cloud orchestration: Step Functions / Temporal workflows where each activity's valid next steps depend on execution state.

docs.title: 6. Practical Use Cases and Scenarios
docs.text:
1. Order lifecycle API: POST /orders/{id}/ship delegates to state; shipping a PENDING order returns 409 with "Cannot ship while PENDING".
  2. Vending machine firmware: coin, select, dispense, and refund buttons each route through the active state; out-of-stock transitions to a service state.
  3. Support tickets: Open → InProgress → WaitingOnCustomer → Resolved; SLA timers attach per state.
  4. Subscription billing: Trial → Active → PastDue → Cancelled, with dunning retries only valid in PastDue.
  5. Elevator control: Idle / MovingUp / MovingDown / Maintenance gate door and motor commands.
  6. Parser/lexer: start, in-string, escaped, comment states consume characters differently.
  7. Hiring pipeline: Applied → Screen → Interview → Offer → Hired, each stage owning its valid moves and emails.

Scenario walkthrough (vending): insertCoin() in IdleState returns HasMoneyState; select() in HasMoneyState returns DispensingState which dispenses then returns IdleState; select() in IdleState is rejected with "insert coins first". No controller if chain exists.

docs.title: 7. When to Use and When Not to Use
docs.text:
Use State when:

  • Behavior and valid actions depend on lifecycle stage (orders, connections, sessions).
  • Methods share large switch(status) blocks that must stay in sync.
  • Transitions are explicit and auditable (compliance, support tooling).
  • New stages arrive over time (returns, refunds, chargebacks) and should not ripple through old code.

Do NOT use State when:

  • There are 2–3 states with one-line behavior — an enum + switch is clearer and fewer files.
  • Transitions are ad-hoc with no rules — a status field plus validation may suffice.
  • State data differs wildly per stage with no shared protocol — consider separate types or a workflow engine.
  • You need caller-chosen algorithms with no lifecycle — that is Strategy, not State.
  • The graph exceeds ~8 states with cross-cutting guards — reach for a state-machine library or table instead of hand-rolled classes.

Rule of thumb: lifecycle drives validity → State. Caller picks among peers → Strategy. Two trivial stages → enum.

docs.title: 8. Do's and Don'ts
docs.text:
Do:

  • Give every (state, event) pair an explicit answer: transition, no-op with log, or typed exception.
  • Log OLD -> NEW on every move; emit metrics on rejections to catch client bugs.
  • Keep states focused; push shared helpers into a base class, not into the context.
  • Document the machine as a diagram in the class or README — code alone hides the graph.
  • Make states immutable/stateless where possible; park per-order data in the context.
  • Test the full transition matrix, including every illegal pair.

Don't:

  • Don't scatter status-string comparisons across services — the state objects are the single source of truth.
  • Don't let the context mutate state directly; all moves go through state methods.
  • Don't share mutable state objects across contexts unless they are truly stateless.
  • Don't silently swallow invalid events in user-facing flows — return 409/validation errors.
  • Don't add a new state by editing five siblings — if that happens, extract a transition table.
  • Don't confuse "mode" flags (dark mode, sort order) with lifecycle states — flags are Strategy/config, not State.

docs.title: 9. Comparison with Other Design Patterns
docs.text:
Aspect State Strategy Template Method Question answered What is valid now, given lifecycle? Which algorithm should run? What is the fixed order of steps? Who switches Current state object returns next Client/context sets explicitly Nobody — skeleton fixed at compile time Transitions Core concern, explicit graph None — peers are independent None — hooks only Client knowledge Sends events, states decide Must know options to choose Picks subclass, inherits order Typical use Orders, TCP, vending, sessions Payments, sorting, routing ETL, JUnit lifecycle, reports Risk Class + transition sprawl Client must choose wisely Rigid hierarchy Aspect State Status enum + switch Rules location One class per stage Spread across every method New stage cost One new class Edit every switch Illegal moves Rejected by type Discovered at runtime (or missed) Readability Graph visible via classes/diagram Compact for ≤3 trivial stages

State vs Strategy (the classic confusion): identical UML, opposite intent. Ask "who triggers the switch?" Lifecycle → State. Caller → Strategy. An order ships because payment completed (State); a checkout pays by card because the user picked it (Strategy).

docs.title: 10. Interview Preparation
docs.text:
Q1: State and Strategy look identical — how do you distinguish them? By intent and switching authority. State: the current state object decides the next state; clients just send events. Strategy: the client picks and injects the algorithm. Probe with "who triggers the switch — lifecycle or caller?"

Q2: Where should transition logic live? Default to state objects (co-located, thin context). Centralize into the context or a transition table when auditors need the whole graph in one place, or past ~8 states when scattering becomes unreviewable.

Q3: How do you handle invalid transitions? Reject explicitly: default methods log + return this for user errors, or throw IllegalStateException for programming errors. Map to 409/422 in APIs, test every illegal pair, and metric rejections.

Q4: Enum switch vs State — when do you graduate? Stay with enum for ≤3 stages with trivial behavior. Graduate when conditionals duplicate across methods, stages carry different data, or transitions need logging/audit. Extract a table/library past ~8 states.

Q5: How do you persist and restore state? Persist the state name (not the object) plus context data; rehydrate via factory State.of(name). Version the names; handle unknown persisted values with a migration or dead-letter. Never serialize behavior objects directly.

Q6: Are state objects shared or per-context? Share when stateless (flyweight singletons); allocate per context when states carry stage data (retry counts, timers). Document the choice — shared mutable states are a classic concurrency bug.

Q7: How do you model hierarchical or parallel states? Nest machines (Payment sub-machine inside Paid) or compose orthogonal regions (connection + subscription states side by side). Beyond two levels, prefer a statechart library over hand-rolled nesting.

Q8: How do you debug a misbehaving machine? Log every transition with (from, event, to, timestamp), expose current state in health/debug endpoints, and add a transition-matrix test that enumerates all pairs. Rejected-transition metrics usually pinpoint the bad caller.

LLD scenario 1 — Design a Vending Machine. Expectation: states Idle / HasMoney / Dispensing / OutOfStock; events coin, select, dispense, refund, restock. Show select() rejected in Idle, change returned in HasMoney, and restock resetting to Idle. Discuss coin inventory and concurrency on dispense.

LLD scenario 2 — Design Order Management with returns. Expectation: extend PENDING → PAID → SHIPPED → DELIVERED with RETURN_REQUESTED → REFUNDED; only Delivered accepts returns. Show terminal-state rejections, refund hook, and persisted state-name rehydration.

LLD scenario 3 — Design a TCP-like connection. Expectation: CLOSED → SYN_SENT → ESTABLISHED → FIN_WAIT → CLOSED with timeout events. Discuss timeout as an event like any other, retransmit counters in state data, and why a table-driven machine fits protocol work.

docs.title: 11. Testing and Best Practices
docs.text:
• Matrix test: enumerate every (state, event) pair; assert each lands on the expected next state or a rejection.
  • Isolation test: unit-test each state with a stub context; verify it returns the right successor without touching real I/O.
  • Rejection test: illegal events log/throw and leave state unchanged; assert no side effects fired.
  • Sequence test: replay golden paths (pay→ship→deliver) and assert the emitted OLD -> NEW log matches.
  • Rehydration test: persist each state name, rebuild, and assert behavior resumes correctly; include unknown-name migration.
  • Concurrency test: concurrent events on one context serialize correctly (synchronized delegate or actor mailbox).
  • Best practice: keep states deterministic and side-effect-light; push I/O (charge, ship label) into context hooks invoked after the transition commits, so retries stay safe.

docs.title: 12. Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• State replaces status-flag conditionals with explicit state objects that own their transitions.
  • Contexts delegate; states decide — that inversion is the whole pattern.
  • Default-reject base classes make illegal moves loud and new stages cheap.
  • Log every transition; metric every rejection — machines are debugged through their trails.
  • Enum for tiny machines, State for lifecycle-driven behavior, tables/libraries for large graphs.
  • Interview one-liner: "State turns each lifecycle stage into an object owning its valid events, so the context just delegates and installs the next state — illegal moves are rejected by type, and new stages arrive as new classes."

docs.title: Strategy Design Pattern
docs.text: Youtube: 2. Strategy Design Pattern explanation (Hindi) | LLD System Design | Design pattern in Java

docs.title: 1. Overview and Fundamentals
docs.text:
The Strategy pattern defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one, and makes them interchangeable — the algorithm varies independently from the clients that use it.

In one sentence: the context delegates work to a swappable strategy object chosen at runtime.

Core roles:

  • Strategy interface: declares the algorithm contract (pay(), route(), sort(), price()).
  • ConcreteStrategy: one implementation per variant (CardPayment, DrivingRoute, QuickSort).
  • Context: holds a strategy reference, exposes setStrategy(), and delegates calls to it (Navigator, Checkout, Sorter).
  • Client/Factory: picks which strategy to inject, often via key, config, or user choice.

Fundamental properties:

  • Composition over inheritance: behavior varies by object wiring, not subclass trees.
  • Runtime swapping: setMode("transit") changes behavior without rebuilding the context.
  • Isolation: each algorithm lives in its own class with its own data and tests.
  • Behavioral: governs how behavior varies, not how objects are created or assembled.

Mental model: navigation app travel modes. The navigator UI is fixed; driving, walking, and transit are plug-in route engines behind one route(from, to) interface. Adding cycling means adding one engine, never editing the navigator.

docs.title: Intent and forces
docs.text:
Strategy solves the algorithm-explosion tension: one class accumulates if (mode == X) branches for every variant, mixing selection logic with algorithm logic. Branches duplicate, testing requires the whole context, and adding a variant edits a method everyone depends on.

Strategy splits the two concerns: the context owns delegation, each strategy owns one algorithm, and a factory owns selection.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Define Strategy with the narrowest parameter list the algorithms need.
  2. Implement one class per variant; keep them stateless where possible.
  3. Context stores Strategy current (constructor default + setStrategy() for swaps).
  4. Client resolves a strategy via factory/map/DI (MODES.get(mode)) and injects it.
  5. Context calls strategy.execute(...) and returns the result untouched.

docs.title: Selection patterns
docs.text: Selector How Best when Client passes object new Checkout(card) Caller legitimately knows the variant Key + factory map MODES.get("transit") UI/config supplies strings, code hides classes DI container Inject by profile/qualifier Environment decides (prod vs test gateway) Auto-selection Factory inspects payload size/type Thresholds pick algorithm (insertion vs quick sort)

docs.title: Sharing data with strategies
docs.text: Pass only what the algorithm needs as parameters (amount, from/to). Inject shared services (HTTP client, config) via constructor. Avoid handing the whole context back-reference — it re-couples what the pattern decoupled. Keep strategies stateless; park session data in the context.

docs.title: Design principles at play
docs.text:
• Open/Closed: new algorithms arrive as new classes.
  • Single Responsibility: one algorithm per class, one delegation job per context.
  • Composition over inheritance: no subclass per variant.
  • Dependency Inversion: context depends on the interface, never concretes.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
• Lambda/functional strategies: single-method strategies as lambdas (Java Comparator, Python callables, Go funcs).
  • Parameterized strategy: one class with enum-tuned behavior when variants differ by value, not logic.
  • Strategy + Factory: the dominant production pairing — factory hides the catalog.
  • Strategy + Decorator: wrap strategies with retry/rate-limit/metrics without touching algorithms.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Benefits: runtime flexibility, isolated testing, no conditionals, independent evolution. Costs: more classes, clients must understand options (mitigate with factory + defaults), and overkill when variants rarely change or differ by a constant.

docs.title: 3. UML and Architecture Diagrams
docs.text:
Static structure: context aggregates one strategy; all variants implement the same interface so they are freely swappable.

classDiagram
    class Navigator {
        -strategy: RouteStrategy
        +Navigator(mode: String)
        +setMode(mode: String)
        +navigate(from: String, to: String) String
    }
    class RouteStrategy {
        <>
        +route(from: String, to: String) String
    }
    class DrivingRoute {
        +route(from: String, to: String) String
    }
    class WalkingRoute {
        +route(from: String, to: String) String
    }
    class TransitRoute {
        +route(from: String, to: String) String
    }
    RouteStrategy <|.. DrivingRoute
    RouteStrategy <|.. WalkingRoute
    RouteStrategy <|.. TransitRoute
    Navigator o--> RouteStrategy : delegates

Explanation: the open diamond marks aggregation — Navigator has a strategy it can re-point at runtime. All route engines share route(from, to), so navigate() never branches on mode strings. A CyclingRoute joins by implementing the interface; Navigator is untouched.

Runtime flow: resolve once via factory, delegate per call, swap whenever the caller decides.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Nav as Context: Navigator
    participant Factory as ModeRegistry
    participant Driving as Strategy: DrivingRoute
    participant Transit as Strategy: TransitRoute
    Client->>Nav: new Navigator("driving")
    Nav->>Factory: MODES.get("driving")
    Factory-->>Nav: DrivingRoute
    Client->>Nav: navigate(Home, Office)
    Nav->>Driving: route(Home, Office)
    Driving-->>Nav: via highway
    Client->>Nav: setMode("transit")
    Nav->>Factory: MODES.get("transit")
    Factory-->>Nav: TransitRoute
    Client->>Nav: navigate(Home, Office)
    Nav->>Transit: route(Home, Office)
    Transit-->>Nav: via metro line 2

Explanation: selection (factory lookup) happens separately from execution (delegation). Swapping mid-session only re-points the reference — in-flight calls finish on the old strategy, new calls use the new one. No context branching exists at either step.

docs.title: 4. Implementation Examples in Java, Python, and Go
docs.text: The domain is route planning: a Navigator context delegates to driving / walking / transit strategies selected by mode string.

docs.title: Java (interface + factory map)
docs.text:
import java.util.Map;

interface RouteStrategy {
    String route(String from, String to);
}

class DrivingRoute implements RouteStrategy {
    public String route(String from, String to) {
        return "Driving " + from + " -> " + to + " via highway";
    }
}

class WalkingRoute implements RouteStrategy {
    public String route(String from, String to) {
        return "Walking " + from + " -> " + to + " via parks";
    }
}

class TransitRoute implements RouteStrategy {
    public String route(String from, String to) {
        return "Transit " + from + " -> " + to + " via metro line 2";
    }
}

class Navigator {
    private RouteStrategy strategy;
    private static final Map<String, RouteStrategy> MODES = Map.of(
        "driving", new DrivingRoute(),
        "walking", new WalkingRoute(),
        "transit", new TransitRoute()
    );
    Navigator(String mode) { setMode(mode); }
    void setMode(String mode) {
        strategy = MODES.getOrDefault(mode.toLowerCase(), MODES.get("driving"));
    }
    String navigate(String from, String to) { return strategy.route(from, to); }
}

class MapsDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Navigator nav = new Navigator("driving");
        System.out.println(nav.navigate("Home", "Office"));
        nav.setMode("transit");
        System.out.println(nav.navigate("Home", "Office"));
        nav.setMode("walking");
        System.out.println(nav.navigate("Home", "Park"));
    }
}

Explanation: the static MODES map is the factory — UI code passes strings, never classes. getOrDefault supplies a safe default. Each engine is independently testable with fixed origin/destination pairs.

Sample I/O:

Driving Home -> Office via highway
Transit Home -> Office via metro line 2
Walking Home -> Park via parks

docs.title: Python (pythonic: Protocol + dict registry, lambdas welcome)
docs.text:
from __future__ import annotations
from typing import Protocol

class RouteStrategy(Protocol):
    def route(self, origin: str, dest: str) -> str: ...

class DrivingRoute:
    def route(self, origin: str, dest: str) -> str:
        return f"Driving {origin} -> {dest} via highway"

class WalkingRoute:
    def route(self, origin: str, dest: str) -> str:
        return f"Walking {origin} -> {dest} via parks"

class TransitRoute:
    def route(self, origin: str, dest: str) -> str:
        return f"Transit {origin} -> {dest} via metro line 2"

class Navigator:
    """Context: delegates route computation to the selected strategy."""

    MODES: dict[str, RouteStrategy] = {
        "driving": DrivingRoute(),
        "walking": WalkingRoute(),
        "transit": TransitRoute(),
    }

    def __init__(self, mode: str = "driving") -> None:
        self.set_mode(mode)

    def set_mode(self, mode: str) -> None:
        self._strategy = self.MODES.get(mode.lower(), self.MODES["driving"])

    def navigate(self, origin: str, dest: str) -> str:
        return self._strategy.route(origin, dest)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    nav = Navigator("driving")
    print(nav.navigate("Home", "Office"))
    nav.set_mode("transit")  # rush hour: swap algorithm
    print(nav.navigate("Home", "Office"))
    nav.set_mode("walking")  # weekend stroll
    print(nav.navigate("Home", "Park"))

Explanation: Protocol enables duck-typed strategies — even a plain function or lambda registers in MODES. Shared stateless instances are reused; the dict acts as the factory so callers never import concrete engines.

Sample I/O: identical to the Java output above.

docs.title: Go (idiomatic: interface + map registry)
docs.text:
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "strings"
)

// RouteStrategy is the algorithm contract.
type RouteStrategy interface {
    Route(from, to string) string
}

type DrivingRoute struct{}

func (DrivingRoute) Route(from, to string) string {
    return "Driving " + from + " -> " + to + " via highway"
}

type WalkingRoute struct{}

func (WalkingRoute) Route(from, to string) string {
    return "Walking " + from + " -> " + to + " via parks"
}

type TransitRoute struct{}

func (TransitRoute) Route(from, to string) string {
    return "Transit " + from + " -> " + to + " via metro line 2"
}

// Navigator is the context.
type Navigator struct{ strategy RouteStrategy }

var modes = map[string]RouteStrategy{
    "driving": DrivingRoute{},
    "walking": WalkingRoute{},
    "transit": TransitRoute{},
}

func NewNavigator(mode string) *Navigator {
    n := &Navigator{}
    n.SetMode(mode)
    return n
}

// SetMode swaps the algorithm at runtime; unknown modes fall back to driving.
func (n *Navigator) SetMode(mode string) {
    s, ok := modes[strings.ToLower(mode)]
    if !ok {
        s = modes["driving"]
    }
    n.strategy = s
}

func (n *Navigator) Navigate(from, to string) string {
    return n.strategy.Route(from, to)
}

func main() {
    nav := NewNavigator("driving")
    fmt.Println(nav.Navigate("Home", "Office"))
    nav.SetMode("transit")
    fmt.Println(nav.Navigate("Home", "Office"))
    nav.SetMode("walking")
    fmt.Println(nav.Navigate("Home", "Park"))
}

Explanation: zero-size structs mean strategies cost nothing to share; the package-level modes map is the registry. SetMode normalizes and defaults, so bad input degrades gracefully instead of nil-panicking.

Sample I/O: identical to the Java output above.

docs.title: 5. Real-World Industry Applications
docs.text:
• Payments: Stripe/Adyen route charges through card, UPI, wallet, BNPL strategy objects per user choice.
  • Spring: PlatformTransactionManager implementations, PasswordEncoder variants, ResourceLoader handlers selected by profile.
  • Sorting/search: Collections.sort with Comparator strategies; database query planners picking scan vs index strategies.
  • Compression/encoding: GZIP vs Snappy vs Zstd strategies negotiated by content type.
  • Maps: Google Maps travel-mode engines — same navigator, different cost functions.
  • Pricing: regular / holiday / clearance / surge strategies behind one price() interface.
  • Auth: OAuth2, JWT, API-key verification strategies per route.
  • Validation: per-tenant or per-role validation rule sets injected into one form pipeline.

docs.title: 6. Practical Use Cases and Scenarios
docs.text:
1. Checkout payments: Checkout.setStrategy(card|upi|wallet); adding BNPL is one class plus one factory entry.
  2. Route planning: driving/walking/transit/cycling engines behind route(from, to); ETA experiments A/B test new engines.
  3. Discount engine: percentage, flat, BOGO, loyalty strategies composed per campaign without touching cart code.
  4. Export formats: CSV / JSON / Parquet writers behind one export(rows) strategy.
  5. Notification channels: email / SMS / push senders chosen by user preference at send time.
  6. Image pipelines: resize algorithms (bilinear, bicubic, Lanczos) swapped by quality setting.
  7. Log routing: console / file / remote strategies chosen by environment profile.

Scenario walkthrough (checkout): user picks UPI at 10:00 and card at 10:05. Same Checkout instance calls setStrategy(upI) then setStrategy(card); each pay(amount) delegates to the current engine. Refund logic stays in the context; gateway specifics stay in engines.

docs.title: 7. When to Use and When Not to Use
docs.text:
Use Strategy when:

  • Multiple variants of one algorithm exist and must swap at runtime (payments, routes, pricing).
  • Conditionals on "which algorithm" spread across methods or classes.
  • Each variant needs independent testing, tuning, or ownership.
  • New variants arrive over time (new payment rail, new codec) and should not touch callers.

Do NOT use Strategy when:

  • Variants rarely change and number one or two — a parameter or if-else is clearer.
  • The choice is driven by object lifecycle, not the caller — that is State.
  • The skeleton is fixed and only steps vary — that is Template Method.
  • Variants differ only by a value (rate = 0.05 vs 0.18) — use config/enum, not a class hierarchy.
  • The caller should not choose (server policy) — hide selection server-side or use a rule engine.

Rule of thumb: caller chooses among peer algorithms → Strategy. Lifecycle dictates validity → State. Fixed order with hook steps → Template Method.

docs.title: 8. Do's and Don'ts
docs.text:
Do:

  • Hide the catalog behind a factory/registry with a documented default.
  • Keep the strategy interface narrow — pass values, not the whole context.
  • Prefer stateless strategies; inject shared dependencies via constructor.
  • Document each variant's trade-offs (cost, latency, accuracy) so callers choose by intent.
  • Name strategies by algorithm (DrivingRoute), not by position (Strategy1).
  • Consider lambdas for single-method strategies in Java/Python/Go funcs.

Don't:

  • Don't leak selection strings through every layer — resolve once at the boundary, inject the object after.
  • Don't give strategies back-references to the context's privates.
  • Don't create a strategy per constant — values belong in config.
  • Don't let strategies accumulate cross-call mutable state unless synchronized and documented.
  • Don't force callers to catch per-strategy checked exceptions — normalize to one domain error.
  • Don't use Strategy to paper over a missing State machine (validity rules belong in states).

docs.title: 9. Comparison with Other Design Patterns
docs.text:
Aspect Strategy State Template Method Mechanism Composition: context holds swappable algorithm Composition: context holds current stage Inheritance: base fixes skeleton Who picks Client/factory explicitly Current state object (lifecycle) Fixed at compile time (subclass) Swappable at runtime Yes — the point Yes — but driven by events No — new subclass per variant Use when Peer algorithms chosen per call Validity depends on stage Order fixed, steps vary Example Payments, routing, sorting Orders, TCP, vending ETL, JUnit lifecycle Aspect Strategy Command Factory Encapsulates How to compute A request to run later/undo Which class to create Executed Immediately by context Later, queued, or undone Creation only Pairs with Factory picks it Queue/invoker runs it Factory often returns a Strategy

Strategy vs State (the classic confusion): same UML, opposite driver. Strategy = caller selects peers (setMode("transit")). State = lifecycle advances itself (pay() returns PaidState). Ask who triggers the switch.

Strategy vs Template Method: Strategy swaps the whole algorithm via composition; Template fixes the skeleton via inheritance and varies steps. Need runtime engine swaps → Strategy. Need enforced order with extension points → Template.

docs.title: 10. Interview Preparation
docs.text:
Q1: How do you stop clients from needing to know every strategy? Hide selection behind a factory/registry: client passes a key ("upi", "transit") and gets an object, with a sensible default. Document trade-offs per variant so callers choose by intent, and resolve at the boundary so inner code only sees the interface.

Q2: Strategy vs if-else — when does it pay off? At three or more algorithms, when algorithms evolve independently, when runtime swapping or isolated testing is needed. For one or two stable branches, if-else wins — refactor once conditionals spread or violate Open/Closed.

Q3: How do strategies share data without leaking internals? Pass needed values as method args, keep strategies stateless, inject shared services via constructor. Never hand the full mutable context to a strategy — it reintroduces the coupling the pattern removed.

Q4: How do you handle a strategy that needs configuration? Inject config at construction (thresholds, keys, clients) so execute() stays pure. Validate config in the factory; fail fast on unknown keys with the default + a warning metric.

Q5: Stateful vs stateless strategies? Prefer stateless (thread-safe, reusable singletons). If state is unavoidable (circuit breaker counters), scope one instance per context, synchronize access, and document lifetime clearly.

Q6: How do you test strategies? Table-driven tests per strategy with fixed inputs/outputs; contract tests asserting every registered strategy satisfies the interface (same edge cases); context tests with stub strategies verifying delegation and swapping.

Q7: Strategy vs polymorphism — isn't it just an interface? An interface is the mechanism; Strategy is the policy: a named family of interchangeable algorithms with explicit selection and swapping. The discipline (factory, defaults, documented trade-offs) is what interviewers probe.

Q8: When do lambdas beat strategy classes? When the algorithm is a few lines with no dependencies — Comparator.comparing(...), Python key funcs, Go sort.Slice closures. Graduate to classes when the algorithm needs config, state, or independent tests.

LLD scenario 1 — Design a Payment Gateway router. Expectation: PayStrategy (card/UPI/wallet/BNPL) + GatewayFactory keyed by user choice + region; Checkout delegates. Discuss idempotency keys per attempt, per-strategy timeouts, fallback strategy on failure, and adding a rail without touching checkout.

LLD scenario 2 — Design a Sort service. Expectation: strategies for insertion (small), quick (general), external (huge); auto-selecting factory by input size. Show benchmark-driven thresholds and contract tests proving identical output ordering.

LLD scenario 3 — Design a Pricing engine. Expectation: regular/holiday/surge strategies behind price(cart, context); factory reads campaign calendar. Discuss stacking with Decorator (coupon on top of campaign) vs baking stacking into strategies.

docs.title: 11. Testing and Best Practices
docs.text:
• Per-strategy tables: fixed inputs → exact outputs, including edge cases (zero amount, same origin/destination, empty list).
  • Contract test: iterate the registry; every strategy handles null/empty/large inputs per the documented policy.
  • Swap test: set A, execute, set B, execute; assert behavior follows the current strategy and prior calls are unaffected.
  • Factory test: every documented key resolves; unknown keys return the default (and log); keys are case-insensitive if specified.
  • Default test: context constructed with no explicit strategy still executes via the default.
  • Isolation test: stub strategies verify the context adds no logic (no branching, no transformation) beyond delegation.
  • Concurrency test: concurrent setMode + navigate never nil-derefs; consider copy-on-write or per-request strategy binding.
  • Best practice: stateless singletons, constructor-injected config, and metrics per strategy (strategy=rides.transit latency) to compare variants in production.

docs.title: 12. Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Strategy = one interface, many encapsulated algorithms, runtime selection via composition.
  • Factory + default hides the catalog; narrow interfaces keep strategies decoupled.
  • Prefer stateless strategies; pass values, inject services, never the whole context.
  • Three-plus evolving variants earn the pattern; one value difference earns config, not classes.
  • Don't confuse with State (lifecycle-driven) or Template (fixed skeleton) — ask who chooses and what varies.
  • Interview one-liner: "Strategy encapsulates each algorithm behind one interface so the context delegates and callers swap behavior at runtime — I hide selection in a factory, keep strategies stateless, and graduate from if-else once variants evolve independently."

docs.title: Template Method Design Pattern
docs.text: Youtube: 39. Template Method Design Pattern Explanation in Java | Concept and Coding LLD | Low Level Design

docs.title: 1. Overview and Fundamentals
docs.text:
The Template Method pattern defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a method, deferring some steps to subclasses — subclasses redefine certain steps without changing the algorithm's structure.

In one sentence: the base class fixes the order; subclasses fill in the varying steps.

Core roles:

  • AbstractClass: declares the final template method plus abstract primitive steps and optional hooks.
  • Template method: the fixed skeleton (importData(), generate(), run()) — usually final so order cannot be broken.
  • Primitive steps: abstract methods subclasses must implement (extract(), transform()).
  • Hooks: concrete methods with defaults subclasses may override (onComplete(), shouldRetry()).
  • ConcreteClass: one subclass per variant (CsvImporter, ApiImporter, PdfReport).

Fundamental properties:

  • Inheritance-based: the one behavioral pattern that deliberately uses subclassing over composition.
  • Inversion of control: the framework calls application code ("Hollywood Principle").
  • Order guarantee: sequencing and invariants enforced once, in one place.
  • Behavioral: governs algorithm structure, not object creation or assembly.

Mental model: a recipe. "Prep → cook → plate" order is fixed by the cookbook; each dish fills in its own cooking step and may optionally garnish (hook). No dish is allowed to plate before cooking.

docs.title: Intent and forces
docs.text:
Template Method solves the duplicated-skeleton tension: several algorithms share the same step order but differ in individual steps. Copy-pasting the sequence into each variant invites drift — one variant skips validation, another reorders load before transform, and fixes must be applied N times.

The pattern extracts the invariant sequence into a final method and quarantines variation into overridable steps. The order is written once and enforced by the compiler.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Identify the invariant order (extract → transform → load → onComplete).
  2. Write it as a final method in the abstract base.
  3. Declare varying steps abstract (or protected in Python/Go-embedding equivalents).
  4. Provide shared steps concretely (load() writes to DB the same way for all sources).
  5. Add hooks with harmless defaults for optional extension (onComplete() no-op).
  6. Subclasses implement only the abstract steps and opt into hooks.

docs.title: Primitive steps vs hooks
docs.text:
Kind Must override? Purpose Example Abstract primitive Yes Required variation extract(), transform(), body() Concrete shared No (can) Reused invariant load(), header(), footer() Hook No (opt-in) Optional extension point onComplete(), validate() default-true

Keep hooks few and documented. A base class with ten hooks is a skeleton nobody understands — that pressure means the order is not actually fixed and Strategy/composition fits better.

docs.title: Design principles at play
docs.text:
• DRY: the sequence lives in exactly one method.
  • Hollywood Principle: base calls subclass code, not vice versa.
  • Open/Closed (narrow): new variants via new subclasses — but base edits ripple to all children.
  • Liskov risk: subclasses must honor the step contracts (no surprising side effects, no skipped writes).

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
• Classic inheritance (this page): abstract base + final template.
  • Compositional template: skeleton function takes step lambdas — same order guarantee without subclassing (preferred in Go/Python).
  • Framework lifecycle: JUnit setUp/test/tearDown, servlet init/service/destroy, Spring JdbcTemplate callbacks.
  • Template + Strategy: a template step delegates to an injected Strategy for runtime-swappable variation inside a fixed order.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Benefits: order enforced, duplication removed, extension points explicit. Costs: inheritance coupling (base change affects every child), rigid order, deep hierarchies when variants multiply, and Liskov violations when a subclass "overrides" by breaking the contract.

docs.title: 3. UML and Architecture Diagrams
docs.text:
Static structure: one abstract base owns the template; each concrete class supplies the varying primitives.

classDiagram
    class DataImporter {
        +importData()*
        #extract()*
        #transform(raw)* 
        #load(rows)
        #onComplete()
    }
    class CsvImporter {
        #extract()
        #transform(raw)
        #onComplete()
    }
    class ApiImporter {
        #extract()
        #transform(raw)
    }
    DataImporter <|-- CsvImporter
    DataImporter <|-- ApiImporter
    note for DataImporter "importData() is final:\nextract → transform → load → onComplete"

Explanation: importData() is the only public entry; its final modifier is the enforcement mechanism. CsvImporter customizes extraction, transformation, and the completion hook; ApiImporter reuses default loading and skips the hook. New sources subclass — they cannot reorder steps even if they try.

Runtime flow: the base orchestrates; control dips into subclass code per step and returns.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Base as DataImporter::importData
    participant Csv as CsvImporter steps
    participant DB as Database
    Client->>Base: importData()
    Base->>Csv: extract()
    Csv-->>Base: raw rows
    Base->>Csv: transform(raw)
    Csv-->>Base: clean rows
    Base->>DB: load(clean)
    DB-->>Base: ack
    Base->>Csv: onComplete() hook
    Csv-->>Base: (notify done)
    Base-->>Client: done

Explanation: sequencing lives entirely in the base — the client sees one call, the subclass sees per-step callbacks. Shared steps (load) never touch subclass code; hooks (onComplete) are the only optional dips. Recording this order in a test with a stub subclass is the canonical verification.

docs.title: 4. Implementation Examples in Java, Python, and Go
docs.text: The domain is a data-import (ETL) pipeline: fixed extract → transform → load → onComplete order; CSV and API importers vary the first two steps.

docs.title: Java (abstract class, final template)
docs.text:
import java.util.List;

abstract class DataImporter {
    final void importData() {                       // Template: fixed skeleton
        List<String> raw = extract();
        List<String> clean = transform(raw);
        load(clean);
        onComplete();                               // Hook
    }
    protected abstract List<String> extract();
    protected abstract List<String> transform(List<String> raw);
    protected void load(List<String> rows) {
        System.out.println("Loading " + rows.size() + " rows into DB");
    }
    protected void onComplete() { }                 // Hook default: no-op
}

class CsvImporter extends DataImporter {
    private final String path;
    CsvImporter(String path) { this.path = path; }
