    protected List<String> extract() {
        System.out.println("Reading CSV: " + path);
        return List.of(" a,1 ", " b,2 ");
    }
    protected List<String> transform(List<String> raw) {
        return raw.stream().map(s -> s.trim().toUpperCase()).toList();
    }
    protected void onComplete() {
        System.out.println("CSV import finished");
    }
}

class ApiImporter extends DataImporter {
    private final String endpoint;
    ApiImporter(String endpoint) { this.endpoint = endpoint; }
    protected List<String> extract() {
        System.out.println("GET " + endpoint);
        return List.of("{\"id\":1}", "{\"id\":2}");
    }
    protected List<String> transform(List<String> raw) {
        return raw.stream().map(s -> s.replaceAll("[^0-9]", "")).toList();
    }
}

class EtlDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new CsvImporter("users.csv").importData();
        new ApiImporter("https://api/users").importData();
    }
}

Explanation: final locks the order; abstract forces variant steps; the no-op hook keeps ApiImporter lean. New sources (S3, Kafka) add one subclass.

Sample I/O:

Reading CSV: users.csv
Loading 2 rows into DB
CSV import finished
GET https://api/users
Loading 2 rows into DB

docs.title: Python (pythonic: ABC + final-by-convention template)
docs.text:
from __future__ import annotations
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class DataImporter(ABC):
    """Skeleton importData() is fixed; subclasses fill extract/transform."""

    def import_data(self) -> None:  # template (do not override)
        raw = self.extract()
        clean = self.transform(raw)
        self.load(clean)
        self.on_complete()  # hook

    @abstractmethod
    def extract(self) -> list[str]: ...
    @abstractmethod
    def transform(self, raw: list[str]) -> list[str]: ...

    def load(self, rows: list[str]) -> None:  # shared step
        print(f"Loading {len(rows)} rows into DB")

    def on_complete(self) -> None:  # hook default: no-op
        pass

class CsvImporter(DataImporter):
    def __init__(self, path: str) -> None:
        self.path = path

    def extract(self) -> list[str]:
        print(f"Reading CSV: {self.path}")
        return [" a,1 ", " b,2 "]

    def transform(self, raw: list[str]) -> list[str]:
        return [s.strip().upper() for s in raw]

    def on_complete(self) -> None:
        print("CSV import finished")

class ApiImporter(DataImporter):
    def __init__(self, endpoint: str) -> None:
        self.endpoint = endpoint

    def extract(self) -> list[str]:
        print(f"GET {self.endpoint}")
        return ['{"id":1}', '{"id":2}']

    def transform(self, raw: list[str]) -> list[str]:
        import re
        return [re.sub(r"[^0-9]", "", s) for s in raw]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    CsvImporter("users.csv").import_data()
    ApiImporter("https://api/users").import_data()

Explanation: Python has no final, so convention + documentation ("do not override") plus a single template test guard the order. List comprehensions keep transforms idiomatic; the ABC enforces the required steps at instantiation.

Sample I/O: identical to the Java output above.

docs.title: Go (idiomatic: compositional template via interface + runner)
docs.text:
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "regexp"
    "strings"
)

// Steps is the variant contract: Go uses composition, not inheritance.
type Steps interface {
    Extract() []string
    Transform(raw []string) []string
    OnComplete()
}

// ImportData is the template function: fixed order for any Steps.
func ImportData(s Steps) {
    raw := s.Extract()
    clean := s.Transform(raw)
    fmt.Printf("Loading %d rows into DB\n", len(clean))
    s.OnComplete()
}

type CsvImporter struct{ Path string }

func (c CsvImporter) Extract() []string {
    fmt.Println("Reading CSV: " + c.Path)
    return []string{" a,1 ", " b,2 "}
}

func (c CsvImporter) Transform(raw []string) []string {
    out := make([]string, len(raw))
    for i, s := range raw {
        out[i] = strings.ToUpper(strings.TrimSpace(s))
    }
    return out
}

func (c CsvImporter) OnComplete() { fmt.Println("CSV import finished") }

type ApiImporter struct{ Endpoint string }

func (a ApiImporter) Extract() []string {
    fmt.Println("GET " + a.Endpoint)
    return []string{`{"id":1}`, `{"id":2}`}
}

var digits = regexp.MustCompile(`[^0-9]`)

func (a ApiImporter) Transform(raw []string) []string {
    out := make([]string, len(raw))
    for i, s := range raw {
        out[i] = digits.ReplaceAllString(s, "")
    }
    return out
}

func (a ApiImporter) OnComplete() {} // hook default: no-op

func main() {
    ImportData(CsvImporter{Path: "users.csv"})
    ImportData(ApiImporter{Endpoint: "https://api/users"})
}

Explanation: Go has no inheritance, so the template is a function parameterized by a Steps interface — same order guarantee, zero hierarchy. Each importer is a plain struct; the no-op OnComplete mirrors the hook default. This compositional style is the idiomatic Go translation reviewers expect.

Sample I/O: identical to the Java output above.

docs.title: 5. Real-World Industry Applications
docs.text:
• JUnit/TestNG: setUp → test → tearDown lifecycle; fixtures override hooks.
  • Spring: JdbcTemplate/RestTemplate fix connect → execute → map → close; callbacks vary mapping.
  • Django: class-based views fix dispatch → get/post → render; subclasses override handlers.
  • Maven/Gradle: lifecycle phases (validate → compile → test → package) with plugin hook points.
  • ETL frameworks: Airflow/Spark job templates fix extract → transform → load with per-job transforms.
  • Game engines: init → update → render loop with per-game update/render.
  • HTTP middleware (template-flavored): frameworks fixing authenticate → authorize → handle → log order.

docs.title: 6. Practical Use Cases and Scenarios
docs.text:
1. CSV/API/S3 importers: one pipeline order, per-source extract/transform — the worked example.
  2. Report generation: header → body → footer with PDF/Excel/HTML bodies sharing chrome.
  3. Test fixtures: shared setup/teardown with per-test body; hooks for optional seeding.
  4. Order fulfillment: validate → reserve → charge → ship → notify with per-channel ship/notify steps.
  5. Build pipelines: checkout → build → test → publish with per-language build/test commands.
  6. Document export: fetch → format → paginate → write with per-format formatters.
  7. Onboarding flows: verify → provision → welcome with per-plan provisioning.

Scenario walkthrough (reports): PdfReport and HtmlReport share header()/footer(); each implements body(). A compliance watermark added to header() propagates to every format with one edit — the DRY payoff — and no subclass can emit the body before the header.

docs.title: 7. When to Use and When Not to Use
docs.text:
Use Template Method when:

  • Multiple variants share one step order with different step bodies (pipelines, reports, lifecycles).
  • Step order is an invariant worth enforcing by construction (extract before load, setup before test).
  • Framework code must call application code at defined points (hooks).
  • Shared steps are substantial enough to merit one maintained copy.

Do NOT use Template when:

  • Step order itself varies per variant — use Strategy or Builder.
  • You need runtime behavior swaps — inheritance binds at compile time; use Strategy/composition.
  • Variants override nearly every step — the "shared" skeleton is fiction; use composition.
  • Hierarchies exceed 2–3 levels — prefer composition to avoid fragile-base-class pain.
  • Language idiom favors functions (Go, modern Python) — use a template function with injected steps.

Rule of thumb: fixed order + varying steps → Template. Swappable whole algorithms → Strategy. Varying order → Builder/Strategy.

docs.title: 8. Do's and Don'ts
docs.text:
Do:

  • Mark the template final (or document do-not-override) and test the order with a recording stub.
  • Keep the skeleton short and readable — 4–7 named steps max.
  • Give hooks harmless defaults and document when each fires.
  • Make primitive steps protected, not public — clients call the template, not the pieces.
  • Push cross-cutting steps (logging, metrics) into the base so variants inherit them.
  • Prefer composition (template function + strategy steps) when the language or team favors it.

Don't:

  • Don't add hooks speculatively — each unused hook is API surface and confusion.
  • Don't let subclasses call the template recursively or skip steps via flags.
  • Don't put variant-specific conditionals in the base (if (this instanceof CsvImporter)) — that defeats the pattern.
  • Don't change shared-step semantics silently — every subclass inherits the blast radius.
  • Don't deepen hierarchies to reuse one step — extract a helper or strategy instead.
  • Don't violate Liskov: subclass steps must honor documented pre/post-conditions (e.g., transform never returns null).

docs.title: 9. Comparison with Other Design Patterns
docs.text:
Aspect Template Method Strategy Factory Method Mechanism Inheritance: base fixes order, children fill steps Composition: context delegates whole algorithm Inheritance: subclass picks created class Binds Compile time (subclass) Runtime (setStrategy) Compile time (subclass) Varies Individual steps Entire algorithm Instantiated type Flexibility Rigid order, designated steps only Fully swappable Creation only Use when Skeleton invariant (ETL, lifecycles) Peer algorithms per call Creator knows when, not which Aspect Template Method Decorator Hook (plain callback) Extension style Subclass override Wrapper stacking Injected function Order control Base enforces Outermost-first, implicit Caller enforces Best for Framework lifecycles Optional stacked features One-off customization

Template vs Strategy (the classic confusion): Template fixes the skeleton and varies steps via inheritance. Strategy swaps the entire algorithm via composition at runtime. If callers must switch engines per request → Strategy. If the framework owns the order → Template. They compose well: a template step delegating to a strategy gives fixed order and runtime-swappable stages.

docs.title: 10. Interview Preparation
docs.text:
Q1: Why is the template method usually final? To lock the skeleton so subclasses cannot reorder or skip steps. Subclasses override designated primitives/hooks only. Without final, a child could load before extracting and silently break invariants the base promised.

Q2: What are hooks, and when do you add one? Hooks are optional overridable steps with safe defaults (onComplete() no-op). Add for discretionary extension; keep them few, named by timing (beforeLoad, onComplete), and documented. Many hooks signal the skeleton is unclear — reach for Strategy.

Q3: How do you test a Template hierarchy? With a recording stub: assert extract → transform → load → onComplete call order once; unit-test each concrete step in isolation; test hooks both default and overridden; assert the template cannot be reordered (final + order test).

Q4: Template vs Strategy — how do you choose on the spot? Ask "does the order stay fixed?" Fixed order + varying steps → Template. Whole algorithm swappable per call → Strategy. Varying order → Builder. Say it as one sentence and give one example each.

Q5: What is the fragile-base-class problem? Base edits (new step, changed hook timing, new exception) silently break subclasses. Mitigate: version the base carefully, keep steps small with contracts, announce hook-timing changes, and prefer composition for fast-moving variation.

Q6: How do you add a step without breaking subclasses? Add it as a hook with a no-op default (backward compatible), or as an optional strategy injection. Forcing a new abstract method breaks every existing subclass — acceptable only in a major version with migration.

Q7: How does Go/Python express Template without inheritance? As a template function taking step interfaces/lambdas (shown in the Go example). Same order guarantee, no hierarchy. Python can also use ABCs classically; Go must compose.

Q8: When do you reject Template outright? When order varies, when runtime swaps are needed, when subclasses override most steps, or past 2–3 hierarchy levels. Then Strategy, Builder, or plain composition wins on flexibility per unit of complexity.

LLD scenario 1 — Design a File Import service (CSV/API/S3). Expectation: DataImporter.importData() template; per-source extract/transform; shared load with batching; onComplete hook for notifications. Discuss poison-row handling inside transform vs load, and adding Kafka source as one subclass.

LLD scenario 2 — Design a Test Framework lifecycle. Expectation: runTest() = setup → execute → verify → teardown with hooks beforeEach/afterEach. Show a DB test overriding setup/teardown while reusing assertion steps; discuss hook ordering with nested suites.

LLD scenario 3 — Design Order Fulfillment with per-channel shipping. Expectation: fulfill() = validate → reserve → charge → ship → notify; standard vs express override ship() only; notify hook per channel. Show how a compliance step inserts once in the base for all channels.

docs.title: 11. Testing and Best Practices
docs.text:
• Order test: stub subclass records calls; assert exact sequence extract → transform → load → onComplete.
  • Step isolation: test each concrete extract/transform with fixture inputs; assert load batching and idempotency separately.
  • Hook coverage: test default no-op path and overridden path; assert hook exceptions propagate per documented policy.
  • Liskov checks: every subclass's steps satisfy base contracts (non-null returns, documented exceptions only).
  • Regression guard: adding a shared-step change runs the full subclass matrix — one base edit, all variants re-verified.
  • Template-function variant (Go/Python lambdas): test the runner with fake steps, including a failing step mid-sequence (assert later steps skipped, cleanup still runs).
  • Best practice: keep templates small, steps pure where possible, and log step boundaries (extract done: N rows) for pipeline observability.

docs.title: 12. Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Template Method fixes the algorithm skeleton once; subclasses supply only varying steps.
  • final template + abstract primitives + defaulted hooks is the complete toolkit.
  • One order, many fillings: pipelines, lifecycles, reports, frameworks.
  • Watch the costs: inheritance coupling, rigid order, fragile base — graduate to Strategy/composition when order itself varies.
  • Test the order once with a stub; test each step in isolation.
  • Interview one-liner: "Template Method puts the invariant step order in a final base method and lets subclasses implement only the varying primitives plus opt-in hooks — order enforced by construction, variants added as subclasses."

docs.title: Visitor Design Pattern
docs.text: Youtube: 36. Visitor Design Pattern | Double Dispatch | Low Level Design

docs.title: 1. Overview and Fundamentals
docs.text:
The Visitor pattern lets you define a new operation without changing the classes of the elements on which it operates — it separates algorithms from the object structure they run over.

In one sentence: elements accept a visitor, and the visitor carries the operation across every element type.

Core roles:

  • Element interface: declares accept(Visitor v) (CartItem, Shape, AstNode).
  • ConcreteElement: implements accept as visitor.visit(this) — the double-dispatch hook (Book, Electronics, Circle).
  • Visitor interface: declares one visit() overload per element type (visit(Book), visit(Electronics)).
  • ConcreteVisitor: implements a whole operation across all types (TaxCalculator, DiscountApplier, AreaCalculator).
  • Object structure: the collection or composite the visitor traverses (cart array, document, AST).

Fundamental properties:

  • Double dispatch: accept dispatches on element type, then visit overload dispatches on visitor logic — two types pick the method.
  • Open for operations, closed for elements: adding an operation is one new visitor class; element classes never change.
  • Behavioral: governs how operations traverse structures, not how objects are built.
  • Stateful visitors: a visitor accumulates results (totalTax) while walking, unlike a plain loop helper.

Mental model: a tax inspector visiting shops. Shops (elements) do not change how they operate; the inspector (visitor) brings the tax rulebook and applies the right page per shop type. A new discount inspector visits the same shops tomorrow with a different rulebook — no shop remodels.

docs.title: Intent and forces
docs.text:
Visitor solves the operation-explosion tension: an object hierarchy is stable (cart items, AST nodes, document blocks), but the operations over it multiply (tax, discount, shipping, export, validation, serialization). Baking each operation into every element class bloats elements, scatters one operation across N files, and forces editing all elements per new rule.

Visitor inverts this: each operation becomes one cohesive class with one method per element type. Elements shrink to accept() plus data accessors.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Define Element.accept(Visitor) in every element type.
  2. Implement each accept as exactly visitor.visit(this) — no logic, just the callback.
  3. Define Visitor with one visit(ConcreteElement) overload per type.
  4. Implement each operation as a ConcreteVisitor with all overloads.
  5. Client walks the structure calling element.accept(visitor) per element (or via Composite traversal).
  6. Visitor accumulates state (totalTax, report string, IR nodes) and exposes it after the walk.

docs.title: Why double dispatch matters
docs.text: Single dispatch picks a method by the receiver type only (element.accept(...) picks Book.accept). Inside accept, the call visitor.visit(this) is statically typed as the concrete element (Book), so the overload resolves to visit(Book). Together the two hops select by both types — operation × element — without instanceof chains or type switches.

docs.title: Design principles at play
docs.text:
• Single Responsibility: one visitor per operation; elements own data, visitors own logic.
  • Open/Closed (operations axis): new operations are new classes, zero element edits.
  • Encapsulation trade-off: visitors need element internals, so elements expose getters — the pattern's honest cost.
  • Cohesion: all tax branches live together instead of one branch per element class.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
• Classic overloaded visitor: one visit() per type (this page; Java/C# idiom).
  • Reflective/switch visitor: single visit(Element) with type switch — simpler for small hierarchies, loses compile-time safety.
  • Acyclic visitor: per-type visitor interfaces so adding a type does not force all visitors to change (breaks the cycle at interface cost).
  • Visitor + Composite: visitor walks tree structures (AST, file system, UI tree) recursively via composite accept.
  • Functional visitor: pattern-match / sealed-type when (Kotlin, Python match, Java sealed + switch) as a lightweight visitor.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Benefits: operations added cheaply, related logic co-located, traversal state accumulates cleanly, no instanceof chains. Costs: adding an element type breaks every visitor (new overload + N implementations), encapsulation weakens, and small hierarchies pay ceremony for little gain.

docs.title: 3. UML and Architecture Diagrams
docs.text:
Static structure: elements know only the visitor interface; visitors know every concrete element — the intentional cycle that enables double dispatch.

classDiagram
    class CartItem {
        <>
        +accept(v: CartVisitor)
        +price() double
    }
    class Book {
        -price: double
        +accept(v: CartVisitor)
        +price() double
    }
    class Electronics {
        -price: double
        +accept(v: CartVisitor)
        +price() double
    }
    class CartVisitor {
        <>
        +visitBook(b: Book)
        +visitElectronics(e: Electronics)
    }
    class TaxCalculator {
        +totalTax: double
        +visitBook(b: Book)
        +visitElectronics(e: Electronics)
    }
    class DiscountApplier {
        +totalDiscount: double
        +visitBook(b: Book)
        +visitElectronics(e: Electronics)
    }
    CartItem <|.. Book
    CartItem <|.. Electronics
    CartVisitor <|.. TaxCalculator
    CartVisitor <|.. DiscountApplier
    Book --> CartVisitor : accept
    Electronics --> CartVisitor : accept

Explanation: Book.accept and Electronics.accept each call back into the visitor with their concrete type, routing to the matching overload. Adding ShippingCalculator means one new class implementing two methods — Book and Electronics are untouched. Adding a Grocery element, by contrast, forces a new overload plus edits in both visitors — the pattern's known asymmetry.

Runtime flow: the client loops over the structure; each element double-dispatches into the visitor, which accumulates results.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Book as Element: Book
    participant Elec as Element: Electronics
    participant Tax as Visitor: TaxCalculator
    participant Disc as Visitor: DiscountApplier
    Client->>Book: accept(Tax)
    Book->>Tax: visitBook(Book)
    Note over Tax: totalTax += price * 0.05
    Client->>Elec: accept(Tax)
    Elec->>Tax: visitElectronics(Electronics)
    Note over Tax: totalTax += price * 0.18
    Client->>Book: accept(Disc)
    Book->>Disc: visitBook(Book)
    Note over Disc: totalDiscount += price * 0.10
    Client->>Elec: accept(Disc)
    Elec->>Disc: visitElectronics(Electronics)
    Note over Disc: no discount on gadgets

Explanation: the first arrow picks the element (Book.accept), the second picks the operation branch (visitBook). The same two elements serve two full operations with no element edits. After the walk the client reads tax.totalTax and discount.totalDiscount — the visitor is both algorithm and accumulator.

docs.title: 4. Implementation Examples in Java, Python, and Go
docs.text: The domain is a shopping cart: Book and Electronics items accept visitors; TaxCalculator and DiscountApplier carry the operations.

docs.title: Java (overloaded visitor, stateful accumulation)
docs.text:
interface CartVisitor {
    void visit(Book b);
    void visit(Electronics e);
}

interface CartItem {
    void accept(CartVisitor v);
    double price();
}

class Book implements CartItem {
    private final double price;
    Book(double price) { this.price = price; }
    public double price() { return price; }
    public void accept(CartVisitor v) { v.visit(this); } // double dispatch
}

class Electronics implements CartItem {
    private final double price;
    Electronics(double price) { this.price = price; }
    public double price() { return price; }
    public void accept(CartVisitor v) { v.visit(this); }
}

class TaxCalculator implements CartVisitor {
    double totalTax = 0;
    public void visit(Book b) { totalTax += b.price() * 0.05; }
    public void visit(Electronics e) { totalTax += e.price() * 0.18; }
}

class DiscountApplier implements CartVisitor {
    double totalDiscount = 0;
    public void visit(Book b) { totalDiscount += b.price() * 0.10; }
    public void visit(Electronics e) { totalDiscount += 0; }
}

class CartDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        CartItem[] cart = { new Book(500), new Electronics(20000) };
        TaxCalculator tax = new TaxCalculator();
        DiscountApplier discount = new DiscountApplier();
        for (CartItem item : cart) {
            item.accept(tax);
            item.accept(discount);
        }
        System.out.println("Tax=" + tax.totalTax + " Discount=" + discount.totalDiscount);
        System.out.println("Payable=" + (20500 + tax.totalTax - discount.totalDiscount));
    }
}

Explanation: accept is one line per element — the whole tax table lives in TaxCalculator, the whole discount table in DiscountApplier. New operations (shipping, gift wrap) add visitors; elements stay frozen.

Sample I/O:

Tax=3625.0 Discount=50.0
Payable=24075.0

docs.title: Python (pythonic: Protocol + single visitor class per operation)
docs.text:
from __future__ import annotations
from typing import Protocol

class CartVisitor(Protocol):
    def visit_book(self, item: Book) -> None: ...
    def visit_electronics(self, item: Electronics) -> None: ...

class Book:
    def __init__(self, price: float) -> None:
        self._price = price

    @property
    def price(self) -> float:
        return self._price

    def accept(self, visitor: CartVisitor) -> None:
        visitor.visit_book(self)  # double dispatch

class Electronics:
    def __init__(self, price: float) -> None:
        self._price = price

    @property
    def price(self) -> float:
        return self._price

    def accept(self, visitor: CartVisitor) -> None:
        visitor.visit_electronics(self)

class TaxCalculator:
    """Concrete visitor: accumulates tax while walking the cart."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.total_tax = 0.0

    def visit_book(self, item: Book) -> None:
        self.total_tax += item.price * 0.05

    def visit_electronics(self, item: Electronics) -> None:
        self.total_tax += item.price * 0.18

class DiscountApplier:
    """Concrete visitor: accumulates discounts while walking the cart."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.total_discount = 0.0

    def visit_book(self, item: Book) -> None:
        self.total_discount += item.price * 0.10

    def visit_electronics(self, item: Electronics) -> None:
        self.total_discount += 0.0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    cart = [Book(500), Electronics(20000)]
    tax, discount = TaxCalculator(), DiscountApplier()
    for item in cart:
        item.accept(tax)
        item.accept(discount)
    print(f"Tax={tax.total_tax} Discount={discount.total_discount}")
    print(f"Payable={20500 + tax.total_tax - discount.total_discount}")

Explanation: Protocol gives structural visitor typing without inheritance ceremony; accept names the concrete hook (visit_book) since Python lacks overloads. Visitors stay stateful accumulators; the walk loop is plain iteration.

Sample I/O:

Tax=3625.0 Discount=50.0
Payable=24075.0

docs.title: Go (idiomatic: explicit per-type visitor methods)
docs.text:
package main

import "fmt"

// CartVisitor declares one method per element type (no overloading in Go).
type CartVisitor interface {
    VisitBook(b *Book)
    VisitElectronics(e *Electronics)
}

// CartItem is the element contract.
type CartItem interface {
    Accept(v CartVisitor)
    Price() float64
}

type Book struct{ price float64 }

func (b *Book) Price() float64      { return b.price }
func (b *Book) Accept(v CartVisitor) { v.VisitBook(b) } // double dispatch

type Electronics struct{ price float64 }

func (e *Electronics) Price() float64      { return e.price }
func (e *Electronics) Accept(v CartVisitor) { v.VisitElectronics(e) }

type TaxCalculator struct{ TotalTax float64 }

func (t *TaxCalculator) VisitBook(b *Book) { t.TotalTax += b.Price() * 0.05 }
func (t *TaxCalculator) VisitElectronics(e *Electronics) {
    t.TotalTax += e.Price() * 0.18
}

type DiscountApplier struct{ TotalDiscount float64 }

func (d *DiscountApplier) VisitBook(b *Book) { d.TotalDiscount += b.Price() * 0.10 }
func (d *DiscountApplier) VisitElectronics(e *Electronics) {}

func main() {
    cart := []CartItem{&Book{price: 500}, &Electronics{price: 20000}}
    tax := &TaxCalculator{}
    discount := &DiscountApplier{}
    for _, item := range cart {
        item.Accept(tax)
        item.Accept(discount)
    }
    fmt.Printf("Tax=%.1f Discount=%.1f\n", tax.TotalTax, discount.TotalDiscount)
    fmt.Printf("Payable=%.1f\n", 20500+tax.TotalTax-discount.TotalDiscount)
}

Explanation: Go spells overloads as VisitBook/VisitElectronics — same double-dispatch shape, explicit names. Pointer receivers let visitors mutate accumulation fields; the Accept one-liners are the entire element-side cost.

Sample I/O:

Tax=3625.0 Discount=50.0
Payable=24075.0

docs.title: 5. Real-World Industry Applications
docs.text:
• Compilers: AST visitors for type-checking, optimization, and codegen (Eclipse JDT, Roslyn, Babel plugins walk nodes with visitors).
  • Tax and pricing engines: per-region tax visitors over invoices, carts, and payroll lines.
  • Reporting/export: PDF, Excel, HTML visitors over the same document model.
  • Serialization: JSON/XML/Protobuf visitors over domain objects without polluting them with format code.
  • Static analysis: lint, dead-code, and security visitors over parsed source trees.
  • File systems: search, backup, antivirus-scan visitors over file/directory composites.
  • Game engines: render, physics, and culling visitors over scene graphs.
  • Spring/Jakarta: BeanDefinitionVisitor, visitor-style RowMapper traversals over result structures.

docs.title: 6. Practical Use Cases and Scenarios
docs.text:
1. Cart totals: tax, discount, shipping, loyalty visitors over book/electronics/grocery items — the worked example.
  2. Document export: one Document of paragraphs/tables/images; PdfExport, HtmlExport, MarkdownExport visitors render each block type.
  3. AST lint + fix: UnusedVarVisitor reports, AutoFixVisitor rewrites — same traversal, two operations.
  4. Org-chart reporting: headcount-cost visitor vs diversity-metric visitor over employee/contractor nodes.
  5. Network inventory: compliance-audit visitor vs firmware-upgrade visitor over router/switch/firewall elements.
  6. Insurance claims: fraud-score visitor vs payout visitor over claim line types.
  7. UI testing: screenshot visitor vs accessibility-check visitor over widget trees.

Scenario walkthrough (documents): adding Markdown export is one MarkdownVisitor with visit(Paragraph), visit(Table), visit(Image). Paragraph, Table, and Image classes gain zero lines. Adding a new Video block, however, forces edits in all three exporters — plan element stability before committing to Visitor.

docs.title: 7. When to Use and When Not to Use
docs.text:
Use Visitor when:

  • Element hierarchy is stable but operations multiply (ASTs, documents, carts, scene graphs).
  • One operation's logic should live together (all tax rules in one class) instead of scattered per element.
  • You need to accumulate traversal state (totals, reports, diagnostics) cleanly.
  • instanceof/type-switch chains repeat in several places — Visitor replaces them with dispatch.

Do NOT use Visitor when:

  • Element types change often — each new type breaks every visitor (the fatal asymmetry).
  • The hierarchy is tiny (2 types, 1–2 operations) — polymorphic methods or a switch win.
  • Traversal is trivial linear iteration with per-item caller logic — use Iterator.
  • Visitors would need deep private internals — the getter sprawl destroys encapsulation; use Strategy or element methods.
  • Operations need only one element type — a plain method call beats double dispatch.

Rule of thumb: stable types × growing operations → Visitor. Growing types × few operations → polymorphism. Simple sequential access → Iterator.

docs.title: 8. Do's and Don'ts
docs.text:
Do:

  • Keep accept() to exactly visitor.visit(this) — no logic, no conditionals inside.
  • Expose the minimal getters visitors need; prefer package-scoped access over public fields.
  • Name visitors by operation (TaxCalculator) and methods by type (visit(Book)).
  • Document the stable-hierarchy contract: adding elements is a breaking change for all visitors.
  • Let visitors accumulate and expose results (totalTax) rather than mutating elements mid-walk.
  • Combine with Composite/Iterator for tree traversal — visitor holds logic, traversal holds walking.

Don't:

  • Don't hide business rules inside accept — operations belong in visitors, never elements.
  • Don't add catch-all visit(Object) fallbacks that silently swallow new types; fail loudly so new elements surface.
  • Don't mutate the structure while visiting without a documented protocol (snapshot first).
  • Don't force every visitor to depend on every element — consider acyclic visitors for large hierarchies.
  • Don't use Visitor to paper over missing polymorphism — if one operation varies per type and nothing else does, a virtual method is simpler.
  • Don't share one stateful visitor across threads — clone per walk or synchronize accumulation.

docs.title: 9. Comparison with Other Design Patterns
docs.text:
Aspect Visitor Iterator Goal Add operations over a stable hierarchy Walk elements hiding storage Who holds logic Visitor object (visit(Book) per type) Client loop body Dispatch Double: accept → visit(this) overload Single: next() yields, client branches State Visitor accumulates across elements Caller accumulates manually Pain New element breaks all visitors No help structuring per-type operations Use when AST analysis, tax/export, reports Collections, cursors, paginated APIs Aspect Visitor (double dispatch) Single dispatch + instanceof Routing Compiler routes to visit(Book) via two hops Manual if (x instanceof Book) chain Safety Missing overload is a compile error Missing branch is a runtime bug Cost Cycle between element and visitor types No cycle, but chains duplicate per operation Use when Many operations over stable types One-off branch, small hierarchy Aspect Visitor Strategy Composite Varies Operations over many types Algorithm for one job Part-whole tree shape Client picks Which visitor to run Which algorithm to inject Nothing — uniform Component API Pairs with Composite for trees Template step for swappable stages Visitor for tree operations

Visitor vs Iterator (the classic confusion): Iterator answers "how do I walk this?"; Visitor answers "what do I compute per type while walking?". A cart loop with Iterator still needs per-type branches; Visitor moves those branches into typed methods. They compose: Iterator/Composite walks, Visitor computes.

docs.title: 10. Interview Preparation
docs.text:
Q1: What is double dispatch and why does Visitor need it? Single dispatch picks by receiver type only. Visitor needs element × operation routing, so accept dispatches on the element, then visit(this) overloads on the concrete element type. The two hops together replace instanceof chains with compiler-checked routing.

Q2: What is Visitor's biggest drawback? Adding an element type breaks every visitor — new overload plus N implementations. Hence Visitor suits stable hierarchies with evolving operations; invert to polymorphism or Strategy when types churn.

Q3: How does Visitor affect encapsulation? Negatively: visitors need internals (price, children), forcing getters that expose representation. Mitigate with minimal, intention-revealing accessors, same-package visitors, or internal accessor interfaces instead of full public state.

Q4: Visitor vs Strategy — when is each right? Strategy swaps one algorithm for one job at runtime (payments, routes). Visitor defines one operation across many element types via double dispatch. Strategy varies which computation; Visitor varies what it computes per type.

Q5: How do you add a new element type with minimal damage? Add the overload to the visitor interface, implement it in each visitor (compiler lists them), and add regression tests per visitor. For large hierarchies, adopt acyclic visitors so only interested visitors implement the new hook.

Q6: How do you traverse trees with Visitor? Combine with Composite: composite accept visits itself then forwards the same visitor to children. The visitor stays order-agnostic; traversal order (pre/post) lives in the composite, logic in the visitor.

Q7: Are visitors stateful or stateless? Typically stateful accumulators (totalTax, report builder) created per walk and read after. Never share one accumulator across threads; for parallel walks, use per-shard visitors merged at the end.

Q8: When do you reject Visitor for a switch or match? For small, fast-moving hierarchies with one or two operations — sealed-type switches (Java switch, Python match, Go type switch) are shorter and survive type additions locally. Graduate to Visitor when operations outnumber types and scattering hurts.

LLD scenario 1 — Design a Document Export service. Expectation: elements Paragraph/Table/Image with accept; visitors PdfExport, HtmlExport, MarkdownExport. Show adding Markdown as one class, and the cost of adding a Video block. Discuss where pagination state lives (visitor) vs traversal (composite).

LLD scenario 2 — Design a Tax engine for a cart. Expectation: TaxCalculator per region (IN/US/EU visitors) over book/electronics/grocery; show rate tables co-located per visitor, accumulation of totalTax, and unit tests per (visitor, item-type) pair including exempt categories.

LLD scenario 3 — Design an AST lint + autofix pass. Expectation: nodes Function/Loop/Var; UnusedVarVisitor collects diagnostics, AutoFixVisitor rewrites. Discuss traversal order in composite accept, diagnostic accumulation, and why new node types are versioned carefully (all visitors break).

docs.title: 11. Testing and Best Practices
docs.text:
• Per-pair tests: every (visitor, element-type) overload gets a case with exact expected contribution (book tax 5%, gadgets 18%).
  • Acceptance test: each element's accept calls exactly the matching overload — verify with a recording visitor.
  • Accumulation test: multi-element walk yields the exact total; empty structure yields zero without errors.
  • New-operation test: adding a visitor (shipping) requires no element edits — assert via diff/review checklist plus passing old suites.
  • New-type impact test: adding a trial element fails compilation/tests in all visitors until handled — assert the breakage is loud, not silent.
  • Traversal test: composite walk visits children in documented order; visitor sees each node exactly once.
  • Encapsulation test: visitors use only approved getters; forbid reflection into privates in review.
  • Best practice: stateless elements, per-walk stateful visitors, table-driven per-pair cases, and traversal/operation separation so ordering bugs and rule bugs are distinguishable.

docs.title: 12. Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Visitor separates operations from structure via double dispatch: elements accept, visitors compute.
  • Adding operations is cheap (one class); adding element types is expensive (all visitors change) — commit only to stable hierarchies.
  • Keep accept trivial, co-locate each operation's branches, and accumulate results in the visitor.
  • Prefer Visitor over instanceof chains once operations outnumber types; prefer switches/polymorphism for tiny or churning hierarchies.
  • Compose with Composite/Iterator for trees; test every (visitor, type) pair.
  • Interview one-liner: "Visitor routes each element to the matching overload through accept-plus-visit double dispatch, so new operations arrive as new visitor classes while element types stay frozen — ideal for compilers, carts, and exporters over stable hierarchies."

docs.title: 1. Overview and Fundamentals
docs.text:
Intent: Provide an interface for creating families of related or dependent objects without specifying their concrete classes.

Problem it solves: Using a Windows button with a macOS checkbox, or an AWS compute client with a GCP bucket, produces incompatible combinations. Scattered new calls let mismatched products slip in.

Solution in one line: One factory per family exposes one creation method per product, so swapping the factory swaps the whole compatible set at once.

GoF category: Creational. Focus is on consistent families rather than a single product.

Core characteristics:

  • AbstractFactory declares createProductA() and createProductB().
  • Each ConcreteFactory builds only its own family's products.
  • Client depends solely on abstract factory and product interfaces.
  • Often each creation method is itself a Factory Method.

Mental model: A themed furniture store. You pick "Scandinavian" or "Industrial" once, and every piece — chair, table, lamp — arrives in the matching style. You never mix collections.

docs.title: 2. Detailed Theory
docs.text:
Mechanics:

  1. Define one product interface per kind: Button, Checkbox, Compute, Storage.
  2. Implement one concrete product per kind per family: WindowsButton, MacButton, AwsCompute, GcpCompute.
  3. Define AbstractFactory with one creation method per product kind.
  4. Implement one ConcreteFactory per family.
  5. Inject the factory into clients; clients never call concrete constructors.

Adding families vs adding products:

  • Adding a family is easy: add one factory class implementing existing methods.
  • Adding a product kind is hard: extend the factory interface and update every concrete factory. Keep product interfaces narrow and factories cohesive.

Principles involved:

  • Dependency Inversion: Client, factory, and products all depend on abstractions.
  • Open/Closed: Open for new families, closed for existing client code.
  • Interface Segregation: Prefer small factories with few methods; split bloated ones.
  • Consistency by construction: Compatibility is enforced because only one family can be built from a given factory.

Consequences:

  • Guarantees that products used together are compatible.
  • Makes switching families a one-line change at the composition root.
  • Increases class count and upfront design cost.
  • Wrong split (too many product kinds in one factory) creates painful interface churn.

Implementation options:

  • Parameterized factories for small families versus one class per family for large ones.
  • Prototype-backed factories that clone registered templates to reduce subclasses.
  • DI containers wiring the right factory per environment or region.

Architecture note: Choose the factory once at startup from config (platform, cloud, region), inject it downward, and keep all downstream code family-agnostic.

docs.title: 4. Implementation Examples in Java, Python, and Go
Java — Cloud family with matched compute plus storage
docs.text:
Steps: 1. Define Compute and Storage interfaces. 2. Implement AWS and GCP variants. 3. Define CloudFactory. 4. Implement one factory per cloud. 5. Inject factory into BackupService.

interface Compute { void start(String name); }
interface Storage { void upload(String key, byte[] data); }
interface CloudFactory {
    Compute createCompute();
    Storage createStorage();
}

class AwsCompute implements Compute {
    public void start(String name) { System.out.println("EC2 starting: " + name); }
}
class AwsStorage implements Storage {
    public void upload(String key, byte[] data) {
        System.out.println("S3 upload: " + key + " (" + data.length + " bytes)");
    }
}
class GcpCompute implements Compute {
    public void start(String name) { System.out.println("GCE starting: " + name); }
}
class GcpStorage implements Storage {
    public void upload(String key, byte[] data) {
        System.out.println("GCS upload: " + key + " (" + data.length + " bytes)");
    }
}

class AwsFactory implements CloudFactory {
    public Compute createCompute() { return new AwsCompute(); }
    public Storage createStorage() { return new AwsStorage(); }
}
class GcpFactory implements CloudFactory {
    public Compute createCompute() { return new GcpCompute(); }
    public Storage createStorage() { return new GcpStorage(); }
}

class BackupService {
    private final Compute compute;
    private final Storage storage;
    BackupService(CloudFactory factory) {
        this.compute = factory.createCompute();
        this.storage = factory.createStorage();
    }
    void nightlyBackup(String job) {
        compute.start(job);
        storage.upload(job + ".snap", new byte[1024]);
    }
}

public class AbstractFactoryDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        CloudFactory factory = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("gcp")
            ? new GcpFactory() : new AwsFactory();
        new BackupService(factory).nightlyBackup("orders-db");
    }
}
// Sample output with no args:
// EC2 starting: orders-db
// S3 upload: orders-db.snap (1024 bytes)
// Sample output with arg gcp:
// GCE starting: orders-db
// GCS upload: orders-db.snap (1024 bytes)

docs.title: Python — Theme family with registry selection, PEP8 style
docs.text:
Steps: 1. Define product classes per theme. 2. Define factory classes with matching methods. 3. Register families by key. 4. Resolve once from config.

"""Abstract factory for light and dark theme widget families."""
from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Dict, Type


class LightButton:
    def render(self) -> str:
        return "light button"


class LightCheckbox:
    def toggle(self) -> str:
        return "light checkbox checked"


class DarkButton:
    def render(self) -> str:
        return "dark button"


class DarkCheckbox:
    def toggle(self) -> str:
        return "dark checkbox checked"


class LightThemeFactory:
    def create_button(self) -> LightButton:
        return LightButton()

    def create_checkbox(self) -> LightCheckbox:
        return LightCheckbox()


class DarkThemeFactory:
    def create_button(self) -> DarkButton:
        return DarkButton()

    def create_checkbox(self) -> DarkCheckbox:
        return DarkCheckbox()


_FAMILIES: Dict[str, Type[object]] = {
    "light": LightThemeFactory,
    "dark": DarkThemeFactory,
}


def factory_for(theme: str):
    try:
        return _FAMILIES[theme]()
    except KeyError as exc:
        raise ValueError(f"unknown theme: {theme}") from exc


def main() -> None:
    factory = factory_for("dark")
    print(factory.create_button().render())
    print(factory.create_checkbox().toggle())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Sample output:
# dark button
# dark checkbox checked

docs.title: Go — Storage family with matched bucket plus queue
docs.text:
Steps: 1. Define Bucket and Queue interfaces. 2. Implement AWS and GCP pairs. 3. Define CloudFactory. 4. Select family in main.

package main

import (
    "errors"
    "fmt"
)

// Bucket stores objects; Queue publishes jobs.
type Bucket interface{ Put(key string) string }
type Queue interface{ Publish(job string) string }

// CloudFactory builds one compatible family.
type CloudFactory interface {
    NewBucket() Bucket
    NewQueue() Queue
}

type awsBucket struct{}

func (awsBucket) Put(key string) string { return "s3 put " + key }

type awsQueue struct{}

func (awsQueue) Publish(job string) string { return "sqs publish " + job }

type gcpBucket struct{}

func (gcpBucket) Put(key string) string { return "gcs put " + key }

type gcpQueue struct{}

func (gcpQueue) Publish(job string) string { return "pubsub publish " + job }

type awsFactory struct{}

func (awsFactory) NewBucket() Bucket { return awsBucket{} }
func (awsFactory) NewQueue() Queue   { return awsQueue{} }

type gcpFactory struct{}

func (gcpFactory) NewBucket() Bucket { return gcpBucket{} }
func (gcpFactory) NewQueue() Queue   { return gcpQueue{} }

// FactoryFor selects the whole family from one key.
func FactoryFor(cloud string) (CloudFactory, error) {
    switch cloud {
    case "aws":
        return awsFactory{}, nil
    case "gcp":
        return gcpFactory{}, nil
    default:
        return nil, errors.New("unknown cloud: " + cloud)
    }
}

func main() {
    factory, _ := FactoryFor("aws")
    fmt.Println(factory.NewBucket().Put("orders.snap"))
    fmt.Println(factory.NewQueue().Publish("backup"))
}

// Sample output:
// s3 put orders.snap
// sqs publish backup

docs.title: 5. Real-World Industry Applications
docs.text:
• UI toolkits: Qt, Flutter, and native widget sets producing matching buttons, inputs, and dialogs per platform.
  • Cloud providers: AWS, Azure, GCP factories for compute, storage, and queue clients.
  • Databases: Connection plus dialect plus transaction triplets per engine (Postgres, MySQL).
  • Theme systems: Light and dark palettes producing colors, fonts, and icons as a set.
  • Document generators: PDF, HTML, Word exporters producing headers, tables, and footers.
  • E-commerce regions: US, EU, Asia factories for currency, tax, and shipping rules.
  • Game engines: Medieval versus sci-fi asset families with matched units and buildings.
  • Spring: FactoryBean hierarchies and profile-specific @Configuration classes.

docs.title: 6. Practical Use Cases and Scenarios
docs.text: Scenario Problem Abstract Factory application Cross-platform UI Mixed widgets look and behave inconsistently One factory per OS builds all widgets Multi-cloud backup Compute and storage must belong to one cloud CloudFactory returns matched pair Regional checkout Tax plus currency plus shipping must agree Region factory returns the legal triplet Document export PDF header with HTML table breaks layout Format factory builds full document kit Test environments Integration tests mix fake DB with real queue Environment factory swaps whole backend Game themes Sci-fi tank beside medieval castle Theme factory builds matched asset set Reporting Chart plus table plus export must share dialect Engine factory per output target

docs.title: 7. When to Use and When Not to Use
docs.text:
Use when:

  • Two or more product kinds must be used together and stay compatible.
  • The system must run against multiple families (platforms, clouds, regions, themes).
  • You want family switching to be a single configuration change.
  • Product constraints should be enforced by construction, not documentation.

Do not use when:

  • Only one product kind varies — prefer Factory.
  • Products are independent and freely mixable — direct factories suffice.
  • The family has one member and no second family is planned — YAGNI applies.
  • Product kinds churn weekly — interface churn across every factory will hurt.

docs.title: 8. Do's and Don'ts
docs.text: Do Don't Inject the factory; select the family at the composition root Instantiate concrete factories deep in domain code Keep factories small and cohesive; split bloated ones Put ten unrelated create methods in one factory Design product interfaces narrowly upfront Add product kinds casually and churn all factories Reuse factories; they are often singletons Create a new factory per request without reason Test family compatibility explicitly Test one product and assume the family works Consider Prototype-backed factories for many variants Subclass endlessly when cloning a template works

docs.title: 9. Comparison with Other Design Patterns
docs.text:
Aspect Abstract Factory Factory Method Builder Prototype Scope Family of related products One product via subclass One complex object stepwise Copies of an existing object Mechanism Composition of creation methods Inheritance and override Fluent assembly plus build Clone plus tweak Compatibility Guarantees family consistency No cross-product guarantee N/A: single product Inherits template state Add family or variant Easy: add one factory Easy: add one subclass Easy: add builder step Easy: register template Add product kind Hard: touches every factory N/A Medium: extend builder Easy: clone new template Best for Platforms, clouds, themes Extension hooks Optional-heavy objects Expensive or stateful templates

Rule of thumb: one varying product points to Factory Method; two or more products that must ship together point to Abstract Factory; stepwise configuration points to Builder; reuse of prepared state points to Prototype.

docs.title: 10. Interview Preparation
docs.text:
Q1 [Beginner]: What problem does Abstract Factory solve? It guarantees that related products come from the same family so incompatible combinations cannot be constructed by accident.

Q2 [Beginner]: How is it a factory of factories? Each concrete factory bundles several Factory Methods — one per product kind — so choosing a factory chooses the whole product set.

Q3 [Intermediate]: Factory Method vs Abstract Factory? Factory Method creates one product through inheritance; Abstract Factory creates a family through composition. Use the former for one hierarchy, the latter for matched sets.

Q4 [Intermediate]: What is the main extension trade-off? Families are cheap to add (one class); product kinds are expensive (every factory plus the interface changes). Mitigate with narrow interfaces and cohesive splits.

Q5 [Intermediate]: How do you select the family at runtime? Read one key (platform, cloud, region) at startup, resolve to a factory via map or DI profile, and inject that factory everywhere downstream.

Q6 [Advanced]: How do you avoid interface explosion? Split by cohesion (compute-plus-storage versus UI widgets), provide default methods or adapters where the language allows, and consider Prototype-backed factories for variant-heavy families.

Q7 [Advanced]: How do you test it? Unit-test clients against fake factories and fake products; add one integration test per real family proving the products interoperate with the real SDK.

Q8 [Scenario]: EU checkout needs new tax rules without touching US — design it? Add EuFactory returning EU tax, currency, and shipping products behind existing interfaces. Wire by region key. US path and shared checkout code stay untouched.

LLD scenario 1 — Cross-platform UI kit: Design button, checkbox, and dialog per OS with native look. Expect factory per OS, program-to-interface clients, and snapshot tests per family.

LLD scenario 2 — Multi-region payments: Design gateway plus currency plus tax per region. Expect region factory, money value objects, and contract tests per region.

LLD scenario 3 — Game world themes: Design matched terrain, units, and buildings for two biomes. Expect theme factory plus Prototype prefabs and asset-budget tests.

docs.title: 11. Testing and Best Practices
docs.text:
• Compatibility tests: every factory must produce products that interoperate; assert pairs, not singles.
  • Switching tests: same client scenario across all families with golden outputs.
  • Negative tests: unknown family key raises a clear error; mixed factories are rejected by types or review.
  • Isolation: fake factories for unit tests; real families only in integration tests with credentials.
  • Best practices: stateless factories, constructor injection, one selection point, metrics on family resolution failures.
Aspect Detail Memory impact Low: factories are thin Creation cost Medium: dominated by real products and SDK clients Scalability High if factories shared and products thread-safe Optimization Reuse factory and heavyweight products; cache SDK clients; lazy-load families

docs.title: 12. Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Abstract Factory answers "which compatible set" — one factory per family, one method per product.
  • Swapping a factory swaps the whole family; clients stay family-agnostic.
  • Families are cheap to add, product kinds are expensive — design interfaces carefully.
  • Test compatibility per family, select the family once, and inject it everywhere.

docs.text: • 23. Builder Design Pattern with Examples, LLD | Low Level Design Interview Question | System Design

docs.title: 1. Overview and Fundamentals
docs.text:
Intent: Separate the construction of a complex object from its representation so the same construction process can create different representations. Build complex objects step by step.

Problem it solves: Telescoping constructors (new Request(a, b, c, d, e, f, g)) are unreadable, error-prone, and break every caller when a field is added. JavaBeans setters fix readability but leave half-built mutable objects.

Solution in one line: Collect parameters in a mutable builder with fluent methods, validate once, then freeze into an immutable product via build().

GoF category: Creational. Focus is on stepwise assembly of one complex type.

Core characteristics:

  • Required fields via builder constructor; optional fields via chained methods with defaults.
  • Single validation gate in build().
  • Immutable product with defensive copies of mutable inputs.
  • Optional Director for standard construction recipes; optional Step Builder for compile-time ordering.

Mental model: Ordering a custom laptop. You pick CPU and RAM first (required), then add storage, warranty, and accessories (optional). The shop validates the full configuration once before sealing the box.

docs.title: 2. Detailed Theory
docs.text:
Mechanics:

  1. Product holds final fields and a private constructor taking the builder.
  2. Static nested Builder holds mutable staging fields with sensible defaults.
  3. Builder constructor takes required fields so they cannot be forgotten.
  4. Chained methods set optional fields and return this.
  5. build() validates cross-field rules and returns the immutable product.

Variants:

  • Fluent Builder: Plain chaining as in the examples below.
  • Step Builder: Each step returns an interface exposing only the next legal call, enforcing order at compile time.
  • Director: Encapsulates standard recipes (buildMinimalReport, buildFullReport) over the builder interface.
  • Lombok @Builder / record builders: Generated builders for routine cases; hand-write when validation is non-trivial.
  • Hierarchical builders: Self-type generics (T extends Builder<T>) for builder inheritance.

Principles involved:

  • Single Responsibility: Construction logic leaves the product; validation lives in one gate.
  • Open/Closed: New optional fields add a method plus default without breaking callers.
  • Encapsulation: Product invariants are established once and never rechecked.
  • Immutability: Frozen product is freely shareable across threads.

Consequences:

  • Call sites name every argument (timeoutMs(8000)), ending boolean-and-int confusion.
  • One extra class per product plus a short-lived builder allocation per build.
  • Builders themselves are single-threaded staging objects — document as not thread-safe.
  • Overkill for two-field value objects where a constructor suffices.

docs.title: 3. UML and Architecture Diagrams
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Director {
        +constructMinimal() Product
        +constructFull() Product
    }
    class Builder {
        <>
        +setPartA(value) Builder
        +setPartB(value) Builder
        +build() Product
    }
    class ConcreteBuilder {
        -partA : String
        -partB : int
        +setPartA(value) Builder
        +setPartB(value) Builder
        +build() Product
    }
    class Product {
        -partA : String
        -partB : int
    }
    Director --> Builder : uses
    Builder <|.. ConcreteBuilder
    ConcreteBuilder ..> Product : builds

The class diagram shows the director driving the builder interface while the concrete builder assembles the immutable product.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant B as Builder
    participant P as Product
    Client->>B: new Builder required fields
    Client->>B: set optional fields
    Client->>B: build
    B->>B: validate all fields
    B->>P: new Product builder state
    P-->>Client: immutable product

The sequence diagram shows staged configuration followed by one validation gate before the frozen product is returned.

Architecture note: Builders belong at API boundaries — HTTP requests, SDK calls, report specs, test fixtures. Domain entities receive the built value object; they never see the builder.

docs.title: 4. Implementation Examples in Java, Python, and Go
Java — HTTP request builder with validation gate
docs.text:
Steps: 1. Make product fields final with private constructor. 2. Require method plus URL in builder constructor. 3. Chain optional fields with defaults. 4. Validate cross-field rules in build(). 5. Defensive-copy mutable state.

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

class HttpRequest {
    private final String method;
    private final String url;
    private final Map<String, String> headers;
    private final int timeoutMs;
    private final int retries;
    private final String body;

    private HttpRequest(Builder builder) {
        this.method = builder.method;
        this.url = builder.url;
        this.headers = Map.copyOf(builder.headers);
        this.timeoutMs = builder.timeoutMs;
        this.retries = builder.retries;
        this.body = builder.body;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return method + " " + url + " timeout=" + timeoutMs
            + " retries=" + retries + " headers=" + headers.size();
    }

    static class Builder {
        private final String method;
        private final String url;
        private final Map<String, String> headers = new HashMap<>();
        private int timeoutMs = 5_000;
        private int retries = 1;
        private String body = "";

        Builder(String method, String url) {
            this.method = method;
            this.url = url;
        }

        Builder header(String key, String value) {
            headers.put(key, value);
            return this;
        }

        Builder timeoutMs(int timeoutMs) {
            this.timeoutMs = timeoutMs;
            return this;
        }

        Builder retries(int retries) {
            this.retries = retries;
            return this;
        }

        Builder body(String body) {
            this.body = body;
            return this;
        }

        HttpRequest build() {
            if (method == null || method.isBlank()) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("method is required");
            }
            if (url == null || url.isBlank()) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("url is required");
            }
            if (timeoutMs <= 0) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("timeout must be positive");
            }
            if (!body.isEmpty() && method.equals("GET")) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("GET must not carry a body");
            }
            return new HttpRequest(this);
        }
    }
}

public class BuilderDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        HttpRequest req = new HttpRequest.Builder("POST", "https://api.shop/orders")
            .header("Authorization", "Bearer tok")
            .timeoutMs(8000).retries(3).body("{\"id\":7}")
            .build();
        System.out.println(req);
    }
}
// Sample output:
// POST https://api.shop/orders timeout=8000 retries=3 headers=1

docs.title: Python — Fluent dataclass builder, PEP8 style
docs.text:
Steps: 1. Model the product as a frozen dataclass. 2. Write a mutable builder with chaining. 3. Apply defaults centrally. 4. Validate in build.

"""Fluent builder producing an immutable email message."""
from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Dict, List


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Email:
    to: str
    subject: str
    body: str = ""
    cc: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    headers: Dict[str, str] = field(default_factory=dict)


class EmailBuilder:
    def __init__(self, to: str, subject: str) -> None:
        self._to = to
        self._subject = subject
        self._body = ""
        self._cc: List[str] = []
        self._headers: Dict[str, str] = {}

    def body(self, text: str) -> EmailBuilder:
        self._body = text
        return self

    def cc(self, *addresses: str) -> EmailBuilder:
        self._cc.extend(addresses)
        return self

    def header(self, key: str, value: str) -> EmailBuilder:
        self._headers[key] = value
        return self

    def build(self) -> Email:
        if "@" not in self._to:
            raise ValueError("valid recipient is required")
        if not self._subject.strip():
            raise ValueError("subject is required")
        return Email(
            to=self._to,
            subject=self._subject,
            body=self._body,
            cc=list(self._cc),
            headers=dict(self._headers),
        )


def main() -> None:
    email = (
        EmailBuilder("a@x.com", "Invoice ready")
        .body("Thanks for your order.")
        .cc("ops@x.com")
        .header("X-Priority", "1")
        .build()
    )
    print(email)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Sample output:
# Email(to='a@x.com', subject='Invoice ready', body='Thanks...', cc=['ops@x.com'], ...)

docs.title: Go — Functional-options builder
docs.text:
Steps: 1. Keep the product struct simple. 2. Define Option functions. 3. Apply defaults first, then options. 4. Validate once before returning.

package main

import (
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "strings"
)

// Server is the immutable-ish product configured step by step.
type Server struct {
    Host string
    Port int
    TLS  bool
    Tags map[string]string
}

// Option mutates the staging config.
type Option func(*Server)

func WithPort(port int) Option {
    return func(s *Server) { s.Port = port }
}

func WithTLS(enabled bool) Option {
    return func(s *Server) { s.TLS = enabled }
}

func WithTag(key, value string) Option {
    return func(s *Server) { s.Tags[key] = value }
}

// NewServer applies defaults, then options, then validates once.
func NewServer(host string, opts ...Option) (Server, error) {
    s := Server{Host: host, Port: 8080, Tags: map[string]string{}}
    for _, opt := range opts {
        opt(&s)
    }
    if strings.TrimSpace(s.Host) == "" {
        return Server{}, errors.New("host is required")
    }
    if s.Port <= 0 || s.Port > 65535 {
        return Server{}, errors.New("port must be 1-65535")
    }
    tags := make(map[string]string, len(s.Tags))
    for k, v := range s.Tags {
        tags[k] = v
    }
    s.Tags = tags
    return s, nil
}

func main() {
    srv, err := NewServer("api.shop", WithPort(443), WithTLS(true), WithTag("env", "prod"))
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("%s:%d tls=%v tags=%v\n", srv.Host, srv.Port, srv.TLS, srv.Tags)
}

// Sample output:
// api.shop:443 tls=true tags=map[env:prod]

  • Android: AlertDialog.Builder, Notification.Builder with chained setters.
  • SQL builders: jOOQ, QueryDSL, Hibernate Criteria, Knex.js, Django ORM chaining.
  • Cloud SDKs: AWS SDK v2 builders for requests, S3 puts, and client configuration.
  • Documents: HTML, XML, JSON, and PDF document builders.

  • Test fixtures: Builder pattern for DTOs and aggregate roots in unit tests.

docs.title: 6. Practical Use Cases and Scenarios
docs.text: Scenario Problem Builder application HTTP request Two required plus six optional fields Builder with build() validation Report export Same data as PDF, HTML, CSV Director plus per-format builder Test user Dozens of nullable fields per test Fixture builder with but() cloning Email send Recipients, CC, body, attachments Fluent builder with size validation Server config Host required, ports and TLS optional Functional options with defaults Query filter Optional predicates in any order Builder accumulating clauses Game character Class required, gear optional Step builder enforcing creation order

docs.title: 7. When to Use and When Not to Use
docs.text:
Use when:

  • An object has four or more parameters, several optional.
  • Construction needs validation across fields, not per setter.
  • You want immutable results with readable call sites.
  • The same process should yield different representations (PDF vs HTML report).
  • Test fixtures need expressive variations from a common base.

Do not use when:

  • The object has two or three simple fields — use a constructor or static factory.
  • All parameters are required and stable — telescoping is not a risk.
  • Builder hierarchies would mirror product hierarchies — consider factories instead.
  • Allocation of one staging object per build is genuinely unacceptable (rare).

docs.title: 8. Do's and Don'ts
docs.text: Do Don't Require mandatory fields in the builder constructor Allow build() with missing required data Validate everything once in build() with clear messages Validate per setter so chaining order matters Defensive-copy mutable inputs into the product Share the builder's map or list with the product Keep defaults in one place and document them Scatter magic defaults across call sites Prefer immutable products; mark builders not thread-safe Share one builder across threads Add but() or copy() for fixture variations Clone products by hand in every test

docs.title: 9. Comparison with Other Design Patterns
docs.text:
Aspect Builder Factory Method Abstract Factory Telescoping constructor Problem Too many parameters, many optional Subclass picks product type Compatible product family N/A: ad-hoc overloads Call shape One type configured stepwise One call, hierarchy decides Several create calls, one family Positional args, easy to swap Validation Once in build() Per product constructor Per product constructor Scattered or absent Readability High: named chained calls Medium: type hidden Medium: family hidden Low: new(a, b, c, d) Immutability Natural: frozen product Depends on product Depends on products Possible but painful Cost Extra builder class Extra subclasses Extra families Combinatorial overloads

Rule of thumb: many optional fields on one type point to Builder; subtype selection points to Factory; matched families point to Abstract Factory; two required fields point to a plain constructor.

docs.title: 10. Interview Preparation
docs.text:
Q1 [Beginner]: What problem does Builder solve? Telescoping constructors and half-built setters. It names every argument, centralizes defaults, and validates the whole object once before freezing it.

Q2 [Beginner]: Where does validation belong? In build(), not in setters. Setters stay order-independent; build() checks required fields plus cross-field rules like GET-must-not-carry-body.

Q3 [Intermediate]: How do you enforce required fields? Pass them through the builder constructor so omission is a compile error. For stronger ordering use a Step Builder where each method returns the next legal step.

Q4 [Intermediate]: Builder vs constructor with defaults? Constructors with defaults work for few stable fields. Builder wins once fields are numerous, optional, or cross-validated, because adding a field never breaks callers.

Q5 [Intermediate]: How do you keep the product immutable? Final fields, private constructor, and defensive copies of collections. The builder stays mutable but is discarded after build().

Q6 [Advanced]: Director vs Step Builder — when? Director encodes reusable recipes over a builder interface (minimal versus full report). Step Builder encodes ordering in types (from plus to required before body). Use both when recipes and ordering matter.

Q7 [Advanced]: Thread-safety story? Builders are single-threaded staging objects. Products are immutable and freely shared. Never publish the builder or reuse it concurrently without explicit reset.

Q8 [Scenario]: Report API needs PDF, HTML, and CSV from one spec — design it? Define a ReportBuilder interface with section methods; write one concrete builder per format; add a Director with minimal() and full() recipes. The service picks the builder by Accept header.

LLD scenario 1 — Pizza order: Design size (required) plus crust, toppings, extras. Expect builder with price computation and validation in build() (vegan cheese versus meat rules).

LLD scenario 2 — Query builder: Design filter, sort, page, and projection for a search API. Expect immutable query object, method chaining, max-page-size guard, and SQL-injection-safe rendering.

LLD scenario 3 — Test data factory: Design user fixtures with admin, guest, and locked variants. Expect base builder plus but() overrides and deterministic faker seeds.

docs.title: 11. Testing and Best Practices
docs.text:
• Combinatorial tests: required-only, all-optional, boundary values, and each default.
  • Validation tests: one failing case per rule with exact message assertions.
  • Immutability tests: mutate builder inputs after build(); assert product unchanged.
  • Recipe tests: Director outputs for minimal and full variants match golden snapshots.
  • Best practices: fail fast with field names, document defaults, keep builders out of product APIs, reuse via but() not shared mutable builders.
Aspect Detail Memory impact Medium: one short-lived builder per product Creation cost Medium: staging plus one validation pass Scalability High: immutable products share freely Optimization Reuse builders only with explicit clear(); cache built templates via Prototype

docs.title: 12. Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Builder turns confusing positional construction into named, validated, stepwise assembly.
  • Required fields ride the constructor; optional fields chain; build() validates once.
  • Products are immutable snapshots; builders are disposable staging objects.
  • Use Directors for recipes and Step Builders for ordering; avoid Builder for trivial objects.

docs.text: • 27. All Creational Design Patterns | Prototype, Singleton, Factory, AbstractFactory, Builder Pattern

docs.title: 1. Overview and Fundamentals
docs.text:
What: Creational patterns control how objects are created, hiding instantiation logic so clients depend on abstractions, not concrete classes.

Family members:

Pattern Answers One-line use Singleton How many? One Shared config, pool manager, registry Factory Method Which type? Via subclass Gateway, parser, sender selection Abstract Factory Which family? Compatible set Platform UI, cloud, region families Builder How assembled? Stepwise Requests, queries, configs, fixtures Prototype From what? Copy template Invoices, prefabs, pipeline configs Object Pool How reused? Bounded lending Connections, threads, bullets, buffers

Shared goal: Decouple use from creation, enforce constraints at construction, and make extension cheap.

docs.title: 2. Detailed Theory
docs.text:
Core ideas: Encapsulate what varies in creation; program to interfaces; let factories own knowledge of concrete classes.

How they combine: Abstract Factory is often built from Factory Methods; factories are often Singleton-scoped; Prototype backs factories to avoid subclass explosion; Builder constructs Composite products.

Key trade-off: Flexibility costs classes. Use a pattern only when creation varies, is expensive, or must enforce compatibility.

Principles applied: Open/Closed (add types without editing clients), Single Responsibility (creation leaves business logic), Dependency Inversion (depend on factory and product abstractions), DRY (centralize construction).

docs.title: 3. UML and Architecture Diagrams
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Client {
        +run() void
    }
    class Factory {
        <>
        +create() Product
    }
    class Product {
        <>
        +use() void
    }
    Client --> Factory : asks
    Factory ..> Product : creates
    Product <|.. ConcreteProduct : implements

The class diagram shows the family-wide rule: clients use factories and products through interfaces only.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Factory
    participant P as Product
    Client->>Factory: create key
    Factory->>P: new or clone or reuse
    P-->>Client: ready product
    Client->>P: use

The sequence diagram shows the uniform flow: resolve, create or reuse, then use through abstraction.

docs.title: 4. Implementation Examples in Java, Python, and Go
Java — Simple factory selecting a product
docs.text:
Steps: 1. Define interface. 2. Implement two products. 3. Select by key in factory.

interface Greeter { String greet(String name); }
class HiGreeter implements Greeter {
    public String greet(String n) { return "hi " + n; }
}
class HelloGreeter implements Greeter {
    public String greet(String n) { return "hello " + n; }
}
class GreeterFactory {
    static Greeter create(boolean formal) {
        return formal ? new HelloGreeter() : new HiGreeter();
    }
}
public class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] a) {
        System.out.println(GreeterFactory.create(true).greet("Asha"));
    }
}
// Sample output: hello Asha
