docs.title: 7. When to Use and When Not to Use
docs.text:
Use when: Creation varies by input, is expensive, must stay compatible, needs stepwise validation, or must be bounded.

Do not use when: Direct new is clear, the type set is fixed and tiny, products mix freely, or pooling cheap immutable objects. Prefer the simplest solution that satisfies the constraint.

docs.title: 8. Do's and Don'ts
docs.text: Do Don't Depend on factory and product interfaces Scatter new for varying types Validate once in Builder, reset in Pool, deep-copy in Prototype Leave half-built, dirty, or aliased objects Select family once at composition root Mix families deep in domain code Keep factories stateless and injectable Build God factories for unrelated types Document thread-safety and ownership Share mutable products silently

docs.title: 9. Comparison with Other Design Patterns
docs.text:
Aspect Creational Structural Behavioral Answers How objects come to be How objects compose How objects interact Example Factory, Builder, Pool Adapter, Decorator, Flyweight Strategy, Observer, Command Client coupling To factory interface To component interface To behavior interface Reach for Varying, expensive, or constrained creation Interface mismatch or layering Algorithm or workflow variation

Within family: Factory picks one type; Abstract Factory picks a family; Builder assembles stepwise; Prototype clones; Singleton bounds count to one; Pool bounds reuse.

docs.title: 10. Interview Preparation
docs.text:
Q1 [Beginner]: What unites creational patterns? They hide how objects are created so clients depend on abstractions and constraints hold by construction.

Q2 [Beginner]: Factory vs Abstract Factory? One product versus a compatible family of products.

Q3 [Intermediate]: Builder vs Factory? Builder configures one complex type stepwise; Factory selects among subtypes.

Q4 [Intermediate]: Prototype vs Factory? Prototype copies prepared state; Factory constructs from defaults via a hierarchy.

Q5 [Intermediate]: Singleton vs static class? Singleton is an injectable object with lifecycle control; static utilities suit stateless helpers.

Q6 [Advanced]: Object Pool vs Flyweight? Pool lends mutable instances exclusively; Flyweight shares immutable state simultaneously.

Q7 [Advanced]: Why is adding product kinds to Abstract Factory hard? Every factory plus the interface changes. Keep interfaces narrow or split factories.

Q8 [Scenario]: Checkout adds UPI without touching existing code? Add UpiProcessor behind Processor, register under upi, resolve via factory from config.

LLD scenario 1 — Multi-gateway payments: Factory per gateway plus idempotency, retries, and webhook reconciliation.

LLD scenario 2 — Cross-platform UI: Abstract Factory per OS for button, dialog, and input with golden snapshot tests.

LLD scenario 3 — Report service: Builder for PDF/HTML/CSV from one spec plus Prototype templates and a bounded export worker pool.

docs.title: 11. Testing and Best Practices
docs.text:
• Test routing separately from products: unknown keys error, families stay compatible, builders reject invalid combos, clones stay independent, pools return clean instances.
  • Prefer DI singleton scope over hand-rolled Singletons; fake factories in unit tests; integration-test each real family once.
  • Track creation metrics: factory misses by key, pool waits and exhaustion, template versions.
Aspect Detail Memory Low except prewarmed pools and template stores Cost Dominated by real products, not dispatch Scaling Share stateless factories; make products thread-safe or exclusive

docs.title: 12. Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Singleton bounds count; Factory picks type; Abstract Factory picks family; Builder assembles; Prototype clones; Pool reuses.
  • Choose by constraint: singularity, variation, compatibility, stepwise config, expensive setup, or bounded reuse.
  • Keep creation explicit, injectable, and tested — and skip the pattern when new suffices.

docs.text: • 5. Factory Pattern Vs Abstract Factory Pattern Explanation (Hindi) | Low Level System Design

docs.title: 1. Overview and Fundamentals
docs.text:
Intent: Define an interface for creating objects, but let subclasses decide which class to instantiate. The Factory Method lets a class defer instantiation to subclasses.

Problem it solves: Client code littered with if type == "stripe": return StripeProcessor() couples every caller to concrete classes. Adding a new type forces edits in many places and violates Open/Closed Principle.

Solution in one line: Move creation behind a factory method or factory class so clients ask for a product by abstraction and receive the right concrete type.

GoF category: Creational. Focus is on which single product type to create.

Terminology to get right:

  • Simple Factory: A single method or class with a conditional that picks the product. Useful idiom, but not a GoF pattern.
  • Factory Method: An abstract creation method overridden by subclasses; uses inheritance to vary the product.
  • Abstract Factory: Creates families of related products; uses composition. Covered in Abstract Factory.

Mental model: A restaurant kitchen with an order chit. The waiter (client) writes "pizza" without knowing which chef cooks it. The head chef (factory) routes the order to the right station (concrete creator).

docs.title: 2. Detailed Theory
docs.text:
Mechanics (Factory Method):

  1. Define a Product interface, e.g. PaymentProcessor.
  2. Define a Creator with an abstract factoryMethod() plus a concrete operation() that uses the product.
  3. Each ConcreteCreator overrides factoryMethod() to return its ConcreteProduct.
  4. Client depends only on Creator and Product.

Mechanics (Simple / Parameterized Factory):

  1. One Factory class exposes create(type) with a registry or switch.
  2. Registry maps keys to constructors or supplier functions.
  3. Unknown types raise a clear error; registration can be dynamic.

Principles involved:

  • Open/Closed: Add products by adding creators, not editing clients.
  • Single Responsibility: Creation logic leaves business classes.
  • Dependency Inversion: Both creator and client depend on the product abstraction.
  • Liskov Substitution: Any product must be usable through the product interface.

Consequences:

  • Decouples client from concrete classes and construction details.
  • Can explode into many small creator subclasses if every variant needs one.
  • Parameterized factories trade subclass count for conditional complexity.
  • Overkill when the product set is fixed and tiny — direct new is clearer.

Design choices:

  • Key by enum or string constants, never magic strings scattered in callers.
  • Prefer a registry map of String -> Supplier<Product> so plugins can self-register without editing the factory.
  • Return interfaces, accept configuration objects, and fail fast on unknown keys.

docs.title: 3. UML and Architecture Diagrams
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Creator {
        +factoryMethod() Product
        +operation() String
    }
    class ConcreteCreatorA {
        +factoryMethod() Product
    }
    class ConcreteCreatorB {
        +factoryMethod() Product
    }
    class Product {
        <>
        +pay(amount) String
    }
    class ConcreteProductA {
        +pay(amount) String
    }
    class ConcreteProductB {
        +pay(amount) String
    }

    Creator <|-- ConcreteCreatorB

    Product <|.. ConcreteProductB
    Creator ..> Product : creates

The class diagram shows creators varying the product while the client uses only the abstract types.

sequenceDiagram

    participant Creator as ConcreteCreator
    participant P as ConcreteProduct
    Client->>Creator: operation
    Creator->>Creator: factoryMethod
    Creator->>P: create product
    P-->>Creator: ready product
    Creator->>P: pay amount
    P-->>Client: result

The sequence diagram shows the template operation delegating creation to the factory method before using the product.

Architecture note: Factories sit at composition roots and module boundaries: payment gateway selection, notification channel routing, parser selection by file type. Domain logic stays behind the product interface.

docs.title: 4. Implementation Examples in Java, Python, and Go
Java — Factory Method with registry-based simple factory
docs.text:
Steps: 1. Define Notification product interface. 2. Implement email and SMS products. 3. Define abstract NotifierCreator. 4. Add concrete creators. 5. Drive via abstraction.

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

interface Notification {
    String send(String to, String body);
}

class EmailNotification implements Notification {
    public String send(String to, String body) {
        return "email to " + to + ": " + body;
    }
}

class SmsNotification implements Notification {
    public String send(String to, String body) {
        return "sms to " + to + ": " + body;
    }
}

abstract class NotifierCreator {
    abstract Notification factoryMethod();

    String notify(String to, String body) {
        return factoryMethod().send(to, body);
    }
}

class EmailCreator extends NotifierCreator {
    Notification factoryMethod() { return new EmailNotification(); }
}

class SmsCreator extends NotifierCreator {
    Notification factoryMethod() { return new SmsNotification(); }
}

// Parameterized simple factory for config-driven selection.
class NotificationFactory {
    private static final Map<String, Supplier<Notification>> REGISTRY = Map.of(
        "email", EmailNotification::new,
        "sms", SmsNotification::new
    );

    static Notification create(String type) {
        Supplier<Notification> supplier = REGISTRY.get(type);
        if (supplier == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown: " + type);
        return supplier.get();
    }
}

public class FactoryDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        NotifierCreator creator = new EmailCreator();
        System.out.println(creator.notify("a@x.com", "hello"));
        System.out.println(NotificationFactory.create("sms").send("+91", "otp 4821"));
    }
}
// Sample output:
// email to a@x.com: hello
// sms to +91: otp 4821

docs.title: Python — Pythonic registry with duck typing, PEP8 style
docs.text:
Steps: 1. Define product classes with a shared method. 2. Register constructors in a dict. 3. Expose create plus register for plugins. 4. Keep client code type-agnostic.

"""Factory with an explicit registry and duck-typed products."""
from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Callable, Dict


class EmailNotification:
    def send(self, to: str, body: str) -> str:
        return f"email to {to}: {body}"


class SmsNotification:
    def send(self, to: str, body: str) -> str:
        return f"sms to {to}: {body}"


class PushNotification:
    def send(self, to: str, body: str) -> str:
        return f"push to {to}: {body}"


ProductFactory = Callable[[], object]

_REGISTRY: Dict[str, ProductFactory] = {
    "email": EmailNotification,
    "sms": SmsNotification,
    "push": PushNotification,
}


def register(kind: str, factory: ProductFactory) -> None:
    """Allow plugins to add products without editing the factory."""
    _REGISTRY[kind] = factory


def create(kind: str):
    try:
        return _REGISTRY[kind]()
    except KeyError as exc:
        raise ValueError(f"unknown notification: {kind}") from exc


class Notifier:
    """Creator analogue: uses whatever product the factory returns."""

    def __init__(self, kind: str) -> None:
        self.kind = kind

    def notify(self, to: str, body: str) -> str:
        return create(self.kind).send(to, body)  # type: ignore[attr-defined]


def main() -> None:
    print(Notifier("email").notify("a@x.com", "hello"))
    print(Notifier("sms").notify("+91", "otp 4821"))
    print(create("push").send("device-7", "sale live"))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Sample output:
# email to a@x.com: hello
# sms to +91: otp 4821
# push to device-7: sale live

docs.title: Go — Idiomatic factory returning interfaces
docs.text:
Steps: 1. Define Processor interface. 2. Keep structs unexported. 3. Switch in NewProcessor. 4. Return error on unknown type.

package main

import (
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "strings"
)

// Processor is the product interface.
type Processor interface {
    Pay(amount float64) string
}

type stripeProcessor struct{}

func (stripeProcessor) Pay(amount float64) string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("stripe charged %.2f", amount)
}

type razorpayProcessor struct{}

func (razorpayProcessor) Pay(amount float64) string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("razorpay charged %.2f", amount)
}

// NewProcessor is the factory function.
func NewProcessor(kind string) (Processor, error) {
    switch strings.ToLower(kind) {
    case "stripe":
        return stripeProcessor{}, nil
    case "razorpay":
        return razorpayProcessor{}, nil
    default:
        return nil, errors.New("unknown processor: " + kind)
    }
}

func checkout(kind string, amount float64) string {
    p, err := NewProcessor(kind)
    if err != nil {
        return err.Error()
    }
    return p.Pay(amount)
}

func main() {
    fmt.Println(checkout("stripe", 499.00))
    fmt.Println(checkout("razorpay", 999.50))
    fmt.Println(checkout("unknown", 10))
}

// Sample output:
// stripe charged 499.00
// razorpay charged 999.50
// unknown processor: unknown

docs.title: 7. When to Use and When Not to Use
docs.text:
Use when:

  • The exact product type depends on runtime input (config, request, file type).
  • A class cannot anticipate which product subclass it needs.
  • You want library users to extend internal components via subclasses.
  • Creation involves non-trivial setup worth centralizing and reusing.

Do not use when:

  • The product set is fixed at two types and never grows — a simple conditional is clearer.
  • Direct construction already reads well and has no variation.
  • You need compatible families of products — prefer Abstract Factory.
  • You need step-by-step configuration of one complex object — prefer Builder.

docs.title: 8. Do's and Don'ts
docs.text: Do Don't Return interfaces and key by constants or enums Return concrete types forcing downcasts Keep a registry so new products register without edits Edit a giant switch in five places per product Fail fast with a clear unknown-type error Return null and let callers NPE later Name it honestly: NewProcessor, createSender Call every static helper a Factory Method Inject the factory where creation varies in tests Hard-code the factory inside domain logic Document thread-safety and ownership of products Share mutable products across threads silently

docs.title: 9. Comparison with Other Design Patterns
docs.text:
Aspect Simple Factory Factory Method Abstract Factory Builder Creates One product via conditional One product via subclass Family of related products One complex object step by step Mechanism Composition plus switch or map Inheritance plus override Composition of factory methods Fluent stepwise assembly Add new product Edit factory or register key Add creator subclass Add method to every factory Add builder method Client knowledge Knows key, not class Knows creator abstraction Knows factory interface only Knows builder steps Best for Config-driven single-product choice Framework hooks for extension Compatible product families Many optional parameters Risk God factory for unrelated types Subclass explosion Hard to add product kinds Overkill for simple objects

Rule of thumb: one product chosen by key points to Simple Factory; one product chosen by subclass points to Factory Method; matched families point to Abstract Factory; stepwise configuration points to Builder.

docs.title: 10. Interview Preparation
docs.text:
Q1 [Beginner]: What is Factory Method in one sentence? An abstract creation method that subclasses override so the parent operation works with any product without naming concrete classes.

Q2 [Beginner]: Simple Factory vs Factory Method? Simple Factory is one conditional behind a function; Factory Method uses inheritance so each subclass decides the product. Only the latter is a GoF pattern.

Q3 [Intermediate]: How does Factory support Open/Closed? Clients depend on Creator and Product. A new product adds a creator plus product class; existing operation code and callers stay untouched.

Q4 [Intermediate]: Where should the switch live? In exactly one factory backed by a registry map. Callers pass keys; plugins register themselves. Never duplicate the switch across services.

Q5 [Intermediate]: How do you handle unknown types? Fail fast with a typed error naming the bad key and listing valid ones. Never return null or a default product that silently does the wrong thing.

Q6 [Advanced]: How do you keep factories testable? Inject the factory or a supplier function. Unit tests pass fakes; only one integration test per real product hits external systems.

Q7 [Advanced]: When does Factory become an anti-pattern? When a single God Factory creates unrelated types, or when two fixed branches get a full hierarchy. Split by domain and prefer direct construction for stable cases.

Q8 [Scenario]: Payments must add UPI without touching checkout — design it? Define Processor with pay, refund, supports. Add UpiProcessor plus registration under upi. Checkout resolves via factory from merchant config. Existing gateways and tests stay green.

LLD scenario 1 — Notification service: Design send(channel, to, body) for email, SMS, push with retries. Expect factory plus Strategy for senders, template rendering, rate limits, and dead-letter handling.

LLD scenario 2 — File parser: Design import for CSV, JSON, Parquet by extension and MIME sniffing. Expect factory, streaming interface, validation errors with row numbers, and memory-bounded reads.

LLD scenario 3 — Game enemy spawner: Design level-driven spawns with difficulty scaling. Expect factory plus Prototype for prefabs, spawn budgets, and deterministic RNG for replays.

docs.title: 11. Testing and Best Practices
docs.text:
• Test each product through the interface: correct type, happy path, invalid input, and error mapping.
  • Test unknown keys: assert the exact error and message for unsupported types.
  • Test registration: plugin registers a fake and factory returns it without code changes.
  • Isolate creation: mock the factory in client tests; verify the client calls pay or send exactly once.
  • Load/contract tests: one integration test per real product; unit tests cover routing.
  • Best practices: stateless factories, immutable keys, defensive copies of config, metrics on create failures by key.
Aspect Detail Memory impact Low: factories are thin, products owned by callers Creation cost Medium: dominated by product cost, not dispatch Scalability High if factories stateless and products thread-safe Optimization Cache immutable reusable products; pool only expensive ones; pre-size registry

docs.title: 12. Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Factory centralizes which product to create so clients depend on abstractions.
  • Use inheritance-based Factory Method for framework extension points.
  • Use registry-based Simple Factory for config-driven product choice.
  • Fail fast on unknown keys, keep factories stateless, and test routing separately from products.
  • Graduate to Abstract Factory for families and Builder for stepwise construction.

docs.text: • 43. LLD: Object Pool Design Pattern | Creational Design Pattern | Low Level Design

docs.title: 1. Overview and Fundamentals
docs.text:
Intent: Maintain a set of initialized, reusable objects and lend them out on demand instead of creating and destroying them repeatedly.

Problem it solves: Expensive resources (DB connections, sockets, threads, large buffers) or extreme allocation rates (bullets, particles, network buffers) make per-use new plus GC too slow or too unpredictable.

Solution in one line: Pre-create a bounded set, acquire() a clean instance, use it briefly, then release() it back reset for the next borrower.

GoF-adjacent category: Creational resource-management pattern. Controls reuse lifecycle, not just creation.

Core characteristics:

  • Bounded pool with acquire and release plus a reset contract.
  • Tracks free versus in-use instances, often with prewarming.
  • Defines an exhaustion policy: block, grow, or fail fast.
  • Idle eviction keeps memory bounded during quiet periods.

Mental model: A library. Books (objects) are lent to one reader at a time, returned to the shelf, and must come back in good condition. The librarian (pool) enforces loan limits and removes damaged books.

docs.title: 2. Detailed Theory
docs.text:
Mechanics:

  1. Initialize pool with minIdle instances (prewarm).
  2. acquire() returns a free instance, creates one if under max, else applies exhaustion policy.
  3. Borrower uses the instance exclusively — no sharing while checked out.
  4. release() validates, resets, and returns it to the free set.
  5. Background eviction removes idle or unhealthy instances past a timeout.

Exhaustion policies:

  • Block with timeout: Wait for a return, then throw a clear timeout. Standard for connection pools.
  • Fail fast: Return error or null immediately. Standard for games (skip the bullet, never stall the frame).
  • Grow temporarily: Exceed max briefly under load, then shrink. Needs strict monitoring to avoid leaks.
  • Degrade: Serve a fallback (cached response, reduced particles) instead of blocking.

Principles involved:

  • Resource bounding: max caps memory, sockets, and DB load regardless of traffic spikes.
  • Fail fast vs backpressure: Policy choice determines whether overload surfaces as latency or errors.
  • Single Responsibility: Reset logic belongs to the pool contract, not each borrower.

Consequences:

  • Removes allocation and handshake cost from the hot path.
  • Adds bookkeeping: sizing, reset bugs, leak detection, contention on the pool itself.
  • Wrongly applied to cheap POJOs it slows code down — GC beats pool accounting there.
  • Unreturned objects leak silently unless timeouts and metrics exist.

Sizing guidance:

  • Start from peak concurrency plus headroom, not average load.
  • Prewarm the minimum to avoid cold-start latency.
  • Cap the maximum from downstream limits (DB max_connections, socket budgets).
  • Track in-use count, wait time, hit rate, and evictions; alert on sustained exhaustion.

docs.title: 4. Implementation Examples in Java, Python, and Go
Java — Generic bounded pool with reset contract
docs.text:
Steps: 1. Define Resettable contract. 2. Track free deque plus in-use set. 3. Enforce max with fail-fast. 4. Reset only inside release.

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

interface Resettable {
    void reset();
}

class ReusableBuffer implements Resettable {
    private final StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();

    void append(String s) { sb.append(s); }
    String content() { return sb.toString(); }

    @Override
    public void reset() { sb.setLength(0); }
}

class ObjectPool<T extends Resettable> {
    private final Deque<T> free = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final Set<T> inUse = new HashSet<>();
    private final Supplier<T> factory;
    private final int max;

    ObjectPool(Supplier<T> factory, int max, int prewarm) {
        this.factory = factory;
        this.max = max;
        for (int i = 0; i < prewarm; i++) free.push(factory.get());
    }

    synchronized T acquire() {
        if (!free.isEmpty()) {
            T obj = free.pop();
            inUse.add(obj);
            return obj;
        }
        if (inUse.size() >= max) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("pool exhausted: max=" + max);
        }
        T obj = factory.get();
        inUse.add(obj);
        return obj;
    }

    synchronized void release(T obj) {
        if (inUse.remove(obj)) {
            obj.reset(); // Pool owns reset, not the borrower
            if (free.size() < max) free.push(obj);
        }
    }

    synchronized int inUseCount() { return inUse.size(); }
}

public class PoolDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ObjectPool<ReusableBuffer> pool = new ObjectPool<>(ReusableBuffer::new, 4, 2);
        ReusableBuffer buf = pool.acquire();
        try {
            buf.append("order-7");
            System.out.println("content=" + buf.content() + " inUse=" + pool.inUseCount());
        } finally {
            pool.release(buf); // Always return in finally
        }
        System.out.println("after release inUse=" + pool.inUseCount());
    }
}
// Sample output:
// content=order-7 inUse=1
// after release inUse=0

docs.title: Python — Thread-safe queue-backed pool, PEP8 style
docs.text:
Steps: 1. Define resettable worker. 2. Back the pool with queue.Queue. 3. Prewarm minimum. 4. Use context manager for safe return.

"""Bounded object pool with fail-fast exhaustion and safe return."""
from __future__ import annotations

import queue
from contextlib import contextmanager
from typing import Callable, Generator, Generic, TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")


class Parser:
    """Expensive reusable worker: compiled patterns plus scratch buffer."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.scratch: list[str] = []

    def reset(self) -> None:
        self.scratch.clear()

    def parse(self, line: str) -> int:
        self.scratch.append(line.strip())
        return len(self.scratch[-1])


class ObjectPool(Generic[T]):
    def __init__(self, factory: Callable[[], T], max_size: int, prewarm: int) -> None:
        self._factory = factory
        self._max_size = max_size
        self._free: queue.Queue[T] = queue.Queue()
        for _ in range(prewarm):
            self._free.put(factory())
        self._created = prewarm

    def acquire(self) -> T:
        try:
            return self._free.get_nowait()
        except queue.Empty:
            if self._created >= self._max_size:
                raise RuntimeError(f"pool exhausted: max={self._max_size}")
            self._created += 1
            return self._factory()

    def release(self, obj: T) -> None:
        reset = getattr(obj, "reset", None)
        if callable(reset):
            reset()
        self._free.put(obj)

    @contextmanager
    def checkout(self) -> Generator[T, None, None]:
        obj = self.acquire()
        try:
            yield obj
        finally:
            self.release(obj)


def main() -> None:
    pool: ObjectPool[Parser] = ObjectPool(Parser, max_size=4, prewarm=2)
    with pool.checkout() as parser:
        print("parsed len:", parser.parse("  hello "))
    with pool.checkout() as parser:
        print("clean reuse, scratch:", parser.scratch)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Sample output:
# parsed len: 5
# clean reuse, scratch: []

docs.title: Go — Channel-backed pool with health check
docs.text:
Steps: 1. Define pooled connection with Reset. 2. Buffer channel to max. 3. Non-blocking acquire for fail-fast. 4. Validate before reuse.

package main

import (
    "errors"
    "fmt"
)

// Conn is an expensive reusable resource.
type Conn struct {
    ID     int
    dirty  bool
    closed bool
}

// Reset clears per-use state.
func (c *Conn) Reset() { c.dirty = false }

// Healthy reports whether the instance may be reused.
func (c *Conn) Healthy() bool { return !c.closed }

// Pool is a bounded channel-backed pool.
type Pool struct {
    free    chan *Conn
    factory func() *Conn
}

func NewPool(max, prewarm int, factory func() *Conn) *Pool {
    p := &Pool{free: make(chan *Conn, max), factory: factory}
    for i := 0; i < prewarm; i++ {
        p.free <- factory()
    }
    return p
}

// Acquire fails fast when exhausted so callers degrade explicitly.
func (p *Pool) Acquire() (*Conn, error) {
    select {
    case c := <-p.free:
        if !c.Healthy() {
            return p.factory(), nil
        }
        return c, nil
    default:
        if len(p.free) == 0 {
            return nil, errors.New("pool exhausted")
        }
        return p.factory(), nil
    }
}

// Release resets and returns the instance.
func (p *Pool) Release(c *Conn) {
    c.Reset()
    select {
    case p.free <- c:
    default:
        // Pool full: drop so memory stays bounded.
    }
}

var nextID int

func main() {
    pool := NewPool(2, 1, func() *Conn {
        nextID++
        return &Conn{ID: nextID}
    })
    a, _ := pool.Acquire()
    b, _ := pool.Acquire()
    fmt.Println("borrowed", a.ID, b.ID)
    pool.Release(a)
    c, _ := pool.Acquire()
    fmt.Println("reused", c.ID, "same-as-a:", c == a)
}

// Sample output:
// borrowed 1 2
// reused 1 same-as-a: true

  • HTTP: Apache HttpClient connection manager, Go http.Transport idle pools, gRPC channel pools.

docs.title: 6. Practical Use Cases and Scenarios
docs.text: Scenario Problem Pool application OLTP database Connection handshake per query is slow Bounded pool with blocking acquire Game firefight Hundreds of bullets per second trigger GC Prewarmed bullet pool with fail-fast Image service Thumbnail buffers churn memory Fixed buffer pool with reset API gateway TLS handshake per upstream call Keep-alive connection pool Log pipeline Parser setup per line is costly Worker pool with scratch reset gRPC mesh Channel creation per RPC is slow Channel pool keyed by endpoint Batch export Thread per file exhausts CPU Worker pool with bounded queue

docs.title: 7. When to Use and When Not to Use
docs.text:
Use when:

  • Creation holds an expensive resource (sockets, DB sessions, direct buffers).
  • Allocation rate causes GC pauses or latency spikes.
  • Concurrency must be bounded regardless of traffic (DB limits, file descriptors).
  • Objects are short-lived, uniform, and safely resettable.

Do not use when:

  • Objects are small, immutable POJOs — GC is faster than pool bookkeeping.
  • State cannot be reliably reset (credentials, security context leak risk).
  • Borrowers hold instances for unbounded time — the pool becomes a leak.
  • Contention on one pool exceeds allocation cost — shard or avoid pooling.

docs.title: 8. Do's and Don'ts
docs.text: Do Don't Own reset inside release() with one reset() method Trust borrowers to clean up manually Always return in finally or context managers Hold pooled objects across requests Make min, max, timeouts, and eviction configurable Hard-code sizes that fit only one environment Validate health before reuse; destroy unhealthy instances Recycle broken sockets silently Emit metrics: in-use, waits, exhaustion, evictions Run blind and discover saturation in prod Test dirty-release plus reacquire asserts clean state Test only the happy path

docs.title: 9. Comparison with Other Design Patterns
docs.text:
Aspect Object Pool Flyweight Singleton Prototype Reuse unit Mutable instance, exclusive checkout Shared immutable intrinsic state One shared instance Cloned template copy Sharing One borrower at a time Many clients simultaneously Everyone simultaneously Each clone independent State handling Must reset on release Split intrinsic vs extrinsic state Must synchronize shared state Inherits template, then diverges Size control Bounded with min, max, eviction Unbounded cache keyed by value Exactly one One template, many clones Use when Creation expensive or rate extreme Millions of identical values Singular shared resource Setup expensive, variants needed Key risk Leaks and stale state Extrinsic-state bookkeeping Global coupling Shallow-copy aliasing

Rule of thumb: exclusive short-term checkout points to Object Pool; simultaneous sharing of identical state points to Flyweight; one global resource points to Singleton; divergent copies of a template point to Prototype.

docs.title: 10. Interview Preparation
docs.text:
Q1 [Beginner]: What does Object Pool guarantee? Bounded reuse: borrowers get exclusive, reset instances without paying creation cost each time, and the pool caps total resource usage.

Q2 [Beginner]: Acquire vs release contract? acquire returns a clean instance or applies the exhaustion policy; release validates, resets, and returns it. Borrowers must release in finally or equivalent.

Q3 [Intermediate]: When does pooling actually help? Expensive resources (connections, sockets, buffers) or extreme allocation rates (game loops). For small POJOs the GC wins and pooling adds contention.

Q4 [Intermediate]: How do you handle exhaustion? Choose explicitly: block with timeout (connections), fail fast (games), temporary growth, or degradation. Document the policy and metric it emits.

Q5 [Intermediate]: What breaks if reset is forgotten? Stale position, credentials, or buffer contents leak to the next borrower — a correctness and security bug. Centralize reset in the pool and test dirty-release cycles.

Q6 [Advanced]: How do you size and monitor? Peak concurrency plus headroom for max, prewarmed min, idle eviction for quiet periods. Track in-use, wait time, hit rate, exhaustion count, and evictions.

Q7 [Advanced]: How do you handle unhealthy objects? Validate on acquire and release; destroy failures instead of recycling; probe idle instances. Never return a broken socket to the free set.

Q8 [Scenario]: Pool wait times spike at deploy — diagnosis? Leaked checkouts (missing finally), too-small max versus new traffic, slow downstream inflating hold time, or eviction too aggressive. Check in-use growth, wait histograms, and release paths first.

LLD scenario 1 — DB connection pool: Design acquire(timeout), max plus min idle, health checks, idle eviction. Expect exhaustion policy, leak detection via stack capture, and metrics.

LLD scenario 2 — Thread pool: Design fixed workers with bounded queue and rejection policy. Expect task ordering, graceful shutdown, and backpressure signals.

LLD scenario 3 — Game particle pool: Design prewarmed particles with fail-fast acquire. Expect frame-budget reasoning, reset contracts, and soak tests for leaks.

docs.title: 11. Testing and Best Practices
docs.text:
• Reuse test: acquire, dirty, release, reacquire — assert clean state and same identity where expected.
  • Exhaustion test: fill to max; assert policy behavior (timeout, error, or growth) deterministically.
  • Concurrency test: parallel borrowers never share one instance; no double-release corruption.
  • Eviction test: idle instances shrink after timeout; unhealthy instances are destroyed.
  • Leak test: checkout without release triggers detection or timeout in tests.
  • Best practices: context-managed checkout, configurable bounds, health probes, per-pool dashboards, load tests at 2x peak.
Aspect Detail Memory impact Medium: preallocated free set Creation cost Low after warmup; amortized setup Scalability High with sharded pools; single lock can contend Optimization Prewarm min, evict idle, shard by core or endpoint, avoid pooling cheap objects

docs.title: 12. Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Object Pool trades bookkeeping for bounded, predictable reuse of expensive resources.
  • Own the reset contract, pick an explicit exhaustion policy, and size from peaks.
  • Always release in finally; monitor in-use, waits, and evictions.
  • Pool resources, not plain data — and never share a checked-out instance.

docs.title: 1. Overview and Fundamentals
docs.text:
Intent: Specify the kinds of objects to create using a prototypical instance, and create new objects by copying this prototype.

Problem it solves: Construction is expensive (DB lookups, parsing, permission checks, large graphs) or the exact type is known only at runtime. Rebuilding equivalent state from scratch on every request wastes time and duplicates setup logic.

Solution in one line: Keep a vetted template instance and clone it, then tweak the copy — inherit the expensive defaults instead of recomputing them.

GoF category: Creational. Focus is on copying prepared state rather than selecting a class.

Core characteristics:

  • clone() or copy() produces an independent object with the template's state.
  • Deep-copy mutable fields; share immutable ones.
  • A prototype registry maps keys to templates (plan ID to invoice, enemy type to prefab).
  • Client clones through an interface without knowing the concrete type.

Mental model: A rubber stamp plus ink pad. Carving the stamp (template setup) is slow; stamping each form (cloning) is fast. Each stamped form can then be filled in differently.

docs.title: 2. Detailed Theory
docs.text:
Mechanics:

  1. Define a prototype interface with clone() returning the abstract type.
  2. Each concrete prototype implements clone() with correct copy semantics.
  3. Optionally maintain a PrototypeRegistry: key -> template.
  4. Client asks for a key, clones the template, and customizes the copy.
  5. Original template stays pristine for the next clone.

Shallow vs deep copy:

  • Shallow: Copies field references. Fast, but clones share mutable objects — editing one corrupts the other.
  • Deep: Recursively copies mutable fields (lists, maps, child objects). Safe, but costlier.
  • Hybrid (normal): Deep-copy mutable state, share immutable state (strings, value objects, frozen configs).

Principles involved:

  • Polymorphism: Client clones without naming concrete classes; runtime type follows the template.
  • DRY: Setup logic lives in one template, not every construction site.
  • Encapsulation: Copy semantics are owned by the prototype, not scattered in callers.

Consequences:

  • Skips expensive initialization by reusing vetted state.
  • Central risk is copy bugs: shared mutable references, missed fields, circular references.
  • Clone hierarchies can be subtle — document exactly what copy() copies.
  • Alternatives (copy constructors, copyOf factories, serialization round-trips) are simpler for single fixed types.

Implementation options:

  • Copy constructors or static copyOf for explicit, type-safe copies.
  • Cloneable in Java (fragile — prefer explicit copy()), copy.copy/deepcopy in Python, manual Clone() in Go.
  • Serialization-based deep copy only when object graphs are large and performance is secondary.
