    Client --> Prototype : clones

The class diagram shows the client depending only on the clone interface while concrete prototypes define their own copy logic.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Registry as PrototypeRegistry
    participant T as Template
    participant C as Clone
    Client->>Registry: get template key
    Registry-->>Client: template reference
    Client->>T: clone
    T->>C: deep copy mutable state
    C-->>Client: independent copy
    Client->>C: customize fields

The sequence diagram shows lookup, cloning with deep copy, and per-use customization leaving the template untouched.

Architecture note: Registries live near composition roots or repositories (billing templates, prefab stores, pipeline configs). Cloning happens per request; templates refresh on versioned updates.

docs.title: 4. Implementation Examples in Java, Python, and Go
Java — Invoice template with deep copy
docs.text:
Steps: 1. Model mutable LineItem with explicit copy(). 2. Give Invoice a copy() that deep-copies the list. 3. Hold templates in a service. 4. Clone per customer.

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

class LineItem {
    String sku;
    int qty;
    double unitPrice;

    LineItem(String sku, int qty, double unitPrice) {
        this.sku = sku;
        this.qty = qty;
        this.unitPrice = unitPrice;
    }

    LineItem copy() {
        return new LineItem(sku, qty, unitPrice); // Strings immutable: share safely
    }
}

class Invoice {
    String planId;
    double taxRate;
    String customerId;
    List<LineItem> items = new ArrayList<>();

    Invoice copy() {
        Invoice clone = new Invoice();
        clone.planId = this.planId;
        clone.taxRate = this.taxRate;
        for (LineItem item : this.items) {
            clone.items.add(item.copy()); // Deep-copy mutable list
        }
        return clone;
    }

    double total() {
        double sub = 0;
        for (LineItem item : items) sub += item.qty * item.unitPrice;
        return sub * (1 + taxRate);
    }
}

class BillingService {
    private final Invoice proTemplate;

    BillingService(Invoice proTemplate) { this.proTemplate = proTemplate; }

    Invoice bill(String customerId) {
        Invoice invoice = proTemplate.copy();
        invoice.customerId = customerId;
        return invoice;
    }
}

public class PrototypeDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Invoice template = new Invoice();
        template.planId = "pro";
        template.taxRate = 0.18;
        template.items.add(new LineItem("seat", 5, 20.0));

        BillingService billing = new BillingService(template);
        Invoice inv = billing.bill("cust-42");
        inv.items.get(0).qty = 6; // Mutate only the copy

        System.out.println("copy total=" + inv.total());
        System.out.println("template qty=" + template.items.get(0).qty);
    }
}
// Sample output:
// copy total=141.6
// template qty=5

docs.title: Python — Prefab registry with copy.deepcopy, PEP8 style
docs.text:
Steps: 1. Define dataclass templates. 2. Register one per key. 3. deepcopy on checkout. 4. Customize the copy.

"""Prototype registry for game enemy prefabs."""
from __future__ import annotations

import copy
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Dict, List


@dataclass
class Enemy:
    kind: str
    hp: int
    loot: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)


class PrefabRegistry:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._templates: Dict[str, Enemy] = {}

    def register(self, key: str, template: Enemy) -> None:
        self._templates[key] = template

    def spawn(self, key: str, hp_boost: int = 0) -> Enemy:
        try:
            template = self._templates[key]
        except KeyError as exc:
            raise ValueError(f"unknown prefab: {key}") from exc
        clone = copy.deepcopy(template)  # lists must not be shared
        clone.hp += hp_boost
        return clone


def main() -> None:
    registry = PrefabRegistry()
    registry.register("goblin", Enemy(kind="goblin", hp=30, loot=["coin"]))
    first = registry.spawn("goblin")
    first.loot.append("dagger")
    second = registry.spawn("goblin", hp_boost=10)
    print(first)
    print(second)
    print(registry.spawn("goblin").loot)  # template loot untouched


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Sample output:
# Enemy(kind='goblin', hp=30, loot=['coin', 'dagger'])
# Enemy(kind='goblin', hp=40, loot=['coin'])
# ['coin']

docs.title: Go — Manual Clone with deep-copied slice
docs.text:
Steps: 1. Define struct with slice field. 2. Write Clone copying the slice. 3. Store templates in a map. 4. Clone per use.

package main

import "fmt"

// Report is the prototype: sections slice must be deep-copied.
type Report struct {
    Title    string
    Sections []string
}

// Clone returns an independent copy.
func (r Report) Clone() Report {
    sections := make([]string, len(r.Sections))
    copy(sections, r.Sections)
    r.Sections = sections
    return r
}

// Registry holds one vetted template per key.
type Registry map[string]Report

func (rg Registry) Build(key, title string) (Report, error) {
    tmpl, ok := rg[key]
    if !ok {
        return Report{}, fmt.Errorf("unknown template: %s", key)
    }
    clone := tmpl.Clone()
    clone.Title = title
    return clone, nil
}

func main() {
    registry := Registry{
        "weekly": {Title: "weekly", Sections: []string{"sales", "churn"}},
    }
    first, _ := registry.Build("weekly", "week-42")
    first.Sections[0] = "edited"
    second, _ := registry.Build("weekly", "week-43")
    fmt.Println(first.Sections)
    fmt.Println(second.Sections)
}

// Sample output:
// [edited churn]
// [sales churn]

docs.title: 5. Real-World Industry Applications
docs.text:
• Game engines: Unity prefabs, Unreal blueprints spawned by cloning.
  • Billing / ERP: Invoice, contract, and report templates cloned per customer.
  • Document editors: Styles, slide masters, and page layouts duplicated per document.
  • ML platforms: Pipeline configs and experiment templates cloned per run.
  • JavaScript: Object.create(prototype) delegation; React element cloning.
  • Java: Object.clone(), prototype bean scope in Spring.
  • Compilers / IDEs: AST node copying during transforms and refactorings.

docs.title: 6. Practical Use Cases and Scenarios
docs.text: Scenario Problem Prototype application SaaS billing Rebuilding tax rules per invoice is slow Clone plan template, set customer Game spawning Constructing enemies per frame is costly Clone prefab, tweak HP and position Report generation Layout lookup per export is expensive Clone layout, fill data ML experiments Config assembly repeated per run Clone base config, override hyperparams Document editor New docs need approved styles Clone style master per document Test fixtures Setup repeated per test Clone base fixture, vary one field Network simulation Topology build is heavy Clone topology, perturb one link

docs.title: 7. When to Use and When Not to Use
docs.text:
Use when:

  • Construction costs more than copying (I/O, parsing, large graphs).
  • Many instances share most state with small per-use differences.
  • The concrete type is known only at runtime (registry key, plugin).
  • You want to avoid parallel factory hierarchies for variants.

Do not use when:

  • Objects are trivial POJOs — new plus setters is clearer.
  • Copy semantics are unclear or circular references abound — prefer explicit builders.
  • Templates change frequently without versioning — stale clones cause bugs.
  • Immutability already lets you share safely — no cloning needed.

docs.title: 8. Do's and Don'ts
docs.text: Do Don't Deep-copy every mutable field; document what is shared Ship shallow copies that alias template state Keep a registry keyed by versioned template names Scatter template instances across call sites Prefer explicit copy() or copy constructors Rely on fragile Cloneable plus super.clone() Test that mutating the clone leaves the template pristine Assume copying works without a mutation test Version templates and refresh clones on update Clone stale configs silently Handle circular references explicitly or forbid them Recurse infinitely on cyclic graphs

docs.title: 9. Comparison with Other Design Patterns
docs.text:
Aspect Prototype Factory Method Builder Object Pool Object source Copies an existing instance Builds new via subclass Assembles stepwise Checks out a reusable instance State inheritance Full template state Constructor defaults Staged builder state Previous borrower residue unless reset Cost model Cheap when setup is expensive Cheap when construction is simple Medium: staging plus validation Cheap when allocation rate is extreme Type flexibility Runtime: whichever template is cloned Compile-time: subclass hierarchy Single type, many configs Fixed pooled type Key risk Shallow-copy aliasing Subclass explosion Overkill for simple objects Leaks and stale state Best for Templates with expensive defaults Extension hooks Optional-heavy objects Short-lived high-frequency reuse

Rule of thumb: clone when a vetted instance already holds the right state; construct via Factory when a hierarchy decides the type; assemble via Builder when configuration is stepwise; pool when allocation rate dominates.

docs.title: 10. Interview Preparation
docs.text:
Q1 [Beginner]: What is Prototype in one sentence? Create new objects by copying a prepared template instead of building from scratch, then customize the copy.

Q2 [Beginner]: Shallow vs deep copy? Shallow copies field references and shares mutable state; deep copies mutable fields recursively so the clone is independent. Share immutable fields, deep-copy mutable ones.

Q3 [Intermediate]: When is Prototype faster than new? When construction involves DB lookups, parsing, permission checks, or large graphs. Cloning skips that work. For trivial objects new is clearer and equally fast.

Q4 [Intermediate]: What is a prototype registry? A map from key to template. Clients request a key and clone the result, centralizing template management and versioning.

Q5 [Intermediate]: Prototype vs copy constructor? Copy constructors are explicit and type-safe for one class. Prototype adds polymorphism — clone through an interface without knowing the concrete type.

Q6 [Advanced]: How do you handle circular references? Track visited objects during deep copy (identity map), or forbid cycles in prototype graphs. Serialization-based copies handle cycles but cost more.

Q7 [Advanced]: How do you version templates safely? Key templates by name plus version, make refresh atomic (swap registry reference), and stamp clones with the template version for traceability.

Q8 [Scenario]: Invoice totals drift after template edits — why? Clones share the items list via shallow copy. Fix with deep copy plus a regression test that mutates the clone and asserts the template is unchanged.

LLD scenario 1 — Game spawner: Design prefab registry with per-level overrides. Expect deep-copy rules, spawn budgets, and deterministic reseeds.

LLD scenario 2 — Report templating: Design layout templates with per-tenant branding. Expect versioned registry, clone-then-fill flow, and golden-output tests.

LLD scenario 3 — Config experiments: Design base ML config with per-run overrides. Expect immutable snapshots, merge semantics, and lineage tracking.

docs.title: 11. Testing and Best Practices
docs.text:
• Independence test: mutate every mutable field of the clone; assert template unchanged.
  • Equality test: clone equals template on creation, diverges after customization.
  • Registry tests: known keys clone, unknown keys error, version upgrade swaps atomically.
  • Performance test: benchmark clone versus fresh construction to justify the pattern.
  • Best practices: document copy semantics per class, prefer explicit copy(), freeze shared state, and treat templates as versioned data.
Aspect Detail Memory impact Medium: templates plus per-use clones Creation cost Low per clone when setup is reused Scalability High for read-mostly templates; copy cost grows with graph size Optimization Share immutable subgraphs; copy-on-write for large fields; cache templates

docs.title: 12. Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Prototype reuses prepared state by cloning instead of reconstructing.
  • Deep-copy mutable fields, share immutable ones, and document the split.
  • Manage templates in a versioned registry; keep originals pristine.
  • Prefer explicit copy methods over magic cloning; test independence on every prototype.

docs.title: Youtube
docs.text: • 28. BUG in Double-Checked Locking of Singleton Pattern & its Fix | Low Level System Design Question

docs.title: 1. Overview and Fundamentals
docs.text:
Intent: Ensure a class has exactly one instance and provide a global point of access to it.

Problem it solves: Uncontrolled object creation leads to multiple instances of resources that must be singular — configuration, connection pools, registries. Direct new everywhere makes lifecycle, consistency, and access coordination impossible.

Solution in one line: Make the constructor private, hold one static instance, and expose it through a controlled static accessor.

GoF category: Creational. It controls how many instances exist, not which subclass is created.

Core characteristics:

  • Single instance guarantee enforced by the class itself.
  • Global access via getInstance().
  • Lazy or eager initialization.
  • Often combined with thread-safety and serialization guards.

Mental model: Think of a building with one reception desk. Everyone enters through the same desk (getInstance()), and the building constructor (private) prevents anyone from building a second desk.

docs.title: 2. Detailed Theory
docs.text:
Mechanics:

  1. Private constructor blocks external new.
  2. Private static field holds the sole instance.
  3. Public static method returns that instance, creating it on first call if lazy.
  4. Guards against reflection, serialization, and cloning that could forge a second instance.

Common variants:

  • Eager initialization: Instance created at class-load time. Simple, thread-safe by default, but pays startup cost even if unused.
  • Lazy with synchronization: Instance created on first use. Needs locking to stay thread-safe.
  • Double-checked locking (DCL): Checks null before and inside synchronized block with volatile. Fixes the classic Java bug where a half-constructed object leaks without volatile.
  • Bill Pugh / Initialization-on-demand holder: Inner static class holds the instance. JVM loads it once, lazily, with no explicit locking.
  • Enum singleton: enum AppConfig { INSTANCE; }. JVM guarantees one constant, with built-in thread safety, serialization safety, and reflection resistance.
  • DI-container singleton: Framework scope (Spring @Scope("singleton"), .NET AddSingleton). The container enforces singularity; preferred in application code.

Principles involved:

  • Single Responsibility tension: The class manages both its lifecycle and its business logic, which is why overuse violates SRP.
  • Encapsulation: Creation knowledge is hidden behind the accessor.
  • Open/Closed: Subclassing a singleton is awkward; prefer composition or DI scopes if extensibility matters.

Consequences:

  • Controlled access and reduced namespace pollution versus raw globals.
  • Hidden dependencies: callers secretly depend on global mutable state.
  • Test coupling: tests share state unless the singleton is resettable or behind an interface.
  • Concurrency risk: lazy singletons without correct locking publish partially constructed objects.

docs.title: 3. UML and Architecture Diagrams
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Singleton {
        -instance : Singleton
        -Singleton()
        +getInstance() Singleton
        +doWork() void
    }
    class Client {
        +run() void
    }
    Client --> Singleton : uses getInstance

The class diagram shows the private constructor plus static accessor that forces all clients through one instance.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C1 as Client A
    participant C2 as Client B
    participant S as Singleton
    C1->>S: getInstance
    S-->>C1: return instance
    C2->>S: getInstance
    S-->>C2: return same instance
    C1->>S: doWork
    C2->>S: doWork

The sequence diagram shows two clients receiving the same instance and sharing its state.

Architecture note: In layered systems the singleton typically lives in the infrastructure layer (config, logging, pool manager). Domain and application layers depend on its interface, not the concrete singleton class, so tests can substitute a fake.

docs.title: 4. Implementation Examples in Java, Python, and Go
Java — Interface-backed enum singleton with lazy holder alternative
docs.text:
Steps: 1. Define ConfigProvider interface. 2. Implement it once. 3. Hide construction. 4. Expose via accessor. 5. Inject the interface into services.

interface ConfigProvider {
    String get(String key);
}

// Enum form: thread-safe, serialization-safe, reflection-safe.
enum AppConfig implements ConfigProvider {
    INSTANCE;
    private final java.util.Map<String, String> values =
        java.util.Map.of("env", "prod", "region", "ap-south-1");

    @Override
    public String get(String key) {
        return values.get(key);
    }
}

// Lazy holder alternative for heavyweight resources.
class MetricsRegistry {
    private final java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap<String,
        java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder> counters =
        new java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    private MetricsRegistry() {}

    private static class Holder {
        static final MetricsRegistry INSTANCE = new MetricsRegistry();
    }

    static MetricsRegistry getInstance() {
        return Holder.INSTANCE;
    }

    void increment(String name) {
        counters.computeIfAbsent(name, k -> new java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder())
            .increment();
    }

    long count(String name) {
        var adder = counters.get(name);
        return adder == null ? 0 : adder.sum();
    }
}

class OrderService {
    private final ConfigProvider config;
    OrderService(ConfigProvider config) { this.config = config; }
    void placeOrder() {
        System.out.println("order in env=" + config.get("env"));
        MetricsRegistry.getInstance().increment("orders.placed");
    }
}

public class SingletonDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        OrderService svc = new OrderService(AppConfig.INSTANCE);
        svc.placeOrder();
        svc.placeOrder();
        System.out.println("count=" + MetricsRegistry.getInstance().count("orders.placed"));
    }
}
// Sample output:
// order in env=prod
// order in env=prod
// count=2

docs.title: Python — Module-friendly Borg / metaclass singleton, PEP8 style
docs.text:
Steps: 1. Use a metaclass to enforce one instance. 2. Guard __init__ against re-running. 3. Inject the instance where needed. 4. Provide reset_for_tests hook.

"""Idiomatic singleton via metaclass with test reset hook."""
from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Any, Dict


class _SingletonMeta(type):
    _instances: Dict[type, Any] = {}

    def __call__(cls, *args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> Any:
        if cls not in cls._instances:
            cls._instances[cls] = super().__call__(*args, **kwargs)
        return cls._instances[cls]


class AppConfig(metaclass=_SingletonMeta):
    """Application configuration loaded once."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        if getattr(self, "_loaded", False):
            return
        self.values = {"env": "prod", "region": "ap-south-1"}
        self._loaded = True

    def get(self, key: str, default: str = "") -> str:
        return self.values.get(key, default)

    @classmethod
    def reset_for_tests(cls) -> None:
        _SingletonMeta._instances.pop(cls, None)


class OrderService:
    def __init__(self, config: AppConfig) -> None:
        self.config = config

    def place_order(self) -> str:
        return f"order in env={self.config.get('env')}"


def main() -> None:
    first = AppConfig()
    second = AppConfig()
    print(first is second)  # True
    print(OrderService(first).place_order())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Sample output:
# True
# order in env=prod

docs.title: Go — sync.Once singleton with interface
docs.text:
Steps: 1. Define ConfigProvider interface. 2. Keep struct unexported. 3. Guard creation with sync.Once. 4. Return interface from GetConfig.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "sync"
)

// ConfigProvider is the abstraction callers depend on.
type ConfigProvider interface {
    Get(key string) string
}

type appConfig struct {
    values map[string]string
}

func (c *appConfig) Get(key string) string { return c.values[key] }

var (
    configOnce     sync.Once
    configInstance ConfigProvider
)

// GetConfig returns the single shared config.
func GetConfig() ConfigProvider {
    configOnce.Do(func() {
        configInstance = &appConfig{
            values: map[string]string{"env": "prod", "region": "ap-south-1"},
        }
    })
    return configInstance
}

type OrderService struct{ Config ConfigProvider }

func (s OrderService) PlaceOrder() string {
    return "order in env=" + s.Config.Get("env")
}

func main() {
    a := GetConfig()
    b := GetConfig()
    fmt.Println(a == b) // true: same pointer-backed instance
    fmt.Println(OrderService{Config: a}.PlaceOrder())
}

// Sample output:
// true
// order in env=prod

docs.title: 5. Real-World Industry Applications
docs.text:
• Spring Framework: Default bean scope is singleton. ApplicationContext, service beans share one instance per container.
  • Django / Flask: Settings object loaded once per process; Flask app extensions often registered once.
  • Logging: Log4j2, SLF4J, Python logging root logger — one hierarchy per process.
  • Connection pools: HikariCP, C3P0, SQLAlchemy engine, Redis client — one pool manager shared by threads.
  • Observability: Prometheus client registries, OpenTelemetry meter providers.
  • OS / platform: File system abstraction, window manager, DriverManager, Android Application class.
  • Cloud SDKs: AWS SDK default clients reused process-wide to share HTTP pools.

docs.title: 6. Practical Use Cases and Scenarios
docs.text: Scenario Problem Singleton application App configuration Config parsed in many places, must agree One AppConfig loaded at startup Structured logging Scattered loggers with different formats One logger hierarchy with shared handlers DB connection pool Too many connections exhaust the DB One pool manager with bounded size Metrics registry Counters fragmented per service One registry scraped by Prometheus Feature flags Inconsistent flag reads during rollout One flag client with cached snapshot Rate limiter Per-instance limits too permissive One token-bucket shared by handlers ID generator Duplicate Snowflake node IDs One generator with claimed node ID

docs.title: 7. When to Use and When Not to Use
docs.text:
Use when:

  • Exactly one instance must exist system-wide (pool manager, registry, scheduler).
  • A well-known global access point is genuinely required (bootstrap code without DI).
  • Lazy startup cost is high and the resource may never be used.
  • The guarantee must hold regardless of container configuration (libraries, agents).

Do not use when:

  • The need is "convenient global access" rather than singularity — use DI or explicit parameters.
  • The object holds request-scoped or user-scoped mutable state.
  • You need subclass polymorphism per context — singletons resist extension.
  • Test isolation matters and no seam exists to substitute the instance.
  • A DI container already offers singleton scope with explicit constructor injection.

docs.title: 8. Do's and Don'ts
docs.text: Do Don't Program callers to an interface and inject it Sprinkle getInstance() calls in every class Prefer enum (Java), holder idiom, or sync.Once (Go) Write broken DCL without volatile / mutex Guard serialization with readResolve and block clone() Assume private constructor alone is enough Keep singletons stateless or carefully synchronized Store request/user state in a singleton Provide a test reset or injectable fake Let global state leak between tests Document thread-safety and lifecycle explicitly Hide blocking or heavy I/O in getInstance()

docs.title: 9. Comparison with Other Design Patterns
docs.text:
Aspect Singleton Static utility class DI singleton scope Monostate Instance Exactly one object No instance, static methods One per container Many instances, shared static state Interface support Yes, can implement interfaces No clean polymorphism Yes, full constructor injection Yes, but state still global Lazy init Yes: holder, enum, Once Class-load timing only Yes, container-managed Per-instance init, shared data Testability Moderate if behind interface Poor, hard to mock Excellent, swap bindings Poor, state leaks silently Subclassing Limited but possible Impossible Easy via bindings Confusing, avoid Best for Singular stateful resource Stateless helpers like Math Application services Rarely; prefer Singleton

Rule of thumb: stateless helpers point to a static utility; application services point to DI scope; a guarantee that must survive outside any container points to a hand-rolled Singleton.

docs.title: 10. Interview Preparation
docs.text:
Q1 [Beginner]: What does Singleton guarantee? Exactly one instance per classloader/process plus global access through a static accessor, enforced by a private constructor and a single stored instance.

Q2 [Beginner]: Why is the Java enum form recommended? The JVM instantiates each enum constant once. That gives thread safety without locking, plus serialization and reflection safety by specification.

Q3 [Intermediate]: What is the DCL bug and its fix? Without volatile, the JVM may publish a partially constructed object because writes can reorder. Declaring the field volatile plus checking null before and inside the synchronized block fixes it. The holder idiom avoids the issue entirely.

Q4 [Intermediate]: How can Singleton be broken? Reflection via setAccessible, deserialization creating a new instance per readObject, cloning, and multiple classloaders each loading their own copy. Mitigate with enum, readResolve, clone() refusal, and constructor guard.

Q5 [Intermediate]: Singleton vs static class? Only Singleton creates an object that can implement interfaces, be injected, lazily initialized, and subclassed in a controlled way. Static utilities suit stateless functions.

Q6 [Advanced]: Why do reviewers call it an anti-pattern? It hides dependencies as global mutable state, couples tests through execution order, and violates SRP. Restrict it to truly singular infrastructure and expose it behind injectable interfaces.

Q7 [Advanced]: How do you make it testable? Depend on the interface, inject the singleton in constructors, and provide a fake plus a reset hook. In Python add reset_for_tests; in Java expose a package-private setter or use DI bindings.

Q8 [Scenario]: Two singletons in microservices — still singular? No. Each process has its own instance. For cross-process singularity use a centralized store (DB advisory lock, Redis lease, coordination service), not an in-process singleton.

LLD scenario 1 — Config manager: Design a reloadable config with get(key) and background refresh. Expect discussion of read-write locks, immutable snapshots, listener notification, and why readers never block on refresh.

LLD scenario 2 — Connection pool manager: Design a bounded pool with acquire(timeout) and release(conn). Expect exhaustion policy, health checks, idle eviction, metrics, and thread-safe bookkeeping.

LLD scenario 3 — Logger: Design per-module loggers sharing one hierarchy with levels and handlers. Expect singleton registry plus Flyweight-like logger cache and async appenders.

docs.title: 11. Testing and Best Practices
docs.text:
• Test the contract: same reference on repeated calls, thread-safety under parallel getInstance(), serialization round-trip preserves identity.
  • Isolate tests: reset between tests or inject fakes; never rely on execution order.
  • Concurrency test: spawn N threads calling the accessor; assert one unique identity and no partial state.
  • Serialization test: serialize and deserialize; assert deserialized is instance.
  • Prefer DI: hand-roll only for libraries, agents, and bootstrap; application code should use container scope.
Aspect Detail Memory impact Low: one instance Creation cost One-time; lazy defers heavy init Scalability High if stateless or lock-free; contention if synchronized hot path Optimization Holder/Once for lazy safety; immutable snapshots for readers; avoid I/O in accessor

docs.title: 12. Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Singleton answers "how many" — exactly one — with a private constructor plus controlled accessor.
  • Prefer enum, holder idiom, or sync.Once over hand-rolled locking.
  • Guard reflection, serialization, and cloning; document thread-safety.
  • Keep singletons for singular infrastructure; use DI scope for everything else.
  • Always program to an interface so tests can substitute the global instance.

docs.title: Youtube
docs.text: • 20. Adapter Design Pattern with Examples, LLD | Low Level Design Interview Question | System Design

docs.title: 1. Overview and Fundamentals
docs.text:
Intent (GoF): Convert the interface of a class into another interface clients expect. Adapter lets classes work together that couldn't otherwise because of incompatible interfaces.

In one line: Adapter is a translator — it implements the interface your code wants and delegates to the thing you actually have.

Real-world analogy: A universal travel plug. Your laptop charger (adaptee) has a US plug, the Indian wall socket (target) expects a different shape. You don't rewire the hotel — you plug an adapter in between.

Family context: Adapter is a structural pattern. Structural patterns deal with how classes and objects are composed into larger structures. Adapter specifically deals with interface mismatch.

Key participants:

  • Target — interface the client depends on (e.g., PaymentProcessor).
  • Client — uses only Target (e.g., CheckoutService).
  • Adaptee — existing class with incompatible API (e.g., StripeGateway, legacy LegacyPlug).
  • Adapter — implements Target, holds/translates to Adaptee.

Core characteristics:

  • Wraps an existing object; does not change its code.
  • Translates method names, signatures, units, protocols, exceptions.
  • Client and adaptee never reference each other directly.
  • Follows Open/Closed Principle: add new providers via new adapters.
  • Typically one adapter per adaptee-to-target mapping.

Mental model:

Client -> Target.pay() -> Adapter.pay() converts -> Adaptee.createCharge()

If the wrapper changes signatures to make code compile, it is an Adapter. If it only simplifies, it is a Facade. If it adds features with the same interface, it is a Decorator.

docs.title: 2. Detailed Theory
docs.text:
Problem: You own clean client code built against interface T. You need to reuse a library, SDK, or legacy class that exposes interface S != T. You cannot (or should not) modify either side — the library is third-party, the client is stable.

Solution: Introduce an Adapter that implements T and internally calls S, performing any data conversion, exception mapping, and sequencing in between.

Two classic variants:

  1. Object Adapter (composition — preferred): Adapter has-a adaptee and delegates. Works in any language, supports multiple adaptees, allows lazy creation and decoration. All examples in Section 4 are object adapters.
  2. Class Adapter (inheritance — Java/C++ only): Adapter extends adaptee and implements target. Only works when you need to override adaptee behaviour and single inheritance permits it. Rare in modern Java; impossible in Go/Python in the same form.

Two-way and pluggable adapters:

  • One-way adapter: Most common — StripeGateway -> PaymentProcessor.
  • Two-way adapter: Implements both interfaces so either side can call; useful for tool interop but doubles surface area.
  • Pluggable adapter with default: Provide a default no-op adaptee so clients can run without the real SDK in tests.

What translation typically includes:

  • Naming: pay() -> createCharge(), sendPayment().
  • Units/types: rupees double -> paise long, INR -> USD, Date -> epoch.
  • Arity/ordering: combining connect() + send() into one publish() call.
  • Error model: SDK exceptions -> domain exceptions (StripeException -> PaymentFailedException).
  • Lifecycle: lazy connect, retry, timeout wrapping around adaptee calls.

SOLID and principles:

  • Open/Closed: New adaptee = new adapter class, zero client edits.
  • Dependency Inversion: Client depends on Target abstraction, not SDK concretes.
  • Single Responsibility: Each adapter owns one integration's quirks (currency, auth, pagination).
  • Interface Segregation: Target should be narrow; don't force adapters to implement methods the adaptee cannot support — split interfaces or throw UnsupportedOperationException explicitly.

Consequences:

  • Reuse without modification, at the cost of one indirection layer.
  • Centralises third-party quirks so vendor swap is localised.
  • Overused, it hides bad domain modelling behind translators — if you own both sides, refactor instead.

docs.title: Diagram 1 — Class structure (object adapter)
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Client {
        +checkout(amount: double)
    }
    class PaymentProcessor {
        <>
        +pay(amountInr: double) String
        +refund(txnId: String, amountInr: double) bool
    }
    class StripeAdapter {
        -stripe: StripeGateway
        +pay(amountInr: double) String
        +refund(txnId: String, amountInr: double) bool
    }
    class PayPalAdapter {
        -paypal: PayPalClient
        +pay(amountInr: double) String
        +refund(txnId: String, amountInr: double) bool
    }
    class StripeGateway {
        +createCharge(paise: long) String
        +reverseCharge(id: String, paise: long) bool
    }
    class PayPalClient {
        +sendPayment(usd: double) String
        +voidPayment(txnId: String) bool
    }
    Client --> PaymentProcessor : uses
    PaymentProcessor <|.. StripeAdapter : implements
    PaymentProcessor <|.. PayPalAdapter : implements
    StripeAdapter --> StripeGateway : adapts
    PayPalAdapter --> PayPalClient : adapts

Explanation: CheckoutService (Client) depends only on PaymentProcessor (Target). StripeAdapter and PayPalAdapter implement that target and each holds a reference to its own adaptee. Adding Razorpay means adding one new class implementing PaymentProcessor — no client change. This is why object adapters scale: N providers need N adapters, not N client branches.

docs.title: Diagram 2 — Runtime call flow (sequence)
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Checkout as CheckoutService
    participant Adapter as StripeAdapter
    participant Adaptee as StripeGateway
    Checkout->>Adapter: pay(500.0)
    Adapter->>Adapter: convert rupees to paise (50000)
    Adapter->>Adaptee: createCharge(50000)
    Adaptee-->>Adapter: stripe_ch_50000
    Adapter-->>Checkout: stripe_ch_50000

Explanation: The sequence shows where translation happens. The client calls the domain method pay() with rupees. The adapter does the unglamorous but critical work — unit conversion, then delegation — before returning the SDK's transaction id unchanged. Error paths follow the same route in reverse: SDK exceptions are caught in the adapter and rethrown as domain exceptions so the client never imports Stripe types.

docs.title: 4. Implementation Examples in Java, Python, and Go
4.1 Java (OOP, object adapter)
docs.text:
Explanation: CheckoutService depends only on PaymentProcessor. StripeAdapter converts rupees to paise and delegates to StripeGateway. The main method wires the adapter in — swapping to PayPalAdapter is a one-line change. This file compiles with javac AdapterDemo.java && java AdapterDemo.

interface PaymentProcessor {
    String pay(double amountInr);
    boolean refund(String txnId, double amountInr);
}

class StripeGateway {
    String createCharge(long amountPaise) {
        return "stripe_ch_" + amountPaise;
    }
    boolean reverseCharge(String chargeId, long amountPaise) {
        return true;
    }
}

class StripeAdapter implements PaymentProcessor {
    private final StripeGateway stripe = new StripeGateway();

    @Override
    public String pay(double amountInr) {
        long paise = Math.round(amountInr * 100);
        return stripe.createCharge(paise);
    }

    @Override
    public boolean refund(String txnId, double amountInr) {
        long paise = Math.round(amountInr * 100);
        return stripe.reverseCharge(txnId, paise);
    }
}

class CheckoutService {
    private final PaymentProcessor payments;
    CheckoutService(PaymentProcessor payments) {
        this.payments = payments;
    }
    void checkout(double amount) {
        String txnId = payments.pay(amount);
        System.out.println("Paid, txn=" + txnId);
        System.out.println("Refunded=" + payments.refund(txnId, amount));
    }
}

public class AdapterDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        CheckoutService checkout = new CheckoutService(new StripeAdapter());
        checkout.checkout(499.50);
    }
}

Sample I/O:

Paid, txn=stripe_ch_49950
Refunded=true

docs.title: 4.2 Python (pythonic, PEP 8, composition + duck typing)
docs.text:
Explanation: Python rarely needs explicit interfaces — duck typing suffices. StripeAdapter wraps stripe_gateway and exposes pay/refund. CheckoutService accepts anything with those methods, so tests can inject a stub. Uses abc.ABC for documentation but works with any duck-typed object. Run with python adapter_demo.py.

"""Adapter pattern: unify Stripe/PayPal SDKs behind PaymentProcessor protocol."""
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod


class PaymentProcessor(ABC):
    """Target interface expected by application code."""

    @abstractmethod
    def pay(self, amount_inr: float) -> str:
        ...

    @abstractmethod
    def refund(self, txn_id: str, amount_inr: float) -> bool:
        ...


class StripeGateway:
    """Adaptee 1: third-party SDK with its own naming and units."""

    def create_charge(self, amount_paise: int) -> str:
        return f"stripe_ch_{amount_paise}"

    def reverse_charge(self, charge_id: str, amount_paise: int) -> bool:
        return True


class PayPalClient:
    """Adaptee 2: different SDK, different currency."""

    INR_TO_USD = 0.012

    def send_payment(self, amount_usd: float) -> str:
        return f"paypal_txn_{amount_usd:.2f}"

    def void_payment(self, txn_id: str) -> bool:
        return True


class StripeAdapter(PaymentProcessor):
    """Adapter: converts pay/refund into Stripe calls."""

    def __init__(self, gateway: StripeGateway | None = None) -> None:
        self._gateway = gateway or StripeGateway()

    def pay(self, amount_inr: float) -> str:
        paise = round(amount_inr * 100)
        return self._gateway.create_charge(paise)

    def refund(self, txn_id: str, amount_inr: float) -> bool:
        paise = round(amount_inr * 100)
        return self._gateway.reverse_charge(txn_id, paise)


class PayPalAdapter(PaymentProcessor):
    """Adapter: converts pay/refund into PayPal calls."""

    def __init__(self, client: PayPalClient | None = None) -> None:
        self._client = client or PayPalClient()

    def pay(self, amount_inr: float) -> str:
        usd = amount_inr * PayPalClient.INR_TO_USD
        return self._client.send_payment(usd)

    def refund(self, txn_id: str, amount_inr: float) -> bool:
        return self._client.void_payment(txn_id)


class CheckoutService:
    """Client: depends only on the target protocol."""

    def __init__(self, payments: PaymentProcessor) -> None:
        self._payments = payments

    def checkout(self, amount: float) -> None:
        txn_id = self._payments.pay(amount)
        print(f"Paid, txn={txn_id}")
        print(f"Refunded={self._payments.refund(txn_id, amount)}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    CheckoutService(StripeAdapter()).checkout(499.50)
    CheckoutService(PayPalAdapter()).checkout(499.50)

Sample I/O:

Paid, txn=stripe_ch_49950
Refunded=True
Paid, txn=paypal_txn_5.99
Refunded=True

docs.title: 4.3 Go (idiomatic, implicit interfaces)
docs.text:
Explanation: Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly, so the adapter needs no implements keyword — defining Pay/Refund methods is enough. StripeAdapter embeds a *StripeGateway and translates units. CheckoutService is a struct holding the PaymentProcessor interface, wired in main. Run with go run adapter_demo.go.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "math"
)

// Target: interface the application expects.
type PaymentProcessor interface {
    Pay(amountInr float64) string
    Refund(txnID string, amountInr float64) bool
}

// Adaptee: third-party SDK with incompatible API.
type StripeGateway struct{}

func (s *StripeGateway) CreateCharge(amountPaise int64) string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("stripe_ch_%d", amountPaise)
}

func (s *StripeGateway) ReverseCharge(chargeID string, amountPaise int64) bool {
    return true
}

// Adapter: implements PaymentProcessor by delegating to StripeGateway.
type StripeAdapter struct {
    gateway *StripeGateway
}

func NewStripeAdapter() *StripeAdapter {
    return &StripeAdapter{gateway: &StripeGateway{}}
}

func (a *StripeAdapter) Pay(amountInr float64) string {
    paise := int64(math.Round(amountInr * 100))
    return a.gateway.CreateCharge(paise)
}

func (a *StripeAdapter) Refund(txnID string, amountInr float64) bool {
    paise := int64(math.Round(amountInr * 100))
    return a.gateway.ReverseCharge(txnID, paise)
}

// Client: depends only on the target interface.
type CheckoutService struct {
    payments PaymentProcessor
}

func (c *CheckoutService) Checkout(amount float64) {
    txnID := c.payments.Pay(amount)
    fmt.Println("Paid, txn=" + txnID)
    fmt.Println("Refunded=", c.payments.Refund(txnID, amount))
}

func main() {
    checkout := &CheckoutService{payments: NewStripeAdapter()}
    checkout.Checkout(499.50)
}

Sample I/O:

Paid, txn=stripe_ch_49950
Refunded= true

docs.title: 5. Real-World Industry Applications
docs.text:
• Payments (Stripe, PayPal, Razorpay, Adyen): Every aggregator (e.g., Shopify, Zerodha Coin, Swiggy checkout) defines one internal PaymentProcessor and writes an adapter per PSP handling currency, webhooks, and idempotency differences.
  • Logging facades (SLF4J, Python logging, Go slog): SLF4J is an adapter layer over Logback, Log4j, and java.util.logging — application code logs once, adapters route to whichever backend is on the classpath.
  • Database drivers (JDBC, ODBC, Python DB-API): java.sql.Driver adapters translate the standard Connection/Statement API into MySQL, Postgres, and Oracle wire protocols.
  • Cloud storage (S3 vs GCS vs Azure Blob): Libraries like Apache Libcloud, Terraform providers, and internal BlobStore interfaces adapt each cloud's SDK (different auth, pagination, error codes) behind Put/Get/Delete.
  • Messaging (Kafka vs SQS vs RabbitMQ): Platform teams expose EventBus.publish() and adapt each broker's producer/consumer semantics, exactly like the payment example.
  • Legacy modernisation (SOAP to REST, XML to JSON): Banks wrap decades-old SOAP services with REST adapters so mobile apps see JSON while the mainframe still sees XML — a textbook anti-corruption layer.

docs.title: 6. Practical Use Cases and Scenarios
docs.text:
1. Multi-PSP checkout: Client code calls pay/refund; each PSP adapter handles unit, currency, and status-code translation. Adding UPI later is one new class.
  2. Third-party SDK upgrade: Vendor releases v2 with renamed methods. Write VendorV2Adapter implementing the old target so the rest of the codebase is untouched during migration.
  3. Legacy printer/file API: Old LegacyPlug.plugIn() or OldLogger.logMsg() must work with new Charger.charge() or Logger.info() — a five-line adapter avoids forking legacy code.
  4. Test seam for external services: Production wires StripeAdapter; tests wire FakePaymentProcessor or InMemoryQueueAdapter — same client, no network.
  5. Protocol bridge (HTTP to gRPC, REST to GraphQL): Edge adapter translates incoming REST JSON into internal gRPC calls, mapping status codes and pagination tokens.
  6. UI toolkit interop: Adapt a D3 chart or legacy Swing widget to a React/Angular component interface so old visualisations embed in a new dashboard.

docs.title: 7. When to Use and When Not to Use
docs.text:
Use Adapter when:

  • You must reuse a third-party or legacy class whose interface does not match.
  • You want one client code path to work with multiple providers (payments, storage, queues).
  • You cannot modify the adaptee (closed source, shared library, frozen legacy).
  • You are building an anti-corruption layer between bounded contexts.
  • You need a test seam to swap real SDKs for fakes.

Do NOT use Adapter when:

  • You own both sides and can refactor to a shared interface — an adapter just hides the design smell.
  • The target and adaptee semantics differ fundamentally (e.g., void-only vs transactional) — a thin translator becomes a lying abstraction; redesign instead.
  • You are tempted to stack adapters on adapters (AdapterA -> AdapterB -> AdapterC) — debugging translation chains is miserable; consolidate.
  • The goal is simplifying a complex subsystem, not fixing mismatch — that is Facade.
  • The goal is adding behaviour with the same interface — that is Decorator.

docs.title: 8. Do's and Don'ts
docs.text:
Do:

  • Depend on the target abstraction in all client code; never import adaptee types into clients.
  • Keep one adapter per adaptee; name it <Adaptee>Adapter (StripeAdapter).
  • Translate errors faithfully: map SDK exceptions to domain exceptions with context preserved.
  • Handle units, timezones, and pagination explicitly and document them.
  • Inject the adaptee (constructor/DI) so tests can mock it.
  • Keep adapters thin — orchestration belongs in services, not translators.

Don't:

  • Don't modify adaptee or target to suit one integration — fix the adapter.
  • Don't let adapters accumulate business rules (pricing, authz) — they are translators, not services.
  • Don't swallow errors or return magic defaults when the adaptee fails.
  • Don't create two-way adapters unless both directions are genuinely needed.
  • Don't expose adaptee return types from adapter methods — that leaks the abstraction.
Do Don't Convert units/currencies inside adapter Force callers to pre-convert units Map exceptions to domain errors Let StripeException propagate to checkout Inject adaptee for testability new StripeGateway() hard-coded with no seam (unless trivial) One focused adapter per provider One giant PaymentAdapter with if provider == X branches

docs.title: 9. Comparison with Other Design Patterns
docs.text:
Aspect Adapter Facade Bridge Intent Convert incompatible interface to expected one Simplify complex subsystem behind one entry point Decouple abstraction from implementation so both vary Timing Retroactive fix for existing mismatch Anytime simplification of verbose subsystem Up-front design for two variation axes Wraps One adaptee (usually) Whole subsystem (many classes) Implementation hierarchy via composition Changes interface? Yes — translates signatures No — orchestrates existing calls No — both sides designed together Client sees Target interface only Facade methods only Abstraction, implementation injected Example StripeAdapter implements PaymentProcessor VideoConverterFacade.convertToMp4() Notification bridging to NotificationChannel Without it Code does not compile/connect Code works but is verbose and error-prone Class explosion (M x N subclasses)

Adapter vs Decorator: Adapter changes the interface; Decorator keeps it and adds behaviour. If method names change, it is an Adapter.

Adapter vs Proxy: Adapter translates so the call can happen at all; Proxy guards/defers the same-interface call. Adapter says "let me rephrase that"; Proxy says "you may / not yet".

When to pick which: Mismatched SDK → Adapter. Verbose multi-step library → Facade. Two dimensions of variation you control → Bridge.

docs.title: 10. Interview Preparation
docs.text:
Q1: What is the Adapter pattern and what problem does it solve? It converts an incompatible interface into one the client expects, letting otherwise incompatible classes collaborate without modifying either side. Example: wrapping StripeGateway.createCharge(paise) and PayPalClient.sendPayment(usd) behind a single PaymentProcessor.pay(rupees) so checkout code is provider-agnostic.

Q2: Class adapter vs object adapter? Class adapter uses inheritance (extends adaptee, implements target); object adapter uses composition (holds adaptee reference). Prefer object adapters — they work with any adaptee, support multiple adaptees, allow lazy/decorated delegation, and avoid single-inheritance limits in Java. Use class adapter only to override adaptee behaviour directly.

Q3: How does Adapter differ from Facade, Bridge, and Decorator? Adapter changes the interface to fix mismatch; Facade simplifies a compatible subsystem without changing interfaces; Bridge is an up-front split of abstraction and implementation you own; Decorator keeps the interface and adds behaviour. Test: renamed signatures → Adapter; one method hiding four subsystems → Facade; two hierarchies varying independently → Bridge; stacked toppings → Decorator.

Q4: When would you NOT use Adapter? When you own both sides — refactor to a shared interface instead. When semantics diverge too far (adapter becomes bloated with edge cases), redesign or build a proper anti-corruption layer. Never stack adapters on adapters; consolidate.

Q5: How do you handle incompatible data types and error models? Convert inside the adapter (units, currencies, date formats, pagination tokens) and map exceptions to domain errors preserving cause chains. Document every conversion; test rounding, null ids, and SDK-specific failures explicitly.

Q6: How does Adapter support Open/Closed Principle? Client depends on Target; each new provider adds one Adapter class. CheckoutService never changes when Razorpay arrives — you write RazorpayAdapter and wire it via DI/config.

Q7: Give a JDK/framework example of Adapter. Arrays.asList() adapts arrays to List; InputStreamReader adapts byte streams to character readers; Spring's HandlerAdapter adapts different controller types to a uniform dispatch interface. SLF4J adapters route to Logback/Log4j.

Q8: Is Adapter an extra hop a performance concern? No — one delegation call is negligible versus network/disk SDK cost. The real cost is cognitive (more classes). Keep adapters thin and avoid reflection-heavy generic adapters on hot paths.

LLD Scenario 1 — Multi-provider payments: Design PaymentProcessor with pay/refund/getStatus. Implement StripeAdapter, PayPalAdapter, RazorpayAdapter. Discuss currency conversion, webhook normalisation, idempotency keys, and how checkout stays untouched. Expected: target interface, per-provider adapters, factory/config wiring, fake for tests.

LLD Scenario 2 — Legacy CSV exporter in new analytics pipeline: Legacy CsvWriter.writeRow(String[]) must fit new Exporter.export(Record) expecting JSON. Design CsvExporterAdapter handling field mapping, escaping, and batching. Discuss error mapping and backpressure. Expected: adapter with schema mapping, buffering, domain exceptions.

LLD Scenario 3 — Unified notification gateway: Email (SMTP), SMS (Twilio), Push (FCM) SDKs each differ. Design NotificationSender.send() plus three adapters handling truncation (SMS 160 chars), retries, and templating. Discuss how to add WhatsApp without touching callers. Expected: target interface, three adapters, factory, ordering of templating vs truncation.

docs.title: 11. Testing and Best Practices
docs.text:
Unit tests:

  • Test each adapter against a mocked adaptee: verify pay(499.50) calls createCharge(49950) exactly once with correct conversion.
  • Assert return-value and exception translation: SDK error → domain PaymentFailedException with cause preserved.
  • Test edge cases introduced by translation: rounding (10.005), zero/negative amounts, null ids, currency precision.
  • Test the client against a stub PaymentProcessor — checkout tests must not import Stripe/PayPal types.

Integration tests:

  • One thin test per adapter against a sandbox/fake SDK proving the real wire mapping works.
  • Contract test: same scenario through every adapter yields equivalent domain outcomes.

Best practices:

  • Constructor-inject adaptees; never hard-code new deep inside business logic (except trivial demos).
  • Keep adapters stateless where possible; if stateful (connections), document lifecycle and thread-safety.
  • Log at the adapter boundary with provider context (provider=stripe txn=...) for debuggability.
  • Version adapters with the SDK (StripeV2Adapter) during migrations; delete old ones after cutover.
Aspect Impact Memory Low (single wrapper per dependency) Runtime cost Low (one delegation + conversion) Scalability High (N providers = N isolated adapters) Risk Leaky abstraction if adaptee types escape — keep signatures clean

docs.title: 12. Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Adapter = translator: Implements the interface the client wants, delegates to the interface that exists.
  • Prefer object adapters (composition) over class adapters (inheritance) for flexibility and testability.
  • Centralise quirks: Units, currencies, error codes, and pagination live in the adapter, not scattered across clients.
  • Open/Closed in action: New providers mean new adapter classes, zero client edits.
  • Don't overuse: If you own both sides, refactor. If semantics diverge wildly, redesign rather than building a bloated translator.
  • Distinguish neighbours: Renamed signatures → Adapter; simplified subsystem → Facade; independent hierarchies → Bridge; added behaviour → Decorator; guarded access → Proxy.
  • Test the seam: Mock adaptee for adapter tests; stub target for client tests; one integration test per provider.

docs.title: Youtube
docs.text: • 26. Bridge Design Pattern | LLD of Bridge Pattern with Example | Low Level Design of Bridge Pattern

docs.title: 1. Overview and Fundamentals
docs.text:
Intent (GoF): Decouple an abstraction from its implementation so that the two can vary independently.

In one line: Bridge splits one exploding class hierarchy into two small hierarchies joined by composition.

Real-world analogy: A TV remote (abstraction) and the TV itself (implementation). You can have basic remotes and smart remotes (abstraction hierarchy) working with Sony, Samsung, or LG TVs (implementation hierarchy). A new TV brand does not force you to redesign remotes, and a new remote type works with all TVs.

Family context: Bridge is a structural pattern. Where Adapter fixes mismatch after the fact, Bridge is designed up front to prevent a Cartesian-product class explosion.

Key participants:

  • Abstraction — high-level interface clients use (e.g., Notification, Remote, Shape).
  • RefinedAbstraction — extends abstraction with variants (e.g., UrgentAlert, GentleReminder).
  • Implementor — low-level interface abstraction delegates to (e.g., NotificationChannel, Device).
  • ConcreteImplementor — specific platform/channel (e.g., SmsChannel, EmailChannel, TV, Radio).

Core characteristics:

  • Uses composition: abstraction has-a implementor, not is-a.
  • Both hierarchies evolve independently — M abstractions x N implementations needs M+N classes, not M*N.
  • Implementation can be swapped at runtime via constructor or setter injection.
  • Clients depend only on abstraction; they never import concrete implementors directly.
  • Implementor interface must stay narrow and stable — it is the bridge contract.

Mental model:

Notification (abstraction) ---> NotificationChannel (implementor)
UrgentAlert / GentleReminder     Email / SMS / Push

If you control both sides and see two orthogonal axes of change, it is a Bridge. If one side is fixed third-party code, it is an Adapter.

docs.title: 2. Detailed Theory
docs.text:
Problem: A single inheritance hierarchy explodes. Classic example: UrgentEmailAlert, UrgentSmsAlert, UrgentPushAlert, ReminderEmail, ReminderSms, ReminderPush — every combination of message type and delivery channel is its own class. Adding WhatsApp means touching every message type; adding a new message type means touching every channel.

Solution: Split along the two axes. Put message semantics in one hierarchy (Notification) and delivery mechanics in another (NotificationChannel). Link them with a reference: Notification holds a NotificationChannel and delegates the actual send.

Structure details:

  • Abstraction defines high-level operations (notifyUser(message)) and holds the implementor reference. It may add pre/post logic (priority headers, quiet-hours checks) before delegating.
  • RefinedAbstractions vary the high-level policy without duplicating delivery code.
  • Implementor defines primitive operations (send(title, body)). It should be minimal — wide interfaces force every channel to implement irrelevant methods.
  • ConcreteImplementors encapsulate platform quirks: SMS truncation to 160 chars, email formatting, push payload limits.

Bridge vs Strategy vs State vs Adapter:

  • Bridge is a long-lived structural split; both sides are hierarchies that grow.
  • Strategy swaps one algorithm for one task at runtime; it is behavioural and typically single-level. The channel side of a Bridge is sometimes implemented with Strategy-style injection, which confuses interviewers — the difference is intent and longevity.
  • Adapter retrofits incompatible code you do not control; Bridge connects two interfaces you designed together.
  • Abstract Factory often creates the right implementor (e.g., ChannelFactory.forRegion("EU")), while Bridge uses it — the two patterns compose well.

SOLID connections:

  • Open/Closed: New channel = one new class; new message type = one new class. Neither touches existing code.
  • Dependency Inversion: Abstraction depends on NotificationChannel interface, not SmsChannel concrete.
  • Single Responsibility: Message policy and transport mechanics live in separate classes.
  • Composition over Inheritance: The core lesson — prefer has-a linkage over is-a explosion.

Consequences:

  • Drastically fewer classes and independent testability, at the cost of an extra indirection and more types to understand for trivial systems.
  • A leaky implementor interface (e.g., abstraction assuming SMS semantics) silently recouples the hierarchies — keep the contract platform-neutral.
  • Overkill when only one implementation will ever exist; introduce when the second one appears.

docs.title: Diagram 1 — Class structure (two hierarchies)
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Notification {
        <>
        #channel: NotificationChannel
        +notifyUser(message: String)
    }
    class UrgentAlert {
        +notifyUser(message: String)
    }
    class GentleReminder {
        +notifyUser(message: String)
    }
    class NotificationChannel {
        <>
        +send(title: String, body: String)
    }
    class EmailChannel {
        +send(title: String, body: String)
    }
    class SmsChannel {
        +send(title: String, body: String)
    }
    class PushChannel {
        +send(title: String, body: String)
    }
    Notification <|-- UrgentAlert : extends
    Notification <|-- GentleReminder : extends
    Notification --> NotificationChannel : bridges to
    NotificationChannel <|.. EmailChannel : implements
    NotificationChannel <|.. SmsChannel : implements
    NotificationChannel <|.. PushChannel : implements

Explanation: The left hierarchy (Notification → UrgentAlert, GentleReminder) captures what to send and with what policy. The right hierarchy (NotificationChannel → Email/SMS/Push) captures how to deliver. The single arrow from Notification to NotificationChannel is the bridge — composition, not inheritance. Adding WhatsAppChannel touches only the right side; adding MarketingPromo touches only the left side.

docs.title: Diagram 2 — Runtime delegation (sequence)
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Application
    participant Alert as UrgentAlert
    participant Channel as SmsChannel
    App->>Alert: notifyUser("CPU > 95%")
    Alert->>Alert: add priority=high, retry=3x
    Alert->>Channel: send("URGENT", "CPU > 95% [priority=high...]")
    Channel->>Channel: truncate to 160 chars
    Channel-->>Alert: sent
    Alert-->>App: done

Explanation: The client talks only to the abstraction. UrgentAlert enriches the message with policy (priority flags) and delegates the transport to whichever channel was injected. The channel handles its own constraint (SMS truncation). Neither side knows the other's concrete type — UrgentAlert works identically with email or push.

docs.title: 4. Implementation Examples in Java, Python, and Go
4.1 Java (OOP, abstraction + implementor hierarchies)
docs.text:
Explanation: Notification holds a NotificationChannel injected via constructor. UrgentAlert and GentleReminder differ in policy; Email/Sms/PushChannel differ in transport. main mixes any pair. Compile with javac BridgeDemo.java && java BridgeDemo.

interface NotificationChannel {
    void send(String title, String body);
}

class EmailChannel implements NotificationChannel {
    @Override
    public void send(String title, String body) {
        System.out.println("[EMAIL] " + title + ": " + body);
    }
}

class SmsChannel implements NotificationChannel {
    @Override
    public void send(String title, String body) {
        String text = title + " " + body;
        if (text.length() > 160) text = text.substring(0, 160);
        System.out.println("[SMS] " + text);
    }
}

class PushChannel implements NotificationChannel {
    @Override
    public void send(String title, String body) {
        System.out.println("[PUSH] " + title + " -> " + body);
    }
}

abstract class Notification {
    protected final NotificationChannel channel;
    protected Notification(NotificationChannel channel) {
        this.channel = channel;
    }
    abstract void notifyUser(String message);
}

class UrgentAlert extends Notification {
    UrgentAlert(NotificationChannel channel) { super(channel); }
    @Override
    void notifyUser(String message) {
        channel.send("URGENT", message + " [priority=high, retry=3x]");
    }
}

class GentleReminder extends Notification {
    GentleReminder(NotificationChannel channel) { super(channel); }
    @Override
    void notifyUser(String message) {
        channel.send("Reminder", message + " [quiet-hours respected]");
    }
}

public class BridgeDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Notification alert = new UrgentAlert(new SmsChannel());
        alert.notifyUser("Server CPU above 95%");
        Notification reminder = new GentleReminder(new EmailChannel());
        reminder.notifyUser("Your report is due Friday");
        Notification push = new UrgentAlert(new PushChannel());
        push.notifyUser("DB failover complete");
    }
}

Sample I/O:

[SMS] URGENT Server CPU above 95% [priority=high, retry=3x]
[EMAIL] Reminder: Your report is due Friday [quiet-hours respected]
[PUSH] URGENT -> DB failover complete [priority=high, retry=3x]

docs.title: 4.2 Python (pythonic, ABC + composition)
docs.text:
Explanation: Notification stores a channel object (duck-typed, documented as NotificationChannel). Subclasses implement policy. Channels implement send. No framework needed — composition plus constructor injection is the whole pattern. Run with python bridge_demo.py.

"""Bridge pattern: message types vary independently from delivery channels."""
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod


class NotificationChannel(ABC):
    """Implementor: how a message is delivered."""

    @abstractmethod
    def send(self, title: str, body: str) -> None:
        ...


class EmailChannel(NotificationChannel):
    def send(self, title: str, body: str) -> None:
        print(f"[EMAIL] {title}: {body}")


class SmsChannel(NotificationChannel):
    def send(self, title: str, body: str) -> None:
        print(f"[SMS] {(title + ' ' + body)[:160]}")


class PushChannel(NotificationChannel):
    def send(self, title: str, body: str) -> None:
        print(f"[PUSH] {title} -> {body}")


class Notification(ABC):
    """Abstraction: what kind of message it is."""

    def __init__(self, channel: NotificationChannel) -> None:
        self._channel = channel

    @abstractmethod
    def notify_user(self, message: str) -> None:
        ...


class UrgentAlert(Notification):
    def notify_user(self, message: str) -> None:
        self._channel.send("URGENT", f"{message} [priority=high, retry=3x]")


class GentleReminder(Notification):
    def notify_user(self, message: str) -> None:
        self._channel.send("Reminder", f"{message} [quiet-hours respected]")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    UrgentAlert(SmsChannel()).notify_user("Server CPU above 95%")
    GentleReminder(EmailChannel()).notify_user("Your report is due Friday")
    UrgentAlert(PushChannel()).notify_user("DB failover complete")

Sample I/O:

[SMS] URGENT Server CPU above 95% [priority=high, retry=3x]
[EMAIL] Reminder: Your report is due Friday [quiet-hours respected]
[PUSH] URGENT -> DB failover complete [priority=high, retry=3x]

docs.title: 4.3 Go (idiomatic, implicit interfaces)
docs.text:
Explanation: Go has no inheritance — the abstraction is a struct holding an interface, and refined abstractions are separate structs sharing that interface field. SmsChannel truncates; UrgentAlert adds priority metadata. Wiring happens in main. Run with go run bridge_demo.go.

package main

import "fmt"

// Implementor: delivery mechanism.
type NotificationChannel interface {
    Send(title, body string)
}

type EmailChannel struct{}

func (e *EmailChannel) Send(title, body string) {
    fmt.Printf("[EMAIL] %s: %s\n", title, body)
}

type SmsChannel struct{}

func (s *SmsChannel) Send(title, body string) {
    text := title + " " + body
    if len(text) > 160 {
        text = text[:160]
    }
    fmt.Println("[SMS] " + text)
}

type PushChannel struct{}

func (p *PushChannel) Send(title, body string) {
    fmt.Printf("[PUSH] %s -> %s\n", title, body)
}

// Abstraction: message policy, bridges to a channel.
type Notifier interface {
    NotifyUser(message string)
}

type UrgentAlert struct {
    channel NotificationChannel
}

func NewUrgentAlert(c NotificationChannel) *UrgentAlert {
    return &UrgentAlert{channel: c}
}

func (u *UrgentAlert) NotifyUser(message string) {
    u.channel.Send("URGENT", message+" [priority=high, retry=3x]")
}

type GentleReminder struct {
    channel NotificationChannel
}

func NewGentleReminder(c NotificationChannel) *GentleReminder {
    return &GentleReminder{channel: c}
}

func (g *GentleReminder) NotifyUser(message string) {
    g.channel.Send("Reminder", message+" [quiet-hours respected]")
}

func main() {
    var n Notifier = NewUrgentAlert(&SmsChannel{})
    n.NotifyUser("Server CPU above 95%")
    n = NewGentleReminder(&EmailChannel{})
    n.NotifyUser("Your report is due Friday")
    n = NewUrgentAlert(&PushChannel{})
    n.NotifyUser("DB failover complete")
}

Sample I/O:

[SMS] URGENT Server CPU above 95% [priority=high, retry=3x]
[EMAIL] Reminder: Your report is due Friday [quiet-hours respected]
[PUSH] URGENT -> DB failover complete [priority=high, retry=3x]

docs.title: 5. Real-World Industry Applications
docs.text:
• JDBC / ODBC drivers: java.sql.Connection is the abstraction; each vendor's driver (Postgres, MySQL, Oracle) is the implementor. Application code never changes when the database does.
  • SLF4J + Logback/Log4j: Logging API (abstraction) bridges to backend appenders (implementors) chosen at deploy time.
  • Cross-platform UI (Flutter, Qt, .NET MAUI): Widget abstraction bridges to native renderers per OS — one Button, many painters.
  • Media players (VLC, FFmpeg): Player controls bridge to codec implementations; new codecs plug in without touching playback logic.
  • Cloud multi-region messaging: EventPublisher abstraction bridges to Kafka/SQS/PubSub implementors selected by environment config.
  • Device drivers / OS kernels: System-call abstraction bridges to hardware-specific drivers; Linux VFS bridges to ext4, XFS, NFS identically.

docs.title: 6. Practical Use Cases and Scenarios
docs.text:
1. Notification platform: 4 message types x 5 channels = 9 classes with Bridge instead of 20 subclasses. Adding WhatsApp is one class.
  2. Shape renderer: Shape (circle, square) bridges to Renderer (vector, raster, SVG). New export format touches only the renderer side.
  3. Remote controls: Remote (basic, voice-enabled) bridges to Device (TV, radio, AC). One voice remote drives every device.
  4. Report exporter: Report (sales, audit) bridges to Formatter (PDF, CSV, HTML). Compliance adds a format without touching report logic.
  5. Multi-cloud file store: FileStore abstraction bridges to S3Driver, GCSDriver, LocalDriver — tests inject the local driver.
  6. Game engine: Character abstraction bridges to PhysicsEngine (Box2D, Havok) so gameplay code is engine-agnostic.

docs.title: 7. When to Use and When Not to Use
docs.text:
Use Bridge when:

  • You see two orthogonal axes of change (message x channel, shape x renderer, remote x device).
  • Both sides need independent extension and independent testing.
  • You want runtime switching of implementation (feature flags, per-tenant drivers).
  • You are building a platform/SDK where third parties supply implementors.
  • Class count is exploding combinatorially (M x N problem).

Do NOT use Bridge when:

  • Only one implementation exists and a second is speculative — start simple, extract the bridge when duplication appears.
  • The two sides are not truly independent (abstraction constantly downcasts to concrete implementor) — the bridge is leaking.
  • A simple Strategy (one swappable algorithm) suffices — do not build two hierarchies for one behaviour.
  • The implementor interface cannot be kept stable — every new method ripples across all implementors.

docs.title: 8. Do's and Don'ts
docs.text:
Do:

  • Keep the implementor interface small, stable, and platform-neutral.
  • Inject the implementor (constructor/DI) so combinations are visible and testable.
  • Put axis-specific logic on its own side: truncation in channels, priority in alerts.
  • Use factories/config to select implementors per environment (dev → local, prod → Kafka).
  • Document which pairs are supported if not all combinations make sense.

Don't:

  • Don't let the abstraction depend on concrete implementors — depend on the interface.
  • Don't stuff business rules that belong in refined abstractions into the implementor.
  • Don't create a bridge for a single fixed pair — plain composition suffices.
  • Don't widen the implementor interface casually — each method is a tax on every implementor.
Do Don't Inject NotificationChannel via constructor new SmsChannel() hard-coded inside UrgentAlert Truncate inside SmsChannel Scatter if channel == SMS checks in alerts Add WhatsAppChannel as one class Create UrgentWhatsAppAlert + ReminderWhatsAppAlert Matrix-test all pairs Test only the pair you demoed

docs.title: 9. Comparison with Other Design Patterns
docs.text:
Aspect Bridge Adapter Strategy Intent Split abstraction from implementation up front Fix incompatible interface after the fact Swap one algorithm at runtime Designed when Proactive, two variation axes foreseen Retroactive, integrating fixed code Anytime a behaviour varies Structure Two hierarchies + composition link One wrapper translating calls One context + interchangeable algorithm Growth M + N classes 1 adapter per mismatch 1 class per algorithm Client role Uses abstraction, injects implementor Uses target, unaware of adaptee Chooses strategy, often per call Example Notification → NotificationChannel StripeAdapter → PaymentProcessor SortContext → QuickSort/MergeSort Without it M x N subclass explosion Code does not compile If/else algorithm branches

Bridge vs Facade: Bridge structures what you own into two axes; Facade simplifies what already exists into fewer calls. Bridge adds types to gain flexibility; Facade hides types to gain simplicity.

Bridge vs State: State changes behaviour by swapping internal state objects opaquely; Bridge lets the client choose and hold the implementor explicitly.

When to pick which: Two axes you control → Bridge. One fixed mismatch → Adapter. One swappable algorithm → Strategy. Verbose subsystem → Facade.

docs.title: 10. Interview Preparation
docs.text:
Q1: What problem does Bridge solve that inheritance cannot? Inheritance multiplies: M abstractions x N implementations needs M*N classes. Bridge composes instead, needing M+N. With 2 message types and 3 channels, Bridge needs 5 classes instead of 6, and the gap widens as either side grows. It also enables runtime swapping by injecting a different implementor.

Q2: How is Bridge different from Strategy? Both use composition, but Bridge splits a design into two long-lived hierarchies that evolve independently, while Strategy swaps a single algorithm for one task. A Bridge implementor is a platform family; a Strategy is an interchangeable behaviour. Structurally similar, intentionally different.

Q3: How is Bridge different from Adapter? Bridge is proactive — you design both sides to vary. Adapter is reactive — you wrap fixed, incompatible code you do not control. If you drew both interfaces, it is Bridge; if one side was forced on you, it is Adapter.

Q4: Give a real framework example of Bridge. JDBC: java.sql interfaces are the abstraction, vendor drivers are implementors. SLF4J bindings, OS window toolkits vs renderers, and Terraform providers vs core follow the same split — application code depends on the abstraction, deployment chooses the implementor.

Q5: What makes a good implementor interface? Small, stable, platform-neutral. It should expose what every implementor can honour without leaking one platform's quirks. If adding a method forces all implementors to throw UnsupportedOperationException, the interface is too wide — split it.

Q6: How do you select implementors in production? Constructor injection plus a factory or DI config: ChannelFactory.forTenant(t) returns SMS for EU, push for mobile. Tests inject fakes. Never hard-code new SmsChannel() inside the abstraction.

Q7: What are the trade-offs? More types and indirection for small systems — overkill for one abstraction plus one implementation. Risk of leaky abstraction if high-level code assumes implementor specifics. Mitigate with narrow interfaces and matrix tests.

Q8: How does Bridge relate to Abstract Factory? Abstract Factory often creates the implementor family (e.g., WindowsFactory vs MacFactory producing buttons and checkboxes), while Bridge consumes it. Together they give platform-independent UI: factory picks the family, bridge wires abstraction to implementation.

LLD Scenario 1 — Cross-platform media player: Design MediaPlayer (basic, premium) bridging to Codec (H264, VP9, AV1). Adding AV1 must not touch player code. Expected: abstraction hierarchy, codec interface, factory wiring, discussion of buffering/payload limits per codec.

LLD Scenario 2 — Multi-tenant notification hub: 3 message priorities x 4 channels with per-tenant channel selection and SMS truncation. Design Bridge plus factory routing. Expected: channel interface, alert abstractions, tenant config, matrix tests, retry policy placement.

LLD Scenario 3 — Shape editor with export formats: Shape (circle, rectangle, group) bridges to Renderer (canvas, SVG, PDF). Discuss where stroke/fill lives vs where serialisation lives. Expected: clean axis split, new-format extensibility, handling of renderer-specific limits.

docs.title: 11. Testing and Best Practices
docs.text:
Unit tests:

  • Test each abstraction against a stub implementor: verify UrgentAlert prefixes URGENT and forwards exactly once regardless of channel.
  • Test each implementor in isolation: SMS truncation, email formatting, push payload — no abstraction involved.
  • Matrix-test every abstraction x implementor pair (2x3 = 6 cases) to catch leaky assumptions.
  • Verify runtime swapping: same alert with different channels produces channel-correct output.

Integration tests:

  • End-to-end with real channels (test SMTP server, fake SMS gateway) for at least one pair per channel.
  • Contract test: any new channel must pass the shared NotificationChannel conformance suite.

Best practices:

  • Constructor-inject implementors; select via factory/config, never via if inside abstraction.
  • Keep implementor methods side-effect-explicit and documented (truncation, retries, rate limits).
  • Prefer immutability on both sides; share implementor instances (they are stateless) across abstractions.
  • Profile before bridging: if only one implementor will ever exist, YAGNI applies.
Aspect Impact Memory Low (one implementor reference per abstraction) Runtime cost Low (single delegation hop) Scalability High (M+N growth, runtime swapping) Risk Leaky implementor interface — keep it narrow and neutral

docs.title: 12. Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Bridge = split and compose: Two small hierarchies joined by a reference beat one giant M*N hierarchy.
  • Design up front when you foresee two axes of change; retrofit with Adapter when code is already fixed.
  • Narrow implementor, rich abstraction: Transport quirks stay in channels; policy stays in alerts.
  • Inject, don't hard-code: Factories and DI choose implementors per environment or tenant.
  • Distinguish neighbours: Two axes → Bridge; one mismatch → Adapter; one algorithm → Strategy; verbose subsystem → Facade.
  • Test the matrix: Every abstraction against every implementor, plus a conformance suite for new implementors.
