docs.text: • 19. Design File System using Composite Design Pattern | Low Level Design Interview Question | LLD

docs.title: 1. Overview and Fundamentals
docs.text:
Intent (GoF): Compose objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies. Composite lets clients treat individual objects and compositions uniformly.

In one line: One interface for a single thing and a group of things — client code never checks which one it holds.

Real-world analogy: A file system. A File is a leaf with a size. A Directory contains files and other directories. Right-click → Properties shows total size either way — Explorer calls the same operation on both.

Family context: Composite is a structural pattern. It structures objects into recursive trees while keeping the client decoupled from tree shape.

Key participants:

  • Component — common interface (FileNode, OrgUnit, Graphic) declaring shared operations (size(), draw(), monthlyCost()).
  • Leaf — single object with no children (File, Developer, Circle).
  • Composite — holds children of type Component and implements operations by delegating/aggregating (Directory, Team).
  • Client — uses Component uniformly, never instanceof-checks leaf vs composite.

Core characteristics:

  • Recursive composition: composites can nest inside composites to any depth.
  • Uniform treatment: one method call works on a leaf or a million-node tree.
  • Aggregation semantics: composites typically sum, count, or concatenate child results.
  • Child management (add/remove/getChild) lives on the composite — or on the component in the transparent variant.
  • Natural fit for part-whole domains: files, orgs, menus, UI trees, graphics groups.

Mental model:

Component.size()
  Leaf.size() -> own size
  Composite.size() -> sum(child.size() for child in children)

If the client should ignore whether it holds one object or a group, use Composite. If wrappers should enrich one object, use Decorator.

docs.title: 2. Detailed Theory
docs.text:
Problem: Client code becomes littered with type checks: if (node.isDirectory()) { for (...) } else { ... }. Every new operation (size, search, print, permissions) duplicates traversal logic. Adding a new node type ripples across all clients.

Solution: Define a Component interface with the operations clients need. Leaves implement them directly. Composites store a List<Component> and implement the same operations by iterating over children. Clients program to Component only.

Transparent vs safe Composite:

  • Transparent: add/remove/getChildren are declared on Component so clients treat everything identically. Cost: leaves must implement meaningless methods (typically throwing UnsupportedOperationException). Best when uniformity matters most (UI toolkits).
  • Safe: Only Composite exposes add/remove. Leaves stay clean and type-safe. Cost: clients must downcast or know the concrete type to build the tree. Best in statically-typed codebases where leaf purity matters.
  • Modern practice favours the safe style plus a builder or factory that assembles trees, keeping traversal uniform while construction is explicit.

Recursive operations and traversal:

  • Operations are naturally recursive: print() prints self then calls child.print(indent+1).
  • Depth-first is default; breadth-first needs a queue and is still expressed via the component interface.
  • Very deep trees risk stack overflow in naive recursion — provide iterative traversal for pathological depths.
  • Expensive aggregates (totalSize, headcount) are O(n) per call; cache them or maintain running totals when reads dominate writes.

Shared vs exclusive children:

  • Classic Composite gives each child one parent (file system, org chart).
  • DAG variants (a file hard-linked into two directories, a shared subtree) allow multiple parents — document ownership and avoid double-counting in aggregates.
  • Flyweight leaves (shared glyphs, shared icons) combine naturally: Composite handles structure, Flyweight shares leaf data.

SOLID connections:

  • Open/Closed: New leaf or composite types implement Component without touching clients.
  • Liskov Substitution: Any Component substitutes for any other — the heart of the pattern.
  • Single Responsibility: Each class owns one node's behaviour; traversal is distributed, not centralised.
  • Interface Segregation: Keep Component focused on client-needed queries; push management methods to Composite (safe style).

Consequences:

  • Beautifully simple clients at the cost of generality: it is hard to restrict which children a composite accepts (a Menu accepting a File compiles but makes no sense).
  • Overly generic trees lose type safety; mitigate with generics, validation in add(), or separate component sub-interfaces per domain.

docs.title: Diagram 1 — Class structure (component, leaf, composite)
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class OrgUnit {
        <>
        +monthlyCost() double
        +headcount() int
        +print(indent: String)
    }
    class Developer {
        -name: String
        -salary: double
        +monthlyCost() double
        +headcount() int
        +print(indent: String)
    }
    class Team {
        -name: String
        -members: List~OrgUnit~
        +add(unit: OrgUnit)
        +remove(unit: OrgUnit)
        +monthlyCost() double
        +headcount() int
        +print(indent: String)
    }
    class PayrollDemo {
        +main()
    }
    OrgUnit <|.. Developer : implements
    OrgUnit <|.. Team : implements
    Team o-- OrgUnit : contains children
    PayrollDemo --> OrgUnit : uses

Explanation: OrgUnit is the component contract. Developer (leaf) implements it with scalar values. Team (composite) holds a list of OrgUnit — which may be developers or sub-teams — and aggregates by looping. The open-diamond o-- denotes aggregation: a team has members but members can outlive reassignment. PayrollDemo depends only on OrgUnit, never on concrete classes, so nesting depth is invisible to it.

docs.title: Diagram 2 — Recursive call flow (sequence)
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client as PayrollDemo
    participant Platform as Team(Platform)
    participant Backend as Team(Backend)
    participant Dev as Developer(Asha)
    Client->>Platform: monthlyCost()
    Platform->>Backend: monthlyCost()
    Backend->>Dev: monthlyCost()
    Dev-->>Backend: 9000
    Backend-->>Platform: 17000
    Platform-->>Client: 26500

Explanation: A single monthlyCost() call on the root cascades down the tree and bubbles back up as partial sums. The client issues one call and receives one total — it never iterates, never checks types, never knows the depth. The same shape applies to headcount(), print(), size(), or render(): delegate down, aggregate up.

docs.title: 4. Implementation Examples in Java, Python, and Go
4.1 Java (OOP, file system)
docs.text:
Explanation: FileNode is the component with size() and print(). File is the leaf. Directory is the composite holding children and aggregating sizes. main builds root/home/docs nesting and prints the tree. Compile with javac CompositeDemo.java && java CompositeDemo.

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

interface FileNode {
    int size();
    void print(String indent);
}

class File implements FileNode {
    private final String name;
    private final int bytes;
    File(String name, int bytes) { this.name = name; this.bytes = bytes; }
    @Override public int size() { return bytes; }
    @Override public void print(String indent) {
        System.out.println(indent + name + " (" + bytes + "B)");
    }
}

class Directory implements FileNode {
    private final String name;
    private final List<FileNode> children = new ArrayList<>();
    Directory(String name) { this.name = name; }
    public void add(FileNode node) { children.add(node); }
    public void remove(FileNode node) { children.remove(node); }
    @Override public int size() {
        int total = 0;
        for (FileNode c : children) total += c.size();
        return total;
    }
    @Override public void print(String indent) {
        System.out.println(indent + name + "/");
        for (FileNode c : children) c.print(indent + "  ");
    }
}

public class CompositeDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Directory root = new Directory("root");
        Directory home = new Directory("home");
        home.add(new File("notes.txt", 120));
        home.add(new File("photo.jpg", 2048));
        Directory docs = new Directory("docs");
        docs.add(new File("resume.pdf", 512));
        home.add(docs);
        root.add(home);
        root.add(new File("readme.md", 64));
        root.print("");
        System.out.println("Total size: " + root.size() + "B");
    }
}

Sample I/O:

root/
  home/
    notes.txt (120B)
    photo.jpg (2048B)
    docs/
      resume.pdf (512B)
  readme.md (64B)
Total size: 2744B

docs.title: 4.2 Python (pythonic, PEP 8, duck-typed component)
docs.text:
Explanation: An abstract OrgUnit defines monthly_cost, headcount, and print. Developer is the leaf; Team aggregates over a plain list and supports nesting plus removal. The demo builds Backend inside Platform and prints payroll. Run with python composite_demo.py.

"""Composite pattern: treat developers and teams uniformly for payroll."""
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod


class OrgUnit(ABC):
    """Component: shared contract for leaves and composites."""

    @abstractmethod
    def monthly_cost(self) -> float:
        ...

    @abstractmethod
    def headcount(self) -> int:
        ...

    @abstractmethod
    def show(self, indent: str = "") -> None:
        ...


class Developer(OrgUnit):
    """Leaf: individual contributor with no reports."""

    def __init__(self, name: str, salary: float) -> None:
        self._name = name
        self._salary = salary

    def monthly_cost(self) -> float:
        return self._salary

    def headcount(self) -> int:
        return 1

    def show(self, indent: str = "") -> None:
        print(f"{indent}- {self._name} (${self._salary:,.0f})")


class Team(OrgUnit):
    """Composite: holds developers and sub-teams."""

    def __init__(self, name: str) -> None:
        self._name = name
        self._members: list[OrgUnit] = []

    def add(self, unit: OrgUnit) -> None:
        self._members.append(unit)

    def remove(self, unit: OrgUnit) -> None:
        self._members.remove(unit)

    def monthly_cost(self) -> float:
        return sum(m.monthly_cost() for m in self._members)

    def headcount(self) -> int:
        return sum(m.headcount() for m in self._members)

    def show(self, indent: str = "") -> None:
        print(f"{indent}+ Team {self._name}")
        for member in self._members:
            member.show(indent + "  ")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    backend = Team("Backend")
    backend.add(Developer("Asha", 9000))
    backend.add(Developer("Ravi", 8000))

    platform = Team("Platform")
    platform.add(backend)
    platform.add(Developer("Mei", 9500))

    platform.show("")
    print(f"Headcount: {platform.headcount()}")
    print(f"Burn: ${platform.monthly_cost():,.0f}")

Sample I/O:

+ Team Platform
  + Team Backend
    - Asha ($9,000)
    - Ravi ($8,000)
  - Mei ($9,500)
Headcount: 3
Burn: $26,500

docs.title: 4.3 Go (idiomatic, implicit interface)
docs.text:
Explanation: Go interfaces are implicit, so FileNode is satisfied by any struct with Size() and Print(). File is the leaf; Directory holds []FileNode and aggregates. main builds the same tree as the Java example. Run with go run composite_demo.go.

package main

import "fmt"

// Component: anything with a size that can print itself.
type FileNode interface {
    Size() int
    Print(indent string)
}

// Leaf: a single file.
type File struct {
    name  string
    bytes int
}

func (f *File) Size() int { return f.bytes }

func (f *File) Print(indent string) {
    fmt.Printf("%s%s (%dB)\n", indent, f.name, f.bytes)
}

// Composite: a directory of files and sub-directories.
type Directory struct {
    name     string
    children []FileNode
}

func (d *Directory) Add(node FileNode) { d.children = append(d.children, node) }

func (d *Directory) Size() int {
    total := 0
    for _, c := range d.children {
        total += c.Size()
    }
    return total
}

func (d *Directory) Print(indent string) {
    fmt.Println(indent + d.name + "/")
    for _, c := range d.children {
        c.Print(indent + "  ")
    }
}

func main() {
    root := &Directory{name: "root"}
    home := &Directory{name: "home"}
    home.Add(&File{name: "notes.txt", bytes: 120})
    home.Add(&File{name: "photo.jpg", bytes: 2048})
    docs := &Directory{name: "docs"}
    docs.Add(&File{name: "resume.pdf", bytes: 512})
    home.Add(docs)
    root.Add(home)
    root.Add(&File{name: "readme.md", bytes: 64})
    root.Print("")
    fmt.Printf("Total size: %dB\n", root.Size())
}

Sample I/O:

root/
  home/
    notes.txt (120B)
    photo.jpg (2048B)
    docs/
      resume.pdf (512B)
  readme.md (64B)
Total size: 2744B

docs.title: 5. Real-World Industry Applications
docs.text:
• File explorers (Windows Explorer, macOS Finder, VS Code tree): Directories and files share selection, drag-drop, size, and permission operations through one node interface.
  • Frontend frameworks (React, Angular, Vue, DOM): Every component renders via the same render() whether it is a leaf <input> or a container <div> of children — the virtual DOM diff walks a Composite.
  • Graphics editors (Figma, Illustrator, Canvas): Groups of shapes rotate, scale, and export as one shape; nested groups recurse identically.
  • Org/HRIS platforms (Workday, BambooHR): Headcount, payroll, and reporting roll up from individuals through teams to the whole company with one code path.
  • Menu and navigation systems: Dropdown menus nest submenus and items; keyboard traversal and access-control checks treat both uniformly.
  • Build systems and test runners (Bazel, JUnit suites): A suite contains tests and sub-suites; run() and report() aggregate results recursively.
  • Game scene graphs (Unity, Unreal): GameObject transforms propagate to children — moving a vehicle moves its wheels and passengers.

docs.title: 6. Practical Use Cases and Scenarios
docs.text:
1. File sync client: upload(), checksum(), and size() work on a file or a folder; sync logic never branches on type.
  2. Payroll roll-up: Finance calls monthlyCost() on any OrgUnit — person, team, or division — for budgets and forecasts.
  3. UI layout engine: measure() and draw() recurse through containers; adding a new widget type needs no layout changes.
  4. Menu permissions: visibleFor(role) aggregates: a submenu is visible if any child is visible; leaves check their own flag.
  5. Test suite runner: Suites nest suites and cases; run() collects pass/fail counts and report() prints the tree.
  6. E-commerce categories: Categories contain products and subcategories; productCount() and search() recurse uniformly.

docs.title: 7. When to Use and When Not to Use
docs.text:
Use Composite when:

  • You model part-whole hierarchies with arbitrary depth (files, orgs, menus, scenes).
  • Clients should treat leaves and groups identically without instanceof checks.
  • Operations naturally aggregate: sum, count, search, render, validate.
  • The tree is built once and traversed often, or structure itself is the domain.

Do NOT use Composite when:

  • The structure is flat or fixed-depth — a list plus a loop is simpler and clearer.
  • Leaf and group operations genuinely differ and forcing one interface creates nonsense methods on both.
  • You need strict type constraints on children (only X inside Y) that the pattern cannot express — consider typed builders or separate classes.
  • Sharing/multiple-parent semantics dominate — a graph model with explicit edges fits better than a tree.
  • Traversal cost on huge trees is unacceptable and cannot be cached — measure first.

docs.title: 8. Do's and Don'ts
docs.text:
Do:

  • Program clients to the Component interface exclusively; assert no instanceof in client code during review.
  • Prefer the safe style: add/remove only on composites; keep leaves minimal.
  • Validate add() (reject nulls, cycles, wrong child types) with clear errors.
  • Cache expensive aggregates or maintain running totals when reads dominate writes.
  • Guard recursion depth; offer iterative traversal for very deep trees.

Don't:

  • Don't put child-management methods on leaves just for uniformity — throwing from leaves is a smell.
  • Don't allow cycles (a team containing itself) without detection — infinite recursion follows.
  • Don't double-count shared children in DAG variants; document ownership semantics.
  • Don't leak child-list internals (return live mutable lists) — return copies or unmodifiable views.
Do Don't Aggregate by delegating to children instanceof-branch in every client Validate add() and reject cycles Let a directory contain itself Cache size() for hot paths Recompute million-node totals per request Return unmodifiable child views Expose the live children list

docs.title: 9. Comparison with Other Design Patterns
docs.text:
Aspect Composite Decorator Flyweight Intent Treat one object and groups uniformly in a tree Add responsibilities to one object dynamically Share fine-grained objects to save memory Structure One composite holds many children One decorator wraps exactly one component Factory pool holds canonical shared instances Children role Peers aggregated (sum, count, render all) Single delegate enriched then returned No children — extrinsic state passed per call Depth meaning Nesting of groups (team in team) Layers of features (milk + sugar) N/A — flat pool keyed by intrinsic state Client view Cannot tell leaf from group Knows it is stacking features Unaware sharing happens Example Org chart, file system, menu tree BufferedInputStream(FileInputStream) Glyph pool, TreeType forest Combines with Flyweight leaves, Decorator on nodes Composite nodes (decorate a whole subtree) Composite trees with shared leaves

Composite vs Iterator: Composite defines the tree; Iterator defines traversal. Expose an iterator over children rather than hard-coding traversal inside every operation.

Composite vs Visitor: Visitor centralises operations over a Composite tree. Use Visitor when operations change often but node types are stable; keep operations on nodes when node types change often.

When to pick which: Uniform group handling → Composite. Stackable features on one object → Decorator. Memory sharing across millions → Flyweight. New operations over stable nodes → Visitor.

docs.title: 10. Interview Preparation
docs.text:
Q1: What is the Composite pattern and why is it useful? It composes objects into trees so clients treat leaves and groups uniformly through a shared component interface. Usefulness: one code path for size, cost, render, or search regardless of depth — e.g., finance calls monthlyCost() on a person or a 500-person org identically.

Q2: Transparent vs safe Composite — which do you prefer? Transparent puts add/remove on the component for total uniformity but forces leaves to implement meaningless methods. Safe exposes management only on composites, keeping leaves clean at the cost of downcasting during assembly. Prefer safe in typed codebases; use builders to keep assembly ergonomic.

Q3: How do you prevent cycles and stack overflows? Reject self-adds and ancestor-adds in add() (track parents or check identity during insertion). Cap depth or switch to iterative traversal with an explicit stack for very deep trees. Test with adversarial nesting (team containing itself, 100k-deep chain).

Q4: Where does aggregation logic live? In the composite, by delegating to children and combining results (sum for cost, AND/OR for permissions, concatenation for rendering). Leaves return base values. Never put aggregation in clients — that reintroduces the type checks the pattern removes.

Q5: How do you restrict which children a composite accepts? Validate in add(): reject nulls, wrong types, or policy violations with descriptive exceptions. Use generics (Team<Engineer>) or separate component sub-interfaces when domains need it. Document constraints — the pattern itself cannot express them structurally.

Q6: How does Composite relate to File, DOM, and UI frameworks? All are canonical instances: file systems (files/directories), DOM (elements containing elements), React trees (components containing components). Each exposes uniform operations (size, render, querySelector) that recurse — interviewers expect at least one of these examples.

Q7: Composite vs Decorator — they both nest, so what differs? Composite holds many children and aggregates across peers; Decorator wraps exactly one object and enriches it. Depth in Composite means group nesting; depth in Decorator means feature layers. A group of shapes is Composite; a shape with border plus shadow wrappers is Decorator.

Q8: What are the performance and memory trade-offs? Traversal is O(n) per aggregate; cache totals or maintain running counts for hot paths. Memory overhead is one child list per composite plus parent pointers if needed. For millions of leaves, combine with Flyweight (share leaf data) and avoid storing redundant parent/child duplicates.

LLD Scenario 1 — File system with size and search: Design FileNode with size(), search(keyword), print(). Directory aggregates. Discuss permission checks, symlink cycles, and caching sizes. Expected: component interface, safe composite, cycle rejection, running totals or memoisation.

LLD Scenario 2 — Org chart with payroll and reporting chain: Design OrgUnit with monthlyCost(), headcount(), findByName(). Support teams in teams, contractors vs FTE leaves, and moving members between teams. Expected: leaf variants, composite moves, uniform queries, removal semantics.

LLD Scenario 3 — Nested comment thread with voting: Comments contain replies to arbitrary depth; score() sums subtree votes; render() indents. Discuss collapsing, pagination of children, and depth limits. Expected: composite with lazy-loaded children, score aggregation, traversal caps.

docs.title: 11. Testing and Best Practices
docs.text:
Unit tests:

  • Test leaves alone: Developer returns own salary, headcount 1; File returns own bytes.
  • Test composites: empty team (cost 0, headcount 0), flat team, 3-level nesting — verify sums and traversal order.
  • Test management: add/remove, removing absent child, rejecting nulls and cycles.
  • Assert client uniformity: same client function produces correct results for leaf and composite inputs without branching.

Integration and property tests:

  • Build randomised trees and compare recursive vs iterative traversal results.
  • Load-test deep/wide trees for stack and time behaviour; set documented depth limits.
  • For permission composites, matrix-test role x tree-shape visibility outcomes.

Best practices:

  • Return unmodifiable views of children; mutate only via add/remove with validation.
  • Keep components immutable where possible; rebuild subtrees instead of mutating shared nodes.
  • Maintain running totals for hot aggregates; invalidate on add/remove.
  • Combine with Iterator for traversal and Visitor for pluggable operations as the design matures.
Aspect Impact Memory Medium (one child list per composite; parent pointers optional) Runtime cost Medium (O(n) traversal per aggregate; cache when hot) Scalability Medium (fine for thousands of nodes; pair with Flyweight for millions) Risk Cycles and over-general types — validate add(), bound depth

docs.title: 12. Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Composite = uniform trees: One interface for leaves and groups; clients never branch on type.
  • Prefer safe over transparent: Management methods belong on composites, not leaves.
  • Aggregate inside composites: Sum, count, and render recurse naturally — never in clients.
  • Guard the tree: Reject nulls and cycles, bound depth, and return unmodifiable child views.
  • Cache hot aggregates when reads dominate; use iterative traversal for extreme depths.
  • Distinguish neighbours: Groups → Composite; stacked features → Decorator; shared instances → Flyweight; traversal abstraction → Iterator; pluggable operations → Visitor.
  • Test shapes, not just values: Empty, flat, nested, cyclic-rejected, and randomised trees.

docs.title: Youtube
docs.text: • 4. Decorator Design Pattern Explanation with Java Coding (Hindi) | LLD System Design

docs.title: 1. Overview and Fundamentals
docs.text:
Intent (GoF): Attach additional responsibilities to an object dynamically. Decorators provide a flexible alternative to subclassing for extending functionality.

In one line: Wrap an object in layers — each layer adds one feature while staying interchangeable with the original.

Real-world analogy: Coffee shop condiments. Base Espresso costs \(2. Add Milk (+\)0.50), Sugar (+\(0.20), WhippedCream (+\)0.70). Each condiment wraps the previous drink, the final object is still a Coffee, and any combination is possible without a MilkySugaryWhippedEspresso subclass.

Family context: Decorator is a structural pattern. It changes the skin and behaviour of objects through composition rather than inheritance hierarchies.

Key participants:

  • Component — common interface (Coffee, Notifier, InputStream).
  • ConcreteComponent — base object with default behaviour (BasicCoffee, EmailNotifier).
  • Decorator — abstract wrapper holding a Component reference and delegating by default.
  • ConcreteDecorator — adds one responsibility (MilkDecorator, EncryptionDecorator, BufferedInputStream).

Core characteristics:

  • Same interface at every layer — a decorated object substitutes anywhere the original fits.
  • Composition at runtime: new Retry(new Encrypt(new Slack(new Email()))).
  • Each decorator has a single responsibility; features mix and match.
  • Order can matter: encrypt-then-log differs from log-then-encrypt.
  • Alternative to subclass explosion: N optional features need N decorators, not 2^N subclasses.

Mental model:

Client -> RetryDecorator -> EncryptionDecorator -> SlackDecorator -> EmailNotifier
  send()      retries          encrypts              also posts       base send

If the caller deliberately stacks toppings, it is a Decorator. If the wrapper secretly guards or defers, it is a Proxy.

docs.title: 2. Detailed Theory
docs.text:
Problem: Subclassing for every feature combination explodes. Three boolean options (milk, sugar, foam) already need 8 subclasses; adding caramel doubles to 16. Static inheritance also locks behaviour at compile time — you cannot add or remove a topping per request.

Solution: Define a Component interface. Implement the base behaviour once. For each optional feature, write a Decorator that implements the same interface, holds a wrapped Component, delegates the core call, and adds its own logic before or after delegation.

How delegation works:

  • Transparent delegation: NotifierDecorator.send() calls wrapped.send() by default so subclasses override only what they change.
  • Before-advice: Validate, transform, or enrich input (encrypt message, check args) then delegate.
  • After-advice: Enrich output or side effects (also post to Slack, record metrics) after delegating.
  • Around-advice: Retry, caching, or timing wraps the delegate call in try/catch or clock logic.
  • Recursive unwrapping: Because every layer honours the interface, depth is invisible to clients.

Ordering semantics:

  • Order is part of the configuration. Encrypt(Slack(Email)) encrypts once then fans out; Slack(Encrypt(Email)) may double-encrypt or leak plaintext to logs.
  • Document valid orderings; provide factory methods for blessed stacks (AlertingPipelines.critical()).
  • When order must not matter, design decorators to be commutative (idempotent headers, independent side channels).

Decorator vs inheritance vs composition helpers:

  • Inheritance: Compile-time, rigid, exponential class growth.
  • Decorator: Runtime, flexible, linear class growth, but longer construction expressions and deeper stack traces.
  • Builder/Factory: Often paired to tame construction — NotifierBuilder.withSlack().withRetry().build() hides nesting.
  • Middleware pipelines (Express, Django, gRPC interceptors): Framework-level decorators where each handler wraps the next — same pattern at architectural scale.

SOLID connections:

  • Open/Closed: New behaviour arrives as a new wrapper; existing components never change.
  • Single Responsibility: Each decorator owns one concern (encryption, retry, fan-out).
  • Liskov Substitution: Any decorated object substitutes for the base component.
  • Dependency Inversion: Clients depend on Notifier, not on any concrete decorator.

Consequences:

  • Maximum combinability at the cost of many small objects and harder debugging through long chains.
  • instanceof checks break — a decorated EmailNotifier is not an EmailNotifier instance in the naive sense.
  • Deep chains add per-call overhead; fuse hot paths or cache when profiling demands it.

docs.title: Diagram 1 — Class structure (stacked wrappers)
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Notifier {
        <>
        +send(message: String)
    }
    class EmailNotifier {
        +send(message: String)
    }
    class NotifierDecorator {
        <>
        #wrapped: Notifier
        +send(message: String)
    }
    class SlackDecorator {
        +send(message: String)
    }
    class EncryptionDecorator {
        +send(message: String)
    }
    class RetryDecorator {
        +send(message: String)
    }
    Notifier <|.. EmailNotifier : implements
    Notifier <|.. NotifierDecorator : implements
    NotifierDecorator <|-- SlackDecorator : extends
    NotifierDecorator <|-- EncryptionDecorator : extends
    NotifierDecorator <|-- RetryDecorator : extends
    NotifierDecorator o-- Notifier : wraps

Explanation: EmailNotifier is the concrete component. NotifierDecorator implements the same Notifier interface and holds a wrapped Notifier (aggregation). Each concrete decorator extends the base decorator and overrides send() to add its bit before or after delegating. Because decorators and components share the interface, they nest arbitrarily: a RetryDecorator can wrap an EncryptionDecorator that wraps a SlackDecorator that wraps the email base.

docs.title: Diagram 2 — Runtime stacking (sequence)
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as AlertingDemo
    participant Retry as RetryDecorator
    participant Enc as EncryptionDecorator
    participant Slack as SlackDecorator
    participant Email as EmailNotifier
    App->>Retry: send("DB latency > 2s")
    Retry->>Enc: send("DB latency > 2s") [attempt 1]
    Enc->>Slack: send("[encrypted]DB latency > 2s")
    Slack->>Email: send("[encrypted]DB latency > 2s")
    Email-->>Slack: EMAIL delivered
    Slack-->>Enc: + SLACK posted
    Enc-->>Retry: ok
    Retry-->>App: success

Explanation: The call flows inward through the stack, each layer transforming or fanning out, then results propagate outward. Encryption happens before fan-out so both email and Slack see ciphertext. Retry surrounds everything, so a failure at any inner layer triggers a full-stack retry. Reordering the nesting would visibly change this trace — which is why order is configuration.

docs.title: 4. Implementation Examples in Java, Python, and Go
4.1 Java (OOP, notifier pipeline)
docs.text:
Explanation: EmailNotifier is the base. NotifierDecorator delegates by default. SlackDecorator, EncryptionDecorator, and RetryDecorator each add one behaviour. AlertingDemo composes the full pipeline in one nested expression. Compile with javac DecoratorDemo.java && java AlertingDemo.

interface Notifier {
    void send(String message);
}

class EmailNotifier implements Notifier {
    @Override
    public void send(String message) {
        System.out.println("EMAIL: " + message);
    }
}

abstract class NotifierDecorator implements Notifier {
    protected final Notifier wrapped;
    protected NotifierDecorator(Notifier wrapped) { this.wrapped = wrapped; }
    @Override
    public void send(String message) { wrapped.send(message); }
}

class SlackDecorator extends NotifierDecorator {
    SlackDecorator(Notifier wrapped) { super(wrapped); }
    @Override
    public void send(String message) {
        super.send(message);
        System.out.println("SLACK: " + message);
    }
}

class EncryptionDecorator extends NotifierDecorator {
    EncryptionDecorator(Notifier wrapped) { super(wrapped); }
    @Override
    public void send(String message) {
        super.send("[encrypted]" + message);
    }
}

class RetryDecorator extends NotifierDecorator {
    RetryDecorator(Notifier wrapped) { super(wrapped); }
    @Override
    public void send(String message) {
        int attempts = 0;
        while (true) {
            try {
                super.send(message);
                return;
            } catch (RuntimeException e) {
                if (++attempts >= 3) throw e;
                System.out.println("Retrying... attempt " + (attempts + 1));
            }
        }
    }
}

class AlertingDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Notifier pipeline = new RetryDecorator(
            new EncryptionDecorator(
                new SlackDecorator(new EmailNotifier())));
        pipeline.send("DB latency above 2s");

        System.out.println("--- plain ---");
        new EmailNotifier().send("plain hello");
    }
}

Sample I/O:

EMAIL: [encrypted]DB latency above 2s
SLACK: [encrypted]DB latency above 2s
--- plain ---
EMAIL: plain hello

docs.title: 4.2 Python (pythonic, PEP 8, callable wrappers)
docs.text:
Explanation: Python's first-class functions make decorators natural, but for LLD parity we use classes sharing a Notifier protocol. Each wrapper stores the inner notifier and delegates. The demo also shows Python's @ syntax alternative in comments. Run with python decorator_demo.py.

"""Decorator pattern: stack Slack, encryption, and retry around email."""
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod


class Notifier(ABC):
    """Component: minimal notification contract."""

    @abstractmethod
    def send(self, message: str) -> None:
        ...


class EmailNotifier(Notifier):
    """Concrete component: plain email delivery."""

    def send(self, message: str) -> None:
        print(f"EMAIL: {message}")


class NotifierDecorator(Notifier):
    """Base decorator: delegates by default."""

    def __init__(self, wrapped: Notifier) -> None:
        self._wrapped = wrapped

    def send(self, message: str) -> None:
        self._wrapped.send(message)


class SlackDecorator(NotifierDecorator):
    """Also posts to Slack after delegating."""

    def send(self, message: str) -> None:
        super().send(message)
        print(f"SLACK: {message}")


class EncryptionDecorator(NotifierDecorator):
    """Encrypts before delegating."""

    def send(self, message: str) -> None:
        super().send(f"[encrypted]{message}")


class RetryDecorator(NotifierDecorator):
    """Retries the whole inner chain up to 3 times."""

    def send(self, message: str) -> None:
        attempts = 0
        while True:
            try:
                super().send(message)
                return
            except RuntimeError:
                attempts += 1
                if attempts >= 3:
                    raise
                print(f"Retrying... attempt {attempts + 1}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    pipeline: Notifier = RetryDecorator(
        EncryptionDecorator(SlackDecorator(EmailNotifier()))
    )
    pipeline.send("DB latency above 2s")
    print("--- plain ---")
    EmailNotifier().send("plain hello")

Sample I/O:

EMAIL: [encrypted]DB latency above 2s
SLACK: [encrypted]DB latency above 2s
--- plain ---
EMAIL: plain hello

docs.title: 4.3 Go (idiomatic, struct embedding via interface field)
docs.text:
Explanation: Go has no inheritance, so each decorator is a struct holding a Notifier interface value. Methods delegate explicitly. Construction nests struct literals. Run with go run decorator_demo.go.

package main

import "fmt"

// Component.
type Notifier interface {
    Send(message string)
}

// Concrete component.
type EmailNotifier struct{}

func (e *EmailNotifier) Send(message string) {
    fmt.Println("EMAIL: " + message)
}

// Concrete decorator: also posts to Slack.
type SlackDecorator struct {
    wrapped Notifier
}

func (d *SlackDecorator) Send(message string) {
    d.wrapped.Send(message)
    fmt.Println("SLACK: " + message)
}

// Concrete decorator: encrypts before delegating.
type EncryptionDecorator struct {
    wrapped Notifier
}

func (d *EncryptionDecorator) Send(message string) {
    d.wrapped.Send("[encrypted]" + message)
}

// Concrete decorator: retries inner chain.
type RetryDecorator struct {
    wrapped Notifier
}

func (d *RetryDecorator) Send(message string) {
    for attempt := 1; attempt <= 3; attempt++ {
        func() {
            defer func() {
                if r := recover(); r != nil && attempt == 3 {
                    panic(r)
                }
            }()
            d.wrapped.Send(message)
            attempt = 4 // success: break loop
        }()
    }
}

func main() {
    var pipeline Notifier = &RetryDecorator{
        wrapped: &EncryptionDecorator{
            wrapped: &SlackDecorator{wrapped: &EmailNotifier{}},
        },
    }
    pipeline.Send("DB latency above 2s")
    fmt.Println("--- plain ---")
    (&EmailNotifier{}).Send("plain hello")
}

Sample I/O:

EMAIL: [encrypted]DB latency above 2s
SLACK: [encrypted]DB latency above 2s
--- plain ---
EMAIL: plain hello

docs.title: 5. Real-World Industry Applications
docs.text:
• Java I/O (BufferedInputStream, GZIPInputStream, DataInputStream): The canonical textbook stack — buffering, decompression, and typed reads layer over any InputStream in any order.
  • HTTP middleware (Express, Django, Spring interceptors, gRPC): Authentication, logging, CORS, rate-limiting, and compression each wrap the next handler — a framework-scale decorator chain.
  • Spring annotations (@Transactional, @Cacheable, @Retryable): AOP proxies decorate bean methods with transactions, caching, and retries without touching business code.
  • OkHttp / Python requests interceptors: Retry, auth-header injection, logging, and metrics wrap a base HTTP client per request.
  • UI adornments: Scrollbars, borders, shadows, and tooltips wrap base widgets in Swing, JavaFX, and web component libraries.
  • Coffee/pizza configurators (Starbucks, Domino's apps): Toppings and size upgrades stack price and description dynamically — the domain that named the pattern.

docs.title: 6. Practical Use Cases and Scenarios
docs.text:
1. Alerting pipeline: Base email plus optional Slack, PagerDuty, encryption, and retry — composed per severity (critical = all layers, info = email only).
  2. Payment processing: Base charge wrapped with fraud-check, idempotency, currency conversion, and audit logging decorators chosen per region.
  3. File stream stack: DataInputStream(BufferedInputStream(GZIPInputStream(FileInputStream))) — buffering, decompression, typed reads in one line.
  4. API client hardening: Base HTTP client decorated with retry, circuit-breaker, auth-refresh, and metrics for production while tests use the bare client.
  5. Text editor formatting: Base text wrapped with bold, italic, hyperlink, and mention decorators for rich rendering.
  6. Data pipeline: Base reader decorated with validation, deduplication, enrichment, and sampling stages toggled by feature flags.

docs.title: 7. When to Use and When Not to Use
docs.text:
Use Decorator when:

  • You need optional, combinable responsibilities chosen at runtime.
  • Subclassing would explode (N features → 2^N subclasses).
  • Responsibilities should be added or removed per object, not per class.
  • You want Open/Closed extension: new feature = new wrapper, zero edits.
  • Each feature is independently testable and order-explicit.

Do NOT use Decorator when:

  • Features are fixed and universal — bake them into the base class instead.
  • Only one combination will ever exist — a single subclass or direct composition is simpler.
  • Order-independence cannot be guaranteed and every permutation behaves differently — consider a pipeline with explicit stages or Chain of Responsibility.
  • Performance-critical hot paths cannot afford per-layer delegation — fuse or inline after profiling.
  • The wrapper must control access or lifecycle rather than add features — that is Proxy.

docs.title: 8. Do's and Don'ts
docs.text:
Do:

  • Keep each decorator focused on exactly one responsibility.
  • Delegate faithfully: forward all interface methods, not just the convenient one.
  • Document ordering constraints and provide factory methods for blessed stacks.
  • Favour constructor injection of the wrapped component for testability.
  • Test each decorator in isolation plus representative compositions.

Don't:

  • Don't let decorators depend on each other directly — they should only know the component interface.
  • Don't use instanceof/type-switches to peek through layers — that defeats substitutability.
  • Don't accumulate business rules across layers opaquely — order bugs become undebuggable.
  • Don't build 10-deep chains on hot paths without profiling delegation cost.
  • Don't expose unwrapping backdoors that let clients bypass layers.
Do Don't new Retry(new Encrypt(new Slack(email))) explicit Hidden global mutation inside decorators One concern per decorator, tested alone God decorator doing auth + retry + logging Factory for standard stacks Force every caller to nest 5 constructors Document encrypt-before-log Log plaintext then encrypt (leak)

docs.title: 9. Comparison with Other Design Patterns
docs.text:
Aspect Decorator Proxy Composite Adapter Intent Add responsibilities dynamically, client-composed Control access (guard, defer, cache), often transparent Treat one and many uniformly in a tree Convert incompatible interface Interface Same as component; stacking normal Same as subject; usually single layer Same for leaf and group Changes to target interface Who builds Client nests wrappers explicitly Framework/factory hides proxy Client assembles tree Client uses target, adapter hidden Cardinality One decorator wraps exactly one component One proxy fronts one subject One composite holds many children One adapter bridges one adaptee Lifecycle Never manages wrapped lifecycle May create/cache/synchronise real object Manages children collection Stateless translator Example EncryptionDecorator(Notifier) AccountProtectionProxy Team of Developers StripeAdapter Without it 2^N subclasses Scattered guards / eager cost Type-check soup Code does not compile

Decorator vs Chain of Responsibility: Decorator always delegates through the full stack; CoR passes along until one handler consumes the request. Decorator enriches; CoR dispatches.

When to pick which: Stackable opt-in features → Decorator. Guard/defer/cache transparently → Proxy. One-or-many uniformity → Composite. Signature mismatch → Adapter.

docs.title: 10. Interview Preparation
docs.text:
Q1: What is Decorator and why prefer it over subclassing? Decorator wraps an object in layers sharing its interface, adding one responsibility per layer at runtime. N optional features need N decorators instead of 2^N subclasses, behaviour composes per object rather than per class, and new features arrive without editing existing code.

Q2: How do Java I/O streams demonstrate Decorator? FileInputStream is the component; BufferedInputStream, GZIPInputStream, DataInputStream are decorators wrapping any InputStream. Nesting them stacks buffering, decompression, and typed reads in any order while downstream code sees only InputStream.

Q3: Decorator vs Proxy — both wrap, so what differs? Decorator openly adds features the client composes (and also); Proxy controls access on the client's behalf (you may not / not yet), often invisibly. Decorators stack many-deep by hand; proxies are usually single-layer and may manage the real object's lifecycle.

Q4: What goes wrong with deep or misordered chains? Deep chains add delegation overhead and long stack traces. Misordering causes semantic bugs: logging before encryption leaks plaintext; retrying inside encryption may resend ciphertext incorrectly. Mitigate with documented orderings, factory-built standard stacks, and integration tests per supported ordering.

Q5: How do middleware pipelines relate to Decorator? Express/Django middleware, Spring interceptors, and gRPC interceptors are Decorator at framework scale: each handler wraps the next, adding auth, logging, or compression. The request flows inward through layers exactly like send() flows through notifier decorators.

Q6: How do you keep construction manageable? Provide builders or factory methods (AlertPipelines.critical()) returning blessed stacks. Use DI to wire common stacks. Keep decorator constructors to one wrapped-component parameter plus its own config.

Q7: Why do instanceof checks break with Decorator? A wrapped object reports the decorator's type, not the inner component's. Code that branches on concrete type fails. Solution: program to the interface and expose capability queries on the interface if needed, never downcast through layers.

Q8: What is the performance cost? One virtual call per layer — negligible for I/O-bound work, measurable for nanosecond hot loops. Profile before fusing. Prefer shallow chains on hot paths; keep deep stacks for configuration-heavy, I/O-bound pipelines.

LLD Scenario 1 — Coffee shop pricing engine: Design Beverage with cost() and description(). Implement Espresso, Milk, Sugar, Whip decorators. Support arbitrary nesting, combo discounts, and receipt printing. Expected: component interface, per-topping decorators, order-independent pricing, builder for common drinks.

LLD Scenario 2 — HTTP client with retry/auth/metrics: Base HttpClient plus AuthDecorator (token refresh), RetryDecorator (exponential backoff), MetricsDecorator (latency histograms). Discuss ordering (auth inside or outside retry?) and testability. Expected: decorator stack, ordering rationale, per-layer unit tests with stubbed inner client.

LLD Scenario 3 — Notification fan-out with encryption: Base email plus Slack, SMS, encryption, and rate-limit decorators. Critical alerts use all layers; info uses email only. Discuss where truncation lives and how to avoid plaintext logs. Expected: stack composition per severity, encrypt-before-log ordering, factory wiring.

docs.title: 11. Testing and Best Practices
docs.text:
Unit tests:

  • Test each decorator against a stub component: assert transformation happens exactly once and delegation happens exactly once (mock verification).
  • Test RetryDecorator with a failing stub: assert 3 attempts then success, and 3 attempts then rethrow.
  • Test order-sensitive pairs both ways (Encrypt(Log(x)) vs Log(Encrypt(x))) and lock the correct one.
  • Test the base component alone to prove it works undecorated.

Integration tests:

  • Representative full stacks (email + Slack + encryption + retry) with fake transports.
  • Concurrency tests when decorators hold state (rate limiters, circuit breakers) — assert thread-safety.
  • Performance smoke test on deepest supported chain to bound latency.

Best practices:

  • Keep decorators stateless where possible; isolate mutable state (counters, caches) with clear thread-safety docs.
  • Forward equals/hashCode/toString thoughtfully or document that identity is layered.
  • Provide unwrap() only for diagnostics, never for bypassing in production paths.
  • Combine with Builder for ergonomic construction and with Strategy inside decorators when the added behaviour itself varies.
Aspect Impact Memory Medium (one object per layer) Runtime cost Medium (one delegation per layer; negligible for I/O) Scalability Medium (chains compose linearly; watch depth on hot paths) Risk Order bugs and debug complexity — document and factory-build stacks

docs.title: 12. Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Decorator = stackable features: Same interface, one responsibility per layer, composed at runtime.
  • N decorators beat 2^N subclasses — linear growth, per-object configurability, Open/Closed extension.
  • Order is configuration: Document it, factory-build blessed stacks, test each supported ordering.
  • Delegate faithfully: Forward the full interface; never peek through layers with type checks.
  • Distinguish neighbours: Stacked features → Decorator; guarded access → Proxy; group uniformity → Composite; signature fix → Adapter; consumed handler → Chain of Responsibility.
  • Test layers then stacks: Isolated decorator tests plus integration tests for real compositions.

docs.title: Youtube
docs.text: • 25. Facade Design Pattern with Example | Facade Low Level Design Pattern | Facade Pattern LLD Java

docs.title: 1. Overview and Fundamentals
docs.text:
Intent (GoF): Provide a unified interface to a set of interfaces in a subsystem. Facade defines a higher-level interface that makes the subsystem easier to use.

In one line: One simple front door hiding a building full of complicated rooms.

Real-world analogy: A hotel concierge. You say "book a cab, reserve dinner, arrange checkout". The concierge coordinates taxi dispatch, restaurant booking, and billing subsystems. You never call each department yourself.

Family context: Facade is a structural pattern. It structures access to a subsystem rather than changing signatures (Adapter) or adding features (Decorator).

Key participants:

  • Facade — simplified entry point exposing coarse-grained operations (OrderFacade.placeOrder(), VideoConverterFacade.convertToMp4()).
  • Subsystem classes — do the real work, remain independently usable (PaymentService, InventoryService, CodecExtractor, Muxer).
  • Client — calls only the facade for common flows; may drop down to subsystem for advanced needs.

Core characteristics:

  • Orchestrates call order: validate → charge → reserve → ship.
  • Does not encapsulate the subsystem — internals stay public for power users.
  • Typically stateless coordination; holds subsystem references via composition.
  • One facade per use case or subsystem view is normal (CheckoutFacade, VideoConverterFacade, ThumbnailFacade).
  • Reduces coupling: client depends on 1 facade instead of N subsystem classes.

Mental model:

Client -> Facade.placeOrder()
            |-> payments.charge()
            |-> stock.reserve()
            |-> shipping.dispatch()

If the pain is "too many steps in the right order", write a Facade. If the pain is "signatures don't match", write an Adapter.

docs.title: 2. Detailed Theory
docs.text:
Problem: A subsystem is powerful but painful: video conversion needs extract → transcode → normalise → mux in exact order with correct options. Checkout needs payment, inventory, shipping, notification, and audit calls. Every caller copy-pastes the sequence, gets ordering wrong, and breaks when a subsystem changes.

Solution: Introduce a Facade that owns the workflow. It exposes intention-revealing methods (convertToMp4(file), placeOrder(order)) and internally wires subsystem calls, default options, error translation, and ordering. Callers go from 15 lines to 1.

Facade vs layers and gateways:

  • Facade object: In-process simplifier over a library or module (this pattern).
  • Layered subsystem: Facade often marks a layer boundary — UI calls service facade, which calls repositories.
  • API Gateway / BFF: Distributed cousin — one HTTP endpoint orchestrating many microservices, same intent at network scale.
  • Anti-corruption layer: Facade plus translation; pure Facade does not translate types, it only orchestrates.

Design choices:

  • Thin vs rich facade: Thin facades only sequence calls; rich facades add defaults, retries, and transaction boundaries. Prefer thin; push business rules into domain services.
  • One vs many facades: Start with one per subsystem; split by client need when it grows (AdminFacade vs CustomerFacade). A single god facade that knows everything is the classic failure mode.
  • Return types: Return subsystem types or simple DTOs — do not rewrap the world. Let callers drill down when needed.
  • Error handling: Translate low-level exceptions (CodecException, SQLException) into facade-level errors (ConversionFailed, OrderFailed) with causes preserved.
  • State: Keep facades stateless; pass context as parameters so they stay thread-safe and testable.

SOLID connections:

  • Single Responsibility: Each facade owns one workflow or view, not all workflows.
  • Dependency Inversion: Clients depend on facade abstraction; facade depends on subsystem abstractions (inject for testability).
  • Open/Closed: New workflows arrive as new facade methods or new facades, not by editing subsystem classes.
  • Interface Segregation: Client-specific facades expose only what each client needs.

Consequences:

  • Dramatically simpler happy paths at the cost of a potential god object and a hiding place for complexity.
  • Well-designed facades are optional — experts can bypass them. Bad facades trap everyone behind a lowest-common-denominator API.

docs.title: Diagram 1 — Class structure (facade over subsystem)
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class UploadController {
        +onUpload(file: String)
    }
    class VideoConverterFacade {
        -extractor: CodecExtractor
        -transcoder: Transcoder
        -audio: AudioNormalizer
        -muxer: Muxer
        +convertToMp4(file: String) String
        +convertToWebm(file: String) String
    }
    class CodecExtractor {
        +extractTrack(file: String) String
    }
    class Transcoder {
        +transcode(track: String, codec: String) String
    }
    class AudioNormalizer {
        +normalize(track: String) String
    }
    class Muxer {
        +mux(video: String, container: String) String
    }
    UploadController --> VideoConverterFacade : uses
    VideoConverterFacade --> CodecExtractor : orchestrates
    VideoConverterFacade --> Transcoder : orchestrates
    VideoConverterFacade --> AudioNormalizer : orchestrates
    VideoConverterFacade --> Muxer : orchestrates

Explanation: The client (UploadController) has exactly one dependency: the facade. The facade holds references to four subsystem classes and encodes the correct pipeline order. Subsystem classes know nothing about the facade, so power users can still call Transcoder directly with custom bitrates. Adding a new output format is a new facade method, not a client change.

docs.title: Diagram 2 — Orchestration flow (sequence)
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as UploadController
    participant F as VideoConverterFacade
    participant E as CodecExtractor
    participant T as Transcoder
    participant A as AudioNormalizer
    participant M as Muxer
    C->>F: convertToMp4("talk.mov")
    F->>E: extractTrack("talk.mov")
    E-->>F: video-track
    F->>T: transcode(video-track, "h264")
    T-->>F: recoded-track
    F->>A: normalize(recoded-track)
    A-->>F: track+audio
    F->>M: mux(track+audio, "mp4")
    M-->>F: final.mp4{...}
    F-->>C: final.mp4{...}

Explanation: The sequence makes the value obvious: five subsystem interactions collapse into one client call. Ordering lives in exactly one place — extract before transcode before mux. Error translation also lives here: if Transcoder throws a codec error, the facade wraps it in a ConversionFailed with the filename attached, so controllers never import codec internals.

docs.title: 4. Implementation Examples in Java, Python, and Go
4.1 Java (OOP, video conversion facade)
docs.text:
Explanation: Four subsystem classes do one job each. VideoConverterFacade wires them with sensible defaults. UploadController calls one method. Compile with javac FacadeDemo.java && java FacadeDemo.

class CodecExtractor {
    String extractTrack(String file) { return "video-track-of:" + file; }
}

class Transcoder {
    String transcode(String track, String codec) { return track + "->" + codec; }
}

class AudioNormalizer {
    String normalize(String track) { return track + "+normalized-audio"; }
}

class Muxer {
    String mux(String video, String container) {
        return "final." + container + "{" + video + "}";
    }
}

class VideoConverterFacade {
    private final CodecExtractor extractor = new CodecExtractor();
    private final Transcoder transcoder = new Transcoder();
    private final AudioNormalizer audio = new AudioNormalizer();
    private final Muxer muxer = new Muxer();

    public String convertToMp4(String sourceFile) {
        String track = extractor.extractTrack(sourceFile);
        String recoded = transcoder.transcode(track, "h264");
        return muxer.mux(audio.normalize(recoded), "mp4");
    }

    public String convertToWebm(String sourceFile) {
        String track = extractor.extractTrack(sourceFile);
        String recoded = transcoder.transcode(track, "vp9");
        return muxer.mux(audio.normalize(recoded), "webm");
    }
}

class UploadController {
    private final VideoConverterFacade videos = new VideoConverterFacade();
    void onUpload(String file) {
        System.out.println("Ready to stream: " + videos.convertToMp4(file));
    }
}

public class FacadeDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new UploadController().onUpload("talk.mov");
    }
}

Sample I/O:

Ready to stream: final.mp4{video-track-of:talk.mov->h264+normalized-audio}

docs.title: 4.2 Python (pythonic, PEP 8, order checkout facade)
docs.text:
Explanation: OrderFacade coordinates payment, inventory, and shipping services behind place_order(). Subsystem classes stay usable alone. Dependency injection via constructor keeps tests hermetic. Run with python facade_demo.py.

"""Facade pattern: one checkout call hiding payment, stock, shipping."""


class PaymentService:
    def charge(self, order_id: str, amount: float) -> str:
        return f"charge:{order_id}:{amount:.2f}"


class InventoryService:
    def reserve(self, order_id: str, sku: str) -> str:
        return f"reserved:{sku}-for-{order_id}"


class ShippingService:
    def dispatch(self, order_id: str, address: str) -> str:
        return f"shipped:{order_id}-to-{address}"


class NotificationService:
    def notify(self, order_id: str) -> str:
        return f"notified:{order_id}"


class OrderFacade:
    """Simplified checkout entry point."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._payments = PaymentService()
        self._stock = InventoryService()
        self._shipping = ShippingService()
        self._notify = NotificationService()

    def place_order(self, order_id: str, sku: str,
                    amount: float, address: str) -> str:
        receipt = self._payments.charge(order_id, amount)
        reservation = self._stock.reserve(order_id, sku)
        shipment = self._shipping.dispatch(order_id, address)
        self._notify.notify(order_id)
        return f"OK {receipt} | {reservation} | {shipment}"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    facade = OrderFacade()
    print(facade.place_order("ord-101", "keyboard", 2499.0, "Bengaluru"))

Sample I/O:

OK charge:ord-101:2499.00 | reserved:keyboard-for-ord-101 | shipped:ord-101-to-Bengaluru

docs.title: 4.3 Go (idiomatic, explicit struct wiring)
docs.text:
Explanation: Same checkout domain in Go. Subsystems are structs with methods; OrderFacade holds them and exposes PlaceOrder. No hidden globals — wiring is visible in NewOrderFacade. Run with go run facade_demo.go.

package main

import "fmt"

type PaymentService struct{}

func (p *PaymentService) Charge(orderID string, amount float64) string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("charge:%s:%.2f", orderID, amount)
}

type InventoryService struct{}

func (s *InventoryService) Reserve(orderID, sku string) string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("reserved:%s-for-%s", sku, orderID)
}

type ShippingService struct{}

func (s *ShippingService) Dispatch(orderID, address string) string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("shipped:%s-to-%s", orderID, address)
}

// Facade: single entry point for checkout.
type OrderFacade struct {
    payments *PaymentService
    stock    *InventoryService
    shipping *ShippingService
}

func NewOrderFacade() *OrderFacade {
    return &OrderFacade{
        payments: &PaymentService{},
        stock:    &InventoryService{},
        shipping: &ShippingService{},
    }
}

func (f *OrderFacade) PlaceOrder(orderID, sku string, amount float64, address string) string {
    receipt := f.payments.Charge(orderID, amount)
    reservation := f.stock.Reserve(orderID, sku)
    shipment := f.shipping.Dispatch(orderID, address)
    return fmt.Sprintf("OK %s | %s | %s", receipt, reservation, shipment)
}

func main() {
    facade := NewOrderFacade()
    fmt.Println(facade.PlaceOrder("ord-101", "keyboard", 2499.0, "Bengaluru"))
}

Sample I/O:

OK charge:ord-101:2499.00 | reserved:keyboard-for-ord-101 | shipped:ord-101-to-Bengaluru

docs.title: 5. Real-World Industry Applications
docs.text:
• E-commerce checkout (Amazon, Flipkart): OrderService.placeOrder() hides payment auth, inventory reservation, fraud check, shipping label, and notification fan-out.
  • Spring Boot starters: spring-boot-starter-web hides dispatcher servlet, Jackson, validation, and Tomcat wiring behind auto-configuration.
  • AWS SDK v2 clients (S3Client, DynamoDbClient): One method hides signing, retries, pagination, endpoint resolution, and error unmarshalling.
  • FFmpeg wrappers / video SaaS (Mux, Cloudinary): uploadAndTranscode(file) hides demux, codec selection, thumbnailing, and CDN publish.
  • Home automation (Home Assistant, Alexa routines): "Good night" routine hides lights, lock, thermostat, and alarm arming.
  • Compiler / build facades (Maven compile, javac driver): One command hides lexing, parsing, analysis, codegen, and linking phases.

docs.title: 6. Practical Use Cases and Scenarios
docs.text:
1. Checkout flow: Charge → reserve → dispatch → notify in one placeOrder(); controllers never sequence payments manually.
  2. Media pipeline: convertToMp4() / thumbnail() hide codec, filter, and muxer orchestration from upload handlers.
  3. Onboarding wizard: onboardEmployee() creates accounts, assigns assets, grants repo access, and sends welcome mail in order.
  4. DevOps deploy: deploy(service, env) hides build, push, migrate, rollout, and health-check steps behind one CLI command.
  5. Report generation: monthlyReport() hides query, aggregate, chart, PDF render, and email steps.
  6. Travel booking: bookTrip() coordinates flights, hotels, cabs, and insurance with rollback on partial failure.

docs.title: 7. When to Use and When Not to Use
docs.text:
Use Facade when:

  • A subsystem needs 3+ calls in a fixed order for every common task.
  • You want to decouple clients from subsystem churn (codec upgrades, provider swaps).
  • You need a layer entry point or a curated default path for most callers.
  • Onboarding to a library is painful — a facade is living documentation.
  • You want one place for cross-cutting defaults: timeouts, retries, error translation.

Do NOT use Facade when:

  • The subsystem is already simple — a facade over two trivial calls adds indirection without value.
  • You need to fix incompatible signatures — that is Adapter, not Facade.
  • One facade would become a god object knowing every subsystem — split by use case instead.
  • Callers genuinely need fine-grained control every time — facades help common paths, not all paths.
  • The goal is adding per-object features — that is Decorator.

docs.title: 8. Do's and Don'ts
docs.text:
Do:

  • Keep facades thin: sequence, default, translate errors — delegate real work.
  • Allow bypass: keep subsystem classes public for advanced use.
  • Inject subsystems (constructor/DI) so tests can mock them.
  • Name by workflow (VideoConverterFacade, CheckoutFacade), not Manager/Util.
  • Split when growing: one facade per subsystem view or client type.

Don't:

  • Don't turn the facade into a god object with 40 methods and mutable state.
  • Don't duplicate subsystem logic inside the facade — call, don't reimplement.
  • Don't swallow subsystem errors or return ambiguous nulls — translate with context.
  • Don't force all clients through the facade when some need lower-level control.
  • Don't hide so much that debugging requires reading facade source to know what ran.
Do Don't One workflow per method, ordered inside Copy-paste sequencing in every controller Translate CodecException to ConversionFailed Leak codec internals to upload code Inject PaymentService for tests new everything inside with no seam Split VideoFacade vs ThumbnailFacade Single MediaGod with 50 methods

docs.title: 9. Comparison with Other Design Patterns
docs.text:
Aspect Facade Mediator Adapter Intent Simplify outside-in access to a subsystem Centralise inside communication between peers Convert one incompatible interface Direction Outside → in: client calls facade instead of internals Peer ↔ peer via hub: colleagues stop referencing each other Old → new: adaptee calls translated to target Knows whom Facade knows subsystem; subsystem unaware of facade Mediator knows colleagues; colleagues know mediator Adapter knows adaptee; client sees only target Reuse Subsystems fully reusable standalone Colleagues usually useless without mediator Adaptee fixed; adapter is new Changes interface? No — orchestrates existing calls Defines new coordination protocol Yes — translates signatures Example VideoConverterFacade.convertToMp4() Chatroom hub, ATC tower, dialog controller StripeAdapter implements PaymentProcessor Without it Verbose, error-prone multi-step code Web of peer-to-peer references Code does not compile

Facade vs Singleton: Facades are often mistakenly made singletons. Prefer injectable instances — singletons hide dependencies and complicate tests.

Facade vs Proxy: Proxy fronts one object with the same interface to control access; Facade fronts many objects with a simpler interface to reduce effort.

When to pick which: Too many steps → Facade. Tangled peers → Mediator. Mismatched signatures → Adapter. Guard/defer one object → Proxy.

docs.title: 10. Interview Preparation
docs.text:
Q1: What is Facade and what problem does it solve? It provides a unified, higher-level interface to a subsystem, collapsing multi-step orchestration into intention-revealing calls. Problem solved: scattered sequencing, ordering bugs, and tight coupling between clients and internals — e.g., convertToMp4() hiding extract/transcode/normalise/mux.

Q2: Does Facade hide or replace the subsystem? It hides complexity but never replaces the subsystem. Internals stay public so experts can bypass the facade. Unlike a wrapper that forbids direct access, a facade is an optional convenience layer — beginners use placeOrder(), experts can still tune Transcoder options directly.

Q3: Facade vs Adapter — how do you tell them apart in code review? Adapter changes signatures so code compiles; Facade keeps signatures and reduces call count. Without an adapter the code breaks; without a facade the code merely becomes verbose. If method names are translated, it is Adapter; if call sequences are orchestrated, it is Facade.

Q4: Facade vs Mediator — both simplify, so what differs? Facade simplifies outside-in: one entry point into a subsystem. Mediator simplifies inside: peers communicate through a hub instead of each other. Facade's subsystem works standalone; Mediator's colleagues typically depend on it. Video converter is Facade; chatroom routing messages between users is Mediator.

Q5: How do you avoid a god-object facade? One facade per subsystem view or client need (VideoConverterFacade vs ThumbnailFacade vs AdminFacade). Delegate instead of reimplementing, return subsystem types rather than rewrapping, keep facades stateless, and move business rules into domain services. If the facade changes for every subsystem tweak, it is too fat.

Q6: Where should error handling live? In the facade: catch subsystem exceptions, attach workflow context (order id, filename), and rethrow domain errors (OrderFailed, ConversionFailed) with causes. Never leak SQLException or CodecException to controllers, and never swallow failures silently.

Q7: Give framework examples of Facade. Spring Boot starters, AWS SDK high-level clients, javax.persistence.EntityManager over JDBC internals, jQuery over DOM APIs, and API gateways over microservices — all collapse multi-step internals behind curated entry points.

Q8: How do you test a Facade? Mock subsystems, verify call order and arguments, and assert error translation. Add one thin end-to-end test with real subsystems proving the pipeline works. Keep client tests on a mocked facade so controller logic is independent of transcoding or payment details.

LLD Scenario 1 — E-commerce checkout: Design OrderFacade.placeOrder() over payment, inventory, shipping, notification. Discuss transactionality, partial-failure rollback (compensating actions), idempotency keys, and where pricing rules live. Expected: facade orchestration, saga/compensation sketch, error translation, bypass for admin flows.

LLD Scenario 2 — Video processing service: Design VideoFacade with convertToMp4, thumbnail, probe. Subsystems: extractor, transcoder, muxer, thumbnailer. Discuss defaults vs custom bitrates, async job handling, and progress callbacks. Expected: thin facade, subsystem injection, async variant with job ids, power-user bypass.

LLD Scenario 3 — Employee onboarding: HR system touches IAM, asset inventory, payroll, and email. Design OnboardingFacade.onboard() sequencing these with rollback. Discuss partial failures and audit trail. Expected: ordered orchestration, compensating deletes, idempotent retries, audit logging placement.

docs.title: 11. Testing and Best Practices
docs.text:
Unit tests:

  • Mock each subsystem; verify the facade calls them in order with correct arguments (mock interaction testing).
  • Assert error translation: subsystem exception → facade domain error with workflow context.
  • Test defaults: convertToMp4 picks h264 without caller input; custom overloads still reachable.
  • Test clients against a mocked facade — controller tests must not spin up transcoders.

Integration tests:

  • One happy-path test per facade method with real (or containerised) subsystems.
  • Failure-injection test: kill inventory mid-checkout, assert compensation/rollback runs.
  • Contract test: subsystem upgrade does not break facade method signatures.

Best practices:

  • Constructor-inject subsystems; select implementations via DI config per environment.
  • Keep facades stateless and thread-safe; pass request context as parameters.
  • Log at facade boundaries with correlation ids for end-to-end tracing.
  • Measure before and after: facade should reduce client code and defect rate, not just move complexity.
Aspect Impact Memory Low (holds subsystem references) Runtime cost Low (one extra hop, no per-item overhead) Scalability High (facades scale with subsystem; split by view when fat) Risk God object and over-hiding — split facades, allow bypass

docs.title: 12. Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Facade = curated front door: One intention-revealing call orchestrating a multi-step subsystem.
  • Optional, not mandatory: Subsystems stay public; experts bypass the facade freely.
  • Thin and focused: Sequence, default, translate — never reimplement subsystem logic.
  • Split by view: One facade per workflow or client type beats one god object.
  • Distinguish neighbours: Many steps → Facade; tangled peers → Mediator; bad signatures → Adapter; guarded object → Proxy.
  • Test the seam: Mocked-subsystem order tests plus one real end-to-end proof per workflow.

docs.title: Youtube
docs.text: • 30. Design Word Processor using Flyweight Design Pattern | Low Level System Design FlyWeight Pattern

docs.title: 1. Overview and Fundamentals
docs.text:
Intent (GoF): Use sharing to support large numbers of fine-grained objects efficiently.

In one line: Share what is common, pass what differs — hold a million objects for the price of a dozen.

Real-world analogy: Printed posters. The printing press holds one metal plate per character design (intrinsic, shared). Each impression's position on the page (extrinsic) is supplied at print time. You do not cast a new "A" plate for every "A" on the page.

Family context: Flyweight is a structural pattern. It restructures how object state is stored — splitting it into shared and per-use parts — rather than changing behaviour.

Key participants:

  • Flyweight — shared object holding intrinsic (immutable, context-free) state (TreeType, Glyph).
  • ConcreteFlyweight — specific shared variant (OakType, Glyph('a', Arial-12-bold)).
  • FlyweightFactory — pool guaranteeing one instance per key (computeIfAbsent, Map cache).
  • Context — tiny per-use object holding extrinsic state plus a flyweight pointer (Tree with x/y/height + TreeType).
  • Client — passes extrinsic state into flyweight operations (type.draw(x, y, height)).

Core characteristics:

  • Intrinsic state: Shareable, immutable, context-independent (character shape, tree texture, font metrics). Lives inside the flyweight.
  • Extrinsic state: Varies per use, supplied by caller (position, size, selection). Lives outside, passed as parameters.
  • Sharing is by identity: every "Oak" reference points to the same instance.
  • Factory-keyed pooling (Map<Key, Flyweight>) enforces canonical instances.
  • Pays off at scale (thousands to millions); overhead is unjustified for hundreds of objects.

Mental model:

Forest: 1_000_000 Tree contexts (x, y, height + pointer)
        ---- share ----> 12 TreeType flyweights (mesh, texture, colour)

If the question is "how do we hold a million of these cheaply", use Flyweight. If it is "how do we ensure only one exists", use Singleton.

docs.title: 2. Detailed Theory
docs.text:
Problem: Naive modelling duplicates heavy data. A game with a million trees storing a 2 MB mesh each needs 2 TB. A text editor storing font, colour, and bitmap per character explodes similarly. Most per-object fields are actually identical across huge groups.

Solution: Split state. Move everything shareable into an immutable Flyweight. Keep only the varying fields plus a reference in a lightweight Context. Serve flyweights from a Factory pool keyed by intrinsic values so duplicates are impossible.

Intrinsic vs extrinsic — the classification discipline:

  • Ask: "Can this field become a method parameter?" If yes, it is probably extrinsic (position, size, cursor).
  • Ask: "Is this identical for all members of a group?" If yes, it is intrinsic (glyph bitmap, tree texture, icon pixels).
  • A field that looks shared but varies (font size affecting line height, colour affecting hit-testing) must be extrinsic or part of the key — misclassification produces visual bugs or breaks sharing.
  • Flyweights must be immutable: one stray setter corrupts every context sharing the instance. Make fields final/readonly and never expose mutators.

Factory design:

  • Key by the full intrinsic tuple (name|colour|texture, char|font|size). A sloppy key merges distinct variants.
  • Use ConcurrentHashMap + computeIfAbsent (Java), functools.lru_cache/dict with lock (Python), sync.Map (Go) for thread-safety.
  • Pre-populate at startup when the variant set is known (ASCII glyphs, tile types); lazily create otherwise.
  • Unlike a cache, entries are never evicted for age — sharing is the correctness mechanism, not a performance hint.

Flyweight vs Cache vs Object Pool vs Singleton:

  • Cache memoises computation and evicts; flyweight pool defines identity and retains.
  • Object Pool recycles mutable instances (connections, threads) to avoid construction cost; flyweights are immutable and never checked in/out.
  • Singleton restricts to one global instance; flyweight maintains many canonical instances keyed by value.

SOLID connections:

  • Single Responsibility: Factories own sharing; contexts own per-use state; flyweights own shared rendering.
  • Open/Closed: New variants arrive as new keys, not new code paths.
  • Interface Segregation: Flyweight interface exposes only operations parameterised by extrinsic state.

Consequences:

  • Orders-of-magnitude memory savings at scale, at the cost of split-state complexity, extrinsic plumbing, and thread-safety care.
  • CPU trade: cheaper allocation but extra parameter passing and pool lookups — profile both sides.

docs.title: Diagram 1 — Class structure (pool, flyweight, context)
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Forest {
        -trees: List~Tree~
        -factory: TreeTypeFactory
        +plant(x, y, h, species, colour, texture)
        +render()
    }
    class TreeTypeFactory {
        -pool: Map~String, TreeType~
        +get(species, colour, texture) TreeType

    }
    class TreeType {
        -name: String
        -colour: String
        -texture: String
        +draw(x, y, height)
    }
    class Tree {
        -x: int

    Forest --> TreeTypeFactory : uses
    Forest --> Tree : contains many
    TreeTypeFactory --> TreeType : pools
    Tree o-- TreeType : shares

Explanation: TreeType (flyweight) holds only intrinsic data and is immutable. TreeTypeFactory guarantees canonical sharing — one instance per species key. Tree (context) is tiny: three ints plus a reference, no texture copy. Forest plants millions of contexts that all point at a handful of flyweights. The o-- from Tree to TreeType shows sharing: thousands of contexts reference one flyweight.

docs.title: Diagram 2 — Shared rendering flow (sequence)
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Application
    participant Forest as Forest
    participant Factory as TreeTypeFactory
    participant T1 as TreeType(Oak)
    participant Tree as Tree(x=10,y=20)
    App->>Forest: plant(10, 20, 5, "Oak", ...)
    Forest->>Factory: get("Oak", ...)
    Factory-->>Forest: existing Oak instance
    Forest->>Forest: trees.add(new Tree(10,20,5,oak))
