Explanation: Planting looks up (or creates once) the shared Oak flyweight, then stores only coordinates in the new context. Rendering passes extrinsic coordinates into the shared instance — the flyweight never stores position. A million plant() calls reuse the same Oak object; only contexts multiply.

docs.title: 4. Implementation Examples in Java, Python, and Go
4.1 Java (OOP, forest with shared tree types)
docs.text:
Explanation: TreeType is the immutable flyweight; TreeTypeFactory pools by key; Tree is the extrinsic context; Forest plants and renders. main plants 5 trees of 2 species and proves only 2 flyweights exist. Compile with javac FlyweightDemo.java && java FlyweightDemo.

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

class TreeType {
    private final String name;
    private final String colour;
    private final String texture;

    TreeType(String name, String colour, String texture) {
        this.name = name;
        this.colour = colour;
        this.texture = texture;
    }

    void draw(int x, int y, int height) {
        System.out.println("Draw " + name + " at (" + x + "," + y
            + ") h=" + height + " [" + colour + "," + texture + "]");
    }
}

class TreeTypeFactory {
    private final Map<String, TreeType> pool = new HashMap<>();

    TreeType get(String name, String colour, String texture) {
        String key = name + "|" + colour;
        TreeType existing = pool.get(key);
        if (existing == null) {
            existing = new TreeType(name, colour, texture);
            pool.put(key, existing);
        }
        return existing;
    }

    int speciesCached() { return pool.size(); }
}

class Tree {
    private final int x, y, height;
    private final TreeType type;

    Tree(int x, int y, int height, TreeType type) {
        this.x = x; this.y = y; this.height = height; this.type = type;
    }

    void draw() { type.draw(x, y, height); }
}

class Forest {
    private final List<Tree> trees = new ArrayList<>();
    private final TreeTypeFactory factory = new TreeTypeFactory();

    void plant(int x, int y, int height, String species,
               String colour, String texture) {
        trees.add(new Tree(x, y, height, factory.get(species, colour, texture)));
    }

    void render() {
        for (Tree t : trees) t.draw();
        System.out.println("Trees=" + trees.size()
            + " species=" + factory.speciesCached());
    }
}

public class FlyweightDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Forest forest = new Forest();
        forest.plant(10, 20, 5, "Oak", "green", "oak.png");
        forest.plant(30, 40, 6, "Oak", "green", "oak.png");
        forest.plant(50, 60, 7, "Oak", "green", "oak.png");
        forest.plant(70, 80, 4, "Pine", "darkgreen", "pine.png");
        forest.plant(90, 15, 5, "Pine", "darkgreen", "pine.png");
        forest.render();
    }
}

Sample I/O:

Draw Oak at (10,20) h=5 [green,oak.png]
Draw Oak at (30,40) h=6 [green,oak.png]
Draw Oak at (50,60) h=7 [green,oak.png]
Draw Pine at (70,80) h=4 [darkgreen,pine.png]
Draw Pine at (90,15) h=5 [darkgreen,pine.png]
Trees=5 species=2

docs.title: 4.2 Python (pythonic, PEP 8, glyph pool)
docs.text:
Explanation: Character glyphs share bitmap data; positions are extrinsic. GlyphFactory interns by (char, font) key. TextChar is the context. The demo renders "hello" proving repeated letters share instances via is. Run with python flyweight_demo.py.

"""Flyweight pattern: share glyph bitmaps, pass positions per use."""


class Glyph:
    """Flyweight: immutable shared bitmap for one (char, font)."""

    __slots__ = ("char", "font", "bitmap")

    def __init__(self, char: str, font: str) -> None:
        self.char = char
        self.font = font
        self.bitmap = f"[{font}:{char}]"  # stand-in for heavy raster data

    def draw(self, x: int, y: int) -> None:
        print(f"Draw {self.bitmap} at ({x},{y})")


class GlyphFactory:
    """Pool: one canonical Glyph per key."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._pool: dict[tuple[str, str], Glyph] = {}

    def get(self, char: str, font: str = "Arial-12") -> Glyph:
        key = (char, font)
        glyph = self._pool.get(key)
        if glyph is None:
            glyph = Glyph(char, font)
            self._pool[key] = glyph
        return glyph

    def cached(self) -> int:
        return len(self._pool)


class TextChar:
    """Context: extrinsic position plus shared glyph pointer."""

    def __init__(self, x: int, y: int, glyph: Glyph) -> None:
        self.x = x
        self.y = y
        self.glyph = glyph

    def draw(self) -> None:
        self.glyph.draw(self.x, self.y)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    factory = GlyphFactory()
    word = [TextChar(i * 10, 0, factory.get(ch)) for i, ch in enumerate("hello")]
    for ch in word:
        ch.draw()
    print(f"Chars={len(word)} glyphs={factory.cached()}")
    print(f"Shared l: {word[2].glyph is word[3].glyph}")

Sample I/O:

Draw [Arial-12:h] at (0,0)
Draw [Arial-12:e] at (10,0)
Draw [Arial-12:l] at (20,0)
Draw [Arial-12:l] at (30,0)
Draw [Arial-12:o] at (40,0)
Chars=5 glyphs=4
Shared l: True

docs.title: 4.3 Go (idiomatic, particle pool)
docs.text:
Explanation: Bullets share sprite/texture; each bullet carries only coordinates and velocity. ParticleFactory pools by kind. The demo spawns 4 bullets of 2 kinds and renders them. Run with go run flyweight_demo.go.

package main

import "fmt"

// Flyweight: shared intrinsic sprite data.
type ParticleType struct {
    kind    string
    sprite  string
    damage  int
}

func (p *ParticleType) Draw(x, y int) {
    fmt.Printf("Draw %s at (%d,%d) [%s dmg=%d]\n", p.kind, x, y, p.sprite, p.damage)
}

// Factory: canonical instance per kind.
type ParticleFactory struct {
    pool map[string]*ParticleType
}

func NewParticleFactory() *ParticleFactory {
    return &ParticleFactory{pool: make(map[string]*ParticleType)}
}

func (f *ParticleFactory) Get(kind, sprite string, damage int) *ParticleType {
    if p, ok := f.pool[kind]; ok {
        return p
    }
    p := &ParticleType{kind: kind, sprite: sprite, damage: damage}
    f.pool[kind] = p
    return p
}

func (f *ParticleFactory) Cached() int { return len(f.pool) }

// Context: extrinsic position plus shared type.
type Bullet struct {
    x, y int
    kind *ParticleType
}

func (b *Bullet) Draw() { b.kind.Draw(b.x, b.y) }

func main() {
    factory := NewParticleFactory()
    bullets := []*Bullet{
        {x: 1, y: 2, kind: factory.Get("plasma", "plasma.png", 10)},
        {x: 3, y: 4, kind: factory.Get("plasma", "plasma.png", 10)},
        {x: 5, y: 6, kind: factory.Get("shell", "shell.png", 25)},
        {x: 7, y: 8, kind: factory.Get("shell", "shell.png", 25)},
    }
    for _, b := range bullets {
        b.Draw()
    }
    fmt.Printf("Bullets=%d types=%d\n", len(bullets), factory.Cached())
    fmt.Println("Shared plasma:", bullets[0].kind == bullets[1].kind)
}

Sample I/O:

Draw plasma at (1,2) [plasma.png dmg=10]
Draw plasma at (3,4) [plasma.png dmg=10]
Draw shell at (5,6) [shell.png dmg=25]
Draw shell at (7,8) [shell.png dmg=25]
Bullets=4 types=2
Shared plasma: true

docs.title: 5. Real-World Industry Applications
docs.text:
• Text editors and browsers (Word, Chrome, Skia): Glyph caches share rasterised characters across every occurrence; layout passes positions per frame.
  • Game engines (Unity, Unreal): Particle systems, bullets, and instanced meshes share textures/materials across thousands of entities.
  • JVM string interning / Python sys.intern: Identical string literals share one heap object automatically.
  • Map renderers (Google Maps, Mapbox): Tile images shared across views, zooms, and sessions; viewport coordinates are extrinsic.
  • UI icon/theme caches: One pixmap per icon shared by every button, menu, and toolbar instance.
  • Regex / font engines: Compiled patterns and font faces cached once, executed with per-call input.

docs.title: 6. Practical Use Cases and Scenarios
docs.text:
1. Word processor: Million-character document shares ~100 glyph flyweights; caret positions and selections stay extrinsic.
  2. Game forest/battlefield: Million trees or particles share a dozen meshes; coordinates and HP are per-context.
  3. Spreadsheet grid: Cells share style flyweights (font, border, format); values and coordinates stay per-cell.
  4. Chat emoji rendering: Each emoji shortcode maps to one shared bitmap; message positions are extrinsic.
  5. Network packet visualisation: Packet kinds share colour/shape; timestamps and routes are per-packet context.
  6. Report charts: Data points share marker/colour styles; x/y values passed per draw call.

docs.title: 7. When to Use and When Not to Use
docs.text:
Use Flyweight when ALL of these hold:

  • Application uses very large numbers of similar objects (thousands+).
  • Memory cost is high and measurable via profiling.
  • Most state can be made extrinsic and passed per call.
  • Object identity is irrelevant — shared instances are interchangeable.
  • Flyweights can be immutable (or safely read-only through sharing).

Do NOT use Flyweight when:

  • Object counts are modest — the pool and split add complexity for no gain.
  • State cannot be cleanly split — smuggling extrinsic fields inside breaks sharing or correctness.
  • Identity matters (each object needs its own lifecycle, listeners, or mutable history) — sharing corrupts peers.
  • A simple cache or pool solves the actual problem (recomputation cost vs memory footprint confusion).
  • Single shared coordinator is the goal — that is Singleton, not Flyweight.

docs.title: 8. Do's and Don'ts
docs.text:
Do:

  • Make flyweights immutable: final fields, no setters, defensive copies on construction.
  • Key the factory on the complete intrinsic tuple; document what the key includes.
  • Pass extrinsic state as parameters to every flyweight operation — never store it inside.
  • Use concurrent maps (ConcurrentHashMap, sync.Map) or pre-populate for thread-safety.
  • Prove value with heap measurements before and after; assert sharing with identity checks in tests.

Don't:

  • Don't store positions, selections, or per-use flags inside the flyweight.
  • Don't use weak/soft keys that let canonical instances vanish mid-render.
  • Don't merge distinct variants with sloppy keys (ignoring font size or colour when it matters).
  • Don't expose the pool's live map — return flyweights, not pool internals.
  • Don't apply flyweight to a few hundred small objects — YAGNI.
Do Don't Immutable TreeType with final fields Setter mutating shared texture at runtime pool.computeIfAbsent(key, ...) atomically Check-then-act race creating duplicates Pass (x, y, height) per draw() Store cursor position inside Glyph Profile heap with/without sharing Assume sharing helps without measuring

docs.title: 9. Comparison with Other Design Patterns
docs.text:
Aspect Flyweight Object Pool Cache Singleton Goal Minimise memory via intrinsic sharing Reuse expensive mutable objects Avoid recomputation via memoisation Ensure exactly one instance Mutability Immutable shared state Mutable, checked in/out Values may expire/invalidate Single mutable global Lookup Pool keyed by intrinsic value, retained forever Acquire/release lifecycle Keyed by input, evicted by policy Global accessor State split Strict intrinsic vs extrinsic None — whole object recycled None — whole result stored None — one state Eviction Never (sharing is correctness) Bounded pool with blocking/creation TTL/LRU eviction routine N/A Example TreeType per species, glyph per char DB connection pool, thread pool HTTP response cache, memoised fib Config holder, logger Without it Memory explosion at scale Construction churn / exhaustion Repeated expensive compute Multiple coordinators diverge

Flyweight vs Prototype: Prototype clones a template per use (each clone independent); Flyweight shares one template across uses (contexts carry differences). Clone when independence matters; share when identity does not.

When to pick which: Millions of similar objects → Flyweight. Expensive reusable resources → Pool. Repeated computation → Cache. One coordinator → Singleton.

docs.title: 10. Interview Preparation
docs.text:
Q1: What is intrinsic vs extrinsic state? Intrinsic is shareable and context-free (glyph bitmap, tree texture) and lives inside the flyweight. Extrinsic varies per use (position, size) and is stored by the caller and passed into each operation. Misclassification breaks either memory savings (extrinsic smuggled inside forces one instance per use) or correctness (shared mutable position corrupts peers).

Q2: How does Flyweight differ from Cache, Pool, and Singleton? Cache memoises computation with eviction to save time; pool recycles mutable resources to save construction cost; Singleton enforces one instance for coordination; Flyweight shares immutable internals across many instances to save memory. Different resource, different lifecycle, different eviction story.

Q3: Why must flyweights be immutable? Because every context shares the same instance — one mutation is visible to all million users of that flyweight. Immutability (final fields, no setters) makes sharing safe. All variation belongs in extrinsic context objects.

Q4: What are the concurrency pitfalls? Check-then-act pool insertion races create duplicates — use computeIfAbsent / sync.Map / locks. Shared mutable fields cause data races across contexts. Key design must be complete: two threads inserting the same logical variant under different keys silently breaks sharing.

Q5: How do you prove Flyweight is worth it? Measure heap with and without sharing over realistic counts. Assert sharing directly (factory.get('a') == factory.get('a'), pool size after duplicates). Load-test render/draw loops for CPU cost of extrinsic passing. Confirm mutating one context never affects siblings.

Q6: Where do extrinsic operations live? Either the client passes extrinsic values into flyweight methods (type.draw(x, y)), or a context object holds extrinsic fields and forwards them. Never store extrinsic fields on the flyweight itself.

Q7: Give JDK/framework examples. String.intern(), Integer.valueOf() caching -128..127, Font/Color factories in UI toolkits, glyph caches in text renderers, and tile caches in map SDKs. Boolean.valueOf() is a degenerate two-instance flyweight.

Q8: What breaks if the key is wrong? Over-broad keys merge distinct variants (12pt and 24pt glyphs sharing bitmaps → rendering bugs). Over-narrow keys split identical variants (including object hash in key → no sharing at all). Key must equal the full intrinsic tuple, nothing more, nothing less.

LLD Scenario 1 — Word processor: Design glyph sharing for a million-character doc with fonts, sizes, colours. Discuss what is intrinsic (bitmap per char+font+size) vs extrinsic (position, selection), factory key, and memory math. Expected: flyweight, context, factory, identity tests, heap proof.

LLD Scenario 2 — Top-down shooter particles: 100k bullets of 8 kinds with position, velocity, TTL. Design ParticleType pool plus Bullet contexts updated per tick. Discuss thread-safety of the pool and where collision state lives. Expected: immutable types, extrinsic motion, concurrent factory, tick-loop rendering.

LLD Scenario 3 — Spreadsheet cell styles: Million cells sharing ~50 style combos (font, border, format). Design style flyweight keyed by full style tuple, cell contexts with values. Discuss adding a new style at runtime and serialisation. Expected: style pool, cell context, key design, style-dedup on paste.

docs.title: 11. Testing and Best Practices
docs.text:
Unit tests:

  • Assert canonical sharing: factory.get(k) == factory.get(k) (reference equality) and pool size stays flat after duplicates.
  • Assert extrinsic isolation: move one context, verify siblings unchanged.
  • Assert immutability: no setters exist; attempt reflective mutation in a dedicated test if paranoid.
  • Assert key correctness: variants differing in any intrinsic field produce distinct instances.

Load and memory tests:

  • Heap-dump with and without sharing at realistic scale; require documented savings before keeping the pattern.
  • Render/draw loop benchmarks proving extrinsic-passing CPU cost is acceptable.
  • Concurrency test: parallel get() calls never create duplicates and never throw.

Best practices:

  • Pre-populate known variants at startup (ASCII set, base tiles) to avoid first-use latency.
  • Keep extrinsic structs tiny and cache-friendly (plain fields, no boxing in hot loops).
  • Combine with Composite (shared leaves in trees) and Prototype (clone-then-share workflows) where natural.
  • Document the intrinsic/extrinsic split in code comments — future maintainers will otherwise "fix" it back together.
Aspect Impact Memory Sharply reduced at scale (12 shared vs 1M copies) Runtime cost Medium (pool lookup once; extrinsic passing per call) Scalability Very high (flat memory as count grows) Risk Misclassification and shared mutation — immutability + key discipline

docs.title: 12. Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Flyweight = share the common, pass the rest: Intrinsic immutable state pooled; extrinsic state supplied per call.
  • Factory guarantees canonical instances keyed by the full intrinsic tuple — sloppy keys break sharing or correctness.
  • Immutability is non-negotiable for shared instances; all mutation belongs in contexts.
  • Measure before adopting: Worth it for thousands+ of heavy similar objects; overhead otherwise.
  • Distinguish neighbours: Memory sharing → Flyweight; time saving → Cache; resource recycling → Pool; one coordinator → Singleton; cloned templates → Prototype.
  • Test identity, isolation, and heap: Reference equality, sibling independence, and measured memory wins.

docs.title: Youtube
docs.text: • 13. Proxy Design Pattern Explanation (Hindi) | LLD | System Design Interview Question | Java

docs.title: 1. Overview and Fundamentals
docs.text:
Intent (GoF): Provide a surrogate or placeholder for another object to control access to it.

In one line: A stand-in with the same face — clients talk to the proxy thinking it is the real thing, while it guards, defers, or enhances access.

Real-world analogy: A bank locker assistant. You cannot walk into the vault yourself. The assistant (proxy) checks your identity, fetches the locker, logs access, and hands you the contents. You use the same request slip either way.

Family context: Proxy is a structural pattern. It structures access to a single object, unlike Facade (many objects) or Composite (tree of objects).

Key participants:

  • Subject — common interface for real and proxy (BankAccount, Image).
  • RealSubject — the actual object doing the work (RealBankAccount, HighResImage).
  • Proxy — implements Subject, holds a reference to RealSubject, adds control logic.
  • Client — depends only on Subject, unaware whether it holds proxy or real object.

Four classic proxy types:

  • Virtual Proxy: Defers expensive creation until first use (lazy image loading, Hibernate entities).
  • Protection Proxy: Checks permissions before delegating (teller limits, Spring Security).
  • Remote Proxy: Local stub for a remote object (gRPC stub, REST client, RMI).
  • Smart / Cache Proxy: Adds bookkeeping — caching, reference counting, logging, metrics — around calls.

Core characteristics:

  • Same interface as the real object — substitutable anywhere.
  • Client ideally does not know the proxy exists; construction is hidden by factory/DI.
  • Typically one proxy per concern; stacking is possible but ordering must be documented.
  • May manage the real object's lifecycle: create lazily, pool, refresh, or evict.
  • Adds one indirection hop — negligible for I/O, measurable for hot loops.

Mental model:

Client -> BankAccount.withdraw()
           |
     AccountProtectionProxy (checks role, audits)
           |
     RealBankAccount (pure ledger math)

If the wrapper says "you may not" or "not yet", it is a Proxy. If it says "and also", it is a Decorator.

docs.title: 2. Detailed Theory
docs.text:
Problem: Direct access to the real object is wrong: creation is too expensive to do eagerly, callers lack permission checks, the object lives on another machine, or every call needs caching/logging. Scattering if (allowed) or if (cached) checks across callers duplicates policy and leaks concerns.

Solution: Introduce a proxy implementing the same interface. Route all client calls through it. The proxy enforces its one concern (auth, laziness, caching, remoteness) and delegates to the real subject only when appropriate.

How each proxy type works:

  • Virtual proxy: Holds a nullable reference; creates RealSubject on first method call (double-checked locking for threads). Later calls reuse it. Ideal for heavy images, large reports, or expensive model loads.
  • Protection proxy: Holds caller identity (role, token, ACL). Each method checks permission before delegating; denied calls never touch the real object and are audited. Keeps security out of domain logic.
  • Remote proxy: Encodes calls (marshalling, HTTP/gRPC), sends over the wire, decodes responses, translates transport errors. Client sees a local interface; network lives inside the proxy.
  • Cache proxy: Stores results keyed by arguments with TTL/invalidation. Read path checks cache first; write path updates or invalidates. Must define coherence rules (write-through vs write-behind).
  • Smart/logging proxy: Records metrics, traces, reference counts, or copy-on-write behaviour transparently.

Static vs dynamic proxies (Java):

  • Static proxy: Hand-written class per interface. Simple, explicit, domain-aware. Best for protection policies with business rules.
  • Dynamic proxy (java.lang.reflect.Proxy): One InvocationHandler generates wrappers for any interface at runtime. Best for cross-cutting concerns (logging, transactions, metrics).
  • Bytecode proxies (CGLib, ByteBuddy): Proxy concrete classes without interfaces by subclassing at runtime. Powers Spring AOP for class-based beans.
  • Python equivalents: __getattr__ delegation, functools.wraps decorators, library proxies. Go equivalents: struct wrapping the interface, http.RoundTripper chains.

Proxy vs Decorator vs Adapter vs Facade:

  • Proxy controls access to one object, same interface, ideally invisible.
  • Decorator adds features to one object, same interface, explicitly stacked by client.
  • Adapter changes the interface to fix mismatch.
  • Facade simplifies many objects behind one entry point.

SOLID connections:

  • Single Responsibility: Each proxy owns one access concern; domain stays pure.
  • Open/Closed: New policy (rate limiting) arrives as a new proxy, not by editing the real subject.
  • Liskov Substitution: Proxy substitutes for real subject in every test and call site.
  • Dependency Inversion: Clients depend on Subject abstraction, never on proxy or real concretes.

Consequences:

  • Clean separation of access policy from domain logic, at the cost of indirection, longer stack traces, and potential surprise (cached denial, unaudited cache hit) when proxies stack.

docs.title: Diagram 1 — Class structure (protection proxy)
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class BankAccount {
        <>
        +deposit(amount: double)
        +withdraw(amount: double) bool
        +balance() double
    }
    class RealBankAccount {
        -balance: double
        +deposit(amount: double)
        +withdraw(amount: double) bool
        +balance() double
    }
    class AccountProtectionProxy {
        -real: BankAccount
        -caller: Role
        +deposit(amount: double)
        +withdraw(amount: double) bool
        +balance() double
    }
    class Role {
        <>
        TELLER
        MANAGER
    }
    class BranchDemo {
        +main()
    }
    BankAccount <|.. RealBankAccount : implements
    BankAccount <|.. AccountProtectionProxy : implements
    AccountProtectionProxy --> BankAccount : guards
    AccountProtectionProxy --> Role : checks
    BranchDemo --> BankAccount : uses

Explanation: Both RealBankAccount and AccountProtectionProxy implement BankAccount, so BranchDemo cannot tell them apart. The proxy holds a reference to the real account plus the caller's role. Withdrawals from tellers above the limit are denied before the real object is touched; manager calls delegate with audit logging. Security lives in one class; ledger math stays pure.

docs.title: Diagram 2 — Guarded call flow (sequence)
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Teller as Teller Client
    participant Proxy as AccountProtectionProxy
    participant Real as RealBankAccount
    Teller->>Proxy: withdraw(25000)
    Proxy->>Proxy: check role=TELLER, limit=10000
    Proxy-->>Teller: DENIED (real never touched)
    participant Mgr as Manager Client
    Mgr->>Proxy: withdraw(25000)
    Proxy->>Proxy: check role=MANAGER: allowed
    Proxy->>Real: withdraw(25000)
    Real-->>Proxy: true (balance updated)
    Proxy->>Proxy: audit log
    Proxy-->>Mgr: true

Explanation: The sequence shows the proxy's gatekeeping. The teller's oversized withdrawal is rejected inside the proxy — no ledger call, no state change. The manager's identical call passes the check, delegates, and gets audited. Both callers use the same withdraw() signature; policy is invisible in the interface but explicit in the trace.

docs.title: 4. Implementation Examples in Java, Python, and Go
4.1 Java (OOP, protection proxy with audit)
docs.text:
Explanation: RealBankAccount holds only balance logic. AccountProtectionProxy enforces teller limits and audits every call. BranchDemo wires the same real account behind two proxies (teller vs manager) proving identical interface, different power. Compile with javac ProxyDemo.java && java BranchDemo.

interface BankAccount {
    void deposit(double amount);
    boolean withdraw(double amount);
    double balance();
}

class RealBankAccount implements BankAccount {
    private double balance;
    RealBankAccount(double opening) { this.balance = opening; }
    @Override public void deposit(double amount) { balance += amount; }
    @Override public boolean withdraw(double amount) {
        if (amount > balance) return false;
        balance -= amount;
        return true;
    }
    @Override public double balance() { return balance; }
}

enum Role { TELLER, MANAGER }

class AccountProtectionProxy implements BankAccount {
    private final BankAccount real;
    private final Role caller;
    private static final double TELLER_LIMIT = 10_000;

    AccountProtectionProxy(BankAccount real, Role caller) {
        this.real = real;
        this.caller = caller;
    }

    @Override
    public void deposit(double amount) {
        real.deposit(amount);
        System.out.println("AUDIT deposit $" + amount + " by " + caller);
    }

    @Override
    public boolean withdraw(double amount) {
        if (caller == Role.TELLER && amount > TELLER_LIMIT) {
            System.out.println("DENIED: teller limit is $" + TELLER_LIMIT);
            return false;
        }
        boolean ok = real.withdraw(amount);
        System.out.println("AUDIT withdraw $" + amount + " by " + caller + " ok=" + ok);
        return ok;
    }

    @Override
    public double balance() { return real.balance(); }
}

class BranchDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        BankAccount account = new RealBankAccount(50_000);
        BankAccount teller = new AccountProtectionProxy(account, Role.TELLER);
        BankAccount manager = new AccountProtectionProxy(account, Role.MANAGER);
        teller.withdraw(25_000);
        manager.withdraw(25_000);
        System.out.println("Final balance: $" + account.balance());
    }
}

Sample I/O:

DENIED: teller limit is $10000.0
AUDIT withdraw $25000.0 by MANAGER ok=true
Final balance: $25000.0

docs.title: 4.2 Python (pythonic, PEP 8, virtual + protection proxy)
docs.text:
Explanation: RealImage simulates expensive loading. ImageProxy defers loading until first display() (virtual proxy). AccountProxy enforces role limits (protection proxy). Both honour their subject protocols so clients are unchanged. Run with python proxy_demo.py.

"""Proxy pattern: virtual image loader and protection proxy for accounts."""
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from enum import Enum


class Image(ABC):
    """Subject for virtual proxy."""

    @abstractmethod
    def display(self) -> None:
        ...


class RealImage(Image):
    """Expensive real subject: loading happens in constructor."""

    def __init__(self, filename: str) -> None:
        self._filename = filename
        print(f"Loading heavy image {filename} from disk...")

    def display(self) -> None:
        print(f"Display {self._filename}")


class ImageProxy(Image):
    """Virtual proxy: lazy-loads RealImage on first use."""

    def __init__(self, filename: str) -> None:
        self._filename = filename
        self._real: RealImage | None = None

    def display(self) -> None:
        if self._real is None:
            self._real = RealImage(self._filename)
        self._real.display()


class Role(Enum):
    TELLER = "TELLER"
    MANAGER = "MANAGER"


class BankAccount(ABC):
    """Subject for protection proxy."""

    @abstractmethod
    def withdraw(self, amount: float) -> bool:
        ...


class RealBankAccount(BankAccount):
    def __init__(self, balance: float) -> None:
        self._balance = balance

    def withdraw(self, amount: float) -> bool:
        if amount > self._balance:
            return False
        self._balance -= amount
        return True

    @property
    def balance(self) -> float:
        return self._balance


class AccountProxy(BankAccount):
    """Protection proxy: enforces teller limits and audits."""

    TELLER_LIMIT = 10_000.0

    def __init__(self, real: BankAccount, caller: Role) -> None:
        self._real = real
        self._caller = caller

    def withdraw(self, amount: float) -> bool:
        if self._caller == Role.TELLER and amount > self.TELLER_LIMIT:
            print(f"DENIED: teller limit is ${self.TELLER_LIMIT:,.0f}")
            return False
        ok = self._real.withdraw(amount)
        print(f"AUDIT withdraw ${amount:,.0f} by {self._caller.value} ok={ok}")
        return ok


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("--- virtual proxy ---")
    img: Image = ImageProxy("photo.jpg")
    print("proxy created, nothing loaded yet")
    img.display()
    img.display()  # second call reuses loaded image

    print("--- protection proxy ---")
    real = RealBankAccount(50_000)
    AccountProxy(real, Role.TELLER).withdraw(25_000)
    AccountProxy(real, Role.MANAGER).withdraw(25_000)
    print(f"Final balance: ${real.balance:,.0f}")

Sample I/O:

--- virtual proxy ---
proxy created, nothing loaded yet
Loading heavy image photo.jpg from disk...
Display photo.jpg
Display photo.jpg
--- protection proxy ---
DENIED: teller limit is $10,000
AUDIT withdraw $25,000 by MANAGER ok=True
Final balance: $25,000

docs.title: 4.3 Go (idiomatic, cache proxy)
docs.text:
Explanation: RealWeatherService simulates a slow upstream call. WeatherCacheProxy implements the same WeatherService interface, caching results by city. The first call for a city is slow; repeats are instant. Run with go run proxy_demo.go.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

// Subject.
type WeatherService interface {
    Temperature(city string) string
}

// RealSubject: slow upstream (simulated with sleep).
type RealWeatherService struct{}

func (r *RealWeatherService) Temperature(city string) string {
    time.Sleep(200 * time.Millisecond) // simulate network
    return "22C in " + city
}

// Cache/smart proxy: memoises per city.
type WeatherCacheProxy struct {
    real  WeatherService
    cache map[string]string
}

func NewWeatherCacheProxy() *WeatherCacheProxy {
    return &WeatherCacheProxy{real: &RealWeatherService{}, cache: make(map[string]string)}
}

func (p *WeatherCacheProxy) Temperature(city string) string {
    if v, ok := p.cache[city]; ok {
        fmt.Println("CACHE hit for " + city)
        return v
    }
    fmt.Println("CACHE miss for " + city)
    v := p.real.Temperature(city)
    p.cache[city] = v
    return v
}

func main() {
    var svc WeatherService = NewWeatherCacheProxy()
    start := time.Now()
    fmt.Println(svc.Temperature("Pune"))
    fmt.Println(svc.Temperature("Pune"))
    fmt.Println("elapsed:", time.Since(start).Round(time.Millisecond))
}

Sample I/O:

CACHE miss for Pune
22C in Pune
CACHE hit for Pune
22C in Pune
elapsed: 200ms

docs.title: 5. Real-World Industry Applications
docs.text:
• Lazy media loading (virtual): Thumbnail grids load full images on demand; Hibernate/JPA lazy-loads entity graphs; java.util.Optional-style holders defer heavy reports.
  • Access control (protection): Spring Security method proxies, database view restrictions, S3 IAM policies enforced in SDK proxies.
  • Remote services (remote): gRPC stubs, Retrofit/Feign HTTP clients, RMI skeletons — local interfaces hiding network marshaling.
  • CDN and edge caching (cache): Cloudflare/Akamai proxies cache origin content; in-app memoising proxies cut repeated pricing or config fetches.
  • API gateways and reverse proxies: Nginx/HAProxy/Envoy front backends with TLS, rate limiting, and routing — infrastructure-scale proxies.
  • Observability (smart/logging): Spring AOP, Micrometer, and OpenTelemetry wrappers add latency histograms and traces around service calls without touching business code.

docs.title: 6. Practical Use Cases and Scenarios
docs.text:
1. Image gallery: Virtual proxy shows thumbnails instantly; full resolution loads on click — startup stays fast.
  2. Branch banking: Protection proxy enforces teller/manager limits and audits, keeping ledger code policy-free.
  3. Microservice client: Remote proxy hides HTTP/gRPC details, retries, and error mapping behind a domain interface.
  4. Weather/pricing feed: Cache proxy memoises slow upstream calls per key with TTL, surviving traffic spikes.
  5. Rate-limited API: Smart proxy throttles and queues calls, returning 429-friendly fallbacks instead of hammering the provider.
  6. Audit trail: Logging proxy records who called what with arguments and duration for compliance, zero business-code changes.

docs.title: 7. When to Use and When Not to Use
docs.text:
Use Proxy when:

  • Object creation is expensive and often unused — defer with virtual proxy.
  • Access needs permission checks, quotas, or auditing — guard with protection proxy.
  • The real object is remote — hide transport with remote proxy.
  • Calls are repeated and cacheable — memoise with cache proxy.
  • Cross-cutting telemetry is needed without polluting domain code.

Do NOT use Proxy when:

  • The goal is adding stackable product features — that is Decorator.
  • The goal is simplifying many objects — that is Facade.
  • The interface itself mismatches — that is Adapter.
  • Every call is unique and cheap — caching/protection overhead buys nothing.
  • A single proxy accumulates auth plus cache plus logging plus retry — split into focused layers with documented order.

docs.title: 8. Do's and Don'ts
docs.text:
Do:

  • Keep one concern per proxy; compose (Cache(Auth(Real))) with explicit ordering.
  • Implement the full subject interface — every method must delegate, guard, or cache faithfully.
  • Make laziness thread-safe (double-checked locking, sync.Once, locks) when shared.
  • Audit denials and cache bypasses so behaviour is observable in production.
  • Hide proxy construction behind factories or DI so clients stay interface-coupled.

Don't:

  • Don't let new interface methods silently bypass the guard — update proxies with the subject.
  • Don't return stale cache entries without TTL/invalidation — define coherence up front.
  • Don't stack proxies so deep that latency and stack traces become undebuggable.
  • Don't put business rules inside proxies — policy (who may) yes, pricing/workflows no.
  • Don't use proxies to hide failures — translate and propagate with context.
Do Don't One focused proxy per concern God proxy doing auth + cache + retry + metrics Thread-safe lazy init Racy if real == null without locking Cache with TTL + invalidation Unbounded cache that serves forever-stale data Factory hides new Proxy(real) Sprinkle new Proxy across callers

docs.title: 9. Comparison with Other Design Patterns
docs.text:
Aspect Proxy Decorator Adapter Intent Control access (guard, defer, cache) Add responsibilities openly Convert incompatible interface Transparency Ideally invisible to client Explicitly composed by client Hidden behind target interface Interface Same as subject; one layer typical Same as component; many layers normal Changes to target Lifecycle role May create, cache, refresh real object Never manages lifecycle Stateless translator Who decides Framework/factory injects proxy Caller nests decorators Adapter fixed at wiring Example AccountProtectionProxy, lazy ImageProxy EncryptionDecorator, BufferedInputStream StripeAdapter Without it Scattered guards / eager cost / leaky remote 2^N subclasses Code does not compile

Proxy vs Facade: Proxy fronts one object with the same interface to control access; Facade fronts many objects with a simpler interface to reduce effort. Proxy says "not yet / you may not"; Facade says "let me do those five steps for you".

Proxy vs Cache (pattern-adjacent): A cache proxy is a proxy whose policy is memoisation. Standalone caches optimise time with eviction; proxy framing adds substitutability — the client cannot tell caching happens.

When to pick which: Guard/defer/cache one object → Proxy. Stack opt-in features → Decorator. Fix signatures → Adapter. Simplify subsystem → Facade.

docs.title: 10. Interview Preparation
docs.text:
Q1: What is Proxy and what are its four classic types? A surrogate with the same interface controlling access to the real object. Virtual defers expensive creation; protection enforces permissions; remote stands in for a distant object; smart/cache adds bookkeeping like caching or logging around calls.

Q2: Proxy vs Decorator — both wrap with the same interface, so what differs? Proxy guards or optimises transparently (you may not / not yet), usually single-layer and framework-injected, and may manage lifecycle. Decorator adds features openly (and also), stacked many-deep by the caller, never managing lifecycle. Teller-limit guard is Proxy; encryption topping is Decorator.

Q3: How do static and dynamic proxies differ in Java? Static proxies are hand-written classes per interface — simple and domain-expressive. Dynamic proxies (java.lang.reflect.Proxy) generate wrappers from one InvocationHandler for any interface — ideal for generic logging/transactions. Spring AOP builds on dynamic proxies plus CGLib/ByteBuddy for class-based beans.

Q4: How do you implement a thread-safe virtual proxy? Guard lazy creation with double-checked locking (Java volatile + synchronized), sync.Once in Go, or a lock in Python. Ensure exactly-once creation under concurrency and publish safely so all threads see the initialised object.

Q5: What are the pitfalls of stacking proxies? Each layer adds latency and stack depth. Interactions surprise: cached denials, unaudited cache hits, retries amplifying non-idempotent calls. Mitigate with one concern per proxy, documented ordering, and measurements on hot paths.

Q6: How do cache proxies stay correct? Key on full request identity, set TTLs, invalidate on writes, and bound size. Distinguish cacheable (idempotent reads) from non-cacheable (withdrawals, mutations) — never cache the latter without explicit versioning.

Q7: Give framework examples of each proxy type. Virtual: Hibernate lazy entities, image lazy-loaders. Protection: Spring Security @PreAuthorize proxies. Remote: gRPC stubs, Feign clients. Cache/smart: CDN edge caches, Spring @Cacheable proxies, ORM second-level cache.

Q8: What is the performance story? One delegation hop is negligible next to I/O; virtual proxies save time by skipping unused work; cache proxies trade memory for latency. Risk is on nanosecond hot loops and deep stacks — profile, keep proxies shallow there, and never proxy what you can inline after measurement.

LLD Scenario 1 — Role-based document vault: Design DocumentStore with read/write plus AccessProxy enforcing owner/editor/viewer rights with audit logs. Discuss where ACLs are stored, denial responses, and test matrix. Expected: subject interface, proxy with policy table, audit seam, bypass-free wiring via factory.

LLD Scenario 2 — Lazy report engine: Reports cost 5s to build and are rarely viewed. Design virtual proxy with exactly-once build, progress callbacks, and cancellation. Discuss thread-safety and cache-after-build. Expected: lazy holder, sync.Once/DCL, state machine (pending/ready/failed), metrics.

LLD Scenario 3 — Cached pricing service: Upstream price API is slow and rate-limited. Design cache proxy with 30s TTL, per-SKU keys, and stampede protection (single-flight). Discuss invalidation on price pushes and fallback when upstream is down. Expected: TTL map, single-flight, stale-while-revalidate policy, fallback semantics.

docs.title: 11. Testing and Best Practices
docs.text:
Unit tests:

  • Test real subject alone for domain correctness (overdrafts, balances) with no proxy involved.
  • Test proxy with stubbed real: allowed calls delegate with identical results; denied calls never reach the real object (mock verifies zero interactions).
  • Test virtual proxy: expensive object created lazily and exactly once, even under concurrent first access.
  • Test cache proxy: miss path delegates and stores; hit path skips delegate; TTL expiry and invalidation behave.

Integration tests:

  • End-to-end through the subject interface proving proxy substitutability (swap real for proxy, same assertions pass plus policy extras).
  • Failure injection: upstream down → cache proxy serves stale-with-warning or fails with domain error, never raw transport exception.
  • Concurrency soak: parallel first-access and parallel cache fills stay correct.

Best practices:

  • Inject the real subject and policy inputs (roles, clocks, TTLs) so tests control them; use fake clocks for TTL tests.
  • Log at proxy boundaries with subject identity and decision (allowed/denied/hit/miss) for production debugging.
  • Keep proxies stateless except for their one concern's state (cache map, lazy holder); document thread-safety.
  • Version remote-proxy contracts with the upstream API; add conformance tests per upstream version.
Aspect Impact Memory Low (one holder per proxy; cache size bounded by policy) Runtime cost Low–medium (one hop; virtual/cache proxies usually save net time) Scalability High (proxies shard with subjects; caches need coherence plan) Risk Stale data and bypassed guards — TTL discipline + full-interface delegation

docs.title: 12. Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Proxy = controlled stand-in: Same interface, plus guarding, deferring, caching, or remoting — invisibly to clients.
  • Name the type: Virtual (lazy), protection (auth), remote (distance), smart/cache (bookkeeping) — each has distinct tests.
  • One concern per proxy: Compose focused layers with documented order instead of building god proxies.
  • Substitutability is the contract: Any client test passing against the real subject must pass against the proxy (plus policy assertions).
  • Distinguish neighbours: Guard/defer → Proxy; stacked features → Decorator; signature fix → Adapter; subsystem simplification → Facade.
  • Test the gate: Denied calls never touch real; lazy builds once; cache hits skip upstream; TTLs expire.

docs.title: All Structural Design Patterns — Family Overview
Youtube
docs.text: • 32. All Structural Design Patterns | Decorator, Proxy, Composite, Adapter, Bridge, Facade, FlyWeight

docs.title: 1. What Are Structural Patterns?
docs.text:
Structural design patterns explain how classes and objects are composed into larger structures while keeping those structures flexible and efficient. If creational patterns are about creating objects and behavioural patterns about communicating, structural patterns are about wiring — interfaces, wrappers, trees, and bridges that let independently-designed parts fit together.

The one-sentence definition: Structural patterns use composition and delegation (has-a) instead of inheritance (is-a) to combine objects into structures that can change at runtime.

Why they exist:

  • Tame complexity: Hide multi-step subsystems behind one call (Facade), or split an exploding hierarchy into two small ones (Bridge).
  • Bridge mismatches: Make incompatible interfaces collaborate without rewriting either side (Adapter).
  • Scale cheaply: Share common state across millions of objects (Flyweight) or treat one object and a million uniformly (Composite).
  • Control and extend: Guard access transparently (Proxy) or stack features at runtime (Decorator).

How to read this family: Each of the seven pattern guides in this directory (adapter.md, bridge.md, composite.md, decorator.md, facade.md, flyweight.md, proxy.md) follows the same 12-section structure — overview, theory, UML (class + sequence), Java/Python/Go examples, industry uses, scenarios, when-to-use, do's and don'ts, comparisons, interviews, testing, and summary. This page is the map; those pages are the territories.

docs.title: 2. The Seven Patterns at a Glance
docs.text:
# Pattern Intent in one line Classic example File 1 Adapter Convert an incompatible interface into one the client expects StripeAdapter implements PaymentProcessor adapter.md 2 Bridge Split abstraction from implementation so both vary independently Notification → NotificationChannel bridge.md 3 Composite Treat single objects and groups uniformly in a tree File system, org chart, menu tree composite.md 4 Decorator Attach responsibilities dynamically by wrapping BufferedInputStream(FileInputStream) decorator.md 5 Facade Provide a simple front door to a complex subsystem VideoConverterFacade.convertToMp4() facade.md 6 Flyweight Share fine-grained objects to support huge numbers cheaply Glyph pool, TreeType forest flyweight.md 7 Proxy Provide a surrogate controlling access to another object Protection, virtual, remote, cache proxies proxy.md

Memory hooks:

  • Adapter: "Translator" — changes the plug shape.
  • Bridge: "Two ladders" — two hierarchies joined by one rung.
  • Composite: "Tree" — one interface, leaves and branches.
  • Decorator: "Toppings" — same drink, stacked extras.
  • Facade: "Concierge" — one call, many departments.
  • Flyweight: "Printing press" — one plate, a million impressions.
  • Proxy: "Bouncer" — same door, checks before entry.

docs.title: 3. Comparison Matrix
docs.text:
Aspect Adapter Bridge Composite Decorator Facade Flyweight Proxy Changes interface? Yes (translates) No (both designed) No (uniform) No (same) No (simplifies) No (splits state) No (same) Wraps One adaptee Implementation hierarchy Many children Exactly one component Whole subsystem Shared pool + contexts One subject Client knows? Sees target only Uses abstraction Cannot tell leaf/group Composes stack Sees facade Unaware of sharing Ideally unaware Timing Retroactive fix Up-front design Anytime tree fits Runtime stacking Anytime simplification At scale Anytime control needed Without it Code won't compile M×N subclasses Type-check soup 2^N subclasses Verbose sequences Memory explosion Scattered guards Memory Low Low Medium Medium Low Sharply reduced Low (+cache if any) Runtime Low Low Medium (traversal) Medium (chain) Low Medium Low–Medium

Most-confused pairs, resolved:

  • Adapter vs Facade: Adapter translates signatures (won't compile without it); Facade orchestrates calls (merely verbose without it).
  • Adapter vs Bridge: Adapter fixes the past (foreign code); Bridge plans the future (your two axes).
  • Decorator vs Proxy: Decorator adds features the client stacks; Proxy guards access invisibly.
  • Decorator vs Composite: Decorator wraps one thing with layers; Composite holds many peers and aggregates.
  • Facade vs Mediator: Facade simplifies outside-in (client to subsystem); Mediator coordinates peer-to-peer (colleagues via hub).
  • Flyweight vs Cache/Pool: Flyweight shares immutable internals permanently; cache memoises results with eviction; pool recycles mutable resources.
  • Proxy vs Decorator vs Adapter: Same-interface guard → Proxy; same-interface enrichment → Decorator; changed-interface translation → Adapter.

docs.title: 4. Design Principles Behind the Family
docs.text:
1. Favour composition over inheritance. Every structural pattern replaces an inheritance tangle (M×N subclasses, 2^N toppings) with a has-a link. This is the family's founding move.
  2. Program to an interface, not an implementation. All seven patterns insert an abstraction (Target, Implementor, Component, Subject) between client and concrete. Concretes vary; contracts hold.
  3. Single Responsibility. Decorator owns one topping; Proxy owns one gate; Facade owns one workflow; Flyweight factory owns sharing. God wrappers are the universal smell.
  4. Open/Closed. New provider → new Adapter. New channel → new Bridge implementor. New topping → new Decorator. Extension without modification is the payoff.
  5. Dependency Inversion. High-level policy (checkout, alerts) depends on abstractions; SDKs, channels, and transports plug in underneath.
  6. Interface Segregation. Narrow Target, Channel, and Subject interfaces keep adapters, bridges, and proxies honest. Wide interfaces force UnsupportedOperationException everywhere.
  7. Liskov Substitution. Any leaf substitutes for any composite; any proxy for its subject; any decorator stack for its component. Tests should prove substitutability explicitly.

docs.title: 5. Patterns Often Combined
docs.text:
• Composite + Flyweight: Trees with shared leaves — DOM nodes sharing style flyweights, org trees sharing role templates, game scene graphs sharing meshes.
  • Composite + Decorator: Decorate a whole subtree — bordered/scrollable panels containing nested components; permission-checked menu trees.
  • Facade + Adapter: E-commerce facade orchestrating per-provider adapters — CheckoutFacade calling StripeAdapter, PayPalAdapter behind one placeOrder().
  • Proxy + Decorator: Guard then enrich — CacheProxy in front of a decorated alerting pipeline; auth proxy outside retry decorator with documented order.
  • Bridge + Abstract Factory: Factory builds the implementor family (EU vs US channels), Bridge consumes it — platform-independent UI and multi-tenant routing.
  • Facade + Mediator: Gateway facade facing clients, mediator coordinating services behind it — API gateway over an event-driven core.
  • Adapter + Anti-Corruption Layer: Legacy SOAP wrapped by adapters, orchestrated by a bounded-context facade — the standard modernisation sandwich.

docs.title: 6. Decision Guide — Which Pattern Do I Need?
docs.text:
Ask in this order:

  1. Do interfaces mismatch so code won't connect? → Adapter.
  2. Is a subsystem usable but painfully verbose? → Facade.
  3. Do you need combinable per-object features at runtime? → Decorator.
  4. Do you need to guard, defer, or cache access to one object? → Proxy.
  5. Should clients ignore one-vs-many? → Composite.
  6. Are two change axes multiplying classes (M×N)? → Bridge.
  7. Are millions of similar objects exhausting memory? → Flyweight.
  8. Are peers tangled in mutual references? → Mediator (behavioural) — not structural, but the usual neighbour.

Decision tree:

Do you need to change an interface?
├─ Yes → ADAPTER
└─ No → Do you need to simplify complex interfaces?
    ├─ Yes → FACADE
    └─ No → Do you need to add behavior?
        ├─ Yes, dynamically stacked → DECORATOR
        ├─ Yes, with access control → PROXY
        └─ No → Do you work with hierarchies?
            ├─ Yes, one-or-many trees → COMPOSITE
            ├─ Yes, two independent axes → BRIDGE
            └─ No, massive similar counts → FLYWEIGHT

Family map:

flowchart TB
    S[Structural patternscompose objects] --> T[Translate: Adapter]
    S --> P[Simplify: Facade]
    S --> W[Wrap one: Decorator, Proxy]
    S --> H[Hierarchies: Composite, Bridge]
    S --> SH[Share many: Flyweight]

Quick smell test: If removing the wrapper breaks compilation → Adapter. If it only makes code longer → Facade. If the caller stacks it → Decorator. If the caller can't tell → Proxy.

docs.title: 7. Performance Cheat Sheet
docs.text:
Pattern Memory Runtime Scales with Watch out for Adapter Low Low (one hop) Provider count Leaky adaptee types Bridge Low Low (one hop) Axes sizes (M+N) Leaky implementor Composite Medium (child lists) Medium (O(n) traversal) Tree size Deep recursion, cycles Decorator Medium (per layer) Medium (per-layer hop) Stack depth Order bugs, deep chains Facade Low Low (one hop) Subsystem size God object Flyweight Sharply reduced Medium (extrinsic passing) Object count (flat) Misclassified state Proxy Low (+bounded cache) Low–Medium Call volume Stale cache, bypassed guards

Rules of thumb: Profile before Flyweight; keep Decorator/Proxy chains shallow on hot paths; cache Composite aggregates when reads dominate; bound Proxy caches with TTL.

docs.title: 8. Structural Patterns in Modern Architectures
docs.text:
• Microservices: Adapter integrates foreign APIs; Facade is the API Gateway/BFF; Proxy is the sidecar (Envoy, Istio) and service client.
  • Cloud-native: Proxy covers load balancers and reverse proxies; Bridge abstracts multi-cloud drivers (S3 vs GCS); Flyweight thinking drives shared caches (Redis, CDN tiles).
  • Frontend: Composite is the component tree (React/Vue/DOM); Decorator is HOCs, hooks, and middleware; Facade is the store API (Redux/Zustand) over reducers and effects.
  • Data/ML: Facade fronts feature pipelines (train() hiding extract/validate/encode); Adapter normalises vendor datasets; Proxy caches feature-store lookups; Flyweight shares embeddings/token tables.
  • DDD: Adapter is the anti-corruption layer between contexts; Facade is the application service; Composite models aggregates containing entities.

docs.title: 9. Anti-Patterns and Code Smells
docs.text:
• Adapter stack: AdapterA(AdapterB(AdapterC(x))) — debugging through three translations. Consolidate or redesign the boundary.
  • God Facade: 40-method SystemManager with mutable state. Split by workflow or client view.
  • Leaky Bridge: Abstraction downcasting to SmsChannel specifics. Narrow the implementor contract.
  • Transparent-everything Composite: Leaves throwing UnsupportedOperationException for add(). Prefer the safe style.
  • Order-fragile Decorators: Five layers where every permutation behaves differently. Bless and factory-build valid orders.
  • God Proxy: Auth + cache + retry + metrics in one class. One concern per proxy, composed explicitly.
  • Premature Flyweight: Pool machinery for 200 small objects. Measure heap first; YAGNI otherwise.

docs.title: 10. Interview Quick-Fire Map
docs.text:
• "Adapter vs Facade vs Bridge?" Signatures fixed → Adapter; steps simplified → Facade; two axes split → Bridge.
  • "Decorator vs Proxy?" Client stacks features → Decorator; wrapper guards invisibly → Proxy.
  • "Composite vs Decorator?" Many peers aggregated → Composite; one object enriched → Decorator.
  • "Flyweight vs Singleton vs Cache?" Many shared instances → Flyweight; one instance → Singleton; memoised results → Cache.
  • "Class vs object adapter?" Inheritance vs composition — prefer object adapters; class adapters only to override adaptee behaviour.
  • "How do you test a Proxy/Adapter/Facade?" Real subject alone; wrapper with stubbed inner; order/translation assertions; one end-to-end proof.
  • Framework examples to cite: JDBC drivers (Bridge), BufferedInputStream (Decorator), SLF4J (Adapter/Bridge), Spring Security/AOP (Proxy), EntityManager (Facade), String.intern() (Flyweight), DOM/React tree (Composite).

docs.title: 11. Suggested Learning Order
docs.text:
1. Facade → Adapter: Simplification first, then translation — the two most common daily needs.
  2. Decorator → Proxy: Same-interface wrapping, first explicit then invisible — the classic confusion pair.
  3. Composite → Flyweight: Trees first, then sharing leaves — the scale story.
  4. Bridge last: The most abstract split — clearest once Adapter (fix) vs Strategy (swap) are understood.
  5. Capstone: Revisit this overview's decision tree and re-derive each choice from a real codebase you own.

Each pattern file ends with 8+ Q&A and 2–3 LLD scenarios — work them in the same order for design-round preparation.

docs.title: 12. Worked Selection Walkthrough
docs.text:
A single evolving scenario shows how the decision tree picks different patterns as the problem changes.

Stage 1 — Messy video library: UploadController calls extractor, transcoder, normaliser, and muxer directly, in an order copied between three controllers. Two bugs this quarter came from swapped steps. Pick Facade: VideoConverterFacade.convertToMp4() owns the order; controllers drop to one call; subsystem stays public for custom-bitrate jobs.

Stage 2 — New cloud encoder SDK: The team wants to swap the in-house transcoder for a vendor SDK whose method names and error codes differ. Pick Adapter: VendorTranscoderAdapter implements the internal Transcoder interface and translates to the SDK. The facade never changes; migration is one wiring edit plus a feature flag.

Stage 3 — Per-customer delivery options: Enterprise tenants want email plus Slack plus encrypted archive; free tier wants email only. Subclassing every mix is hopeless. Pick Decorator: Retry(Encrypt(Slack(Email))) for enterprise, bare Email for free — composed per tenant at runtime.

Stage 4 — Abuse and cost: Alerts now fire 10k times per incident because every retry re-sends. Pick Proxy: a rate-limiting proxy and a cache proxy (dedupe identical alerts within 5 minutes) sit in front of the pipeline. Product features untouched; access policy centralised.

Stage 5 — Two delivery axes: Message kinds (urgent, reminder, marketing) multiply against channels (email, SMS, push, WhatsApp) — 12 subclasses and counting. Pick Bridge: Notification hierarchy × NotificationChannel hierarchy, wired by tenant config. Twelve classes collapse to seven, and the next channel is one class.

Stage 6 — Org-wide rollout: Notifications now target teams with nested sub-teams, and finance needs cost roll-ups. Pick Composite: OrgUnit with Developer leaves and Team composites; notifyAll() and monthlyCost() recurse uniformly.

Stage 7 — Million-device fan-out: Device tokens and message templates repeat enormously; heap pressure spikes. Pick Flyweight: share template/style flyweights across contexts, pass device id and position extrinsically. Memory flattens while throughput holds.

The lesson: each stage's pain maps to exactly one decision-tree question, and patterns compose — the final system runs Facade over Adapters, Decorators behind Proxies, Bridges feeding Composites with Flyweight leaves.

docs.title: 13. Minimal Skeleton Comparison
docs.text:
When reviewing code, these skeletons distinguish the patterns faster than prose:

import java.util.*;

// ADAPTER: translates signatures
interface PaymentProcessor { String pay(double inr); }
class StripeGateway { String createCharge(long paise) { return "ch_" + paise; } }
class StripeAdapter implements PaymentProcessor {
    private final StripeGateway adaptee = new StripeGateway();
    public String pay(double inr) { return adaptee.createCharge(Math.round(inr * 100)); }
}

// BRIDGE: two hierarchies, one composition link
interface NotificationChannel { void send(String m); }
abstract class Notification {
    protected final NotificationChannel channel; // bridge
    Notification(NotificationChannel c) { channel = c; }
    abstract void notify(String m);
}

// COMPOSITE: one holds many of the same interface
interface OrgUnit { double monthlyCost(); }
class Team implements OrgUnit {
    private final List<OrgUnit> members = new ArrayList<>();
    public double monthlyCost() { return members.stream().mapToDouble(OrgUnit::monthlyCost).sum(); }
}

// DECORATOR: one wraps exactly one, same interface
interface Notifier { void send(String m); }
class RetryDecorator implements Notifier {
    private final Notifier wrapped;
    RetryDecorator(Notifier w) { wrapped = w; }
    public void send(String m) { wrapped.send(m); }
}

// FACADE: one method orchestrates many subsystems
class Order {}
class Payments { void charge(Order o) {} }
class Stock { void reserve(Order o) {} }
class Shipping { void dispatch(Order o) {} }
class OrderFacade {
    private final Payments payments = new Payments();
    private final Stock stock = new Stock();
    private final Shipping shipping = new Shipping();
    public void placeOrder(Order o) { payments.charge(o); stock.reserve(o); shipping.dispatch(o); }
}

// FLYWEIGHT: pool + tiny contexts
class Glyph { Glyph(String c) {} }
class GlyphFactory {
    private final Map<String, Glyph> pool = new HashMap<>();
    Glyph get(char c) { return pool.computeIfAbsent(String.valueOf(c), Glyph::new); }
}

// PROXY: same interface, gate in front
class Doc {}
class Denied extends RuntimeException {}
class Role { boolean canRead() { return true; } }
interface DocumentStore { Doc read(String id); }
class RealStore implements DocumentStore { public Doc read(String id) { return new Doc(); } }
class AccessProxy implements DocumentStore {
    private final DocumentStore real = new RealStore(); private final Role caller = new Role();
    public Doc read(String id) { if (!caller.canRead()) throw new Denied(); return real.read(id); }
}

Review heuristic: count what the wrapper holds — one adaptee with renamed methods (Adapter), one implementation hierarchy (Bridge), many children (Composite), one component with extras (Decorator), many subsystems (Facade), a pool with contexts (Flyweight), one subject with a gate (Proxy).

docs.title: 14. Family-Wide Testing and Adoption Checklist
docs.text:
• Substitutability first: every wrapper (Adapter, Decorator, Proxy) and every node (Composite leaf/group) must pass the same interface-level tests. Write one contract suite per interface and run all implementations through it.
  • Order and translation assertions: Facade tests verify call order; Adapter tests verify unit/error translation; Decorator/Proxy tests verify delegation counts with mocked inners.
  • Matrix and identity tests: Bridge needs abstraction × implementor matrix tests; Flyweight needs reference-equality (get(k) == get(k)) and sibling-isolation tests.
  • One real end-to-end per seam: a thin integration test with genuine subsystems (sandbox SDK, test SMTP, in-memory channel) proves the wiring beyond mocks.
  • Adoption checklist: name the pain with the decision tree, keep wrappers thin and single-concern, inject dependencies for tests, document ordering and key design, measure (heap/latency) before and after Flyweight/Proxy changes, and allow Facade bypass for power users.

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
Design an access-control service that decides who can do what on which resource. Covers user authentication and authorization via role/permission mappings enforced on every protected action. Key entities: User, Role, Permission, Resource, AccessPolicy. Core operations: assign roles, grant/revoke permissions, authorize requests.

This guide turns that stub into an interview-ready low-level design: you will clarify an intentionally ambiguous enterprise access-control service, model clean OOP entities around User, Role, Permission, Resource, and AccessPolicy, choose RBAC evaluation (role inheritance plus permission union plus explicit deny) behind a pluggable PolicyEngine evaluated at a central DecisionPoint, gate every protected action behind an authenticated principal plus a cached allow-or-deny verdict plus an auditable decision record, and write plain Java 17 code an interviewer can trace on a whiteboard. The emphasis is on object modeling, evaluation mechanics, and deny-correctness — not SSO protocols, OAuth token cryptography, or distributed session replication.

Scope note: this is LLD (class design, patterns, in-process concurrency). Company-wide SSO federation, OAuth2/OIDC token issuance, LDAP directory sync, and multi-service distributed policy replication belong to HLD and are mentioned only where they constrain the object model (for example, every authorization carries subjectId plus resourceId plus action plus context so a stale role cache or revoked permission never grants access it should deny).

docs.text:
1. Problem Statement
  2. Functional / Non-Functional Requirements
